### Pattern 19: `browserContext.storageState()` with IndexedDB Backup/Restore (v1.51+) [official]

Before v1.51, `storageState()` captured only cookies and `localStorage`. From v1.51 onward, it also serializes and restores **IndexedDB** data, enabling auth flows that store tokens in IndexedDB (common in PWA and Firebase Auth apps) to be captured once and replayed across workers without re-authenticating.

```typescript
// e2e/auth.setup.ts — capture IndexedDB alongside cookies + localStorage
import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';

const AUTH_FILE = 'playwright/.auth/user.json';

setup('firebase auth — capture full storage state incl. IndexedDB', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(process.env.E2E_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.E2E_PASS!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  // Wait until Firebase stores the ID token in IndexedDB
  await page.waitForFunction(() =>
    new Promise<boolean>(resolve => {
      const req = indexedDB.open('firebaseLocalStorageDb');
      req.onsuccess = () => {
        const db     = req.result;
        const tx     = db.transaction('firebaseLocalStorage', 'readonly');
        const store  = tx.objectStore('firebaseLocalStorage');
        const getAll = store.getAll();
        getAll.onsuccess = () => resolve(getAll.result.length > 0);
      };
    })
  );

  // v1.51+: IndexedDB is included automatically
  await page.context().storageState({ path: AUTH_FILE });
  console.log('[setup] Auth file with IndexedDB saved to', AUTH_FILE);
});

// playwright.config.ts — use saved state in all tests
export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name:        'setup',
      testMatch:   /auth\.setup\.ts/,
    },
    {
      name:         'chromium',
      use:          { storageState: AUTH_FILE },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
  ],
});
```

**When to use:** Applications that use Firebase Auth, Dexie.js, or any library that persists authentication tokens in IndexedDB. Without this pattern, tests open a logged-in page and immediately see a login redirect because the IndexedDB state was missing.

**When NOT to use:** IndexedDB capture increases auth file size substantially (can be 5–50 KB vs. a few hundred bytes for cookie-only auth). If your app uses cookies or `localStorage` exclusively, omit IndexedDB capture — it adds I/O cost per worker startup for no benefit.

**Alternatives:** Intercept the auth API endpoint and inject tokens via `page.evaluate()` + `localStorage.setItem()`; use `addInitScript()` to seed IndexedDB programmatically before navigation. [official]

---

### Pattern 20: `snapshotPathTemplate` with `{kind}` — Separate Visual from ARIA Snapshot Directories (v1.53+) [official]

By default, all snapshots (visual, ARIA, text) share the same `__snapshots__` directory, causing name collisions when a test produces both `toHaveScreenshot` and `toMatchAriaSnapshot` outputs. The `{kind}` placeholder in `snapshotPathTemplate` lets you route each snapshot type to its own subdirectory.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — separate snapshot dirs per kind
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // {kind} expands to 'png' | 'aria' | 'txt'
  snapshotPathTemplate:
    '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{kind}/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',

  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot:    { maxDiffPixels: 100 },
    toMatchAriaSnapshot: { children: 'contain' },
  },
});
```

```typescript
// e2e/specs/homepage.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('homepage — visual + ARIA regression', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Stored in __snapshots__/png/homepage.spec.ts/hero-area.png
  await expect(page.getByRole('banner')).toHaveScreenshot('hero-area.png');

  // Stored in __snapshots__/aria/homepage.spec.ts/nav-structure.aria.yml
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toMatchAriaSnapshot({
    name: 'nav-structure.aria.yml',
  });

  // Stored in __snapshots__/txt/homepage.spec.ts/seo-headings.txt
  const headings = await page.getByRole('heading').allTextContents();
  expect(headings.join('\n')).toMatchSnapshot('seo-headings.txt');
});
```

**When to use:** Any project that uses both `toHaveScreenshot` and `toMatchAriaSnapshot` in the same test file. Without the `{kind}` template, Playwright appends numeric suffixes to avoid collisions — making snapshot names unpredictable and diff reviews confusing.

**When NOT to use:** Projects with only one snapshot type (e.g., pure visual regression) — the extra directory nesting adds complexity with no benefit. Also, the `{kind}` placeholder requires Playwright >= v1.53; fall back to manual name differentiation on older versions.

**Alternatives:** Use unique names per call (`'hero-area.png'` vs `'nav.aria.yml'`); configure separate test projects for visual vs. ARIA tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 21: `testProject.workers` — Per-Project Parallelism Tuning (v1.52+) [official]

The top-level `workers` config applies globally, but different test projects may have wildly different resource demands. `testProject.workers` overrides concurrency per project, enabling you to run I/O-heavy API tests at maximum parallelism while throttling database-mutating integration tests to prevent deadlocks.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: 8,  // global pool: 8 workers total across all projects

  projects: [
    // Unit/API tests — no shared DB state, safe to run at full pool size
    {
      name:    'api-tests',
      testDir: './e2e/api',
      workers: 8,   // use all 8 workers for stateless API tests
    },

    // Integration tests — mutate a shared staging DB, must run serially
    {
      name:    'integration',
      testDir: './e2e/integration',
      workers: 1,   // serial execution prevents DB conflicts
    },

    // E2E browser tests — balanced parallelism
    {
      name:    'chromium',
      testDir: './e2e/browser',
      use:     devices['Desktop Chrome'],
      workers: 4,  // half the pool for browser tests
    },

    // Visual regression — GPU/screenshot-heavy, keep concurrency low
    {
      name:    'visual',
      testDir: './e2e/visual',
      workers: 2,
      use:     devices['Desktop Chrome'],
    },
  ],
});
```

**When to use:** Monorepo test suites where different test categories have different resource profiles. API tests are cheap and parallel-safe; browser tests consume more memory; database-mutation tests require serialization.

**When NOT to use:** Simple projects with a single test type — the extra configuration overhead is not justified. Note: `testProject.workers` is a cap against the global pool, not a guaranteed allocation — it cannot exceed the global `workers` value.

**Alternatives:** Separate `playwright.config.ts` files per test type (verbose but clean isolation); `--workers` CLI flag (overrides config but applies globally); test sharding across CI machines. [official]

---

### Pattern 22: Service Worker Network Routing in Chromium (v1.57+) [official]

From v1.57+, Playwright exposes Service Worker network requests as first-class routeable entities in Chromium. Previously, requests intercepted by a Service Worker were invisible to `page.route()` — they would proceed or fail without Playwright being able to observe or modify them.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Service worker requests are now reported and routeable in Chromium (v1.57+)
test('SW-cached assets served correctly on repeat visit', async ({ page, context }) => {
  const swRequests: string[] = [];
  context.on('request', req => {
    if (req.serviceWorker()) {
      swRequests.push(req.url());
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/');       // first visit — SW installs and caches
  await page.reload();        // second visit — SW intercepts from cache
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

  // Verify the SW handled at least one navigation request
  expect(
    swRequests.some(url => url.includes('/index.html')),
    'SW should intercept navigation',
  ).toBe(true);
});

test('intercept SW fetch — inject offline mock response', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // context.route() catches SW-proxied requests too in Chromium v1.57+
  await context.route('**/api/products', route =>
    route.fulfill({
      status:      200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body:        JSON.stringify({ items: [], offline: true }),
    }),
  );

  await page.goto('/products');
  await expect(page.getByText('offline')).toBeVisible();
});

test('block SW entirely to test online-only code path', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({ serviceWorkers: 'block' });
  const page    = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText(/offline/i)).not.toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});
```

**When to use:** PWA testing where the Service Worker implements caching, push notifications, or background sync. Previously required `serviceWorkers: 'block'` to test reliably; now you can route SW fetch events selectively.

**When NOT to use:** Firefox and WebKit do not support Service Worker routing in Playwright — these patterns are Chromium-only. For cross-browser tests, fall back to `serviceWorkers: 'block'` to ensure consistent behavior.

**Alternatives:** `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in context options disables SW entirely; `context.route()` without SW support (pre-v1.57 behavior); testing the SW script in isolation with unit tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 23: `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` — Fail CI on Detected Flakiness (v1.52+) [official]

Flaky tests erode suite credibility. `failOnFlakyTests: true` causes Playwright to exit with code 1 if any test is marked flaky (passed on retry after failing on the first attempt). Paired with `retries: 1`, this transforms retries from a "hide the flake" mechanism into a "surface the flake" signal.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,

  // Exit with code 1 if any test passed only after retrying
  failOnFlakyTests: process.env.CI ? true : false,

  reporter: [
    ['github'],
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
  ],

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',  // capture trace on the flaky run for investigation
  },
});
```

```bash
# PR gate: fail if any test is flaky, run only changed files
npx playwright test --only-changed=origin/main --fail-on-flaky-tests

# Flake audit: run full suite with retries, surface all flaky tests
npx playwright test --retries=2 --fail-on-flaky-tests
```

**When to use:** Any CI pipeline where flaky tests reaching `main` is unacceptable. Particularly useful for merge-queue gates where each PR must prove its tests are deterministic. Pair with `retries: 1` so legitimate flakes are caught without masking real failures.

**When NOT to use:** Do not enable in local development runs — developers running tests while actively writing code expect retries to be a convenience, not a gate. Also, avoid enabling if your suite has known infrastructure flakes (slow containers, shared staging DB timeouts) that you have not yet fixed — it will block every PR until those are resolved.

**Alternatives:** External flake-tracking dashboards (Currents, Argos); manually annotating known flaky tests with `test.fixme()`; increasing `retries` without failing on flake (hides the problem). [official]

---

### Pattern 24: `test.step()` with `timeout` and `step.skip()` — Granular Step Control (v1.50+) [official]

`test.step()` gained two power features in v1.50: a `timeout` option that time-bounds individual steps, and `test.step.skip()` that conditionally skips a step at runtime. Together they enable conditional test flows and time-budgeted smoke checks without splitting tests into multiple files.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow with conditional payment step', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Step 1: Verify the product catalog loads within 5 seconds
  await test.step('load product catalog', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products');
    await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Products' })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 5_000 }); // this step fails (not skips) if it takes > 5s

  // Step 2: Add item to cart — inherits test-level timeout
  await test.step('add widget to cart', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add Widget Pro' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status', { name: /cart/i })).toContainText('1');
  });

  // Step 3: Skip payment if the payment gateway is unavailable
  const gatewayStatus = await request.get('/health/payment-gateway');
  await test.step('complete checkout', async (step) => {
    if (gatewayStatus.status() !== 200) {
      await step.skip(); // step shows as skipped; test continues to next step
      return;
    }
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111 1111 1111 1111');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  // Step 4: Verify order in history — always runs regardless of step 3
  await test.step('verify order history', async () => {
    await page.goto('/orders');
    await expect(page.getByRole('row').first()).toContainText('Widget Pro');
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Long multi-phase tests where individual steps have different SLA requirements (fast navigation vs. slow payment API). Also useful for tests that cover multiple features with optional steps dependent on third-party service availability.

**When NOT to use:** Do not use `step.skip()` to hide expected failures — if a step is always expected to fail, use `test.fixme()` or `test.skip()` at the test level. Do not confuse step `timeout` with a budget that allows continuation — a step timeout is a hard failure, not a soft cap.

**Alternatives:** Split into separate tests with `test.describe`; use `test.slow()` to triple the entire test timeout; use individual `expect` timeout options. [official]

---

### Pattern 25: `locator.and()` and `locator.or()` — Boolean Locator Composition [official]

`locator.and(other)` returns a locator that matches elements satisfying both the original and the additional locator. `locator.or(other)` matches elements satisfying either locator. Together they replace brittle compound CSS selectors with readable, composable locator chains.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('locator.and() — narrow to the single enabled submit button', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Matches the button with the right name AND that is not disabled
  const submitBtn = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: /submit|place order/i })
    .and(page.locator(':not([disabled])'));

  await expect(submitBtn).toBeEnabled();
  await submitBtn.click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});

test('locator.and() — element must match both role and test-id', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Target the primary action button identified by BOTH role AND testId
  const primaryAction = page
    .getByRole('button')
    .and(page.getByTestId('primary-cta'));

  await expect(primaryAction).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(primaryAction).toBeVisible();
  await primaryAction.click();
});

test('locator.or() — handle two authentication UI states', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // App may render either a sign-in button OR a user avatar — accept both
  const authIndicator = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' })
    .or(page.getByRole('img', { name: /avatar|profile/i }));

  await expect(authIndicator).toBeVisible();

  const isLoggedIn = await page.getByRole('img', { name: /avatar/i }).isVisible();
  if (!isLoggedIn) {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /sign in/i })).toBeVisible();
  }
});
```

**When to use:** `locator.and()` is ideal for narrowing locators when multiple attributes must be satisfied simultaneously (role + state + test-id). `locator.or()` is ideal for handling components with multiple possible rendered states (A/B variants, loading vs. loaded, logged-in vs. guest).

**When NOT to use:** Avoid chaining more than two or three `and()`/`or()` conditions — deeply nested compositions are hard to read and debug. Prefer adding a specific test-id to the element or improving the ARIA markup instead of constructing complex boolean locators.

**Alternatives:** `locator.filter({ has, hasText })` for child-based filtering; compound CSS selectors (fragile); separate `if/else` locator choices with `isVisible()` checks. [official]

---

### Pattern 26: `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` — Form Validation Assertion (v1.50+) [official]

`toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` asserts the computed `aria-errormessage` association of an input — the accessible name of the element pointed to by the input's `aria-errormessage` attribute. This is the semantically correct way to assert form validation messages in accessible forms.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('email field shows accessible validation error on blur', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('not-an-email');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').blur();

  // Assert the computed aria-errormessage content
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Email')).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(
    /please enter a valid email/i,
  );

  // Belt-and-suspenders: also assert the error is visually visible
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/valid email/i);
});

test('password field clears error message after correction', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  const passwordInput = page.getByLabel('Password');

  // Trigger the validation error
  await passwordInput.fill('abc');
  await passwordInput.blur();
  await expect(passwordInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/at least 8 characters/i);

  // Fix the input — error should clear
  await passwordInput.fill('Str0ng!Pass#1');
  await passwordInput.blur();
  await expect(passwordInput).not.toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage();
});

test('form submit with empty fields surfaces errors on all required inputs', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');
  // Submit without filling any fields
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click();

  const emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email');
  const nameInput  = page.getByLabel('Name');
  const bodyInput  = page.getByLabel('Message');

  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/required/i);
  await expect(nameInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/required/i);
  await expect(bodyInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/required/i);
});
```

**When to use:** Any form that follows ARIA best practices by wiring `aria-errormessage` on inputs. This assertion follows the semantic association — even if the error element is visually repositioned by a redesign, the assertion still passes.

**When NOT to use:** Do not use this assertion on forms that use legacy inline error display (error text immediately following the input with no `aria-errormessage`). In that case, use `toContainText()` or `toBeVisible()` on the error element directly.

**Alternatives:** `expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(msg)`; `expect(input).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true')`; full ARIA snapshot with `toMatchAriaSnapshot()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 27: `page.pickLocator()` — Interactive Locator Discovery in Headed Mode (v1.59+) [official]

`page.pickLocator()` enters an interactive mode where the developer hovers over elements in the browser, and Playwright returns the best-practice locator string for the highlighted element. This is the programmatic equivalent of the VS Code "Pick locator" button and is designed for headed development workflows.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Run in headed mode for interactive use:
// npx playwright test --headed --debug locator-discovery.spec.ts
test('interactive locator discovery helper', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Execution pauses — hover over an element in the browser window
  // Playwright returns the recommended locator for the hovered element
  const locatorString = await page.pickLocator();

  // Example output: getByRole('button', { name: 'Export CSV' })
  console.log('Recommended locator:', locatorString);

  // The returned string is ready for use as a Playwright locator
  const el = page.locator(locatorString);
  await expect(el).toBeVisible();
});

// Practical audit: discover locators for all interactive elements on a new page
test.skip('locator audit helper — for spec authoring only', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/new-feature-page');
  // Use page.pause() to open the interactive inspector,
  // then call page.pickLocator() from the console to pick elements
  await page.pause();
});
```

**When to use:** During initial test authoring on new or poorly-labeled pages where you need to discover resilient locators. Also useful in `--debug` sessions when an existing locator stops matching and you want Playwright to suggest a better one.

**When NOT to use:** Do not include `page.pickLocator()` calls in CI-facing spec files — in headless mode it returns a heuristic immediately without awaiting user interaction, which may produce unexpected locator strings. It is a developer tooling API, not an assertion.

**Alternatives:** `npx playwright codegen <url>` (full interactive code generation); VS Code Playwright extension "Pick locator" button; `page.pause()` + Inspector "Pick" button. [official]

---

### Pattern 28: `locator.normalize()` — Convert Heuristic Locators to Best-Practice Form (v1.59+) [official]

`locator.normalize()` inspects an existing locator and returns a new locator expressing the same element using Playwright's recommended patterns (preferring `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByTestId` over raw CSS or XPath). This is designed for automated locator migration and test-healer workflows.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('normalize migrates a CSS locator to a role-based locator', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');

  // Legacy locator written with CSS class and attribute selector
  const legacyCssLocator = page.locator('button.btn-primary[type="submit"]');

  // Get the normalized, best-practice equivalent
  const normalizedLocator = await legacyCssLocator.normalize();
  console.log('Normalized:', normalizedLocator.toString());
  // Example output: getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' })

  // The normalized locator targets the same element
  await expect(normalizedLocator).toBeVisible();
  await expect(normalizedLocator).toHaveText('Sign in');
});

// Practical: audit legacy locators across a new page during test maintenance
test.skip('locator audit — log normalized forms for manual review', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  const legacyLocators = [
    page.locator('.data-table tbody tr'),
    page.locator('input[name="search"]'),
    page.locator('#export-btn'),
    page.locator('[data-qa="user-menu"]'),
  ];

  for (const loc of legacyLocators) {
    const normalized = await loc.normalize();
    console.log(`BEFORE: ${loc.toString()}`);
    console.log(`AFTER:  ${normalized.toString()}`);
    console.log('---');
  }
});
```

**When to use:** Automated test maintenance pipelines that scan for fragile CSS/XPath locators and suggest replacements. Valuable in AI-assisted test healers (Playwright Test Agents) that detect broken locators after UI changes and generate repaired versions.

**When NOT to use:** Do not call `normalize()` in production CI test specs as a runtime step — it is a developer-time introspection tool. Always review normalized suggestions before committing; a deliberately precise CSS locator may exist for valid disambiguation reasons.

**Alternatives:** Manual locator review; `npx playwright codegen` for fresh locator generation; `page.pickLocator()` for interactive discovery. [official]

---

### Pattern 29: `consoleMessage.timestamp()` — Time-Correlate Console Logs with Network Events (v1.59+) [official]

`consoleMessage.timestamp()` returns the milliseconds-since-epoch timestamp of when the browser emitted a console message. This enables correlating console logs with network events and test actions — critical for diagnosing race conditions where a log appears before or after a specific network response.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('data-loaded log fires within 200ms of API response', async ({ page }) => {
  const logTimeline: Array<{ text: string; ts: number }> = [];
  const netTimeline: Array<{ url: string; ts: number }> = [];

  page.on('console', msg => {
    logTimeline.push({ text: msg.text(), ts: msg.timestamp() }); // v1.59+
  });

  page.on('response', res => {
    if (res.url().includes('/api/')) {
      netTimeline.push({ url: res.url(), ts: Date.now() });
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('table')).toBeVisible();

  const dataLog = logTimeline.find(l => l.text.includes('data-loaded'));
  const apiResp = netTimeline.find(r => r.url.includes('/api/dashboard'));

  if (dataLog && apiResp) {
    const lagMs = dataLog.ts - apiResp.ts;
    console.log(`data-loaded fired ${lagMs}ms after /api/dashboard response`);
    // Assert the app emits the log promptly — not in a deferred microtask
    expect(lagMs, 'log should fire within 200ms of API response').toBeLessThan(200);
  }
});

test('no error-level console messages on initial page load', async ({ page }) => {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  page.on('console', msg => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') {
      errors.push(`[t=${msg.timestamp()}] ${msg.text()}`);
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  expect(errors, 'no console errors on load').toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**When to use:** Diagnosing race conditions between browser-side logging and network events. Useful in flaky-test post-mortems where the order of operations matters and you need to prove whether a log preceded or followed a network call.

**When NOT to use:** Do not use `timestamp()` for assertions in fast-path CI tests — timing assertions are inherently brittle on busy CI machines. Use it for local debugging; remove timing-based assertions before committing to CI.

**Alternatives:** Playwright Trace Viewer captures all events with timestamps automatically; `page.consoleMessages()` for post-hoc access; `Date.now()` recorded at `page.on('console')` handler time (less precise but cross-version compatible). [official]

---

### Pattern 30: `response.httpVersion()` and `request.existingResponse()` — Protocol-Level Regression Testing (v1.59+) [official]

`response.httpVersion()` returns `'HTTP/1.1'`, `'HTTP/2'`, or `'HTTP/3'` for a given response. `request.existingResponse()` returns a response that is already available without waiting — useful for asserting HTTP/2 server-push or pre-fetched resources. Together they enable protocol-level CI assertions after infrastructure changes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('critical static assets are served over HTTP/2', async ({ page }) => {
  const versions: Record<string, string> = {};

  page.on('response', res => {
    const url = res.url();
    if (url.includes('/static/') || url.includes('/api/')) {
      versions[url] = res.httpVersion(); // v1.59+
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

  // Assert no static assets fell back to HTTP/1.1
  const h1Assets = Object.entries(versions)
    .filter(([, v]) => v === 'HTTP/1.1')
    .map(([url]) => url);

  expect(
    h1Assets,
    `These assets are not on HTTP/2: ${h1Assets.join(', ')}`,
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});

test('pre-fetched resource available without waiting', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const req = await page.waitForRequest('**/critical.css');

  // existingResponse() returns immediately if response is already buffered
  const existingRes = req.existingResponse(); // v1.59+
  if (existingRes) {
    console.log(`critical.css pushed — protocol: ${existingRes.httpVersion()}`);
    expect(existingRes.status()).toBe(200);
  } else {
    console.log('critical.css loaded on demand (no server push detected)');
  }
});

test('API endpoint uses modern HTTP protocol in staging', async ({ request }) => {
  const apiRes = await request.get(process.env.BASE_URL + '/api/products');
  expect(apiRes.status()).toBe(200);

  const version = apiRes.httpVersion();
  expect(
    ['HTTP/2', 'HTTP/3'],
    `Expected modern protocol, got ${version}`,
  ).toContain(version);
});
```

**When to use:** Protocol-level smoke tests asserting that your CDN or load balancer correctly negotiates HTTP/2 for static assets and API endpoints. Run after infrastructure changes (NGINX config, ALB protocol settings, CDN migrations) to catch regressions.

**When NOT to use:** Do not assert HTTP version in local development or against `localhost` — local dev servers typically serve HTTP/1.1. These assertions only make sense in staging or production-mirror environments with TLS and a real load balancer.

**Alternatives:** `curl --http2 -I <url>` for manual protocol checks; Chrome DevTools Network panel Protocol column; infrastructure-level health checks in your deployment pipeline. [official]

## Cycle 31 — Community Gotchas

### 105. `locator.filter({ visible: true })` does not filter elements clipped by `overflow: hidden` — they report as visible [community]

**What:** An element scrolled out of view inside a container with `overflow: hidden` is considered visible by Playwright's visibility check. Only elements with `display:none`, `visibility:hidden`, or `opacity:0` are filtered out by `{ visible: true }`.

**WHY:** Playwright's visibility check mirrors the CSS-level visibility definition — `display:none` and `visibility:hidden` make an element invisible. Overflow clipping is a layout constraint that does not change the element's CSS visibility property. The browser's `checkVisibility()` API (which Playwright uses internally) considers clipped elements visible because they remain in the rendering tree — they just have no visible pixels in the current scroll position. Developers expect "visible" to mean "I can see it on screen," but Playwright means "not CSS-hidden."

**Fix:** If you need only elements within the visible viewport, use `locator.isInViewport()` or check `locator.boundingBox()` intersection with `page.viewportSize()`. For interaction, call `locator.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded()` first.

```typescript
// ❌ Matches all items including those clipped by overflow:hidden
const visibleItems = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ visible: true });

// ✅ Scroll the target into view before interacting
const targetItem = page.getByRole('listitem', { name: 'Target Product' });
await targetItem.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded();
await expect(targetItem).toBeInViewport();
await targetItem.click();
```

---

### 106. `page.clock.install()` must be called BEFORE `page.goto()` to intercept module-level timers [community]

**What:** If you call `page.clock.install()` after `page.goto()`, any timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`) registered during the page's script evaluation phase are not under clock control. The fake clock only intercepts timers registered after `install()` runs.

**WHY:** `page.clock.install()` works by replacing `window.setTimeout`, `window.setInterval`, and related globals. If the page has already evaluated its scripts by the time `install()` is called, module-level timers have already been registered with the real `setTimeout` — not the fake one. Those timers fire on wall-clock time, making `runFor()` and `fastForward()` have no effect on them. This is the same constraint as `page.addInitScript()` — the injection must happen before script evaluation.

**Fix:** Always call `page.clock.install()` (or `page.clock.setFixedTime()`) before `page.goto()`. Pass the `time` option to set the starting instant.

```typescript
// ❌ Module-level setInterval already registered — clock.runFor() has no effect
await page.goto('/dashboard');
await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01') }); // too late

// ✅ Install before navigation — all page scripts see the fake clock
await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01') });
await page.goto('/dashboard');
await page.clock.runFor('1m'); // now advances all timers as expected
```

---

### 107. `test.step()` with `timeout` throws `TimeoutError` and fails the whole test — it does not skip or continue [community]

**What:** When a `test.step()` call exceeds its `timeout` option, Playwright throws a `TimeoutError` inside the step. This error propagates and fails the entire test — it does not skip the step or move to the next one. This surprises developers who expect `{ timeout }` to work like a conditional skip budget.

**WHY:** `timeout` on `test.step()` is a hard invariant — exceeding it signals a defect (the action was too slow). It is architecturally analogous to Playwright's action timeout: exceeding it means the test should fail. If you want to skip a step conditionally, use `step.skip()` instead. The two mechanisms serve opposite purposes: `timeout` says "this must finish in time," while `step.skip()` says "this step is optional."

**Fix:** Use `step.skip()` for optional or environment-conditional steps. Use `timeout` on steps where slowness itself is a test failure. Wrap a step in `try/catch` only if you intend to record the timeout error and continue — and attach the error to the report explicitly.

```typescript
// ❌ Timeout does not skip — it fails the entire test with TimeoutError
await test.step('optional slow check', async () => {
  await page.waitForSelector('.slow-component');  // may be slow
}, { timeout: 2_000 });  // TimeoutError → test FAILS

// ✅ Skip the step conditionally instead
await test.step('optional slow check', async (step) => {
  const isReady = await page.locator('.slow-component').isVisible();
  if (!isReady) { await step.skip(); return; }
  await expect(page.locator('.slow-component')).toBeVisible();
});
```

---

### 108. `--only-changed` does not detect changes to shared fixtures, helpers, or `playwright.config.ts` [community]

**What:** `--only-changed` compares the git diff at the test file level only. Modifying a shared fixture (`e2e/fixtures/auth.ts`), a POM class, or `playwright.config.ts` without touching any spec file causes `--only-changed` to run zero tests — even though those changes affect many tests.

**WHY:** Playwright's `--only-changed` diffs paths matching `testDir` globs. It has no dependency graph awareness and does not trace TypeScript imports to find which spec files consume the modified fixture. This is a deliberate design choice for speed; full dependency analysis would require a TypeScript compiler integration that would be slow for large suites.

**Fix:** Do not use `--only-changed` as the sole CI gate when modifying shared infrastructure files. Detect such changes and fall back to running the full suite.

```bash
# ❌ Runs 0 tests — only a fixture file changed, no spec files modified
npx playwright test --only-changed=origin/main

# ✅ Detect fixture/config changes and run full suite as fallback
CHANGED=$(git diff --name-only origin/main)
if echo "$CHANGED" | grep -qE "e2e/fixtures|e2e/pages|playwright\.config"; then
  echo "Shared infrastructure changed — running full suite"
  npx playwright test
else
  npx playwright test --only-changed=origin/main
fi
```

---

### 109. `browserContext.storageState()` with IndexedDB captures only committed transactions — async writes in-flight are not included [community]

**What:** When you call `await page.context().storageState({ path })`, Playwright reads IndexedDB state at that instant. If your application has an async IndexedDB write in progress (e.g., a Firebase Auth token refresh completing in the background), that write may not be committed before `storageState()` reads — resulting in an auth file missing the latest token.

**WHY:** IndexedDB operations are asynchronous and transactional. When Playwright serializes IndexedDB via the Chrome DevTools Protocol, it reads the current committed state. Any transaction that has been initiated but not yet committed at the JS level is not captured. This is especially common with Firebase Auth's token refresh, which writes to IndexedDB asynchronously after login completes at the UI layer.

**Fix:** Before calling `storageState()`, use `page.waitForFunction()` to poll until the expected IndexedDB record is present and committed.

```typescript
// ❌ storageState() called too early — Firebase token write may still be in-flight
await loginPage.login(email, password);
await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile }); // may miss the token

// ✅ Wait for the IndexedDB write to commit before capturing state
await page.waitForFunction(() =>
  new Promise<boolean>(resolve => {
    const req = indexedDB.open('firebaseLocalStorageDb');
    req.onsuccess = () => {
      const tx    = req.result.transaction('firebaseLocalStorage', 'readonly');
      const store = tx.objectStore('firebaseLocalStorage');
      const all   = store.getAll();
      all.onsuccess = () => resolve(all.result.length > 0);
      all.onerror   = () => resolve(false);
    };
    req.onerror = () => resolve(false);
  }),
);
await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile }); // now safe
```

---

### 110. `testProject.workers` is capped by the global `workers` setting — project values exceeding the global are silently ignored [community]

**What:** `testProject.workers` cannot exceed the global `workers` value. If you set `workers: 2` globally and `testProject.workers: 8` for an API project, the API project runs with at most 2 workers — the project-level setting is silently capped without a warning.

**WHY:** The global `workers` setting represents the total Playwright runner worker pool. All projects share this pool — they do not each receive an independent pool. `testProject.workers` sets the maximum concurrent workers a specific project may claim from the global pool, but it cannot expand the pool itself. The documentation phrasing "specifies concurrent workers per project" is misleading — it is a per-project cap, not a per-project allocation from a separate pool.

**Fix:** Set the global `workers` to the maximum you need across all projects combined, then use `testProject.workers` to restrict individual projects that should run with fewer workers (not more).

```typescript
// ❌ API project wants 8 workers but the global pool is 2 — silently runs at 2
export default defineConfig({
  workers: 2,
  projects: [
    { name: 'api-tests', workers: 8, testDir: './e2e/api' }, // capped at 2 silently
  ],
});

// ✅ Set global pool large enough; use per-project limits to restrict noisy neighbors
export default defineConfig({
  workers: 8,
  projects: [
    { name: 'api-tests',   workers: 8, testDir: './e2e/api' },         // up to 8
    { name: 'integration', workers: 1, testDir: './e2e/integration' }, // serial
    { name: 'visual',      workers: 2, testDir: './e2e/visual' },      // limited
  ],
});
```

---

### 111. `page.requests()` stores only the last 100 requests per navigation — high-traffic pages silently lose earlier entries [community]

**What:** `page.requests()` maintains a rolling buffer of the last 100 network requests since the most recent top-level navigation. If a page fires more than 100 requests (common in data-heavy dashboards loading charts, ads, and analytics), the earliest requests are silently dropped.

**WHY:** The 100-entry cap is a deliberate memory bound to prevent long-running tests from accumulating thousands of request objects. The buffer resets on each `page.goto()` call, consistent with `page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` scoping. There is no warning or error when the cap is reached — entries are simply evicted FIFO.

**Fix:** For pages with more than 100 requests, use `page.on('request')` to stream all requests into a custom array before the test begins. This has no cap and does not reset on navigation unless you clear the array manually.

```typescript
// ❌ High-traffic page — requests beyond the 100th are silently dropped
await page.goto('/analytics-dashboard');
const allRequests = page.requests(); // may be missing the first ~50 requests

// ✅ Stream all requests via listener — no cap
const allRequests: import('@playwright/test').Request[] = [];
page.on('request', req => allRequests.push(req));

await page.goto('/analytics-dashboard');
await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

const analyticsReqs = allRequests.filter(r => r.url().includes('/collect'));
expect(analyticsReqs.length, 'analytics events fired').toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(5);
```
