## Cycle 34 — 2026-05-14

### 122. `locator.describe()` for human-readable labels in trace viewer and reports [official]

**Description:** `locator.describe(label)` attaches a human-readable description to any locator without changing which element it targets. The description surfaces in the Playwright Trace Viewer action list and in HTML report step details, replacing the raw selector string with the label you provide. This is especially valuable for complex chained locators or test-ID-based selectors whose raw form is opaque to reviewers. Call `locator.description()` to retrieve the label programmatically when building custom reporter logic.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Locators use internal test IDs or data attributes that are meaningless to anyone reading a trace or report — add a business-domain label to make failures instantly understandable.
- **Do NOT use when:** The locator is already human-readable (e.g., `getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })`) — the description adds noise without benefit.
- **Alternative:** Add `data-testid` values that already encode semantic meaning (e.g., `data-testid="checkout-submit-btn"`) so the raw selector is self-documenting.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('described locators appear in trace viewer', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Attach business-domain labels to opaque selectors
  const submitBtn = page
    .locator('[data-qa="btn-7f3a"]')
    .describe('Checkout submit button');

  const promoInput = page
    .getByTestId('promo-field-v2')
    .describe('Promotional code input');

  await promoInput.fill('SAVE20');
  await submitBtn.click();

  // Retrieve the label for custom reporting
  console.log(submitBtn.description()); // "Checkout submit button"

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' }))
    .toBeVisible();
});
```

---

### 123. `page.ariaSnapshot()` for programmatic accessibility tree inspection [official]

**Description:** `page.ariaSnapshot()` (and its per-locator variant `locator.ariaSnapshot()`) returns the current ARIA accessibility tree as a YAML string without performing any assertion. This is the read side of the aria snapshot system: use it to capture a baseline during exploratory testing, diff trees across page states, or feed snapshot text into a custom accessibility linter. Unlike `toMatchAriaSnapshot()`, it never fails a test — it only returns data. The returned YAML uses the same template syntax supported by `toMatchAriaSnapshot()`, so snapshots captured with this method can be pasted directly into assertion arguments.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You want to log, inspect, or conditionally branch on the current accessibility tree without asserting against a fixed expected value.
- **Do NOT use when:** You want to assert that the tree matches a known-good baseline — use `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` instead.
- **Alternative:** `page.accessibility.snapshot()` was the legacy equivalent but was removed in v1.57; `page.ariaSnapshot()` is the replacement.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('capture and compare aria snapshots across nav states', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Capture the initial navigation tree
  const navRegion = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' });
  const initialSnapshot = await navRegion.ariaSnapshot();
  console.log('Initial nav ARIA:', initialSnapshot);

  // Expand a menu item and capture the updated tree
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Reports' }).click();
  const expandedSnapshot = await navRegion.ariaSnapshot();

  // Programmatic diff — verify the expanded tree is strictly larger
  expect(expandedSnapshot.length).toBeGreaterThan(initialSnapshot.length);

  // Full assertion using the captured baseline
  await expect(navRegion).toMatchAriaSnapshot(expandedSnapshot);
});
```

---

### 124. `page.requests()`, `page.consoleMessages()`, `page.pageErrors()` — bounded history APIs [official]

**Description:** Playwright v1.56 added three "pull" APIs that return recent page activity without requiring event listeners to be registered in advance: `page.requests()` (up to 100 network requests), `page.consoleMessages()` (up to 200 console messages), and `page.pageErrors()` (up to 200 uncaught errors). These are ideal for post-hoc diagnostics at assertion time — you can check whether a specific XHR fired or whether a JS error occurred after a user action without wiring listeners at setup. In v1.59, `consoleMessages()` and `pageErrors()` gained a `filter` option accepting `'all'` (default) or `'since-navigation'` to scope results to the current page load.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You need lightweight, zero-setup access to recent page activity for assertion-time diagnostics, especially in shared fixtures where installing listeners is inconvenient.
- **Do NOT use when:** You need guaranteed capture of every event — these buffers are bounded and drop the oldest entries; use `page.on('request', ...)` listeners for exhaustive capture.
- **Alternative:** `page.on('request')` / `page.on('console')` / `page.on('pageerror')` for complete event streams; `page.route()` for interception rather than observation.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('verify analytics beacon fired and no JS errors occurred', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/product/123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();

  // Check requests post-hoc — no listener needed at setup time
  const requests = page.requests();
  const beaconFired = requests.some(r =>
    r.url().includes('/analytics/add-to-cart')
  );
  expect(beaconFired).toBe(true);

  // Check for JS errors since the last navigation
  const errors = page.pageErrors({ filter: 'since-navigation' });
  expect(errors).toHaveLength(0);

  // Inspect console messages for unexpected warnings
  const warnings = page
    .consoleMessages({ filter: 'since-navigation' })
    .filter(m => m.type() === 'warning');
  expect(warnings).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

---

### 125. `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` — hard-fail CI on detected flakiness [official]

**Description:** Setting `failOnFlakyTests: true` (or `!!process.env.CI`) causes the test run to exit with a non-zero code whenever any test passes on a retry after initially failing, which Playwright classifies as "flaky". Without this flag, flaky tests are reported in the HTML report but the run exits with code 0 — builds pass and flakiness accumulates silently. Enabling `failOnFlakyTests` forces engineers to resolve flakiness before merging, rather than accumulating a growing backlog of unreliable tests that pass "most of the time" in CI. Combine this with `retries: 2` in CI to give tests a genuine retry window before classifying them as flaky.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your CI pipeline should enforce zero-tolerance for flaky tests — any test that needed a retry is a signal requiring investigation, not a silent pass.
- **Do NOT use when:** Your test suite is in active development and some expected test instability exists during the stabilization period — the flag will block all merges until every test is stable.
- **Alternative:** Use the `--reporter=json` output to track `flaky` status metrics in a custom dashboard without blocking the pipeline.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // Any test that passes only on retry fails the CI run
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['github']]
    : [['list']],

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
});
```

---

### 126. `testConfig.webServer.wait` with named capture groups as environment variables [official]

**Description:** The `webServer.wait` field (added in v1.57) accepts a `stdout` or `stderr` regex that Playwright monitors during server startup. When the pattern matches, Playwright considers the server ready and proceeds with the test run. Named capture groups in the regex are automatically uppercased and injected as environment variables — for example, `(?<port>\d+)` makes the matched port available as `process.env['PORT']`. This eliminates the need to hardcode dynamic ports in `baseURL` or test helpers, enabling integration with dev servers that bind to ephemeral ports.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your dev server binds to an ephemeral or configurable port logged to stdout (e.g., Vite, Express, Next.js with `--port 0`).
- **Do NOT use when:** Your server always starts on a fixed port — use `url` instead of `wait` for faster readiness checks via HTTP polling.
- **Alternative:** `webServer.url` with a fixed URL for polling-based readiness; set `baseURL` statically for deterministic port environments.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    // Named capture group 'server_port' becomes process.env['SERVER_PORT']
    wait: {
      stdout: /Local:\s+http:\/\/localhost:(?<server_port>\d+)/,
    },
    // Use the captured port in baseURL via env var
    url: `http://localhost:${process.env['SERVER_PORT'] ?? 5173}`,
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
  use: {
    baseURL: `http://localhost:${process.env['SERVER_PORT'] ?? 5173}`,
  },
});
```

---

### 127. `test.abort()` for immediate test termination from fixtures and route handlers [official]

**Description:** `test.abort(message?)` (v1.60+) immediately fails the currently running test and stops execution. Unlike `expect().toBe()` which throws an assertion error, `test.abort()` is designed to be called from fixtures, `page.route()` handlers, or `page.on()` event listeners where throwing is not practical. When `abort()` is called from a fixture, teardown still runs — but `afterEach` hooks are skipped since the test is already marked as failed. This is ideal for "canary" patterns where an unexpected network call or console error should immediately fail the test rather than polluting later assertions.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You want a fixture or route handler to act as an invariant enforcer — if a production API key leaks into a test request, abort immediately.
- **Do NOT use when:** The failure condition is something you can check with a normal `expect()` at the end of the test — `test.abort()` skips `afterEach` hooks and may leave cleanup undone if your teardown depends on them.
- **Alternative:** Throw an `Error` inside a `page.on('request')` listener for simpler cases; use `page.route()` with `route.abort()` to block specific requests rather than failing the test.

```typescript
import { test, expect, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

// Fixture that aborts if any request leaks to a production endpoint
const strictNetworkTest = test.extend<{ page: Page }>({
  page: async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
    page.on('request', request => {
      if (request.url().includes('api.production.example.com')) {
        testInfo.abort(
          `Production API called in test: ${request.url()}`
        );
      }
    });
    await use(page);
    // Fixture teardown still runs even after abort()
  },
});

strictNetworkTest('checkout does not call production API', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});
```

---

### 128. `page.screencast` API for programmatic video recording and visual overlays [official]

**Description:** The `page.screencast` API (v1.59+) exposes video recording as an explicit, controllable interface rather than a passive `recordVideo` context option. `screencast.start()` begins recording to a file or a per-frame callback, `screencast.stop()` finalizes the file, and `showActions()` overlays visual annotations on interacted elements during recording. `showChapter(title, description)` displays a centered slide-style overlay for demo narration, while `showOverlay(html)` injects arbitrary HTML overlays. This API is particularly useful for generating annotated demo recordings, visual regression videos, and debugging videos that highlight the exact elements Playwright is interacting with.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You need recording control beyond "always record" or "record on failure" — e.g., start recording only after login completes, or overlay step labels for stakeholder demos.
- **Do NOT use when:** You just want to capture failure videos — `video: 'on-first-retry'` in `use` config is simpler and requires no test changes.
- **Alternative:** `use: { video: 'on' }` context option for passive recording; Playwright Trace Viewer (`trace: 'on'`) for interactive post-hoc replay.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('annotated checkout flow recording', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.screencast.start({
    path: 'recordings/checkout-demo.webm',
    size: { width: 1280, height: 800 },
  });

  // Show visual annotations on every interaction
  await page.screencast.showActions({ duration: 1500 });

  await page.screencast.showChapter('Step 1: Navigate to Checkout');
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  await page.screencast.showChapter('Step 2: Enter payment details');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');

  await page.screencast.showChapter('Step 3: Submit order');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' }))
    .toBeVisible();

  await page.screencast.stop();
});
```

---

### 129. Async disposables with `await using` for automatic route and listener cleanup [official]

**Description:** Playwright's `Disposable` interface (surfaced in v1.59) enables TypeScript's `await using` syntax with APIs that return `Promise<Disposable>` — including `browserContext.route()`, `page.route()`, `browserContext.addInitScript()`, `browserContext.exposeFunction()`, and similar registrations. When the `await using` variable goes out of scope, the registered handler or script is automatically removed without an explicit `dispose()` call. This eliminates a common source of test pollution where routes registered inside a `test.step()` or helper function accidentally persist to the next assertion or test.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You register a route or init script that should only apply for a specific portion of a test — scoped cleanup is guaranteed even if an exception is thrown.
- **Do NOT use when:** Your TypeScript target is below `ES2022` or you are not using `"useDefineForClassFields": false` — `await using` requires `target: 'ES2022'` or higher in `tsconfig.json`.
- **Alternative:** Explicit `disposable.dispose()` in a `try/finally` block; `page.unrouteAll()` for bulk route cleanup at test end.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('route cleanup with await using', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Route is automatically removed when this block ends
  {
    await using _slowNetwork = await context.route(
      '**/api/products',
      async route => {
        await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500)); // simulate slow API
        await route.continue();
      }
    );

    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Load more' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(20);
    // _slowNetwork.dispose() is called automatically at block end
  }

  // This request is no longer intercepted — tests real API latency
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Load more' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(40);
});
```

---

### 130. `tracing.startHar()` / `tracing.stopHar()` — first-class HAR recording API [official]

**Description:** Playwright v1.60 promoted HAR recording from an option on `browserContext.newContext({ recordHar })` to a first-class tracing API: `context.tracing.startHar(path)` begins recording and `context.tracing.stopHar()` finalizes the HAR file to disk. Using the tracing API makes HAR recording composable with other tracing operations and enables starting/stopping HAR recording mid-test without recreating the context. The resulting HAR files can be replayed in `page.routeFromHAR()` for deterministic offline test replay, or analyzed externally to diagnose latency, header, and payload issues.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You need to record HAR archives for a specific sequence of interactions (e.g., only the checkout flow, not the entire test) and want to compose this with tracing.
- **Do NOT use when:** You need full-context HAR from test start — `recordHar` in `use` config is simpler and covers the entire browser context lifecycle automatically.
- **Alternative:** `use: { recordHar: { path: 'har/test.har' } }` for always-on HAR recording; `page.routeFromHAR()` for replaying recorded HARs in isolation tests.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('record HAR for checkout flow only', async ({ context, page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Shop' }).click();

  // Start HAR recording only from this point forward
  await context.tracing.startHar('hars/checkout-flow.har');

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();

  // Finalize and write the HAR file
  await context.tracing.stopHar();

  // HAR can now be replayed via page.routeFromHAR('hars/checkout-flow.har')
});
```

---

### 131. `locator.drop()` — simulate external drag-and-drop from files or clipboard [official]

**Description:** `locator.drop()` (v1.60+) simulates dropping external data (files, clipboard content, or custom `DataTransfer` objects) onto a target element, distinct from `locator.dragTo()` which drags one page element onto another. This enables testing file upload drop zones, external content paste targets, and drag-and-drop interactions that originate outside the browser window. The `dataTransfer` option accepts a `DataTransfer` object created via `page.evaluateHandle(() => new DataTransfer())`, allowing fine-grained control over MIME types, file lists, and custom data items.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your application accepts files or content dragged from outside the browser (e.g., drop zones for PDF upload, Figma-style external asset import).
- **Do NOT use when:** You are dragging one element within the page to another — use `locator.dragTo(target)` for intra-page drag-and-drop.
- **Alternative:** `page.setInputFiles()` for file uploads via `<input type="file">`; `locator.dragTo()` for in-page element dragging.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

test('drop external file onto upload zone', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/upload');

  // Build a DataTransfer with the file to drop
  const fileBuffer = fs.readFileSync(
    path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures/report.pdf')
  );
  const dataTransfer = await page.evaluateHandle(
    ([name, buffer]) => {
      const dt = new DataTransfer();
      const file = new File([new Uint8Array(buffer)], name, {
        type: 'application/pdf',
      });
      dt.items.add(file);
      return dt;
    },
    [path.basename('fixtures/report.pdf'), Array.from(fileBuffer)] as const
  );

  // Drop the external file onto the drop zone
  const dropZone = page.getByRole('region', { name: 'Upload area' });
  await dropZone.drop({ dataTransfer });

  await expect(page.getByText('report.pdf')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Process' })).toBeEnabled();
});
```

---

### 132. `browser.on('context')` — monitor programmatically created contexts in multi-tenant tests [official]

**Description:** The `browser.on('context')` event (v1.60+) fires whenever a new `BrowserContext` is created on a browser instance, including contexts created by `browser.newContext()`, `browser.newPage()` (which implicitly creates a context), and contexts opened by popup windows. This is invaluable in test infrastructure that launches a shared browser and needs to apply global policies — such as route interception, authentication state injection, or network monitoring — to every context regardless of how it was created. Previously, applying uniform context configuration required wrapping every `browser.newContext()` call.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You build shared browser infrastructure (BrowserPool, multi-tenant test runners) where every context should receive the same route handlers, headers, or state without per-call configuration.
- **Do NOT use when:** You only create one context per test via the standard `{ page }` fixture — Playwright's fixture system already provides isolation without needing this event.
- **Alternative:** Playwright fixtures with `scope: 'worker'` to share a configured context across tests in a worker; `test.use({ extraHTTPHeaders })` for header injection without event listeners.

```typescript
import { chromium, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

// Shared infrastructure: inject auth headers into every new context
async function launchTrackedBrowser() {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();

  browser.on('context', async (context: BrowserContext) => {
    // Apply global route interceptor to every context automatically
    await context.route('**/api/**', async route => {
      await route.continue({
        headers: {
          ...route.request().headers(),
          'X-Test-Run-Id': process.env['TEST_RUN_ID'] ?? 'local',
        },
      });
    });
  });

  return browser;
}

// Every context.newPage() now has the injected header — no per-call config needed
const browser = await launchTrackedBrowser();
const page1 = await browser.newPage();
const page2 = await browser.newPage();
await browser.close();
```

---

### 133. CHIPS partitioned cookies with `partitionKey` for third-party storage testing [official]

**Description:** Playwright v1.54 added `partitionKey` support to `browserContext.addCookies()` and the cookies returned by `browserContext.cookies()`. Partitioned cookies (CHIPS — Cookies Having Independent Partitioned State) are isolated per top-level site, enabling cross-site embed testing without third-party cookie access. This is critical for testing embedded widgets, payment iframes, SSO flows, and analytics tags that must function under modern browser privacy restrictions. Setting `partitionKey` to a top-level site origin reproduces the partitioned context Chrome enforces for iframes from a different origin.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your application embeds third-party iframes (payment widgets, SSO providers, analytics) that set or read cookies, and you need to verify behavior under CHIPS-compliant browsers.
- **Do NOT use when:** You are testing first-party cookies set by your own domain — standard `addCookies()` without `partitionKey` is sufficient and simpler.
- **Alternative:** Frame fixtures that navigate directly to the embedded origin in isolation; `page.route()` to mock embedded service responses rather than testing cookie propagation.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('embedded payment widget reads its partitioned session cookie', async ({
  context,
  page,
}) => {
  // Add a CHIPS-partitioned cookie as a third-party payment provider would set it
  await context.addCookies([
    {
      name: 'psp_session',
      value: 'tok_test_abc123',
      domain: 'pay.example-psp.com',
      path: '/',
      // partitionKey = top-level site that embeds the iframe
      partitionKey: { sourceScheme: 'https', hasCrossSiteAncestor: true },
    },
  ]);

  await page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout');

  // The embedded PSP iframe should read its partitioned cookie
  const pspFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[src*="pay.example-psp.com"]');
  await expect(
    pspFrame.getByText('Session active')
  ).toBeVisible();

  // Verify cookie is partitioned — not accessible from main frame context
  const cookies = await context.cookies('https://pay.example-psp.com');
  expect(cookies[0].partitionKey).toBeDefined();
});
```

---

### 134. `testAnnotation.location` — trace annotation origins back to source files [official]

**Description:** Test annotations added via `test.info().annotations.push()` or the declarative `test()` options now include a `location` property (added in v1.54) that records the file path and line number where the annotation was created. In HTML reports and custom reporters, `annotation.location` lets you hyperlink directly to the source code that added the annotation — critical for tags like `{ type: 'jira', description: 'BUG-1234' }` where a one-click link to the tagging location accelerates triage. The `location` property is populated automatically; no extra code is required in the annotation itself.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You build custom reporters or dashboards that need to link annotation events (bug tags, skip reasons, retry contexts) back to the exact test file line that added them.
- **Do NOT use when:** You only consume annotations in the standard HTML reporter — the built-in reporter already uses location data; you need this only for custom reporter integrations.
- **Alternative:** `testInfo.annotations` for reading all annotations at test runtime; `test.info().line` for the current test file location independently of annotations.

```typescript
import { test, type Reporter, type TestCase, type TestResult } from '@playwright/test';

// Custom reporter that links annotation sources
class AnnotationLinkReporter implements Reporter {
  onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult): void {
    for (const annotation of result.annotations ?? []) {
      if (annotation.type === 'jira' && annotation.location) {
        console.log(
          `[JIRA ${annotation.description}] annotated at ` +
          `${annotation.location.file}:${annotation.location.line}`
        );
      }
    }
  }
}

// In a test: annotate with a Jira ticket reference
test('checkout total calculation', async ({ page }) => {
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'jira',
    description: 'BUG-9821',
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  // location is auto-populated — points to the annotations.push() call above
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-total')).toContainText('€');
});
```

---

### 135. `testStepInfo.titlePath` — full hierarchical step title for structured test reporting [official]

**Description:** `TestStepInfo.titlePath` (v1.55+) returns an array of strings representing the full title path from the test root to the current step, including all parent `describe` block names and step names. This is analogous to `test.info().titlePath` but scoped to the active step, enabling reporters to build hierarchical step trees or structured JSON logs without parsing slash-delimited title strings. Use `titlePath` inside a `test.step()` callback to capture the full context for logging or analytics systems that consume structured step data.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You build a custom step reporter or structured JSON logger that needs the full hierarchical path for each step without string manipulation.
- **Do NOT use when:** You only need the step's own title — use `step.title` directly rather than `titlePath.at(-1)`.
- **Alternative:** `testInfo.titlePath` for the full test title path (describe + test name) without step granularity; `step.title` for just the current step name.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const stepLog: Array<{ path: string[]; durationMs: number }> = [];

test.describe('Checkout flow', () => {
  test('complete purchase', async ({ page }) => {
    await test.step(
      'Navigate to checkout',
      async step => {
        // titlePath: ['Checkout flow', 'complete purchase', 'Navigate to checkout']
        const start = Date.now();
        await page.goto('/checkout');
        stepLog.push({
          path: step.titlePath,
          durationMs: Date.now() - start,
        });
      }
    );

    await test.step(
      'Submit order',
      async step => {
        const start = Date.now();
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
        await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
        stepLog.push({
          path: step.titlePath,
          durationMs: Date.now() - start,
        });
      }
    );

    // Emit structured step log for external analytics
    console.log(JSON.stringify(stepLog, null, 2));
  });
});
```

---

### 136. `page.consoleMessages()` with `filter: 'since-navigation'` — scoped console inspection [official]

**Description:** The `filter: 'since-navigation'` option on `page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` (v1.59+) restricts results to messages logged after the most recent navigation event, eliminating noise from messages logged during page initialization or previous route changes. Without this filter, assertions against `consoleMessages()` can fail due to vendor script warnings logged during initial hydration that are unrelated to the action under test. The `'all'` default includes every buffered message since the page was created (up to 200), while `'since-navigation'` creates a clean boundary at each `goto()` or navigation.

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You assert the absence of errors or warnings following a specific user action — filter to `'since-navigation'` to avoid false positives from unrelated initialization-time messages.
- **Do NOT use when:** You need to assert that no errors occurred during the initial page load itself — use `'all'` or install a `page.on('pageerror')` listener before `goto()`.
- **Alternative:** `page.on('pageerror', handler)` before `page.goto()` for exhaustive pre-navigation error capture; `page.on('console', handler)` for real-time processing.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('no console errors after adding item to cart', async ({ page }) => {
  // Navigate — this becomes the 'since-navigation' boundary
  await page.goto('/product/sneakers-42');

  // Initial page may have benign hydration warnings — ignore them
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.goto('/cart'); // <-- new navigation boundary

  // Only check messages logged after the /cart navigation
  const errors = page
    .consoleMessages({ filter: 'since-navigation' })
    .filter(m => m.type() === 'error');

  const pageErrors = page.pageErrors({ filter: 'since-navigation' });

  expect(errors).toHaveLength(0);
  expect(pageErrors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

---

## Cycle 34 — Community Gotchas

### 137. `page.requests()` returns stale references — access immediately after the action [community]

**What:** `page.requests()` documents that returned requests "should be accessed immediately, otherwise they might be collected." In practice, Playwright uses a circular buffer capped at 100 entries: every new request evicts the oldest entry once the buffer is full. On high-traffic pages (dashboards with WebSocket polling, analytics-heavy storefronts), the specific XHR you want to assert against may already have been evicted by the time you call `page.requests()` if many other requests fired in the interim.

**WHY:** The bounded buffer is intentional — storing an unbounded list of all `Request` objects would prevent garbage collection of request/response body memory, causing heap growth across long test runs. The buffer size (100) was chosen to cover typical assertion windows, but high-frequency request pages (> 100 requests per action) can exhaust it before your assertion runs. There is no mechanism to increase the buffer size via config.

**Fix:** For high-traffic pages, install a `page.on('request', handler)` listener before the action under test to capture requests into your own unbounded array. Reserve `page.requests()` for low-traffic pages where the 100-entry buffer is never at risk of overflow.

```typescript
// ❌ Unreliable on high-traffic pages — beacon may be evicted from 100-entry buffer
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
const captured = page.requests().find(r => r.url().includes('/beacon'));
expect(captured).toBeDefined(); // may be undefined on busy pages

// ✅ Install listener BEFORE the action — unbounded, guaranteed capture
const beaconRequests: string[] = [];
page.on('request', req => {
  if (req.url().includes('/beacon')) beaconRequests.push(req.url());
});
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
expect(beaconRequests.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
```

---

### 138. `page.accessibility.snapshot()` was removed in v1.57 — `page.ariaSnapshot()` is the replacement [community]

**What:** `page.accessibility.snapshot()` was the legacy API for reading the accessibility tree as a JSON object. It was deprecated in Playwright v1.15 and fully removed in v1.57. Projects that still reference `page.accessibility.snapshot()` after upgrading to v1.57+ receive a `TypeError: page.accessibility is undefined` at runtime — not a compile-time TypeScript error, because the `page.accessibility` property was typed as potentially undefined in the deprecation period.

**WHY:** The `page.accessibility` object was a thin wrapper around Chrome DevTools Protocol's `Accessibility.getFullAXTree` command, which did not align with ARIA standards and had known issues with virtual accessibility trees used by screen readers. Playwright replaced it with `page.ariaSnapshot()` which produces ARIA-spec-compliant YAML output and integrates with `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` for snapshot-based regression testing. The removal was announced in v1.15 release notes but teams running long-lived test suites often miss deprecation notices and discover the break only when upgrading.

**Fix:** Replace `page.accessibility.snapshot()` calls with `page.ariaSnapshot()` or `locator.ariaSnapshot()`. The output format is YAML instead of JSON, so any downstream parsing code also needs updating.

```typescript
// ❌ Removed in v1.57 — throws TypeError: page.accessibility is undefined
const tree = await page.accessibility.snapshot();
const button = tree?.children?.find(n => n.role === 'button');

// ✅ Replacement: page.ariaSnapshot() returns ARIA-compliant YAML string
const yamlTree = await page.ariaSnapshot();
// Parse or assert directly
await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
  - list:
    - listitem: Home
    - listitem: Products
`);
```

---

### 139. `await using` requires `"target": "ES2022"` in tsconfig — silently falls back to JS errors without it [community]

**What:** Playwright v1.59+ APIs that return `Promise<Disposable>` (e.g., `context.route()`, `page.addInitScript()`) can be used with TypeScript's `await using` syntax for automatic cleanup. However, `await using` is a TypeScript 5.2+ feature that requires `"target": "ES2022"` (or higher) in `tsconfig.json`. Projects using `"target": "ES2015"` or `"ES2016"` will receive a TypeScript compile error ("Decorators are not valid here" or "Property Symbol.asyncDispose does not exist"), not a runtime polyfill. This surprises teams that assume the TypeScript compiler handles the downleveling automatically.

**WHY:** `await using` desugars to `Symbol.asyncDispose` — a well-known symbol introduced in ES2022. TypeScript emits code that calls `Symbol.asyncDispose` directly without any polyfill, so if the JavaScript runtime (Node.js < 20) or the `lib` configuration doesn't define `Symbol.asyncDispose`, the code throws a `ReferenceError` at runtime even if it compiled successfully with `"target": "ES2022"`. Node.js 18 LTS does not natively support `Symbol.asyncDispose`; Node.js 20+ does.

**Fix:** Set `"target": "ES2022"` and ensure `"lib"` includes `"ES2022"`. For Node 18 environments, polyfill `Symbol.asyncDispose` in `globalSetup.ts` or use `disposable.dispose()` in a `try/finally` instead.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — required for await using to compile and run
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "target": "ES2022",
//     "lib": ["ES2022"],
//     "module": "Node16"
//   }
// }

// globalSetup.ts — Node 18 polyfill for Symbol.asyncDispose
export default async function globalSetup() {
  // Node 18 does not define Symbol.asyncDispose natively
  if (typeof Symbol.asyncDispose === 'undefined') {
    (Symbol as unknown as Record<string, symbol>).asyncDispose =
      Symbol('Symbol.asyncDispose');
  }
}

// ✅ With target ES2022 + Node 20: await using works natively
// ❌ Without it: ReferenceError: Symbol.asyncDispose is not defined
```

---

### 140. Chrome for Testing (v1.57+) headers differ from Chromium — third-party SDK detection breaks [community]

**What:** Playwright v1.57 switched its default Chromium channel from a stripped Chromium build to "Chrome for Testing" (CfT). CfT reports a full Chrome user-agent string (`Chrome/NNN`) and sets `navigator.userAgent` identically to a production Chrome installation. This breaks a class of tests and mocked responses that relied on the old Chromium build's user-agent fragment (`HeadlessChrome` or `Chromium`) to detect Playwright-controlled sessions and route them to stub endpoints. Additionally, some third-party SDKs (Intercom, Segment, Braze) changed initialization behavior when they detect a real Chrome user-agent, causing unexpected network calls that were absent with the old headless Chromium.

**WHY:** CfT is the same binary distributed to end users through Chrome's standard channel, making it more representative for regression testing. The tradeoff is that all heuristics based on distinguishing headless Chromium from real Chrome break silently — there is no `HeadlessChrome/NNN` substring in the user-agent in headed mode, and the `--headless` flag no longer leaks into the user-agent string by default. Tests that used `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders` to inject a custom sentinel header as a workaround for the Chromium detection pattern need to be updated.

**Fix:** Do not rely on the user-agent to detect Playwright-controlled sessions. Inject a custom request header (`X-Playwright-Test: 1`) at the context level and key your stub routing logic on that header instead of the user-agent.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — inject sentinel header instead of relying on UA detection
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    extraHTTPHeaders: {
      'X-Playwright-Test': '1', // key stubs on this, not on user-agent
    },
  },
});

// server-side middleware (Express example):
// ❌ Old pattern — breaks with Chrome for Testing (no 'HeadlessChrome' in UA)
// if (req.headers['user-agent']?.includes('HeadlessChrome')) {
//   return res.json(stubbedResponse);
// }

// ✅ New pattern — keyed on injected header, stable across Playwright versions
// if (req.headers['x-playwright-test'] === '1') {
//   return res.json(stubbedResponse);
// }
```

---

### 141. `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` marks slow retry-passing tests as flaky — not just unreliable ones [community]

**What:** When `failOnFlakyTests: true` is enabled and `retries > 0`, any test that fails on attempt 1 but passes on attempt 2 is classified as "flaky" and causes the run to exit non-zero — regardless of whether the failure was due to genuine test flakiness or a legitimate environmental issue (CI runner throttling, cold-start database connection, first-request SSL handshake latency). Teams enabling `failOnFlakyTests` for the first time discover that tests which were "reliably passing" in reports were quietly relying on `retries` to absorb infrastructure-level slowness, and these now block CI.

**WHY:** Playwright's flakiness detection is purely behavioral: a test that fails on attempt N and passes on attempt N+1 is flaky by definition. The runner has no way to distinguish an inherently unreliable test from one that needed a retry due to a cold start or CI resource contention. The `failOnFlakyTests` flag is intentionally strict because the distinction between "environment flakiness" and "test flakiness" is irrelevant from a reliability standpoint — both are reliability failures that should be investigated, not silently retried away.

**Fix:** Before enabling `failOnFlakyTests` in CI, audit which tests are currently passing only via retries. Fix their root causes (add `waitForLoadState`, increase `actionTimeout`, add explicit waits for database readiness) so they pass on the first attempt. Then enable the flag.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — staged rollout: fix flaky tests before enforcing
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // Step 1: enable reporting without blocking — track flaky count over time
  // reporter: [['html'], ['json', { outputFile: 'results.json' }]],

  // Step 2 (after fixing root causes): enforce flakiness as a build failure
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.ENFORCE_FLAKY_POLICY,

  use: {
    // Increase global action timeout to absorb legitimate cold-start latency
    actionTimeout: 15_000,
    navigationTimeout: 30_000,
  },
});
```

### 142. `test.step()` timeout — per-step independent deadlines [official]

Since v1.50, `test.step()` accepts a `timeout` option that enforces an independent time limit on the step body, separate from the overall test timeout. A step that exceeds its timeout causes the step to fail (and the test to fail) without waiting for the full test timeout to expire. This is particularly useful for steps that call slow external services or perform I/O-heavy setup, where you want tight observability on which step is the bottleneck. Without per-step timeouts, a single slow setup step can silently consume the entire test budget, making the failure message uninformative. Steps inherit the parent test timeout unless a `timeout` is explicitly provided, so adding a step timeout is always a tightening constraint, never an extension.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow with per-step timeouts', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('load product page', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/42');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /product/i })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 5_000 }); // fail fast if product page hangs

  await test.step('add to cart', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText('1 item');
  }, { timeout: 3_000 });

  await test.step('proceed to checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: /checkout/i }).click();
    await page.waitForURL(/checkout/);
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /checkout/i })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 8_000 }); // checkout page may redirect slowly
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** An individual step involves a slow external dependency (payment gateway, image processing) and you want precise failure attribution in the trace viewer.
- **Do NOT use when:** The step timeout is shorter than `actionTimeout` — the first auto-waiting action will exceed it and mask the actual bottleneck.
- **Alternative:** Increase `actionTimeout` globally instead if all steps are slow; use `test.step()` timeout only for steps with known upper-bound SLAs.

---

### 143. `test.step.skip()` — conditionally disable steps without removing them [official]

Since v1.50, `test.step.skip(title, body)` provides a static skip API that bypasses execution entirely without entering the step body. It differs from `testStepInfo.skip()` (the instance method inside the step) in that `test.step.skip` is called at the call site, before the async body ever runs. Use it when a step is temporarily broken or not yet implemented, and you want it to appear as "skipped" in reports rather than removing it and losing traceability. The skipped step is still visible in the HTML report and trace viewer with a "skipped" badge, preserving test intent documentation. Skipped steps do not count against the test timeout and do not affect pass/fail status of the parent test (unless `testInfo.annotations` is programmatically checked in a reporter).

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('full registration flow', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('fill registration form', async () => {
    await page.goto('/register');
    await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill('user@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill('SecurePass1!');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /register/i }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
  });

  // Step exists in report; body never executes
  await test.step.skip('verify welcome email sent', async () => {
    // TODO: mailhog integration not ready in this environment
    const inbox = await fetchMailhogInbox('user@example.com');
    expect(inbox.items).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(inbox.items[0].subject).toContain('Welcome');
  });

  await test.step('complete profile setup', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel(/display name/i).fill('Test User');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Profile saved');
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** A step depends on infrastructure not available in all environments (email server, S3, external API), and you want the step to appear in reports for tracking.
- **Do NOT use when:** The entire test should be skipped — use `test.skip()` or `test.fixme()` at the test level; `test.step.skip` only skips the step body.
- **Alternative:** Use `test.step('...', async step => { step.skip(condition, 'reason'); ... })` for runtime-conditional skip with access to test context.

---

### 144. `TestStepInfo.skip()` and `TestStepInfo.attach()` — runtime step control [official]

Since v1.51, `test.step()` passes a `TestStepInfo` object as the first argument of the step function, enabling runtime conditional skipping and per-step artifact attachment. `step.skip(condition?, message?)` aborts execution from inside the step at the point of call, marking it skipped in reports — unlike the static `test.step.skip`, this version can use runtime values such as browser name, feature flags, or API responses. `step.attach()` attaches a buffer, string, or file to the step specifically (not the test), so attachments appear nested under the correct step in the HTML reporter and trace viewer rather than floating at the test level. The `step.titlePath` property returns a `string[]` of all ancestor titles for structured logging.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment with runtime step control', async ({ page, browserName }) => {
  await test.step('verify payment gateway UI', async (step) => {
    // Runtime conditional skip based on environment variable
    step.skip(
      process.env.PAYMENT_MOCK === 'true',
      'Payment gateway mocked — UI verification skipped'
    );
    await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
    await expect(page.getByText(/credit card/i)).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('capture payment form screenshot', async (step) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
    const screenshot = await page.screenshot({ fullPage: false });
    // Attaches under this step, not at the test root
    await step.attach('payment-form.png', {
      body: screenshot,
      contentType: 'image/png',
    });
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay now/i })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('submit and confirm', async (step) => {
    step.skip(browserName === 'webkit', 'Payment redirect broken on WebKit — tracked in #1234');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay now/i }).click();
    await page.waitForURL(/confirmation/);
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toContainText('Order confirmed');
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Skip conditions are only known at runtime (feature flags, browser-specific issues), or you want attachments scoped to a specific step for traceability.
- **Do NOT use when:** The step has no runtime context to inspect — prefer `test.step.skip` at the call site for static skips to avoid unnecessary step body invocations.
- **Alternative:** `testInfo.skip()` to skip the whole test; `testInfo.attach()` to attach at the test level without step scoping.

---

### 145. `locator.filter({ visible: true })` — narrow a locator set to visible elements only [official]

Since v1.51, `locator.filter()` accepts a `visible` boolean option to match only elements that are currently visible (equivalent to `element.isVisible()` returning `true`). This is distinct from standard Playwright auto-waiting: the `filter({ visible: true })` narrows a locator before it resolves, so `expect(locator.filter({ visible: true })).toHaveCount(n)` will retry until exactly `n` visible matches exist. This is especially useful with lists that mix visible and hidden rows (e.g., virtualized tables, conditionally rendered items) where a count assertion on the full locator would include DOM-attached but visually hidden nodes. The `visible: false` variant is equally useful to assert that no visible instances of a pattern exist, while preserving attached-but-hidden DOM nodes for other assertions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('filter panel shows only active items', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard/items');

  // Toggle "active only" filter
  await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /active only/i }).check();

  const allItems    = page.getByTestId('item-row');
  const visibleItems = allItems.filter({ visible: true });
  const hiddenItems  = allItems.filter({ visible: false });

  // Wait until exactly 5 active rows are visible
  await expect(visibleItems).toHaveCount(5);

  // Hidden rows are still in DOM (virtualization / CSS display:none)
  const hiddenCount = await hiddenItems.count();
  expect(hiddenCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Each visible row has no 'inactive' badge
  for (const item of await visibleItems.all()) {
    await expect(item.getByTestId('inactive-badge')).not.toBeAttached();
  }
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** The DOM contains multiple elements matching a selector where some are hidden by CSS, and you need a count or action only on visible ones.
- **Do NOT use when:** You simply need to assert one element is visible — `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` is more readable for single-element visibility.
- **Alternative:** `locator.filter({ hasText: /active/i })` to narrow by content; `locator.and(page.locator(':visible'))` (CSS pseudo-class) for a non-retrying snapshot.

---

### 146. `expect(locator).toContainClass()` — ergonomic individual CSS class assertion [official]

Since v1.52, `toContainClass()` asserts that an element's `class` attribute contains a specific class name, without requiring an exact match of all classes on the element. Before this API, developers used `toHaveClass(/myClass/)` (regex) or destructured `getAttribute('class')` manually — both brittle approaches when class names are generated or prefixed. `toContainClass()` is an auto-retrying assertion that re-checks until the class is present (or the timeout elapses), making it safe in dynamic UIs where classes are toggled asynchronously. It accepts a string or an array of strings, all of which must be present simultaneously.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('task completion toggles class state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/tasks');

  const taskItem = page.getByTestId('task-42');

  // Before completion: should have 'pending' class
  await expect(taskItem).toContainClass('pending');

  // Complete the task
  await taskItem.getByRole('checkbox').check();

  // After completion: class switches from 'pending' to 'done'
  await expect(taskItem).toContainClass('done');
  await expect(taskItem).not.toContainClass('pending');

  // Assert multiple required classes simultaneously (all must be present)
  await expect(taskItem).toContainClass(['done', 'highlighted']);
});

// Old fragile approach — not auto-retrying, nullable type unsafe:
// const classes = await taskItem.getAttribute('class');
// expect(classes).toContain('done'); // ❌ no retry, string | null type
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You need to assert the presence or absence of one or more specific class names on an element whose full class list may include framework-generated utility classes you don't control.
- **Do NOT use when:** You need to assert the exact and complete class list — use `toHaveClass('exact-class-string')` with exact match.
- **Alternative:** `toHaveClass(/pattern/)` for regex-based class matching (less readable for literal names).

---

### 147. `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` — ARIA error message assertion [official]

Since v1.50, `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` asserts that an element's `aria-errormessage` attribute points to an element whose text matches the expected value. This completes the ARIA assertion triad alongside `toHaveAccessibleName()` (v1.44) and `toHaveAccessibleDescription()` (v1.44), covering the full set of user-facing ARIA properties. The distinction matters because `aria-errormessage` is specifically for form validation feedback and is different from `aria-describedby` — screen readers announce error messages through a different narration path than descriptions. Testing this attribute programmatically ensures accessible form error flows without visual regression testing. Like all Playwright assertions it auto-retries, so it works correctly with asynchronously displayed validation messages.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form validation error messages are accessible', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/register');

  // Submit with empty required field to trigger validation
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /register/i }).click();

  const emailField = page.getByLabel(/email/i);

  // Assert the full ARIA triad: name + description + error
  await expect(emailField).toHaveAccessibleName('Email address');
  await expect(emailField).toHaveAccessibleDescription(/required field/i);
  await expect(emailField).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Email is required.');

  // Regex variant for partial matching
  await expect(emailField).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/email.*required/i);

  // Test format validation error
  await emailField.fill('not-an-email');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /register/i }).click();
  await expect(emailField).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Enter a valid email address.');
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your app uses `aria-errormessage` (ARIA 1.1+) for field-level validation, and you need to ensure screen reader users receive the correct error message.
- **Do NOT use when:** Your app uses `aria-describedby` to convey error text — use `toHaveAccessibleDescription()` instead.
- **Alternative:** `expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText()` for inline error displays not linked via `aria-errormessage`.

---

### 148. `browserContext.storageState({ indexedDB: true })` — capture and restore IndexedDB state [official]

Since v1.51, `browserContext.storageState()` accepts an `indexedDB: true` option that includes all IndexedDB databases in the saved state file. Without this flag, `storageState()` only captures cookies and `localStorage`/`sessionStorage`, which is insufficient for applications that store auth tokens, user preferences, or sync state in IndexedDB (common in PWAs, offline-first apps, and apps using Dexie.js or localForage). When restoring state via `use: { storageState: 'state.json' }`, IndexedDB contents are automatically re-populated if they were included at capture time. This enables full offline-app session warm-starts in auth setup files.

```typescript
import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const authFile = path.join(__dirname, '.auth/user-with-idb.json');

setup('authenticate and capture IndexedDB state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill(process.env.E2E_USER!);
  await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill(process.env.E2E_PASS!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);

  // Wait for app to populate IndexedDB after login
  await page.waitForFunction(() =>
    new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => {
      const req = indexedDB.open('app-db');
      req.onsuccess = () => resolve(true);
      req.onerror   = () => resolve(false);
    })
  );

  // Capture cookies + localStorage + IndexedDB in one file
  await page.context().storageState({
    path: authFile,
    indexedDB: true, // v1.51+ — include all IndexedDB databases
  });
});
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — restore full state including IndexedDB
projects: [
  { name: 'setup', testMatch: /auth\.setup\.ts/ },
  {
    name: 'chromium',
    use: {
      ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
      storageState: 'e2e/.auth/user-with-idb.json',
    },
    dependencies: ['setup'],
  },
],
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your app stores authentication tokens, user preferences, or sync data in IndexedDB (Dexie.js, localForage, Firebase offline, PouchDB).
- **Do NOT use when:** Your app uses only cookies and `localStorage` — the default `storageState()` without `indexedDB` is lighter and sufficient.
- **Alternative:** `page.evaluate()` to manually read/write IndexedDB in `globalSetup`; more verbose but works for all Playwright versions.

---

### 149. `testConfig.captureGitInfo` — embed git commit and diff metadata in HTML reports [official]

Since v1.51, `testConfig.captureGitInfo` accepts an object with `{ commit: boolean, diff: boolean }` that instructs Playwright to capture the current git commit hash, author, message, and optionally the full staged diff at test run time. This metadata is embedded in the HTML report's "Metadata" panel, making it trivial to correlate a CI test failure report with the exact commit that caused it — without cross-referencing build logs. When `diff: true` is set, the full `git diff HEAD` output is embedded, enabling reviewers to see the precise code change that broke a test directly in the Playwright report.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Embed git metadata into every HTML report
  captureGitInfo: {
    commit: true,  // captures: hash, message, author, date, branch
    diff:   false, // true only in pre-merge pipelines (large diffs inflate report size)
  },

  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never', outputFolder: 'playwright-report' }],
    ['blob', { outputDir: 'blob-report' }], // for sharded run merging
  ],

  use: { baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000' },
});
```

```typescript
// Custom reporter accessing captured git metadata
import type { FullConfig, Reporter } from '@playwright/test/reporter';

class GitInfoReporter implements Reporter {
  onBegin(config: FullConfig) {
    // Available when captureGitInfo.commit: true
    const meta   = config.metadata as Record<string, string>;
    const branch = meta.gitBranch  ?? 'unknown';
    const commit = meta.gitCommit  ?? 'unknown';
    console.log(`Run: branch=${branch} commit=${commit.slice(0, 8)}`);
  }
}
export default GitInfoReporter;
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your team shares HTML reports from CI and needs to know which commit triggered a failure without leaving the report UI.
- **Do NOT use when:** `diff: true` in monorepos — the embedded diff can inflate report size significantly.
- **Alternative:** Inject `process.env.GITHUB_SHA` into `testConfig.metadata` in `globalSetup` for environments without git CLI access (Docker containers).

---

### 150. `testConfig.updateSnapshots: 'changed'` and `updateSourceMethod: '3way'` — surgical snapshot update strategies [official]

Since v1.50, `updateSnapshots` accepts four enum values: `'none'` (never update), `'missing'` (default — create only new), `'changed'` (update snapshots that fail), and `'all'` (update every snapshot regardless of pass/fail). The `updateSourceMethod` option (also v1.50) controls how inline snapshot values are written back to `.spec.ts` files: `'overwrite'` (destructive in-place replacement), `'patch'` (creates a `.patch` file for review), and `'3way'` (inserts Git-style merge conflict markers for manual resolution). The `'3way'` + `'changed'` combination is the safest update workflow — only failing snapshots are flagged, and conflict markers let reviewers accept or reject each change individually using standard merge tools.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — safe snapshot update configuration
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Only update snapshots that actually failed — never reset passing baselines
  updateSnapshots: (process.env.UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS as
    'none' | 'missing' | 'changed' | 'all') ?? 'missing',

  // CI: generate diff patch; Local: 3-way merge markers for IDE resolution
  updateSourceMethod: process.env.CI ? 'patch' : '3way',

  expect: {
    snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{testFileName}/{arg}{ext}',
  },
});
```

```bash
# CI: generate patch file for snapshot review PR
UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=changed npx playwright test --reporter=html

# Local: update only changed, get merge conflict markers in spec files
UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=changed npx playwright test
# Then open .spec.ts — accept/reject each snapshot change with IDE merge tool
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Multiple developers touch the same components and snapshot diffs need review; `'3way'` surfaces changes as standard merge conflicts.
- **Do NOT use when:** Snapshots are binary screenshot images — `'3way'` only applies to inline text/ARIA snapshots; for image snapshots use the HTML reporter's visual diff.
- **Alternative:** `--update-snapshots` CLI flag for one-off local updates without touching the config.

---

### 151. `testProject.workers` — per-project parallelism control [official]

Since v1.52, individual projects in `playwright.config.ts` can declare their own `workers` count via `testProject.workers`. Previously, `testConfig.workers` was the only parallelism control and applied globally. With per-project workers, you can run CPU-intensive visual regression projects at lower parallelism (to reduce screenshot variability) while running lightweight API smoke tests at maximum concurrency. The value accepts a number (absolute count) or a percentage string like `'50%'` (relative to available CPU cores, resolved at runtime).

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — heterogeneous worker allocation per project
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: '50%', // global default: half of available CPUs

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'api-smoke',
      testMatch: /api\.spec\.ts/,
      workers: 8,  // API tests are I/O-bound — run many in parallel
      use: { baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL },
    },
    {
      name: 'visual-regression',
      testMatch: /visual\.spec\.ts/,
      workers: 2,  // Screenshot tests need stable CPU; limit to reduce variance
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'e2e-chromium',
      testMatch: /e2e\.spec\.ts/,
      // No explicit workers — inherits global '50%'
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Your test suite mixes fast I/O-bound API tests and slow CPU-bound visual tests that have different optimal parallelism levels.
- **Do NOT use when:** All projects have similar resource profiles — per-project workers adds configuration overhead without benefit.
- **Alternative:** Run projects in separate CI jobs with different `--workers` CLI flags instead of per-project config.

---

### 152. HTML reporter `!@tag` NOT-filter syntax — exclude tests by tag in CI reports [official]

Since v1.52, the Playwright HTML reporter and UI Mode support `!@tagname` as a filter expression to exclude tests bearing a specific tag. This works as a complement to positive tag filtering (`@tagname`) and supports combining filters: `@smoke !@broken` shows all smoke tests except those tagged broken. In CI pipelines, this enables a "run everything except known-broken" filter without enumerating every broken test individually. Tags applied via `test.describe('...', { tag: ['@broken'] })` or inline `test('...', { tag: '@broken' }, ...)` are immediately filterable via this syntax.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — tag-driven project routing with negation
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'smoke-stable',
      testMatch: /e2e/,
      grep:        /@smoke/,
      grepInvert:  /@broken|@skip-ci/, // exclude multiple tags via regex union
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// Tagging tests for both inclusion and exclusion filtering
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('stable smoke test', { tag: '@smoke' }, async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
});

test.describe('payment flow', { tag: ['@smoke', '@broken'] }, () => {
  test('pay with card', async ({ page }) => {
    // Tagged @broken — excluded by grepInvert or by !@broken in HTML reporter
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** You have known-broken tests checked into main that should be excluded from CI failure counts but preserved in source for tracking.
- **Do NOT use when:** The set of broken tests changes very frequently — `test.fixme()` at the test level is more maintainable than keeping tag lists in sync.
- **Alternative:** `grepInvert` in `playwright.config.ts` for CI exclusion; `--grep-invert /@broken/` via CLI for one-off local runs.

### 153. `testConfig.webServer.gracefulShutdown` — custom termination signal for dev servers [official]

Since v1.50, `testConfig.webServer` accepts a `gracefulShutdown` object with a `signal` string and optional `timeout` (ms). By default, Playwright sends `SIGTERM` to the dev server process and waits 5 seconds before forcibly killing it. Many modern dev servers (Vite, Turbopack, webpack-dev-server) trap `SIGTERM` and perform cleanup — but some require `SIGINT` to trigger the correct shutdown path, and others need longer to flush write-ahead logs or close database connections. Misconfigured shutdown causes port binding failures on rapid test re-runs and leaks background processes in CI containers.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — explicit graceful shutdown per webServer
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: [
    {
      command: 'npm run dev:api',
      url:     'http://localhost:4000/health',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      gracefulShutdown: {
        signal:  'SIGINT',  // API server traps SIGINT for DB connection cleanup
        timeout: 10_000,    // Allow 10s for graceful drain
      },
    },
    {
      command: 'npm run dev:web',
      url:     'http://localhost:3000',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      gracefulShutdown: {
        signal:  'SIGTERM', // Vite default — explicit is more readable
        timeout: 3_000,
      },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** CI runs fail intermittently with "EADDRINUSE" errors (port already in use from a previous run's leaked server process).
- **Do NOT use when:** Your dev server has no meaningful cleanup on shutdown — focus on `reuseExistingServer: true` for local efficiency instead.
- **Alternative:** `pkill -f dev-server-name` in a `globalTeardown` script as a fallback for servers that ignore all signals.

---

### 154. Playwright Test Agents (`init-agents`) — LLM-driven planner, generator, and healer workflow [official]

Since v1.56, `npx playwright init-agents` scaffolds three agent definition files (planner, generator, healer) that guide an LLM through the full test authoring lifecycle within an agentic loop. The **planner** agent navigates the application and produces a Markdown spec file describing user scenarios. The **generator** agent transforms specs into executable Playwright TypeScript test files while verifying selectors against the live DOM. The **healer** agent runs the test suite, analyzes failures, and proposes patches. This workflow targets teams with rapidly evolving UIs where manual test maintenance is the bottleneck. Generated agent files are version-locked at scaffold time and should be regenerated after major Playwright upgrades.

```bash
# Scaffold for your preferred agentic loop client
npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude    # Claude Code integration
npx playwright init-agents --loop=vscode    # VS Code Copilot Edits
npx playwright init-agents --loop=opencode  # OpenCode CLI

# Resulting directory structure:
# .playwright/agents/
#   planner.md    — explores app, outputs specs/*.md test plans
#   generator.md  — reads specs/*.md, outputs tests/*.spec.ts
#   healer.md     — runs suite, patches failing assertions
# e2e/seed.spec.ts — style reference example for the generator
```

```typescript
// e2e/seed.spec.ts — generator uses this as a style reference
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('homepage loads correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/My App/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Writing tests for a new feature area with no existing coverage and you want an AI-assisted first-pass for code review.
- **Do NOT use when:** Tests require deep business logic knowledge the LLM planner cannot infer from the UI alone — human-authored specs remain superior for complex flows with invisible state.
- **Alternative:** Playwright `codegen` (`npx playwright codegen <url>`) for interactive recording without LLM scaffolding; simpler for single-page flows.

---

### 155. `testConfig.tsconfig` — single tsconfig path for all test files [official]

Since v1.49, `testConfig.tsconfig` specifies a single `tsconfig.json` file that Playwright uses when compiling all test files, regardless of per-directory `tsconfig.json` files that TypeScript project references would normally resolve. Without this option, Playwright's TypeScript compilation heuristic walks the directory tree looking for the nearest `tsconfig.json` to each file — in monorepos with nested configs this can cause different test files to compile under different settings. Setting `tsconfig` explicitly ensures consistent compiler options, path aliases, and strict mode across the entire test suite.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — explicit tsconfig for test compilation
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  tsconfig: path.resolve(__dirname, 'tsconfig.playwright.json'),
  testDir:  './e2e',
  use:      { baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000' },
});
```

```json
// tsconfig.playwright.json — dedicated test compiler config
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "Node16",
    "moduleResolution": "Node16",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "paths": {
      "@fixtures/*": ["./e2e/fixtures/*"],
      "@pages/*":    ["./e2e/pages/*"]
    }
  },
  "include": ["e2e/**/*.ts", "playwright.config.ts"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Monorepo with multiple nested `tsconfig.json` files — without an explicit `testConfig.tsconfig`, Playwright's nearest-config heuristic causes inconsistent strictness or missing path aliases.
- **Do NOT use when:** Single-package repo with one root `tsconfig.json` — Playwright finds it automatically; `testConfig.tsconfig` adds no value.
- **Alternative:** `--tsconfig` CLI flag (`npx playwright test --tsconfig tsconfig.playwright.json`) for per-run override without changing the config file.

---

### 156. `apiRequest.newContext()` `maxRedirects` option — control redirect follow behavior in API tests [official]

Since v1.52, `apiRequest.newContext()` and `apiRequestContext.fetch()` accept a `maxRedirects` integer option that limits how many HTTP redirects the API client will follow before throwing. The default is unlimited (follows all redirects). Setting `maxRedirects: 0` disables redirect following entirely, enabling tests that assert the exact redirect response (`301`/`302`/`307`) rather than the final destination. Setting `maxRedirects: 1` allows exactly one redirect and throws on the second, which detects redirect chains longer than intended (infinite redirect bugs, login loop regressions). This option is unavailable on `page.request` (the page-bound API client) — use `apiRequest.newContext()` for redirect control.

```typescript
import { test, expect, request } from '@playwright/test';

test('login endpoint returns 302 to dashboard', async () => {
  const api = await request.newContext({
    baseURL:      'http://localhost:3000',
    maxRedirects: 0, // Do not follow — assert the redirect itself
  });

  const response = await api.post('/login', {
    data: { email: 'admin@example.com', password: 'secret' },
  });

  expect(response.status()).toBe(302);
  expect(response.headers()['location']).toMatch(/\/dashboard/);
  await api.dispose();
});

test('URL migration is exactly one hop (no redirect chains)', async () => {
  const api = await request.newContext({
    baseURL:      'http://localhost:3000',
    maxRedirects: 1, // Allow exactly one; throw if a second redirect occurs
  });

  // Single redirect /old-path → /new-path should succeed
  const response = await api.get('/old-path');
  expect(response.ok()).toBe(true);
  expect(response.url()).toContain('/new-path');
  await api.dispose();
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**
- **Use when:** Testing authentication redirect flows, URL migration (301 permanent redirects), or detecting unintended redirect chains (login loops, double-redirect bugs).
- **Do NOT use when:** Your test needs to assert the final page state after a redirect — use `page.goto()` which follows redirects and lands on the destination.
- **Alternative:** `response.request().redirectedFrom()` to inspect the redirect chain on responses from `page.goto()` in a browser context.
