### Gotcha #70: `page.consoleMessages()` does not capture messages from cross-origin iframes [community]

`page.consoleMessages()` only includes messages from the top-level page frame. Console output from cross-origin iframes — payment widgets, embedded maps, social share buttons — is silently excluded due to browser security isolation.

```typescript
// ❌ Misuse: expecting Stripe iframe console errors to appear here
const errors = page.consoleMessages().filter(m => m.type() === 'error');
// errors will be empty even if the Stripe iframe threw a configuration error

// ✅ Correct: inject onerror into same-origin iframes only
await page.evaluate(() => {
  document.querySelectorAll('iframe').forEach(iframe => {
    try {
      iframe.contentWindow!.onerror = (msg, src, line) => {
        console.error(`[iframe ${src}:${line}] ${msg}`);
      };
    } catch { /* cross-origin — security boundary, cannot inject */ }
  });
});

// ✅ For cross-origin iframes: monitor only what is observable from the parent
// (network requests, postMessage events, DOM changes in the host page)
page.on('response', response => {
  if (response.url().includes('stripe') && !response.ok()) {
    console.warn(`Stripe resource failed: ${response.url()} [${response.status()}]`);
  }
});
```

> **WHY:** The `ConsoleMessage` API is scoped to the `Page` object's main frame and same-origin child frames. Cross-origin iframes run in separate renderer processes under Chrome's site-isolation model, which prevents the DevTools Protocol listener attached to the parent page from receiving their console events. This is not a Playwright limitation — it is an intentional browser security boundary. [community]

---

### Gotcha #71: `expect.configure({ soft: true })` failures do not surface unless you explicitly check `testInfo.errors` [community]

Soft assertions accumulated via `expect.configure({ soft: true })` or `expect.soft()` do NOT automatically fail the test when the test body completes. The failures live in `testInfo.errors`, and without a final hard assertion to check that array, the test passes with hidden failures.

```typescript
// ❌ Silent pass: soft errors accumulated but never surfaced
test('form validation shows all errors', async ({ page }) => {
  const soft = expect.configure({ soft: true });
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
  await soft(page.getByTestId('name-error')).toBeVisible();   // fails silently
  await soft(page.getByTestId('email-error')).toBeVisible();  // fails silently
  // Test PASSES — no hard assertion forced the failure
});

// ✅ Correct: end with an explicit guard
test('form validation shows all errors', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  const soft = expect.configure({ soft: true });
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
  await soft(page.getByTestId('name-error')).toBeVisible();
  await soft(page.getByTestId('email-error')).toBeVisible();

  // Force failure if any soft assertion failed
  expect(testInfo.errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

> **WHY:** Soft assertions are designed for report enrichment — they collect all failures so the engineer sees every broken assertion, not just the first. But the test runner's pass/fail decision is based on whether the test throws an uncaught exception. The `testInfo.errors` array is the bridge between soft-failure accumulation and hard-failure signaling. Omitting the final guard is the single most common soft-assertion footgun — always add it at the end of any test that uses soft assertions. [community]

---

### Gotcha #72: `testConfig.captureGitInfo` fails silently in Docker containers without `git` on PATH [community]

`captureGitInfo: { commit: true }` shells out to `git` to read commit metadata. In minimal Docker images built from `node:slim` or `node:alpine` that do not include `git`, the command is absent and Playwright silently omits all git fields from reports — no error is thrown.

```dockerfile
# ❌ Missing git: captureGitInfo silently produces null metadata
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci && npx playwright install chromium --with-deps
# No git → report.json shows gitInfo: null for every field

# ✅ Install git before running tests
FROM node:20-alpine
RUN apk add --no-cache git
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci && npx playwright install chromium --with-deps
```

```typescript
// Post-run CI assertion to catch this regression early
import fs from 'fs';
const report   = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('test-results/report.json', 'utf-8'));
const commitId = report?.gitInfo?.commit?.id ?? null;
if (!commitId) {
  console.error('ERROR: git metadata missing — install git in CI Docker image');
  process.exit(1);
}
```

> **WHY:** The `captureGitInfo` implementation calls `execSync('git log ...')` internally. When `git` is absent from PATH, Node.js throws `ENOENT`, which Playwright catches and silently logs at `verbose` level only. Teams not running with `--verbose` or not inspecting verbose CI logs never see the warning, and reports ship without commit traceability. The `apk add --no-cache git` (Alpine) or `apt-get install -y git` (Debian) is the one-line fix. [community]

---

### Gotcha #73: `clearCookies({ name })` is exact-match only and never throws on zero matches — typos are silent no-ops [community]

`browserContext.clearCookies({ name: 'session' })` deletes only cookies with that exact name. Cookies named `session_token`, `SESSION`, or `_session` are untouched. Unlike many Playwright filter APIs that accept regex, the cookie name filter accepts only exact strings.

```typescript
// ❌ Silent no-op: 'session' does not match 'session_token'
await context.clearCookies({ name: 'session' });
const remaining = await context.cookies();
// remaining STILL contains 'session_token' — it was NOT cleared

// ✅ Use the exact name
await context.clearCookies({ name: 'session_token' });

// ✅ For prefixed/suffixed names: clear all and restore what you need
const allCookies        = await context.cookies();
const nonSessionCookies = allCookies.filter(c => !c.name.startsWith('session'));
await context.clearCookies();               // wipe all
await context.addCookies(nonSessionCookies); // restore non-session ones
```

> **WHY:** The cookie spec (RFC 6265) treats cookie names as case-sensitive exact strings; Playwright mirrors this strictly. `clearCookies({ name: 'x' })` succeeds with a no-op even if no cookie named `x` exists — the "idempotent delete" semantic is intentional. The footgun is that typos or prefix mismatches leave the target cookie alive with zero feedback. Add a post-clear assertion (`expect((await context.cookies()).find(c => c.name === 'session_token')).toBeUndefined()`) to catch silent no-ops in teardown fixtures. [community]

---

### Gotcha #74: `filter({ hasNotText })` matches against full `textContent` including visually hidden sr-only text [community]

`locator.filter({ hasNotText: /pattern/ })` uses the element's full `textContent`, which includes text from visually hidden elements (sr-only spans, `aria-label` fallback text, hidden child nodes). A row that appears visually empty may still be excluded if it contains a hidden screen-reader label that matches the pattern.

```typescript
// HTML: <tr>
//   <td>Item A</td>
//   <td><span class="sr-only">status: completed</span></td>
// </tr>
// Visually the second cell is invisible but textContent includes "status: completed"

// ❌ Unexpected exclusion: row IS removed because "completed" in sr-only span
const pendingRows = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasNotText: /completed/i });
// The "Item A" row is EXCLUDED even though visually it shows no status badge

// ✅ Correct: use filter({ hasNot: visibleElement }) to require a rendered node
const statusBadge    = page.getByRole('status').filter({ hasText: /completed/i });
const pendingVisible = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasNot: statusBadge });
// Only excludes rows that have a RENDERED, visible "completed" status badge
```

> **WHY:** `textContent` is a DOM property that returns the concatenated text of ALL descendant text nodes regardless of their CSS `visibility` or `display` value. Playwright's `hasText` / `hasNotText` filters use `textContent`, not `innerText`. The practical difference: `innerText` respects CSS visibility; `textContent` does not. When building exclusion filters that must reflect what the user actually sees, always compose `filter({ hasNot: locator })` with a visible element target rather than relying on `hasNotText` alone. [community]

### Pattern 216: `expect.extend()` — Custom Domain-Specific Matchers with Full TypeScript Support [official]

`expect.extend()` lets you define project-specific assertion verbs that read like business language in test reports. Each custom matcher receives the subject locator plus any arguments, performs its checks using the base `expect` API internally, and returns a structured result object. Extending the TypeScript interface via `interface` merging exposes the new matchers to IDE autocomplete across the entire project.

```typescript
// e2e/matchers/toHavePrice.ts
import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHavePrice(locator: Locator, expected: number, opts?: { timeout?: number }) {
    const name = 'toHavePrice';
    let pass: boolean;
    let actual: string | undefined;
    try {
      const text = await locator.textContent({ timeout: opts?.timeout ?? 5_000 });
      actual = text ?? '';
      const numeric = parseFloat(actual.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ''));
      pass = Math.abs(numeric - expected) < 0.005;
    } catch {
      pass = false;
    }
    const message = () =>
      this.utils.matcherHint(name, undefined, undefined, { isNot: this.isNot }) +
      `\n\nExpected price: ${expected}\nReceived text:  ${actual ?? '<empty>'}`;
    return { pass, message, name, expected, actual };
  },
});

// TypeScript interface augmentation — place in e2e/global.d.ts
declare namespace PlaywrightTest {
  interface Matchers<R> {
    toHavePrice(expected: number, opts?: { timeout?: number }): Promise<R>;
  }
}
```

```typescript
// e2e/specs/cart.spec.ts
import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import { expect } from '../matchers/toHavePrice';

test('cart line item shows correct price', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  const lineItem = page.getByRole('row', { name: 'Widget Pro' });
  await expect(lineItem.getByTestId('price')).toHavePrice(29.99);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `expect.extend()` registers matchers on a *new* `expect` instance — not on Playwright's global `expect`. All imports in spec files must use the extended instance from your fixtures file, not `@playwright/test`'s default `expect`. Mixing both in one file is a common source of "matcher not found" runtime errors. Export a single composed `expect` from a central `fixtures.ts` and import only from there.

---

### Pattern 217: `locator.or()` — Resilient Handling of Alternate UI States [official]

`locator.or()` creates a locator that matches when *either* the primary or the alternate selector is present. This is the idiomatic Playwright pattern for handling UIs that show different elements depending on login state, feature flags, or A/B test buckets — without adding conditional `if` branches inside tests.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can reach account settings', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Some builds show "My Account" button; others show an avatar menu icon
  const accountEntry = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'My Account' })
    .or(page.getByRole('button', { name: /avatar|profile/i }));

  await accountEntry.click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/account/);
});

// Handling cookie consent OR an existing-session banner (appears one, not both)
test('dashboard loads after consent is dismissed', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  const blocker = page
    .getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie|consent/i })
    .or(page.getByRole('banner', { name: /session expired/i }));

  // Dismiss whichever barrier appears — if neither is present, skip
  if (await blocker.isVisible({ timeout: 2_000 }).catch(() => false)) {
    await blocker.getByRole('button', { name: /accept|dismiss|ok/i }).click();
  }

  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** When *both* alternatives are simultaneously present on the page, `locator.or()` throws a strict-mode violation ("resolved to N elements"). This is intentional — the strict mode guard prevents accidentally acting on the wrong element. If both can coexist, use `locator.first()` or narrow each alternative further with `.filter()` before combining with `.or()`. Do not use `locator.or()` as a generic "try one then the other" fallback pattern in a single steady-state UI.

---

### Pattern 218: `locator.filter({ visible: true })` — Excluding Detached and Hidden Duplicates (v1.51+) [official]

`locator.filter({ visible: true })` restricts a multi-match locator to only the elements that are currently attached, rendered, and not `display:none` / `visibility:hidden`. It eliminates the class of failures caused by animated elements that briefly remain in the DOM while fading out, or server-rendered HTML that duplicates visible/hidden toggle pairs.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dropdown shows exactly one active option', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings');
  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Theme' }).click();

  // The DOM may contain both a mobile-hidden and a desktop-visible copy
  const visibleOptions = page
    .getByRole('option')
    .filter({ visible: true });

  // Only the rendered, user-visible options count toward uniqueness
  await expect(visibleOptions).toHaveCount(5);
  await visibleOptions.filter({ hasText: 'Dark' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Theme' })).toHaveValue('dark');
});

// Pattern: safe first-element click on animated lists that leave fading ghosts
test('notification bell clears the topmost alert', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/notifications');
  const visibleAlerts = page
    .getByRole('listitem', { name: /alert/i })
    .filter({ visible: true });

  await expect(visibleAlerts).not.toHaveCount(0);
  const initialCount = await visibleAlerts.count();
  await visibleAlerts.first().getByRole('button', { name: 'Dismiss' }).click();
  await expect(visibleAlerts).toHaveCount(initialCount - 1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `filter({ visible: true })` adds a runtime visibility check to each locator evaluation and makes tests slightly slower when used in tight loops. More importantly, it is a symptom treatment — if the application leaves duplicate hidden DOM nodes across both mobile and desktop breakpoints, the real fix is cleaning up the markup or isolating tests to a single viewport. Reserve `filter({ visible: true })` for third-party widgets and legacy components where you cannot control the DOM structure.

---

### Pattern 219: `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` — Firebase and IndexedDB Authentication Persistence (v1.51+) [official]

Setting `indexedDB: true` in the `storageState()` call captures the full IndexedDB snapshot alongside cookies and localStorage. This is essential for apps that store auth tokens in IndexedDB — most notably Firebase Authentication — where the default `storageState()` produces a valid-looking but authentication-less state file that causes every test to redirect to login.

```typescript
// e2e/auth/firebase-setup.ts
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';
import type { FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page    = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto(config.projects[0].use.baseURL + '/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(process.env.TEST_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');

  // Capture IndexedDB — Firebase stores auth tokens there, not in localStorage
  await context.storageState({
    path: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
    indexedDB: true,           // required for Firebase
  });

  await browser.close();
}

export default globalSetup;
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: './e2e/auth/firebase-setup.ts',
  use: {
    storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** IndexedDB serialization is performed via CDP's `IndexedDB.requestData` API, which traverses the entire database synchronously at capture time. For applications with large IndexedDB stores (offline caches, large data blobs), the `storageState()` call can take several seconds and produce megabyte-sized state files. Only enable `indexedDB: true` for auth-only state files, and use separate storage state paths for different user roles to avoid re-serializing unnecessarily.

---

### Pattern 220: `page.requestGC()` — Memory Leak Detection with `WeakRef` (v1.48+) [official]

`page.requestGC()` asks the browser's JavaScript engine to perform a garbage collection pass. Paired with `WeakRef`, it verifies that a reference-counted object was properly released — turning memory leak detection from a profiler exercise into a deterministic assertion in a normal test file.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('closing a modal releases its component from memory', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/app');

  // Open a modal and plant a WeakRef to its root DOM node in page scope
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open settings' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Settings' })).toBeVisible();

  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const dialog = document.querySelector('[role="dialog"][aria-label="Settings"]');
    (window as any).__testRef = new WeakRef(dialog);
  });

  // Close the modal — the component should become eligible for GC
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Close settings' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Settings' })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Request GC and assert the WeakRef no longer resolves to the original node
  await page.requestGC();

  const isLeaking = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return (window as any).__testRef?.deref() !== undefined;
  });

  expect(isLeaking, 'Modal component was not garbage collected — possible memory leak').toBe(false);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `requestGC()` asks the JS engine to run GC — it does not *guarantee* that specific objects are collected in a single pass. Engines may defer collection of objects with finalizers or complex prototype chains. A `false` leak result does not prove the object was released; it only proves it was not held in this particular GC cycle. For production leak detection, run the scenario multiple times and look for a consistent pattern, or use Chrome DevTools Memory panel for authoritative heap snapshots.

---

### Pattern 221: `testConfig.tsconfig` — Single TypeScript Config for All Tests (v1.49+) [official]

Setting `testConfig.tsconfig` to a single path stops Playwright from performing per-file `tsconfig.json` lookup, which can discover the wrong config when tests live alongside application source code with conflicting `moduleResolution` or `paths` settings. A dedicated `tsconfig.test.json` in the project root is the idiomatic pattern.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  tsconfig: path.resolve(__dirname, 'tsconfig.test.json'),  // absolute — CWD-safe

  testDir: './e2e',
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});
```

```json
// tsconfig.test.json
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "paths": {
      "@fixtures": ["./e2e/fixtures/index.ts"],
      "@pages/*":  ["./e2e/pages/*"]
    },
    "types": ["@playwright/test", "node"]
  },
  "include": [
    "e2e/**/*.ts",
    "playwright.config.ts"
  ],
  "exclude": [
    "node_modules",
    "src/**"
  ]
}
```

```typescript
// e2e/specs/example.spec.ts — path alias resolved via tsconfig.test.json
import { test, expect } from '@fixtures';
import { LoginPage } from '@pages/LoginPage';

test('alias imports resolve correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  const login = new LoginPage(page);
  await login.goto();
  await expect(login.emailInput).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Setting `testConfig.tsconfig` globally disables per-directory config lookup for the entire test suite. If you have intentionally different TypeScript settings for different test directories (e.g., one directory testing ES modules with `"module": "ESNext"` and another using CommonJS fixtures), a single global tsconfig can break one or the other. In this case, revert to per-file lookup (omit `tsconfig` from config) and fix path collisions by restructuring directories rather than controlling config selection.

---

### Pattern 222: `testProject.workers` — Per-Project Parallelism Caps for Resource-Constrained Tests (v1.52+) [official]

`workers` on a `testProject` limits concurrency for that project independently of the global `workers` setting. This enables you to run most projects at full parallelism while constraining projects whose tests share a limited external resource — a single test database, a licensed third-party API, or a Stripe sandbox account with rate limits.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: 8,                        // global: up to 8 workers total

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      // No per-project workers → inherits global (up to 8)
    },
    {
      name: 'payment-flow',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      testMatch: '**/payment/**',
      workers: 1,                    // serialised: 1 worker for Stripe sandbox
    },
    {
      name: 'db-migration-tests',
      testMatch: '**/migration/**',
      workers: 2,                    // limited: only 2 connections to test DB
    },
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// e2e/payment/checkout.spec.ts — runs serially within payment-flow project
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });   // belt-and-suspenders for serial project

test('guest checkout completes with Stripe test card', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /payment successful/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Per-project `workers` does not reserve workers — the global pool is shared. If other projects are already consuming all 8 global workers, the payment-flow project waits until one frees up before scheduling its next test, even with `workers: 1`. For strict serial guarantees across the entire run, also set `fullyParallel: false` on the constrained project and use `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` inside spec files.

---

### Pattern 223: `expect.extend()` — `this.isNot` Double-Negation Guard for Asymmetric Matchers [official]

When writing a custom matcher that calls `baseExpect(...).toBe*(...)` internally, the `isNot` flag received by the matcher already represents the *outer* negation (`expect(...).not.toHaveFoo()`). Calling `baseExpect(...).not.*` inside the matcher on top of an `isNot: true` invocation produces a double negation — the assertion passes when it should fail. The correct pattern is to always call the *positive* internal assertion and return the `pass` boolean, letting Playwright's negation logic handle `.not` inversion.

```typescript
import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { Locator } from '@playwright/test';

// ❌ Double-negation bug: isNot flipped again inside the matcher
export const buggyExpect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveStatusBadge(locator: Locator, status: string) {
    const badge = locator.getByTestId('status-badge');
    // BUG: this.isNot=true + .not inside = double negation → always passes
    if (this.isNot) {
      await baseExpect(badge).not.toHaveText(status);
    } else {
      await baseExpect(badge).toHaveText(status);
    }
    return { pass: !this.isNot, message: () => '' };
  },
});

// ✅ Correct: always call the positive assertion; return pass truthfully
export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveStatusBadge(locator: Locator, status: string, opts?: { timeout?: number }) {
    const badge = locator.getByTestId('status-badge');
    let pass: boolean;
    try {
      await baseExpect(badge).toHaveText(status, { timeout: opts?.timeout ?? 5_000 });
      pass = true;
    } catch {
      pass = false;
    }
    const message = () =>
      `Expected status badge to${this.isNot ? ' not' : ''} contain "${status}"`;
    return { pass, message };
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Always running the positive internal assertion means the matcher throws an exception on failure rather than returning `pass: false` directly. Wrapping the internal call in `try/catch` is required for the matcher to compose correctly with `.not`. If you forget the `try/catch` and the assertion throws, the test fails with an unhandled promise rejection rather than a clean matcher failure message — making the error harder to diagnose in CI reports.

---

### Pattern 224: `test.step()` with `box: true` — Hiding Implementation Details in Trace Reports [official]

Setting `box: true` on a `test.step()` call causes all errors inside the step to be reported at the step's *call site* rather than at the internal line that threw. This is the idiomatic pattern for shared step utilities in helper files — consumers of the utility see "failed at `await login(page, user)`" in spec files rather than "failed at `this.submitButton.click()`" somewhere deep in the page object internals.

```typescript
// e2e/helpers/auth.ts
import { Page, expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

export async function login(page: Page, email: string, password: string) {
  // box: true → any error inside surfaces at the login() call site in reports
  await test.step('Login as ' + email, async () => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard', { timeout: 10_000 });
  }, { box: true });
}
```

```typescript
// e2e/specs/orders.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { login } from '../helpers/auth';

test('order history lists recent purchases', async ({ page }) => {
  // If login fails, the trace shows the error at THIS line — not inside auth.ts
  await login(page, 'buyer@example.com', 'password123');

  await page.goto('/orders');
  await expect(page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Order history' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('row').filter({ has: page.locator('td') }),
  ).not.toHaveCount(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `box: true` deliberately hides the internal call stack from the trace viewer — helpful for consumer readability but harmful when debugging the helper implementation itself. When a boxed step fails in CI and the failure is unclear from the step label alone, temporarily remove `box: true` from the helper, re-run, and inspect the full inner trace. Restore `box: true` before merging to keep reports clean. Never use `box: true` on steps that are themselves still under development.

---

### Pattern 225: `page.addLocatorHandler()` with `times` — Dismissing Transient Overlays Automatically [official]

`page.addLocatorHandler()` registers a callback that fires whenever an overlay locator becomes visible *during* another action. The `times` option limits how many times the handler fires, preventing indefinite loops if the overlay reappears unexpectedly after dismissal. This is the recommended replacement for the fragile "check if cookie banner exists then click" preamble pattern at the start of every test.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Register handler once per test — fires at most twice (handles reappearance)
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie|privacy/i }),
    async (overlay) => {
      await overlay.getByRole('button', { name: /accept|agree/i }).click();
    },
    { times: 2 },   // fire at most 2 times per test to prevent infinite loops
  );
});

test('product page shows correct price after cookie consent', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
  // If the cookie dialog appears during navigation, handler auto-dismisses it

  await expect(page.getByRole('main').getByTestId('price')).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status', { name: /added to cart/i })).toBeVisible();
});

test('search results load without overlay interference', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search?q=widget');
  // Handler fires if GDPR banner re-appears after navigation
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Search results' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).not.toHaveCount(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addLocatorHandler()` inserts extra roundtrips between each action to check whether the overlay locator has appeared. On fast, overlay-free pages this adds ~5–15 ms per action. For test suites that do not hit overlays in most runs, the cumulative overhead across thousands of actions is measurable. Register handlers only in `beforeEach` blocks that target spec files where the overlay is known to appear — do not register them globally in `playwright.config.ts`'s `use` block.

---

### Pattern 226: `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` with `children: 'equal'` — Strict Accessibility Tree Assertions (v1.52+) [official]

The `children` option on `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` controls how child nodes are matched: `'contain'` (default) passes if the expected children are a subset; `'equal'` requires an exact match with no extra children. Setting `children: 'equal'` globally in `playwright.config.ts` turns accessibility snapshots into strict contract tests that catch unexpected DOM additions — for example, injected analytics scripts adding `aria-live` regions.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toMatchAriaSnapshot: {
      children: 'equal',   // strict: no unexpected extra children allowed globally
    },
  },
});
```

```typescript
// e2e/specs/nav.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('primary navigation matches baseline', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Primary' });

  // children:'equal' → snapshot must list EVERY child node exactly
  await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Primary":
      - link "Home"
      - link "Products"
      - link "Pricing"
      - link "Contact"
  `);
  // If a new "Blog" link is added, this test fails — intentional contract enforcement
});

// Override to 'contain' for a single relaxed assertion
test('sidebar has at least a home link', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const sidebar = page.getByRole('complementary');
  await expect(sidebar).toMatchAriaSnapshot(
    `- complementary:\n  - link "Home"`,
    { children: 'contain' },   // local override allows extra siblings
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Global `children: 'equal'` makes every accessibility snapshot test brittle to intentional additions — adding a new nav link breaks every navigation snapshot in CI. This is the right tradeoff for accessibility contract testing (you *want* to know about unexpected additions), but burdensome during rapid feature development. Toggle the global default to `'contain'` during sprint development and switch back to `'equal'` for release branches, or use the local per-assertion override to selectively enforce strictness only on stabilized components.

---

### Pattern 227: Blob Reporter + `npx playwright merge-reports` — Multi-Shard CI with Unified HTML Report [official]

Blob reporter emits a compact binary artifact per shard; `merge-reports` combines all shards into a single HTML report after the matrix jobs complete. This is the official recommended pattern for GitHub Actions matrix runs and avoids the common anti-pattern of uploading separate HTML reports per shard (which produces N disconnected reports with no cross-shard summary).

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [['blob', { outputDir: './blob-report' }]]   // CI: binary artifact per shard
    : [['html', { open: 'on-failure' }]],          // local: immediate HTML report
  fullyParallel: true,
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/playwright.yml (abridged)
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20' }
      - run: npm ci && npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-report-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 1

  merge-reports:
    needs: test
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20' }
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { pattern: 'blob-report-shard-*', path: all-blob-reports, merge-multiple: true }
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-html-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14
```

**Tradeoff:** The `merge-reports` step adds a serial job after all shards complete. If any shard upload fails or times out, the artifact download in `merge-reports` will be incomplete and the final report will silently miss results from that shard. Add an explicit artifact-count guard before running `merge-reports` — compare the number of downloaded blob files against the expected shard count and exit non-zero if any are missing. This catches partial uploads before they produce a silently truncated report.

---

### Pattern 228: `page.route()` Priority — Last-Registered Handler Wins and `route.fallback()` [official]

Multiple `page.route()` calls for the same URL pattern stack in LIFO order — the *last* registered handler runs first. Use `route.fallback()` to pass control to the previously registered handler, enabling composable middleware-style intercept chains where a logging layer and a mocking layer coexist independently without coupling their implementations.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('request is logged then answered by mock', async ({ page }) => {
  const requestLog: string[] = [];

  // Layer 1: Logging (registered first → runs LAST — receives fallback from layer 2)
  await page.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
    requestLog.push(route.request().url());
    await route.fallback();   // pass to next handler in LIFO chain (network)
  });

  // Layer 2: Mocking (registered second → runs FIRST when URL matches)
  await page.route('**/api/products', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      json: { products: [{ id: 1, name: 'Widget Pro', price: 29.99 }] },
    });
    // Does not call fallback → logging layer above never fires for /api/products
  });

  await page.goto('/products');
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Products' })).toBeVisible();

  // /api/products was mocked (not logged); other /api/* calls were logged
  expect(requestLog.some(u => u.includes('/api/'))).toBe(true);
});

// Correct composable pattern: mock calls fallback so logger fires too
test('mock and log compose correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  const log: string[] = [];
  await page.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
    log.push(route.request().url());
    await route.fallback();
  });
  await page.route('**/api/products', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({ json: { products: [] } });
    // Note: calling fallback() after fulfill() is a no-op — fulfill wins
  });
  await page.goto('/products');
  // To have both: log FIRST by registering mock THEN logger (LIFO means logger runs first)
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Handler registration order is effectively reversed at execution time — the last `page.route()` call is the first to execute. This is counter-intuitive and regularly causes bugs when a global logging fixture is added *after* per-test route mocks, because in the fixture chain the global fixture registers its route handler before the test's own handlers. Document the "last-in, first-out" execution order prominently in your fixture readme, and verify the intended layer ordering with an integration test when adding a new route middleware layer.

---

### Pattern 229: `page.screenshot({ mask, maskColor })` — Redacting Dynamic Content in Visual Snapshots [official]

The `mask` option accepts an array of locators whose bounding boxes are painted over with a solid `maskColor` before the screenshot is taken. This stabilizes visual regression snapshots for pages with timestamps, user avatars, ad content, or other dynamic regions that would otherwise cause false failures on every run.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard visual baseline ignores dynamic widgets', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

  const screenshot = await page.screenshot({
    fullPage: true,
    mask: [
      page.getByTestId('live-clock'),             // real-time clock widget
      page.getByTestId('user-avatar'),            // profile picture (CDN URL varies)
      page.getByRole('img', { name: /ad/i }),     // ad banners
      page.locator('[data-testid*="timestamp"]'), // all timestamp cells
    ],
    maskColor: '#e2e8f0',   // light gray — visually distinct but not distracting
  });

  expect(screenshot).toMatchSnapshot('dashboard-baseline.png', {
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.005,
  });
});

// Locator-level masking for component snapshots
test('product card hides stale price badge', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  const card = page.getByTestId('product-card').first();

  await expect(card).toMatchSnapshot('product-card.png', {
    mask: [card.getByTestId('sale-timer')],   // sale countdown is dynamic
    maskColor: '#f1f5f9',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Masked regions are painted *after* the browser renders the page — the dynamic content still loads and may affect surrounding layout before the mask is applied. If a dynamic element such as a lazy-loaded ad changes the page height or shifts adjacent elements, masking its visual output will not prevent the snapshot from diffing. For layout-shifting dynamics, wait for the layout to stabilize (`await expect(page.locator('.ad-slot')).toHaveCSS('height', /[1-9]/)`) before taking the screenshot, or use `page.clock.setFixedTime()` to freeze timestamps before navigation.

---

### Pattern 230: `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with Predicate Function — Dynamic URL Assertions (v1.51+) [official]

`toHaveURL()` accepts a predicate function `(url: URL) => boolean` in addition to string and regex patterns. This enables assertions against specific URL components — `searchParams`, `pathname`, `hostname`, `hash` — without writing fragile regex that must account for URL encoding, query parameter ordering, or trailing slashes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search redirects to results page with query params preserved', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search' }).fill('playwright testing');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  // Predicate: assert specific search params without a brittle regex
  await expect(page).toHaveURL((url) => {
    return (
      url.pathname === '/search' &&
      url.searchParams.get('q') === 'playwright testing' &&
      url.searchParams.has('page')
    );
  });
});

test('OAuth callback strips sensitive state param from URL', async ({ page }) => {
  // Simulate returning from OAuth provider with auth params
  await page.goto('/auth/callback?code=abc123&state=xyz789');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Assert the app cleaned up sensitive params from the final URL
  await expect(page).toHaveURL((url) =>
    !url.searchParams.has('state') && !url.searchParams.has('code'),
  );
});

test('pagination preserves filter params across pages', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products?category=electronics&sort=price-asc');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Next page' }).click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL((url) => {
    const params = url.searchParams;
    return (
      params.get('category') === 'electronics' &&
      params.get('sort') === 'price-asc' &&
      Number(params.get('page') ?? '1') >= 2
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Predicate-based `toHaveURL()` assertions are not displayed as human-readable values in failure messages — Playwright reports the function's source code rather than a diff of expected vs actual URL. When a predicate assertion fails in CI, the engineer must mentally parse the function to determine which constraint was violated. For frequently-asserted URL patterns, consider wrapping the predicate in a named helper function (e.g., `isSearchResultsUrl(url)`) so the function name appears in the stack trace and makes the failure self-documenting.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 40

---

### Gotcha #75: `locator.or()` throws a strict-mode violation when both alternatives are simultaneously present [community]

`locator.or()` creates a locator that matches *any* element from either branch. When *both* alternatives exist in the DOM at the same time — for example, a "New email" button and a security dialog that appears before the button is hidden — the combined locator resolves to multiple elements and Playwright throws `"strict mode violation: resolved to N elements"`.

```typescript
// ❌ Breaks when both are visible simultaneously
const target = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'New email' })
  .or(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Security check' }));
await target.click();  // throws if both are present at once

// ✅ Narrow with first() only after checking actual count
const count = await target.count();
if (count > 1) {
  // Both present: prioritise the dialog (blocking action)
  await page
    .getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Security check' })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' })
    .click();
} else {
  await target.click();
}
```

> **WHY:** `locator.or()` is a *union* locator — it returns all elements matched by either branch, not the first branch that matches. Strict mode requires exactly one matching element for interactive actions (`click`, `fill`, `check`). Teams that introduce `locator.or()` to handle intermittent overlays are often surprised when the overlay and the underlying control briefly co-exist during the overlay's fade-out animation, causing a strict-mode error that only appears on slow CI runners where the animation takes longer to complete. [community]

---

### Gotcha #76: `route.fallback()` in a globally-registered fixture handler is silently skipped when the test-level mock fulfills without calling `fallback()` [community]

When a `page.route()` handler calls `route.fallback()` but the *subsequent* handler in the LIFO chain fulfills the request without also calling `fallback()`, the earlier handler never fires for that URL. Engineers who register a global logging handler in a fixture and expect it to capture every request are surprised to find that test-level mocks silently suppress the logging layer.

```typescript
// ❌ Logger never fires for /api/products because mock fulfills without fallback
// Fixture (registered first → runs SECOND):
await page.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
  logRequest(route.request().url());  // never called for /api/products
  await route.fallback();
});
// Per-test mock (registered second → runs FIRST):
await page.route('**/api/products', async (route) => {
  await route.fulfill({ json: mockProducts });
  // No fallback() call → logger above is never invoked
});

// ✅ Call fallback() from the mock too, or accept the LIFO semantics
await page.route('**/api/products', async (route) => {
  logRequest(route.request().url());  // log inline before fulfilling
  await route.fulfill({ json: mockProducts });
});
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's route handler stack is LIFO: the most recently registered handler gets first access to each matching request. Calling `route.fallback()` passes to the *previously* registered handler — the one registered *before* the current one in source order. When the innermost handler fulfills the request, the chain is terminated and earlier handlers in the stack never receive control. The mental model of "first registered = first to run" (common from `addEventListener` and Express middleware) is the wrong model here. Always document route handler registration order in your fixture file as a comment showing each handler's position in the execution chain. [community]

---

### Gotcha #77: `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` silently captures an empty database when IndexedDB writes are still in-flight at capture time [community]

`browserContext.storageState({ indexedDB: true })` captures IndexedDB via CDP at the moment the call is made. If the application has not yet committed an open transaction — for example, because a post-login Firebase write is still in-flight — the snapshot captures the database in its pre-commit state: structurally present but data-empty.

```typescript
// ❌ Capture race: Firebase write may still be in-flight when storageState is called
await page.goto('/login');
await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email);
await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');  // navigation resolves before IndexedDB write commits
await context.storageState({ path: 'auth.json', indexedDB: true });
// auth.json may have firebaseLocalStorage DB with EMPTY user record

// ✅ Wait for a DOM signal that confirms IndexedDB has committed before capturing
await page.waitForFunction(() =>
  new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => {
    const req = indexedDB.open('firebaseLocalStorage');
    req.onsuccess = () => {
      const db    = req.result;
      const tx    = db.transaction('firebaseLocalStorage', 'readonly');
      const store = tx.objectStore('firebaseLocalStorage');
      const get   = store.getAll();
      get.onsuccess = () => resolve(get.result.length > 0);
      get.onerror   = () => resolve(false);
    };
    req.onerror = () => resolve(false);
  }),
);
await context.storageState({ path: 'auth.json', indexedDB: true });
```

> **WHY:** Firebase Authentication's `setPersistence(browserLocalPersistence)` writes auth tokens to IndexedDB asynchronously after the sign-in promise resolves. The `waitForURL('/dashboard')` navigation completes when the HTTP response returns — which is earlier than the IndexedDB write callback fires. The result is a storage state snapshot that contains correct cookies and localStorage keys but an empty Firebase auth database, causing every test that restores this state to silently fail authentication and redirect back to the login page. [community]

---

### Gotcha #78: Custom matchers registered with `expect.extend()` are invisible on `expect.configure()` instances created from the base `expect` [community]

Custom matchers registered via `expect.extend()` are available on the returned extended instance. However, a `expect.configure()` instance created from the *base* `expect` (before or after extension) does not inherit matchers registered on a separately extended instance — each call to `extend()` or `configure()` creates a new snapshot of the matcher registry at that moment.

```typescript
import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { Locator } from '@playwright/test';

// ❌ softExpect does not have toHaveStatusBadge
const myExpect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveStatusBadge(locator: Locator, status: string) {
    // ...
    return { pass: true, message: () => '' };
  },
});
const softExpect = baseExpect.configure({ soft: true });  // based on baseExpect, NOT myExpect
// softExpect.toHaveStatusBadge → TypeError: not a function

// ✅ Configure FROM the extended instance
const myExtended = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveStatusBadge(locator: Locator, status: string) {
    // ...
    return { pass: true, message: () => '' };
  },
});
const softMyExpect = myExtended.configure({ soft: true });  // inherits toHaveStatusBadge

// ✅ Best practice: single composed expect in fixtures.ts
export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveStatusBadge(locator: Locator, status: string) {
    return { pass: true, message: () => '' };
  },
  async toHavePrice(locator: Locator, price: number) {
    return { pass: true, message: () => '' };
  },
});
export const softExpect  = expect.configure({ soft: true });
export const quickExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 2_000 });
```

> **WHY:** `expect.configure()` creates a new object that copies the matcher registry at call time using a shallow clone of the base instance. Registering matchers on a separate `extend()` call does not retroactively update other derived instances. The rule is: extend first, configure second, always from the same source instance. Teams that split matcher registrations across multiple files and call `configure()` in a shared module frequently discover this ordering issue only in tests that use both a configured preset and a custom matcher simultaneously — and only after migrating to a pattern where `configure()` is used early for module-level preset creation. [community]

---

### Gotcha #79: `testConfig.tsconfig` is silently overridden by the `--tsconfig` CLI flag, which resolves the path relative to CWD — not to `playwright.config.ts` [community]

`testConfig.tsconfig` in `playwright.config.ts` is resolved relative to the config file's directory — making it stable regardless of where `npx playwright test` is invoked. However, the `--tsconfig` CLI flag resolves relative to the *current working directory* at invocation time and silently overrides the config-file setting, causing "Cannot find tsconfig" errors when tests are run from a different directory.

```bash
# ❌ CLI flag with relative path: breaks when CWD is not the project root
npx playwright test --tsconfig tsconfig.test.json
# Works from project root, but fails from CI workspace root in a monorepo

# ❌ The flag silently overrides testConfig.tsconfig — no warning emitted
```

```typescript
// ✅ playwright.config.ts — use path.resolve for CWD-safe absolute path
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  // Resolved at config-load time relative to this file's directory
  tsconfig: path.resolve(__dirname, 'tsconfig.test.json'),
  testDir: './e2e',
});
```

```json
// package.json — if CLI flag is needed, use an absolute-path script
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:e2e": "playwright test",
    "test:e2e:debug": "playwright test --debug"
  }
}
```

> **WHY:** Playwright resolves `testConfig.tsconfig` relative to the directory containing `playwright.config.ts`, making it robust to CWD variation. The `--tsconfig` CLI flag uses `process.cwd()` at invocation time. In monorepos where tests run from workspace root with `-c packages/app/playwright.config.ts`, the CWD is the workspace root but a relative flag path expects the app subdirectory. The safest pattern is to set `tsconfig: path.resolve(__dirname, ...)` in the config file and avoid the `--tsconfig` CLI flag entirely, letting the config-file value take precedence. [community]

## Cycle 41 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 231: `test.step()` `timeout` Option — Per-Step Execution Budgets (v1.50+) [official]

Individual test steps can now carry their own timeout budget independent of the overall test timeout. Passing `{ timeout: ms }` as the third argument to `test.step()` causes Playwright to throw a `TimeoutError` and fail the step (and thus the test) if the step body does not resolve within the allotted time. This lets you enforce SLA-style contracts on critical UI interactions — for example, requiring that a checkout flow completes within 5 seconds — without tightening the global test timeout and breaking unrelated steps. Combined with the `box` option, step timeouts provide both a capped execution budget and a clean call-site error location.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout must complete within budget', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /your cart/i })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 3_000 });

  const orderId = await test.step('submit order and capture confirmation', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }).click();
    const confirmation = page.getByTestId('order-id');
    await expect(confirmation).toBeVisible();
    return await confirmation.textContent();
  }, { timeout: 5_000, box: true });  // box=true → error points to this call-site

  await test.step('verify confirmation number format', async () => {
    expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-\d{6}$/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** A per-step timeout creates a hard ceiling that is additive — if all steps fire their maximum timeout the test could run `sum(step timeouts)` milliseconds before the outer test timeout intervenes. Set step timeouts conservatively and below the outer `testInfo.timeout` to prevent the outer timeout from masking which step was the bottleneck. Do not apply step timeouts to steps that wrap assertions only (those are nearly instant); reserve them for steps containing network-bound `waitForURL` or `waitForResponse` calls.
