### Pattern 232: `test.step.skip()` — Programmatic Step Exclusion (v1.50+) [official]

`test.step.skip()` is a static method on the `test.step` function that marks an entire step as skipped without executing its body. This mirrors `test.skip()` semantics but scoped to a step, allowing feature-flagged steps, environment-gated verifications, or "not yet implemented" scaffolding that should show up in reports without breaking the suite. The skip shows as a distinct status in HTML and trace reports so it is never confused with a missing step or an accidental no-op.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const DARK_MODE_ENABLED = process.env.FEATURE_DARK_MODE === '1';

test('profile settings page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings/profile');

  await test.step('verify basic profile fields are visible', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByLabel(/display name/i)).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByLabel(/email address/i)).toBeVisible();
  });

  // Conditionally skip based on feature flag — step appears in report as skipped
  await test.step.skip('verify dark mode toggle (feature-flagged)', async () => {
    const toggle = page.getByRole('switch', { name: /dark mode/i });
    await expect(toggle).toBeVisible();
    await toggle.click();
    await expect(page.locator('html')).toHaveClass(/theme-dark/);
  }, !DARK_MODE_ENABLED, 'dark-mode feature flag is off in this environment');

  await test.step('save settings and verify success toast', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: /save changes/i }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/saved successfully/i);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Unlike `test.skip()`, which aborts the entire test, `test.step.skip()` continues execution of subsequent steps. This is powerful for optional verification steps but can mask regressions when a skipped step covered behavior that should have been tested. Audit skipped steps regularly; treat persistent skips as technical debt that needs a resolution date tracked via `test.step`'s description field or a linked issue annotation on the parent test.

---

### Pattern 233: `TestStepInfo.attach()` — Step-Scoped Attachments (v1.51+) [official]

When a `test.step()` body receives its `TestStepInfo` object as a parameter, calling `stepInfo.attach()` associates the file or buffer with that specific step in reports and traces rather than with the top-level test. Step-scoped attachments make long test traces dramatically easier to navigate: screenshots, downloaded files, and API response bodies appear directly under the step that generated them instead of in a flat attachment list at the test level. This is especially valuable in data-driven loops where each iteration produces its own diagnostic artefacts.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('bulk data import validates each row', async ({ page }) => {
  const rows = [
    { sku: 'A001', price: 9.99 },
    { sku: 'B042', price: 24.50 },
    { sku: 'C100', price: 4.75 },
  ];

  for (const row of rows) {
    await test.step(`import row ${row.sku}`, async (step) => {
      // Navigate and fill form
      await page.goto('/admin/products/import');
      await page.getByLabel(/sku/i).fill(row.sku);
      await page.getByLabel(/price/i).fill(String(row.price));
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: /import/i }).click();

      // Capture screenshot scoped to THIS step — not the whole test
      const screenshot = await page.screenshot();
      await step.attach(`${row.sku} result`, {
        body: screenshot,
        contentType: 'image/png',
      });

      // Also attach the API confirmation response body
      const response = await page.waitForResponse('/api/products');
      const body = await response.json();
      await step.attach(`${row.sku} api-response`, {
        body: JSON.stringify(body, null, 2),
        contentType: 'application/json',
      });

      await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/imported/i);
    });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Step-scoped attachments increase report size proportionally to the number of iterations. In suites running hundreds of data-driven rows, screenshot attachments per step can exhaust disk space on CI agents — especially when combined with `trace: 'on'`. Apply `step.attach()` selectively: only capture on explicit assertion failure branches (`if (!pass) await step.attach(...)`) or limit attachments to the first N failures using a counter fixture.

---

### Pattern 234: `locator.filter({ visible: true })` — Visibility-Aware Locator Narrowing (v1.51+) [official]

`locator.filter({ visible: true })` narrows a multi-match locator to only the subset of matched elements that are currently visible in the layout. Before v1.51, filtering for visibility required combining `locator.all()` with a manual `isVisible()` loop or using `:visible` pseudo-class strings — both of which either escape Playwright's retry engine or couple tests to CSS semantics. The `visible` option participates fully in Playwright's retry loop: if no visible match exists yet, the assertion retries until the timeout, making it suitable for animations that gradually reveal list items.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('only active notifications are actionable', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/notifications');

  // Page renders a mix of visible and CSS-hidden (archived) notification rows
  const allRows = page.getByRole('listitem', { name: /notification/i });

  // Narrow to only the currently visible rows — participates in retry loop
  const visibleRows = allRows.filter({ visible: true });

  await expect(visibleRows).toHaveCount(3);

  // Dismiss each visible notification — invisible ones are untouched
  for (const row of await visibleRows.all()) {
    await row.getByRole('button', { name: /dismiss/i }).click();
  }

  // After dismissal all visible rows gone — hidden rows remain in DOM
  await expect(visibleRows).toHaveCount(0);
  await expect(allRows).not.toHaveCount(0);  // hidden rows still in DOM
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `visible: true` in `locator.filter()` uses the same layout-visibility heuristic as `locator.isVisible()` — an element with `opacity: 0` or `visibility: hidden` is considered invisible, but an element clipped outside the viewport scroll boundary is considered visible. For off-viewport list virtualization patterns, combine with `locator.filter({ hasText })` or a scroll-and-check strategy. Never use `visible: true` as a substitute for waiting for an animation to complete — prefer `toBeVisible()` on the specific element instead.

---

### Pattern 235: `expect(locator).toContainClass()` — Individual CSS Class Assertions (v1.52+) [official]

`toContainClass()` asserts that an element's `classList` contains every class in the expected value without requiring an exact match of the full class string. Before v1.52, teams used `toHaveClass(/expected-class/)` with a regex, which is brittle when class names are generated (e.g., CSS Modules hashes) or when the expected class appears as a substring of another class name. `toContainClass()` is space-separated: passing `'active selected'` asserts both classes are present independently, equivalent to two separate `toHaveClass(/active/)` and `toHaveClass(/selected/)` calls but with a single readable assertion. It also accepts an array for asserting against multiple elements simultaneously.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('data table row state classes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports/table');

  const rows = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: /in progress/i });

  // Single element — assert multiple classes without caring about others
  const firstRow = rows.first();
  await expect(firstRow).toContainClass('highlighted editable');

  // After clicking to select it
  await firstRow.click();
  await expect(firstRow).toContainClass('selected');
  // Does NOT assert that 'highlighted' or 'editable' were removed — use toHaveClass for that

  // Array form: assert different class on each row simultaneously
  const statusRows = page.locator('tr[data-status]');
  await expect(statusRows).toContainClass([
    'status-pending',
    'status-active',
    'status-complete',
  ]);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `toContainClass()` asserts inclusion, not exclusivity. If a class is unexpectedly removed, `toContainClass()` will not catch it — use `toHaveClass()` with an exact string or regex when the absence of a class also matters. Avoid using this assertion to test CSS Module hash classes (`_abc123_` style) — those leak implementation details. Instead, pair `toContainClass()` with semantic BEM or utility class names that have stable meaning across deploys.

---

### Pattern 236: `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` — ARIA Error State Assertions (v1.50+) [official]

`toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` asserts the value of an element's `aria-errormessage` attribute linkage — it resolves the referenced element and checks its `textContent` rather than checking the attribute value string. This is the correct way to assert form validation error messages in accessible UIs: the error paragraph is typically a separate DOM node referenced by `aria-errormessage="error-id"` on the input. Using `toHaveText()` on the error node directly works but decouples the assertion from the semantic relationship — if the `aria-errormessage` reference is broken, the test passes even though screen readers cannot find the error.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('registration form shows accessible validation errors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/register');

  const emailInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /email address/i });
  const passwordInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /password/i });

  // Submit empty form to trigger validation
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /create account/i }).click();

  // Assert via the aria-errormessage relationship — not just visible text
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Email address is required.');
  await expect(passwordInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/at least 8 characters/i);

  // Fill email, re-validate
  await emailInput.fill('not-an-email');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /create account/i }).click();
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/valid email/i);

  // Correct email clears the error
  await emailInput.fill('user@example.com');
  await emailInput.blur();
  await expect(emailInput).not.toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` requires that the element has a valid `aria-errormessage` attribute pointing to an element in the DOM with a matching `id`. If the application uses `aria-describedby` instead (common in older component libraries), this assertion will not find the message — use `toHaveAccessibleDescription()` instead. The two attributes have subtly different semantics: `aria-describedby` is for supplemental description, `aria-errormessage` is specifically for invalid-state error messages. Mixing them is an accessibility defect this assertion can expose.

---

### Pattern 237: `expect(checkbox).toBeChecked({ indeterminate: true })` — Tri-State Checkbox Assertions (v1.50+) [official]

HTML checkboxes support a tri-state `indeterminate` property used in "select all" patterns and tree structures where a parent checkbox reflects partial child selection. The `indeterminate` state is set programmatically via JavaScript (`element.indeterminate = true`) and cannot be set via the `checked` HTML attribute — meaning a checkbox in this state has `checked: false` in the DOM while visually showing a dash indicator. Before v1.50, asserting this state required `page.evaluate()` or a custom matcher. The `{ indeterminate: true }` option makes this a first-class assertion.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('select-all checkbox reflects partial selection state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/tasks');

  const selectAll = page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /select all/i });
  const taskBoxes = page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /^task/i });

  // Initially all unchecked
  await expect(selectAll).not.toBeChecked();
  await expect(selectAll).not.toBeChecked({ indeterminate: true });

  // Select first task — parent becomes indeterminate
  await taskBoxes.first().check();
  await expect(selectAll).not.toBeChecked();
  await expect(selectAll).toBeChecked({ indeterminate: true });

  // Select all tasks — parent becomes fully checked
  await taskBoxes.last().check();
  await expect(selectAll).toBeChecked();
  await expect(selectAll).not.toBeChecked({ indeterminate: true });

  // Deselect one — back to indeterminate
  await taskBoxes.first().uncheck();
  await expect(selectAll).toBeChecked({ indeterminate: true });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `indeterminate` property is not reflected in the `checked` attribute or accessible name — screen readers announce indeterminate checkboxes differently depending on the ARIA implementation. If the component uses `aria-checked="mixed"` instead of the native `indeterminate` property (common in custom React/Vue components), `toBeChecked({ indeterminate: true })` may not detect it. In that case use `expect(locator).toHaveAttribute('aria-checked', 'mixed')` and file the discrepancy as a test gap note.

---

### Pattern 238: `testConfig.captureGitInfo` — Git Metadata in HTML Reports (v1.51+) [official]

`captureGitInfo` attaches commit metadata (hash, author, branch, timestamp, PR number) to the HTML report, enriching it with the exact code version under test. This eliminates the need to manually copy `git log` output into report annotations or CI job summaries. Setting `{ commit: true, diff: true }` also captures the commit diff so reviewers can trace which code change introduced a new failure directly from the report UI. The feature integrates with blob reporter merge-reports: shards from different machines each capture the same commit SHA, producing a consistent merged report.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Capture commit metadata + diff for enriched HTML reports
  captureGitInfo: {
    commit: true,   // hash, author, branch, timestamp, PR info
    diff:   true,   // commit diff (caution: large diffs increase report size)
  },

  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
    ['blob'],  // for shard merging — git info is carried through merge
  ],

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
});
```

```bash
# CI: merge sharded blob reports — git info from each shard is preserved
npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports

# Verify git is available in Docker — captureGitInfo silently produces empty fields without git
which git || echo "WARN: git not found — captureGitInfo will return empty metadata"
```

**Tradeoff:** `captureGitInfo.diff` produces a full `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD` output that can be very large for commits with many changed files, significantly increasing report size. In monorepos disable `diff: true` and rely on `commit: true` alone — the commit SHA provides enough information to reconstruct the diff from the repository. The feature silently falls back to empty strings when `git` is not on `PATH` (common in minimal Docker images), so validate availability during CI setup rather than discovering it in production reports.

---

### Pattern 239: `testConfig.updateSourceMethod: '3way'` — Merge-Conflict Snapshot Updates (v1.50+) [official]

When `updateSourceMethod` is set to `'3way'`, running `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` writes Git-style merge conflict markers directly into snapshot files rather than overwriting them. This lets developers review both the old baseline and the new captured value in a `<<<`/`===`/`>>>` diff block and choose which to keep — useful in CI where a snapshot update is non-obvious (e.g., a minor copy change or a loading-state animation frame). The default `'overwrite'` mode silently replaces the baseline, making it impossible to diff without a separate Git checkout. The `'patch'` mode writes a separate `.patch` file that must be applied manually.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — use 3way for team code-review workflows
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  updateSourceMethod: process.env.CI ? '3way' : 'overwrite',

  expect: {
    toMatchAriaSnapshot: {
      children: 'contain',  // default — less brittle for 3way review workflows
    },
    toHaveScreenshot: {
      maxDiffPixels: 50,
    },
  },
});
```

```bash
# Update snapshots with 3way conflict markers in CI
npx playwright test --update-snapshots

# After reviewing conflict markers in spec files, accept all new values:
# Open the spec files and resolve conflict markers manually, keeping the new (>>>>>) side
# Then commit the resolved files to finalize the snapshot update
```

**Tradeoff:** The `'3way'` mode breaks snapshot files (they contain merge conflict syntax and fail to parse) until conflicts are resolved — which means the test suite cannot run in its current state after an `--update-snapshots` run on CI. This is intentional as a forcing function for review, but it is disruptive if a CI job re-runs before the branch is updated. Use `'3way'` on a dedicated "snapshot update" CI job that posts conflicts as PR comments, and keep the main CI job on `'overwrite'` or `'patch'` so reruns still function.

---

### Pattern 240: `apiRequest.newContext()` `maxRedirects` Option — Redirect Control in API Testing (v1.52+) [official]

`apiRequest.newContext()` accepts a `maxRedirects` option that caps the number of HTTP redirects the context will automatically follow. The default behaviour follows redirects indefinitely (up to a browser-internal limit). Setting `maxRedirects: 0` causes the context to return the redirect response directly without following it, allowing tests to assert the redirect target URL, status code, and `Location` header without making the subsequent request. This is essential for testing OAuth callback flows, shortened URL resolvers, and SAML assertion endpoints where the redirect itself is the meaningful response.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('OAuth callback issues a 302 redirect to the correct return URL', async ({ playwright }) => {
  // Context that will NOT follow redirects — returns the 302 directly
  const api = await playwright.request.newContext({
    baseURL:      'https://auth.example.com',
    maxRedirects: 0,
    extraHTTPHeaders: {
      'Accept': 'application/json',
    },
  });

  const response = await api.post('/oauth/token', {
    form: {
      grant_type:   'authorization_code',
      code:         'test-code-abc123',
      redirect_uri: 'https://app.example.com/callback',
      client_id:    process.env.OAUTH_CLIENT_ID!,
    },
  });

  // Assert on the redirect itself — not on the final destination
  expect(response.status()).toBe(302);
  const location = response.headers()['location'];
  expect(location).toMatch(/^https:\/\/app\.example\.com\/callback\?code=/);
  expect(location).not.toContain('error=');

  await api.dispose();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Setting `maxRedirects: 0` means every subsequent request in the context will also not follow redirects, including requests that legitimately should (e.g., fetching a resource after auth). Create a dedicated `newContext()` instance with `maxRedirects: 0` only for the specific redirect-assertion requests, and use a separate default context for remaining API calls within the same test. Do not reuse the no-redirect context across fixtures — the accidental propagation of `maxRedirects: 0` to utility requests produces confusing 3xx response errors that are hard to trace.

---

### Pattern 241: `testInfo.snapshotPath(name, { kind })` — Explicit Snapshot Kind Resolution (v1.53+) [official]

`testInfo.snapshotPath()` now accepts a `kind` option that selects which of the three snapshot path templates to evaluate: `'screenshot'`, `'aria'`, or `'snapshot'` (the default). This matters because each kind has a separate configuration key (`snapshotPathTemplate`, `screenshotPathTemplate`, and the aria path template) that can resolve to different directories. Before v1.53, custom helper functions computing snapshot paths for comparison or pre-population had to replicate Playwright's internal path logic. The `kind` option exposes the canonical resolution so helpers stay in sync with configuration changes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

// Fixture: pre-populate aria snapshots from a shared fixture directory
const baseTest = test.extend<{ ensureAriaBaseline: void }>({
  ensureAriaBaseline: [async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    // Compute the canonical path Playwright uses for aria snapshots
    const safeTitle = testInfo.title.replace(/\s+/g, '-');
    const ariaPath = testInfo.snapshotPath(
      `${safeTitle}.aria.yml`,
      { kind: 'aria' }
    );

    // Seed the baseline from shared fixtures if it doesn't exist yet
    if (!fs.existsSync(ariaPath)) {
      const fixtureSource = path.join('tests', 'fixtures', 'aria', `${safeTitle}.aria.yml`);
      if (fs.existsSync(fixtureSource)) {
        fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(ariaPath), { recursive: true });
        fs.copyFileSync(fixtureSource, ariaPath);
      }
    }

    await use();
  }, { auto: true }],
});

baseTest('navigation menu accessible structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: /main/i });
  await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot({ name: 'nav-main.aria.yml' });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `kind` option only affects path template resolution — it does not validate that the file at the resolved path is actually a valid aria YAML or screenshot PNG. Using `kind: 'aria'` on a helper that then writes arbitrary content to the resolved path can silently corrupt Playwright's snapshot store. Treat `snapshotPath()` as a read-only path resolver for comparison and seeding logic; never write snapshot content manually unless mirroring what `--update-snapshots` would produce.

---

### Pattern 242: Component Testing `mount.update()` + `unmount()` — Lifecycle Coverage for React/Vue Components [official]

Playwright Component Testing exposes `mount.update()` to re-render a component with new props/events and `mount.unmount()` to remove it from the DOM. These lifecycle operations are essential for testing components whose behavior changes in response to prop transitions (e.g., `loading: true` to `loading: false`) and for asserting cleanup effects (event listener removal, subscription teardown). Without `update()`, teams resort to unmounting and re-mounting with new props — which resets all state and does not exercise the component's prop-change code path.

```typescript
// tests/DataTable.spec.tsx  (React CT — @playwright/experimental-ct-react)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import { DataTable } from '../src/DataTable';

test('DataTable transitions from loading skeleton to populated rows', async ({ mount }) => {
  // Mount in loading state
  const component = await mount(
    <DataTable loading={true} rows={[]} onRowClick={() => {}} />
  );

  await expect(component.getByRole('status', { name: /loading/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(component.getByRole('row')).toHaveCount(0);

  // Simulate parent re-render with loaded data — exercises componentDidUpdate path
  await component.update(
    <DataTable loading={false} rows={[
      { id: '1', name: 'Alpha', status: 'active' },
      { id: '2', name: 'Beta',  status: 'pending' },
    ]} onRowClick={() => {}} />
  );

  await expect(component.getByRole('status', { name: /loading/i })).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(component.getByRole('row', { name: /alpha/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Unmount — assert element is removed from DOM
  await component.unmount();
  await expect(component).not.toBeAttached();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `mount.update()` only re-renders props passed directly to the component — it cannot update context providers or routing context injected via `hooksConfig`. If the component reads from React Context or a router, update the context wrapper instead: unmount and re-mount with a new `hooksConfig` providing updated context values. The Node/browser boundary also means that callback props cannot return live objects from the Node side — only serializable values like strings, numbers, and plain objects can cross the boundary, so avoid expecting `onRowClick` to receive a DOM `Event` instance in Node-side assertions.

---

### Pattern 243: `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` — Capturing Firebase/IDB Auth State (v1.51+) [official]

Setting `indexedDB: true` in `browserContext.storageState()` includes IndexedDB databases in the captured state file, enabling full restoration of auth tokens stored by Firebase Auth SDK, Supabase, and other libraries that use IDB as their persistence layer. Without this option, `storageState()` captures only cookies and `localStorage`, leaving IDB-backed sessions invalid after restoration — causing signed-in test users to silently appear as signed-out on first page load. Restoring IDB state via `context.storageState()` at context creation replays all database writes atomically before the first page navigation.

```typescript
// global-setup.ts — capture auth state including IndexedDB
import { chromium, type FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page    = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto(config.webServer!.url + '/login');
  await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill(process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill(process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();

  // Wait for Firebase to write the auth token to IndexedDB
  await page.waitForFunction(() =>
    indexedDB.databases().then(dbs =>
      dbs.some((db: IDBDatabaseInfo) => db.name?.includes('firebaseLocalStorage'))
    )
  );
  // Extra tick to ensure IDB write transaction has committed
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);

  // Capture full state including IndexedDB
  await context.storageState({
    path:      'playwright/.auth/firebase-user.json',
    indexedDB: true,
  });

  await browser.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff:** IDB capture serializes all object store data as JSON, which can be very large for applications that cache API responses or document content in IDB (e.g., offline-capable PWAs). A 10 MB IDB database produces a 10 MB auth file that is loaded on every test worker startup. Inspect the captured file to identify cacheable object stores that do not contribute to auth state, and exclude them by clearing the relevant IDB databases before calling `storageState()`. Firebase Auth specifically uses a small `firebaseLocalStorage` store — all other stores can typically be purged without affecting test sessions.

---

### Pattern 244: Session Storage Restoration via `addInitScript()` — Bridging the `storageState` Gap [community]

`storageState()` captures and restores cookies and `localStorage` but not `sessionStorage` — which is cleared on every page navigation by design. Applications that use `sessionStorage` to carry ephemeral auth tokens, wizard state, or tab-specific context cannot be restored through the standard auth workflow. The canonical workaround is to serialize the required `sessionStorage` keys during the auth setup phase and inject them via `page.addInitScript()` before each navigation. The init script runs before any page scripts execute, so the storage is available to framework bootstrapping code on the first tick.

```typescript
// fixtures/sessionAuth.ts
import { test as base, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';

// Capture sessionStorage keys during global-setup (run once)
export async function captureSessionStorage(
  context: BrowserContext, url: string
): Promise<Record<string, string>> {
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto(url);
  const sessionData = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const data: Record<string, string> = {};
    for (let i = 0; i < sessionStorage.length; i++) {
      const key = sessionStorage.key(i)!;
      data[key] = sessionStorage.getItem(key)!;
    }
    return data;
  });
  await page.close();
  return sessionData;
}

export const test = base.extend<object, { workerSessionData: Record<string, string> }>({
  workerSessionData: [async ({}, use) => {
    const data = JSON.parse(
      fs.readFileSync('playwright/.auth/session-storage.json', 'utf8')
    );
    await use(data);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  // Override page to inject sessionStorage before each navigation
  page: async ({ browser, workerSessionData }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    // Guard injection to app origin only — avoid polluting third-party pages
    await context.addInitScript((data) => {
      if (window.location.origin === 'https://app.example.com') {
        for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(data)) {
          sessionStorage.setItem(key, value as string);
        }
      }
    }, workerSessionData);
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await use(page);
    await context.close();
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addInitScript()` runs the injection on every page navigation in the context, including navigations to third-party URLs (analytics endpoints, OAuth providers). If a `sessionStorage` key collides with a third-party page's own storage, the injection can corrupt third-party flows. Always scope the init script with a `window.location.origin` guard as shown above. Additionally, if `sessionStorage` contains CSRF tokens or short-lived JWTs, they expire between the setup capture and test execution — regenerate these tokens programmatically in a `beforeEach` hook rather than relying on the captured snapshot. [community]

---

### Pattern 245: `test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } })` — Per-File Auth Opt-Out [official]

When a Playwright project is configured with a default `storageState` (e.g., `use: { storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' }`), every test in that project inherits the authenticated session. Tests that specifically verify unauthenticated behavior — login page rendering, anonymous access restrictions, sign-up flows — need to opt out of the project-level auth. Placing `test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } })` at the top of a spec file resets the storage state for all tests in that file to an empty (anonymous) context without requiring a separate project definition.

```typescript
// e2e/auth/login-page.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/pages';

// Override project-level storageState — tests in THIS file run unauthenticated
test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } });

test('login page renders correctly for anonymous users', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  // Without the override above, this would redirect to /dashboard (authenticated)
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /sign in/i })).toBeVisible();
});

test('redirects to login when accessing protected route', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login\?.*returnUrl/);
});

test('sign up link navigates to registration', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /create account/i }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/register/);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** This pattern only works cleanly when the authenticated `storageState` file is always present (i.e., the auth setup project has already run). In CI sharding configurations where auth setup runs as a dependency project, a shard that somehow skips the dependency may not have the auth file — but because the spec that opts out never reads the file, it succeeds silently while the project configuration has a latent breakage. Always validate that the auth file exists in CI setup scripts independent of whether the current shard happens to need it.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 41

### Gotcha #80: `test.step()` per-step `timeout` is NOT deducted from the parent test timeout — both clocks run concurrently [community]

A step timeout and the test's overall timeout are independent countdown timers that run in parallel. If a step timeout fires, it throws a `TimeoutError` and fails the test — but the test timeout was also ticking the whole time. This means a test with `timeout: 30_000` and a step with `{ timeout: 5_000 }` does not get 35 seconds; it gets at most 30 seconds, with the step failing at 5 seconds. The confusion arises because developers expect step timeouts to be "sub-allocations" of the test budget, but they are independent constraints. Setting a step timeout *shorter* than the test timeout creates a meaningful early-failure signal; setting it *longer* is a no-op because the test timeout will fire first.

```typescript
// ❌ Misleading: step timeout 60s > test timeout 30s — step timeout never fires
test('submit order', async ({ page }) => {
  test.setTimeout(30_000);
  await test.step('wait for confirmation', async () => {
    await page.waitForURL('/confirmation');
  }, { timeout: 60_000 });  // dead code — test dies at 30s first
});

// ✅ Step timeout shorter than test timeout — meaningful early-failure budget
test('submit order', async ({ page }) => {
  test.setTimeout(30_000);
  await test.step('wait for confirmation', async () => {
    await page.waitForURL('/confirmation');
  }, { timeout: 5_000 });  // fires at 5s — clear which step was slow
});
```

> **WHY:** Playwright implements step timeouts as a `Promise.race()` between the step body and a `setTimeout` at the step level. The outer test timeout is a separate timer managed by the test runner's worker process. Neither timer "pauses" the other — they are independent racing promises. The error message from a step timeout (`TimeoutError: Test step exceeded timeout of 5000ms`) is distinct from an outer test timeout (`Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded`) so the failure message does identify which timer fired, but developers only discover the independence when both timers fire unexpectedly close together. [community]

---

### Gotcha #81: `locator.filter({ visible: true })` counts elements positioned off-scroll as visible — combine with viewport-aware guards for absolute-positioned lists [community]

`filter({ visible: true })` uses the CSS visibility model: an element is "visible" if it has non-zero layout dimensions and is not hidden via `visibility: hidden`, `display: none`, or `opacity: 0`. An element positioned below the fold or outside the current scroll position still passes this check. In virtualized lists where only rendered-window items exist in the DOM at all, this is fine. But in infinite-scroll lists where all items are always in the DOM but some are positioned off-screen via `position: absolute; top: -9999px`, `filter({ visible: true })` captures the off-screen items, inflating counts and causing unexpected element interactions.

```typescript
// ❌ Captures CSS-visible but off-viewport items in absolute-positioned lists
const visibleItems = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ visible: true });
await expect(visibleItems).toHaveCount(5);  // may return 25 if off-screen items are CSS-visible

// ✅ Rely on app-provided data attribute set by IntersectionObserver
const viewportItems = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({
  has: page.locator('[data-in-viewport="true"]'),  // app sets via IntersectionObserver
});

// ✅ Alternatively, combine visible:true with hasText to narrow to known-content rows
const activeItems = page.getByRole('listitem')
  .filter({ visible: true })
  .filter({ hasText: /active|pending/ });
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's visibility check calls the browser's `getBoundingClientRect()` and checks that width and height are non-zero, then checks computed style for `visibility` and `display`. It does NOT check whether the element intersects the current viewport scroll window. Elements with `position: absolute` and a large negative `top` value have real dimensions (non-zero bounding box) and valid computed styles, so they are considered visible. The only browser-native way to detect viewport intersection is the `IntersectionObserver` API, which Playwright does not invoke for the `visible` filter check. [community]

---

### Gotcha #82: `captureGitInfo` silently produces empty metadata in Docker images without `git` on `PATH` — no error, no warning [community]

When `captureGitInfo: { commit: true, diff: true }` is set in `playwright.config.ts` and the test runs in a Docker image that does not have `git` installed (common in minimal `node:alpine` images), Playwright executes the `git log` and `git diff` commands, catches the `ENOENT` / command-not-found error silently, and populates all metadata fields with empty strings. The HTML report renders without any git information but does not indicate that metadata capture failed. CI engineers often diagnose this as a configuration error in `captureGitInfo` when it is actually a missing system dependency.

```dockerfile
# ❌ node:alpine has no git — captureGitInfo produces empty metadata silently
FROM node:20-alpine
RUN npm ci
RUN npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

# ✅ Install git explicitly before running tests
FROM node:20-alpine
RUN apk add --no-cache git
RUN npm ci
RUN npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — emit a clear warning if git is unavailable
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

let hasGit = true;
try { execSync('git --version', { stdio: 'ignore' }); }
catch { hasGit = false; console.warn('[playwright] git not found — captureGitInfo will be empty'); }

export default defineConfig({
  captureGitInfo: hasGit ? { commit: true, diff: false } : undefined,
});
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's git info capture uses Node.js `child_process.execFile('git', ...)` and wraps the call in a try/catch that swallows all errors to avoid crashing the test suite over a non-critical metadata feature. This defensive approach prevents noise but creates a silent-failure mode. The design choice prioritizes not breaking CI over surfacing configuration issues. Teams that discovered this issue did so by comparing two HTML reports — one from local machine (with git) and one from CI (without git) — and noticing the "Commit" section was missing from the CI report. [community]

---

### Gotcha #83: `test.step.skip()` skipped steps still appear in the report step tree with status `'skipped'` — they are not invisible and count in total step metrics [community]

When `test.step.skip()` marks a step as skipped, the step appears in the HTML report, JSON reporter output, and trace viewer with a "skipped" status — it is not omitted from the step list. Automation scripts that parse the JSON reporter output and count total/passed/failed steps to derive a completeness score will include skipped steps in the total, inflating the denominator. If the expectation was that skipped steps would be invisible (as if the `test.step()` call never existed), the actual behavior is closer to `test.skip()` on a test: the entry exists, it has a defined title, and it has status `'skipped'`.

```typescript
// JSON reporter output for a skipped step:
// {
//   "title": "verify dark mode toggle (feature-flagged)",
//   "status": "skipped",
//   "duration": 0,
//   "steps": []
// }

// ❌ Script assumes steps with status !== 'passed' are failures:
const failedSteps = results.steps.filter((s: any) => s.status !== 'passed');
// Includes skipped steps — inflates failure count

// ✅ Account for skipped status explicitly in any step-counting automation:
const failedSteps = results.steps.filter(
  (s: any) => s.status !== 'passed' && s.status !== 'skipped'
);
const completedSteps = results.steps.filter(
  (s: any) => s.status === 'passed' || s.status === 'skipped'
);
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's reporter data model uses the same `TestStep` type for all step states, and `'skipped'` is a valid status value alongside `'passed'` and `'failed'`. This is the correct behavior — skipped steps represent intentional non-execution of a branch, which is different from absence. The confusion arises from teams that treat test steps as analogous to test cases (where skipped tests are often excluded from pass-rate calculations) and write step-counting automation without reading the API documentation for the complete set of step status values. [community]

---

### Gotcha #84: `expect(locator).toContainClass('')` with an empty string always passes — it is NOT a "has no classes" assertion [community]

Calling `toContainClass('')` succeeds for any element regardless of its `classList` contents. An empty string split on spaces produces an empty array, and the "all expected classes present" check vacuously passes over an empty expected set. This is correct subset-check behavior but is a frequent copy-paste bug: developers writing `toContainClass('')` to assert that an element has no classes get a false-positive pass on every element. The correct assertion for "element has no CSS classes" is `toHaveClass('')` (exact match against the full class string) or `not.toHaveClass(/\S/)`.

```typescript
// ❌ Always passes — does NOT assert element has no classes
await expect(page.locator('#status-badge')).toContainClass('');

// ✅ Assert element has no classes — exact empty class string match
await expect(page.locator('#status-badge')).toHaveClass('');

// ✅ Assert element has no non-whitespace class tokens (regex)
await expect(page.locator('#status-badge')).not.toHaveClass(/\S/);

// ✅ Preferred pattern: assert a specific class was removed (tests behavior, not absence)
await page.getByRole('button', { name: /dismiss/i }).click();
await expect(page.locator('#status-badge')).not.toContainClass('error');
```

> **WHY:** `toContainClass()` implements a mathematical subset check: the assertion passes if every element in the expected set is present in the actual `classList`. A subset check with an empty expected set is trivially true (the empty set is a subset of every set). This is standard set theory behavior, not a Playwright bug. The root cause of the gotcha is that `toContainClass('')` and `toHaveClass('')` look nearly identical but have completely different semantics — one is a vacuous truth and the other is an exact-match assertion against the full class attribute. [community]

### Pattern 246: `page.screencast` API — Programmatic Video Recording with Frame Callbacks (v1.59+) [official]

The `page.screencast` property provides a first-class API for capturing video recordings without relying on Playwright's built-in `recordVideo` fixture option. `screencast.start({ path })` begins recording to a `.webm` file; `screencast.stop()` finalizes it. The key differentiator from `recordVideo` is the `onFrame` callback, which delivers raw frame buffers in real time, enabling integration with vision-model pipelines or custom streaming targets. `screencast.start()` returns a `Promise<Disposable>`, meaning it pairs naturally with TypeScript's `await using` pattern for automatic cleanup.

```typescript
// e2e/screencast/vision-capture.spec.ts
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('capture screencast frames for vision-model analysis', async ({ page }) => {
  const frames: Buffer[] = [];

  // Start screencast with frame callback — returns Disposable for auto-cleanup
  await using _sc = await page.screencast.start({
    size: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
    onFrame: async ({ data }) => {
      // Collect every 30th frame (~1 fps at 30 fps capture rate)
      if (frames.length % 30 === 0) frames.push(data);
    },
  });

  // Enable action annotations so AI can correlate gestures with frames
  await using _actions = await page.screencast.showActions({
    duration: 800,
    fontSize: 28,
    position: 'bottom-right',
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /proceed to checkout/i }).click();

  // _actions and _sc are disposed automatically via 'await using' at block end
  console.log(`Captured ${frames.length} sample frames for analysis`);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `onFrame` fires on every raw frame, which can be CPU-intensive if the callback does synchronous work. Buffer every N-th frame or push to a queue for async processing. Unlike `recordVideo`, `screencast.start()` does not automatically attach the output file to `testInfo`; you must call `testInfo.attach()` manually if the video should appear in the HTML report.

---

### Pattern 247: `page.screencast.showChapter()` and `showOverlay()` — Human-Readable Video Narration [official]

`showChapter(title, { description, duration })` renders a centered overlay that fades out after `duration` ms (default 2000), acting like a slate card for a section of the recording. `showOverlay(html, { duration })` injects arbitrary HTML over the viewport — useful for stamping timestamps, test metadata, or custom branding onto screen recordings. Both `showChapter` and `showOverlay` are distinct from `showActions`: `showChapter` and `showOverlay` return `Promise<void>` (fire-and-forget after injection) while `showActions` returns `Promise<Disposable>` for persistent annotation control.

```typescript
// e2e/screencast/narrated-walkthrough.spec.ts
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('narrated checkout flow recording', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  await using _sc = await page.screencast.start({
    path: testInfo.outputPath('checkout-flow.webm'),
    size: { width: 1280, height: 800 },
  });

  // Chapter header — centred slate visible for 3 seconds before fading
  await page.screencast.showChapter('Step 1: Product Selection', {
    description: 'User browses catalog and adds item to cart',
    duration: 3000,
  });
  await page.goto('/catalog');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).first().click();

  // Persistent metadata overlay — no duration means it stays until disposed
  const metaHtml = `<div style="position:fixed;bottom:8px;left:8px;background:rgba(0,0,0,.65);
    color:#fff;padding:4px 8px;font:12px monospace;border-radius:4px">
    TEST: ${testInfo.title} | ${new Date().toISOString()}
  </div>`;
  await using _meta = await page.screencast.showOverlay(metaHtml);

  await page.screencast.showChapter('Step 2: Checkout', { duration: 2000 });
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /checkout/i }).click();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Awaiting `showChapter()` only confirms the overlay was injected — not that its fade-out animation has completed. If the next action should occur after the slate is fully visible (for a polished recording), add a `page.waitForTimeout(duration)` after the call; this is one of the rare legitimate uses of an explicit sleep. Overlays add visual noise if the same recording is used for accessibility audits.

---

### Pattern 248: `browserContext.debugger` — Programmatic Step-Through Debugging (v1.59+) [official]

`browserContext.debugger` exposes a `Debugger` instance that lets test code pause and step through Playwright actions without using the `--debug` CLI flag or inserting `page.pause()` calls. `debugger.requestPause()` sets a "pause before next statement" flag; the next Playwright action halts before execution. `debugger.pausedDetails()` returns the current pause position (file, line, column, title) or `null` when running. `debugger.next()` steps to the following action; `debugger.resume()` continues normally. The `'pausedstatechanged'` event fires on every paused/resumed transition.

```typescript
// e2e/debug/conditional-pause.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('pause on unexpected JS error for live inspection', async ({ page, context }, testInfo) => {
  const dbg = context.debugger;
  let errorCount = 0;

  // Request a pause whenever the page fires a JS error
  page.on('pageerror', async (err) => {
    errorCount++;
    console.error('[pageerror]', err.message);
    // Only pause in headed / interactive debug sessions — never in headless CI
    const isInteractive = process.env.PWDEBUG === '1' &&
      testInfo.project.use.headless === false;
    if (isInteractive) await dbg.requestPause();
  });

  dbg.on('pausedstatechanged', () => {
    const details = dbg.pausedDetails();
    if (details) {
      console.log(`Paused at: ${details.file}:${details.line} — "${details.title}"`);
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /refresh data/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('table')).toBeVisible();

  if (errorCount > 0) await dbg.resume(); // ensure test always continues
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `requestPause()` only works meaningfully in headed mode or `--debug=cli`; in headless CI, the next action blocks indefinitely waiting for a resume signal that never arrives. Always guard `requestPause()` behind `process.env.PWDEBUG` or an explicit `headless !== false` check. `page.pause()` is simpler for ad-hoc debugging; `browserContext.debugger` is for programmatic, condition-triggered pausing where the test code itself decides when to interrupt.

---

### Pattern 249: `page.pickLocator()` / `page.cancelPickLocator()` — Interactive Locator Discovery (v1.59+) [official]

`page.pickLocator()` activates an interactive pick mode: hovering over elements highlights them and displays the recommended Playwright locator string. Clicking an element deactivates the mode and resolves the returned `Promise<Locator>` with a `Locator` object pointing to the clicked element. `page.cancelPickLocator()` cancels an active pick session and is a no-op when no session is active. This API enables developer scripts that capture locators dynamically rather than hardcoding them, and integrates with Playwright's code-generation workflow.

```typescript
// scripts/interactive-locator-capture.ts
// Run: npx tsx scripts/interactive-locator-capture.ts
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';

async function captureLocators() {
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto(process.env.APP_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000');

  console.log('Click any element to capture its locator (5 captures total).');

  const captured: string[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    // Enter pick mode — blocks until user clicks an element
    const locator = await page.pickLocator();
    const locatorStr = locator.toString();
    console.log(`[${i + 1}/5] Captured: ${locatorStr}`);
    captured.push(locatorStr);
  }

  console.log('\nAdd these to your POM:');
  captured.forEach((l) => console.log(`  ${l}`));

  await browser.close();
}

captureLocators().catch(console.error);
```

**Tradeoff:** `pickLocator()` is a development-time tool — never call it in a CI spec file since it requires user interaction and blocks indefinitely without a click. The returned `Locator` reflects Playwright's current best-practice recommendations (typically `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, or `getByText`) but may need manual adjustment for app-specific locator conventions that deviate from ARIA patterns.

---

### Pattern 250: `await using` with Playwright Disposables — Automatic Cleanup for Recording and Route Handles (v1.59+) [official]

Several Playwright v1.59+ APIs return `Promise<Disposable>` objects, supporting TypeScript's `await using` syntax (TC39 Explicit Resource Management, Stage 4). When a variable is declared with `await using`, the runtime calls its `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` method automatically at the end of the enclosing block — even if an error is thrown — eliminating try/finally teardown boilerplate. Applicable APIs include `screencast.start()`, `screencast.showActions()`, `screencast.showOverlay()`, `page.exposeFunction()`, `page.addInitScript()`, and `page.route()`.

```typescript
// e2e/screencast/disposable-cleanup.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs/promises';

test('all disposables cleaned up automatically even on assertion failure', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // Each 'await using' calls [Symbol.asyncDispose] at block end — order is LIFO
  await using _sc = await page.screencast.start({
    path: testInfo.outputPath('test-recording.webm'),
    size: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
  });

  await using _actions = await page.screencast.showActions({ duration: 600 });

  // page.route() also returns Disposable in v1.59+ — auto-removed at block end
  await using _route = await page.route('**/api/flags', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({ json: { newCheckout: true } });
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByText(/new checkout/i)).toBeVisible();

  // _route.dispose() → removes route intercept
  // _actions.dispose() → stops action annotations
  // _sc.dispose() → finalizes video file
  // All called automatically in LIFO order, even if the assertion above threw
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `await using` requires TypeScript 5.2+ and `"lib": ["ES2022", "ESNext.Disposable"]` in `tsconfig.json`. On older TypeScript or without the correct lib entry, `[Symbol.asyncDispose]` resolves to `any` and cleanup silently never fires. Teams on TypeScript < 5.2 must use explicit `try/finally` with `await disposable.dispose()`. Never assign a disposable to a plain `const` variable — it will not be auto-disposed even though no compile error is raised.

---

### Pattern 251: `testConfig.webServer.wait` with Named Capture Groups — Dynamic Port Binding (v1.57+) [official]

The `webServer.wait` field accepts `{ stdout: RegExp, stderr: RegExp }`. When the server's stdout/stderr matches the pattern, Playwright marks the server as ready. Named capture groups are automatically promoted to environment variables using SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE keys. For example, `/Listening on port (?<app_port>\d+)/` exports `process.env.APP_PORT`. This enables dynamic port assignment (port 0) to eliminate port-conflict flakiness in parallel CI without a separate output-parsing script.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'node server.js --port 0',  // OS assigns a free port
    wait: {
      // Named capture group 'app_port' → process.env.APP_PORT after server starts
      stdout: /Server running on port (?<app_port>\d+)/,
    },
    timeout: 30_000,
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
  use: {
    // process.env.APP_PORT is populated AFTER webServer starts —
    // use a lazy arrow function so it is evaluated at test time, not config load time
    baseURL: () => `http://localhost:${process.env.APP_PORT ?? 3000}`,
  },
});

// In any test — dynamic port is transparent
// test('homepage loads', async ({ page }) => {
//   await page.goto('/');  // uses lazy baseURL
// });
```

**Tradeoff:** Named capture group promotion only works via the `webServer.wait` field — the legacy `url` readiness check does not promote groups. The env var is written at server-ready time, *after* `playwright.config.ts` is evaluated; referencing it as a plain string in `use.baseURL` captures `undefined` at module load. Always use a function (`() => ...`) for `baseURL` when relying on `wait` capture groups to defer evaluation. Group names are upper-cased and non-alphanumeric characters become underscores.

---

### Pattern 252: `testProject.workers` — Per-Project Worker Concurrency (v1.52+) [official]

`testProject.workers` overrides the global `workers` setting for a single project, allowing heavy E2E projects to run with fewer parallel workers while fast API or unit projects use more. Without per-project control, a global `workers: 4` setting splits resources equally, under-utilizing fast projects or overwhelming stateful ones. Setting `workers: 1` on a specific project serializes only that project without disabling parallelism elsewhere.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: 4,  // global default applied to projects without an override
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'api-smoke',
      testMatch: '**/*.api.spec.ts',
      workers: 8,   // API tests are fast + I/O-bound — use more concurrency
    },
    {
      name: 'checkout-e2e',
      testMatch: '**/checkout/**/*.spec.ts',
      workers: 1,   // checkout modifies shared cart state — serialize to prevent conflicts
    },
    {
      name: 'dashboard-e2e',
      testMatch: '**/dashboard/**/*.spec.ts',
      // No override — inherits global workers: 4
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Per-project `workers` values are independent limits, not slices of a shared pool. Setting `workers: 8` on two projects simultaneously may consume 16 logical workers on a 4-core machine, causing CPU contention and slowdown. On self-hosted CI with constrained resources, prefer a global percentage (`workers: '50%'`) and use `workers: 1` only for explicitly serial projects rather than inflating worker counts across multiple projects simultaneously.

---

### Pattern 253: Cookie `partitionKey` — CHIPS Third-Party Cookie Isolation (v1.54+) [official]

Playwright v1.54 added `partitionKey` to `browserContext.addCookies()`, `browserContext.cookies()`, and `browserContext.storageState()`. The `partitionKey` maps to the Cookies Having Independent Partitioned State (CHIPS) spec, which isolates third-party cookies by the top-level site that set them. In tests embedding third-party widgets (payment iframes, analytics, embedded auth), cookies set by the third-party origin must be visible only when accessed from the correct top-level site. Setting `partitionKey` explicitly in test cookies ensures this partitioning behavior is faithfully simulated.

```typescript
// e2e/auth/third-party-widget.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment widget cookie is scoped to checkout partition only', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // Simulate payment processor setting a partitioned session cookie
  await context.addCookies([
    {
      name: 'psp-session',
      value: 'tok_test_abc123',
      domain: 'payments.example.com',
      path: '/',
      secure: true,
      // Cookie only visible when the top-level origin is store.example.com
      partitionKey: 'https://store.example.com',
    },
  ]);

  await page.goto('https://store.example.com/checkout');
  // payments.example.com iframe should receive the partitioned cookie
  const paymentFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[src*="payments.example.com"]');
  await expect(paymentFrame.getByText(/card details/i)).toBeVisible();

  // Verify the cookie does NOT leak to a different top-level context
  const cookiesForOtherSite = await context.cookies('https://other-store.example.com');
  const pspCookie = cookiesForOtherSite.find((c) => c.name === 'psp-session');
  expect(pspCookie).toBeUndefined();  // partition isolation confirmed
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `partitionKey` is only meaningful when testing genuine CHIPS-partitioned cookie behavior. For ordinary first-party cookie testing, omit `partitionKey` entirely — adding it to first-party cookies changes their semantics. CHIPS enforcement depends on Chromium's implementation of the `Partitioned` cookie attribute; confirm your Playwright version's bundled Chromium supports it before adding `partitionKey` to a baseline auth fixture.

---

### Pattern 254: `test.step({ box: true })` — Collapsing Noisy Helper Steps in Traces (v1.51+) [official]

The `box: true` option collapses a `test.step()` block and all its inner steps into a single entry in the HTML report and trace viewer. Only the boxed step's title and pass/fail status are shown; inner actions are hidden from the trace. This is ideal for setup helpers, fixture actions, and validation utilities that generate many low-signal trace entries. Without boxing, a `login()` helper that calls `goto`, two `fill()` calls, `click`, and `waitForURL` produces 5+ trace entries before the actual test assertions even begin.

```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/auth.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  authenticatedPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // 'box: true' collapses the entire login sequence into one trace entry
    await base.step('login as test user', async () => {
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill('user@example.com');
      await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill('password123');
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
      await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
    }, { box: true });

    await use(page);
  },
});

// e2e/dashboard/widgets.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/auth.fixture';

test('dashboard renders all widgets after login', async ({ authenticatedPage: page }) => {
  // Trace shows: [login as test user ✓] then the actual test actions
  // NOT: [goto] [fill email] [fill password] [click sign in] [waitForURL] ...
  await expect(page.getByRole('region', { name: /analytics/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('region', { name: /recent activity/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Boxed steps hide ALL inner steps from the report — including failures. If an assertion inside a boxed step fails, the trace shows the boxed step as failed but does not reveal which inner action triggered the failure. Use boxing only for stable, hardened helpers where the error message alone is sufficient for diagnosis. Never box steps containing assertions you need to distinguish in failure reports during active development.

---

### Pattern 255: `locator.drop()` — Simulating External File and Clipboard Drop Events (v1.60+) [official]

`locator.drop(payload, options)` simulates a drag-and-drop event onto an element as if files or clipboard data originated from outside the browser window. The `payload.files` property accepts file paths or `Buffer` objects; `payload.data` accepts a MIME-type-to-content map for clipboard payloads. This is distinct from `locator.dragTo()` (which drags between two elements within the page) and from `page.setInputFiles()` (which sets a file input's value directly without drag events). `drop()` is the correct API for file upload drop zones and rich-text paste-via-drop flows.

```typescript
// e2e/upload/drop-zone.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as path from 'path';

test('drop CSV file onto upload zone renders parsed rows', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/data-import');
  const dropZone = page.getByRole('region', { name: /drop files here/i });

  await dropZone.drop({
    files: [path.resolve('fixtures/sample-data.csv')],
  });

  // Confirm application-level result — not just that drop() resolved
  await expect(page.getByText(/sample-data\.csv/)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('row')).toHaveCount(6);  // header + 5 data rows
});

test('drop rich-text clipboard data onto content editor', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/editor');
  const editor = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /content editor/i });

  await editor.drop({
    data: {
      'text/plain': 'Hello world',
      'text/html': '<b>Hello</b> <em>world</em>',
    },
  });

  // Editor should prefer the richer HTML MIME type
  await expect(editor.locator('b')).toHaveText('Hello');
  await expect(editor.locator('em')).toHaveText('world');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The drop target's JavaScript must call `event.preventDefault()` on `dragover`; without it, the browser discards the `drop` event entirely and `drop()` resolves silently with no error. If `drop()` appears to have no effect, add a `page.on('console')` listener to verify `dragover` is handled. `drop()` with `files` bypasses the OS file chooser entirely — it does not exercise the `<input type="file">` selection path, so use `page.setInputFiles()` when testing the file input itself.

---

### Pattern 256: `page.clearConsoleMessages()` / `page.clearPageErrors()` — Per-Step Error Monitoring in Long Tests (v1.59+) [official]

`page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` maintain rolling buffers of up to 200 messages accumulated since page creation. In long tests that perform multiple logical operations, the buffer fills with messages from early steps that are irrelevant to later assertions. `page.clearConsoleMessages()` and `page.clearPageErrors()` reset the buffers at any point, enabling per-operation error isolation without spinning up a new page instance. These methods are synchronous and return `void`.

```typescript
// e2e/checkout/step-error-monitoring.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('no JS errors occur during any checkout step', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/cart');

  // Step 1: cart → shipping — clear BEFORE measuring this step
  page.clearPageErrors();
  page.clearConsoleMessages();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /proceed to shipping/i }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/checkout/shipping');
  expect(page.pageErrors(), 'Cart step produced JS errors').toHaveLength(0);

  // Step 2: shipping → payment — clear again for this step's isolation
  page.clearPageErrors();
  await page.getByLabel(/street address/i).fill('123 Test St');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /continue to payment/i }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/checkout/payment');
  expect(page.pageErrors(), 'Shipping step produced JS errors').toHaveLength(0);

  // Step 3: payment page console error check
  page.clearConsoleMessages();
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  const consoleErrors = page.consoleMessages().filter((m) => m.type() === 'error');
  expect(consoleErrors, 'Payment page console errors').toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `clearConsoleMessages()` and `clearPageErrors()` are synchronous and cannot be awaited. Always call them *before* the operation you want to measure — clearing after an async action risks discarding messages that arrived during the action itself. There is no `clearRequests()` equivalent for `page.requests()`; use an array-length baseline index for network request isolation (see Pattern 259).

---

### Pattern 257: Test Agents Workflow (`npx playwright init-agents`) — AI-Assisted Spec Generation (v1.56+) [official]

`npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude` (or `--loop=vscode`, `--loop=opencode`) generates three static agent definition files: a Planner (explores the app and produces a markdown test plan), a Generator (converts the plan to executable specs with live selector verification), and a Healer (runs failing specs and auto-suggests locator/wait repairs). Re-running `init-agents` after a Playwright update refreshes the embedded instructions to stay synchronized with the current API surface. The generated specs are drafts — always review assertions before committing.

```bash
# One-time project setup — generates agent definition files
npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude
# Output: .github/playwright-planner.md, playwright-generator.md, playwright-healer.md
```

```typescript
// tests/seed.spec.ts — the Planner executes this to bootstrap its session
// Keep it minimal: establish auth context so Planner explores authenticated pages
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('seed: authenticated context for agent exploration', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel(/email/i).fill(process.env.SEED_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel(/password/i).fill(process.env.SEED_PASS!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
  // Planner now runs in an authenticated session to map the app
});

// After Planner produces specs/checkout-flow.md, run the Generator:
// "Generate Playwright tests from specs/checkout-flow.md"
// After Generator creates tests, run the Healer:
// npx playwright test --project=e2e > results.json → pass results to Healer for repair
```

**Tradeoff:** Agent-generated tests require human review before committing — the Healer can "fix" a test by weakening assertions to match broken behavior rather than surfacing a real defect. Treat generated specs as first drafts: verify every assertion the Generator creates and every patch the Healer proposes. `init-agents` output is static documentation, not live tooling; the agents use your installed AI loop to execute the embedded instructions at authoring time.

---

### Pattern 258: Fixture `{ box: true }` — Invisible Infrastructure Fixtures in Reports (v1.51+) [official]

The `{ box: true }` option in a fixture's options object hides all the fixture's setup and teardown actions from the HTML report and trace viewer — they collapse into a single named entry. This mirrors `test.step({ box: true })` but applies to the fixture lifecycle rather than a step block. Boxed fixtures are ideal for database seeders, server stubs, and auth helpers whose internals are stable and whose trace entries add noise without diagnostic value.

```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/db-seed.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type DbFixtures = { seededDb: { userId: string; orderId: string } };

export const test = base.extend<DbFixtures>({
  seededDb: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // All four DB calls appear as one "seededDb" trace entry — not four separate ones
      const userId = await createTestUser();
      const productId = await createTestProduct();
      const orderId = await createTestOrder({ userId, productId });
      await seedInventory(productId, 10);

      await use({ userId, orderId });

      // Teardown is also hidden under a single "seededDb teardown" trace entry
      await deleteOrder(orderId);
      await deleteUser(userId);
    },
    { box: true },  // hides all inner actions from HTML report and trace viewer
  ],
});

// Usage — trace shows [seededDb ✓] then actual test actions
// import { test } from '../fixtures/db-seed.fixture';
// test('order summary shows correct items', async ({ page, seededDb }) => {
//   await page.goto(`/orders/${seededDb.orderId}`);
//   await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order #/i })).toBeVisible();
// });
```

**Tradeoff:** Like boxed steps, boxed fixtures conceal the specific action that fails. If `createTestUser()` throws a DB connection error, the trace shows "seededDb setup failed" without the inner stack location. Reserve `{ box: true }` for fixture code that is stable and well-tested. During fixture development, remove `box: true` temporarily to preserve full trace visibility until the fixture is hardened.

---

### Pattern 259: `page.requests()` — Synchronous Recent Request Inspection for Post-Hoc Auditing (v1.56+) [official]

`page.requests()` returns a snapshot of up to 100 recent network requests as `Request` objects without requiring a pre-registered `page.on('request')` listener. This enables post-hoc request auditing after an interaction completes, without modifying the test setup to add listeners before the action. Use an array-length baseline captured before the operation to isolate requests generated by a specific user action, since the buffer is append-only and cannot be cleared.

```typescript
// e2e/analytics/event-tracking.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('add-to-cart button fires exactly one analytics event', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/product/widget-pro');

  // Capture baseline before the action — requests() buffer is NOT clearable
  const baseline = page.requests().length;

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i }).click();
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Slice to only requests generated after the button click
  const newRequests = page.requests().slice(baseline);
  const analyticsHits = newRequests.filter((r) =>
    r.url().includes('analytics.example.com/event')
  );

  expect(analyticsHits).toHaveLength(1);
  const body = JSON.parse(analyticsHits[0].postData() ?? '{}');
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ event: 'add_to_cart', productId: 'widget-pro' });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.requests()` is a point-in-time snapshot — requests fired after the call are not captured. The 100-request buffer can overflow in network-heavy SPAs, causing the oldest requests to fall off. For exhaustive tracking, prefer `page.on('request', handler)` registered before navigation. Unlike `consoleMessages` and `pageErrors`, `requests()` has no `clearRequests()` companion — the baseline-index pattern is the only isolation mechanism.

---

### Pattern 260: Fixture `{ auto: true }` — Global Test Lifecycle Hooks via Auto-Fixtures [official]

Fixtures with `{ auto: true }` run for every test using the fixture module, regardless of whether the test explicitly requests them. Combined with `testInfo`, auto-fixtures implement cross-cutting behaviors: attaching console errors on failure, recording per-test performance metrics, or resetting shared resources after each test. Unlike `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks (which require co-location in the spec file), a single auto-fixture defined in a shared fixture file applies globally without modifying any test file.

```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/auto-error-monitor.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  // Runs before and after every test — no test needs to declare it
  _errorMonitor: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
      const jsErrors: string[] = [];
      const consoleErrors: string[] = [];

      page.on('pageerror', (err) => jsErrors.push(err.message));
      page.on('console', (msg) => {
        if (msg.type() === 'error') consoleErrors.push(msg.text());
      });

      await use(undefined);  // test body executes here

      // On a passing test that still had JS/console errors — attach as diagnostic warning
      if (testInfo.status === 'passed' && (jsErrors.length || consoleErrors.length)) {
        if (jsErrors.length) {
          await testInfo.attach('js-errors', {
            body: jsErrors.join('\n'), contentType: 'text/plain',
          });
        }
        if (consoleErrors.length) {
          await testInfo.attach('console-errors', {
            body: consoleErrors.join('\n'), contentType: 'text/plain',
          });
        }
      }
    },
    { auto: true },  // fires for every test using this fixture module
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** An `{ auto: true }` fixture that throws during teardown will mark an otherwise-passing test as failed. Wrap teardown logic in try/catch and use `testInfo.attach()` to surface information rather than throwing. The auto-fixture's setup phase runs even for `test.skip()` tests — add an early `if (testInfo.expectedStatus === 'skipped') return;` guard if setup has side effects. Use `{ auto: true, scope: 'worker' }` to run the fixture once per worker instead of once per test when setup is expensive.
