## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 291 — `tracing.startHar()` / `tracing.stopHar()` — First-Class HAR Recording via Tracing API (v1.60+) [official]

Playwright v1.60 promotes HAR recording to a first-class tracing operation. `context.tracing.startHar(path, options)` begins capturing all network activity into an HTTP Archive file, while `context.tracing.stopHar()` flushes and closes it. Options include `content` (`'omit'` | `'embed'` | `'attach'`), `mode` (`'full'` | `'minimal'`), `urlFilter` to restrict which URLs are captured, and `resourcesDir` for external response body storage when using `content: 'attach'`. Only one active HAR per `BrowserContext` is allowed simultaneously. The resulting `.har` or `.zip` file is consumable directly by `context.routeFromHAR()` for deterministic replay.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow — record + replay HAR', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // Start HAR recording; embed small resources, attach large ones separately
  await context.tracing.startHar('checkout.har.zip', {
    content: 'embed',
    mode: 'full',
    urlFilter: '**/api/**',
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();

  await context.tracing.stopHar();

  // Later test: replay from recorded HAR for deterministic offline verification
  await context.routeFromHAR('checkout.har.zip', { url: '**/api/**', notFound: 'fallthrough' });
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `mode: 'minimal'` records only data needed to reconstruct routing (method, URL, headers, status) and significantly reduces file size, but omits response bodies — use `mode: 'full'` when you intend to replay with `routeFromHAR()`. Only one HAR recording per `BrowserContext` is permitted; calling `startHar()` a second time without `stopHar()` throws. The `urlFilter` option does not suppress network traffic — it controls what gets *written* to the file, so sensitive credentials in unfiltered responses will still be captured.

---

### Pattern 292 — `browser.on('context')` — Centralized Instrumentation for Every New BrowserContext [official]

The `browser.on('context', (context) => {})` event, added in v1.60, fires synchronously whenever a new `BrowserContext` is created on the browser instance. This provides a single attachment point to install route handlers, storage state, or listeners on every context without modifying individual test fixtures. The event fires before the context is returned to the caller, so handlers installed inside the callback are active before the first `newPage()` call on that context.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — global setup via browser event
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({ use: { baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000' } });

// fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  browser: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    // Intercept all API errors globally on every context this browser creates
    browser.on('context', (ctx) => {
      ctx.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
        const response = await route.fetch();
        if (response.status() >= 500) {
          console.error(`API 5xx on ${route.request().url()}: ${response.status()}`);
        }
        await route.fulfill({ response });
      });
    });
    await use(browser);
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `browser.on('context')` handler fires for *all* contexts on the browser instance, including any ephemeral contexts created by internal Playwright machinery or third-party plugins. Guard instrumentation with `if (!ctx.pages().length)` style checks only when you need to exclude tool-created contexts. The handler is synchronous but the body can be async — however, `context.route()` itself returns a Promise that must be awaited; fire-and-forget async calls inside the handler may race with the first `page.goto()`.

---

### Pattern 293 — `browserContext.on('download')` / `'pageload'` / `'pageclose'` — Context-Level Page Lifecycle Monitoring (v1.60+) [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds six context-level lifecycle events that mirror page-level events but aggregate across every page opened in the context: `download`, `frameattached`, `framedetached`, `framenavigated`, `pageclose`, and `pageload`. These eliminate the need to attach the same listener to every `page` object individually — a single handler on the context covers all current and future pages. The `pageload` event fires when *any* page in the context reaches `load` state; `pageclose` fires when a page is closed (whether by test code or triggered by the application).

```typescript
test('multi-tab download tracking', async ({ context, page }) => {
  const downloads: string[] = [];

  // Single attachment point covers all tabs opened during the test
  context.on('download', (download) => {
    downloads.push(download.suggestedFilename());
  });

  context.on('pageclose', (closedPage) => {
    console.log(`Tab closed: ${closedPage.url()}`);
  });

  // Action opens a new tab that triggers a download
  await page.goto('/reports');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export All' }).click();

  // New tab may open and then auto-close after download starts
  await expect.poll(() => downloads.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(downloads[0]).toMatch(/^report-\d{4}\.csv$/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Context-level `frameattached` fires for *every* iframe on every page, including third-party ad iframes and Playwright's own internal frames (used by `addLocatorHandler`). Filter by `frame.parentFrame() !== null && frame.page() === targetPage` before acting on frames. The `pageload` event is equivalent to `page.on('load')` but aggregated — it does not equate to `'networkidle'`; follow up with `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` if API calls after load are required for assertions.

---

### Pattern 294 — `expect(locator).toContainClass(name)` — Partial CSS Class Membership Assertions (v1.52+) [official]

`expect(locator).toContainClass(expected)` asserts that an element's `classList` contains *all* classes listed in `expected` — as a space-separated string, a `RegExp`, or an array of strings for multi-element assertions. Unlike `toHaveClass()`, which matches the full class attribute, `toContainClass()` succeeds as long as the specified classes are a subset of the element's actual classes. Passing an array asserts one entry per element in the locator's matched set, enabling bulk class checks across repeated elements in a list.

```typescript
test('product card state classes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/catalog');

  // ✅ toContainClass passes even if element also has 'card shadow-lg rounded'
  const featured = page.getByTestId('product-card').filter({ hasText: 'Featured' });
  await expect(featured).toContainClass('featured');

  // ✅ Multi-class check — all three must be present
  const selectedRow = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Selected Item' });
  await expect(selectedRow).toContainClass('row selected highlighted');

  // ✅ Array form: assert class per matched element (index 0 → first card, etc.)
  const cards = page.getByTestId('product-card');
  await expect(cards).toContainClass(['card available', 'card out-of-stock', 'card available']);

  // ❌ toHaveClass would FAIL if element has extra classes beyond 'featured'
  // await expect(featured).toHaveClass('featured');  // matches EXACT class string
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toContainClass()` with an array argument asserts *exactly as many elements* as array entries — if the locator matches more elements than the array length, the assertion fails. Use `locator.first()` / `locator.nth(n)` to target specific elements when the list size is variable. The assertion retries until the timeout elapses (auto-waiting) so transient CSS class transitions (e.g., loading spinners adding `'loading'` before `'loaded'`) will be tolerated and eventually pass once the target class arrives.

---

### Pattern 295 — `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(message)` — Asserting ARIA Error Messages on Form Controls (v1.50+) [official]

`expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(message)` asserts the *computed* ARIA error message for a form control — the string resolved by following the `aria-errormessage` attribute to its referenced element and reading that element's text content. This is distinct from `aria-describedby` (general descriptions) and `title` attributes. The assertion accepts a string (exact or substring via `toContainText` semantics), a `RegExp`, or an object with `{ ignoreCase: true }`. It retries until the message matches or the timeout expires, making it reliable for async validation patterns that show error text after a server response.

```typescript
test('form validation shows accessible error on submit', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  // Submit empty form to trigger server-side validation
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign Up' }).click();

  // Assert the accessible error message on the email field
  const emailInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Email address' });
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Please enter a valid email address');

  // Assert case-insensitively for flexible server message matching
  const passwordInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Password' });
  await expect(passwordInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(
    /at least 8 characters/i,
  );

  // Assert field is invalid so assistive tech announces it
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The assertion resolves `aria-errormessage` by ID lookup (`getElementById`), not by DOM proximity — the error `<span>` must have an `id` matching the input's `aria-errormessage` value. If the error element is rendered conditionally (only in DOM when an error exists), the assertion will fail with "element not found" rather than "error message mismatch" during the period before the element mounts. Combine with `await expect(errorSpan).toBeVisible()` in a `beforeEach` gate when testing async server-validated forms to get clearer failure messages.

---

### Pattern 296 — `locator.describe(label)` / `locator.description()` — Human-Readable Locator Labels for Traces and Reports (v1.53+/v1.57+) [official]

`locator.describe(label)` attaches a human-readable string label to any locator. The label appears in the Playwright trace viewer, HTML reports, and step titles, replacing the raw CSS/ARIA selector with an intent-driven name. The method returns the original locator unchanged (fluent chaining), so all selector mechanics are unaffected. `locator.description()` (v1.57+) retrieves the currently set label, returning `null` if none was set — useful for dynamically generating report annotations from locator metadata.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('order summary displays correct totals', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  // Describe locators for trace clarity — raw selector is still used for matching
  const subtotalCell = page
    .getByRole('cell', { name: /^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/ })
    .first()
    .describe('Cart subtotal cell');

  const taxCell = page
    .getByRole('cell', { name: /^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/ })
    .nth(1)
    .describe('Tax amount cell');

  const totalCell = page
    .getByRole('cell', { name: /^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/ })
    .last()
    .describe('Order total cell');

  // These assertions appear in traces as "Cart subtotal cell", "Tax amount cell", etc.
  await expect(subtotalCell).toBeVisible();
  await expect(taxCell).toBeVisible();
  await expect(totalCell).toBeVisible();

  // Dynamic use: read label for step annotation
  await test.step(`Verify ${totalCell.description()} is non-zero`, async () => {
    await expect(totalCell).not.toHaveText('$0.00');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.describe()` labels affect only the display layer (trace viewer, HTML reports) — they have no effect on selector resolution, `waitFor`, or assertion retries. Labels are not serialized across `page.evaluate()` or `frame.locator()` — if you derive a new locator from a described one (e.g., `describedLocator.locator('.child')`), the child locator has no description. Re-describe derived locators explicitly in complex selector chains to maintain trace readability.

---

### Pattern 297 — `locator.click({ steps: N })` / `locator.dragTo(target, { steps: N })` — Granular Mouse-Move Interpolation for Canvas and Drag Interactions (v1.57+) [official]

The `steps` option on `locator.click()` and `locator.dragTo()` controls how many intermediate `mousemove` events are dispatched between the current pointer position and the target. The default is `1` (a single `mousemove` directly to the destination). Increasing `steps` inserts evenly spaced `mousemove` events along the linear path, which is required for canvas-based drawing tools, SVG path editors, and drag-to-resize handles that compute deltas between consecutive `mousemove` events rather than reading the final position.

```typescript
test('canvas drawing tool traces a diagonal stroke', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/canvas-editor');

  const canvas = page.getByRole('img', { name: 'Drawing canvas' });

  // Select the pencil tool
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pencil' }).click();

  // Click with 10 intermediate steps — canvas onmousemove fires 10 times along the path
  await canvas.click({
    position: { x: 50, y: 50 },
    steps: 10,
  });

  // Drag with 20 steps to draw a diagonal line — each step triggers a delta calculation
  const handle = page.getByTestId('resize-handle');
  await handle.dragTo(page.getByTestId('resize-target'), { steps: 20 });

  // Verify stroke count or canvas pixel changes
  const strokeCount = await page.evaluate(() => window.__strokeCount__);
  expect(strokeCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `steps` emits synchronous `mousemove` events in rapid succession within a single CDP input dispatch — there is no time delay between steps. If the application uses `requestAnimationFrame` throttling to rate-limit processing of `mousemove` events (only handling one per animation frame), many intermediate steps may be silently dropped. For rAF-throttled drawing tools, prefer `page.mouse.move(x, y, { steps: N })` with `page.waitForTimeout(16)` between moves, or use `page.clock.install()` + `page.clock.runFor()` to control frame timing.

---

### Pattern 298 — `testProject.workers` — Per-Project Worker Concurrency Caps for Shared-Resource Projects (v1.52+) [official]

`testProject.workers` sets an upper bound on the number of Playwright worker processes that may run tests from that specific project simultaneously. It accepts an absolute integer or a percentage string (e.g., `'50%'` of logical CPUs). The global `testConfig.workers` cap still applies across all projects; `testProject.workers` adds a *per-project* sub-limit. This allows high-parallelism projects (e.g., unit-style API tests) to share the worker pool with low-concurrency projects (e.g., tests against a single shared staging database) without complex sharding or separate config files.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: 8, // global cap: 8 workers total across all projects

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'api-tests',
      testDir: './tests/api',
      // No per-project limit — can use all 8 workers
    },
    {
      name: 'e2e-shared-db',
      testDir: './tests/e2e',
      workers: 2,  // Only 2 workers ever run e2e tests simultaneously
      // Prevents contention on the shared staging database seeded in globalSetup
    },
    {
      name: 'visual-regression',
      testDir: './tests/visual',
      workers: 1,  // Run visuals serially — screenshot comparison needs deterministic GPU
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `testProject.workers` constrains concurrency but does not affect test *distribution* — tests from the constrained project may still be interleaved with other projects' tests on the remaining workers. If your constrained project requires an exclusive database lock for its entire run (not just per-test), use a `globalSetup` mutex file or switch to `fullyParallel: false` for that project. Setting `workers: 1` on a project guarantees serial execution within the project but not isolation from other projects' workers running concurrently on the same machine.

---

### Pattern 299 — `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` — Enforcing Zero-Flakiness Policy in CI (v1.52+) [official]

`testConfig.failOnFlakyTests: true` causes the `playwright test` process to exit with a non-zero code if any tests are detected as flaky during the run (i.e., they passed after one or more retries). When `retries` is zero, no test can be flaky by definition — enable `retries: 1` or higher in CI alongside `failOnFlakyTests: true` to allow one retry for genuine transient failures while still failing the build when flakiness is detected. The flag is independent of the overall pass/fail status — the build fails even if all tests ultimately pass after retries.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Allow 1 retry to distinguish genuine failures from transient network blips
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,

  // Fail CI build when any test passes only after retrying — surfacing flakiness
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',  // Capture trace on the retry run for diagnosis
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `failOnFlakyTests` is most useful when `retries >= 1` — without retries there are no "passed after retry" outcomes to detect. Setting `retries: 2` with `failOnFlakyTests: true` means a test that fails twice and passes on the third attempt counts as flaky (build fails), whereas a test that fails once and passes on the first retry also counts as flaky. Teams should tune `retries` carefully: too many retries mask true flakiness, too few make transient infrastructure failures indistinguishable from code bugs.

---

### Pattern 300 — `testConfig.captureGitInfo` — Embedding Commit Metadata in Test Reports (v1.51+) [official]

`testConfig.captureGitInfo` enriches the Playwright HTML report and test result metadata with the current git commit hash, author, timestamp, and optionally the full diff. This data surfaces in the HTML report header and is available programmatically via the reporter API's `suite.entries()` metadata. Enabling `{ commit: true, diff: true }` in CI provides full traceability from a test failure back to the exact code change that introduced it, without cross-referencing CI logs.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  captureGitInfo: {
    commit: true,  // captures hash, author, branch, timestamp
    diff: process.env.CI ? true : false,  // skip diff in local runs (can be large)
  },

  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
    ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results/results.json' }],
  ],
});

// In a custom reporter, read captured metadata:
// class GitReporter implements Reporter {
//   onBegin(config, suite) {
//     const gitInfo = config.metadata?.git;
//     console.log(`Running tests on commit: ${gitInfo?.commit}`);
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** `diff: true` captures the entire `git diff HEAD` at test run time, which can be megabytes for large changesets. The diff is embedded in the report JSON, increasing file size and slowing HTML report generation. For repositories with large binary or generated files, add `.gitattributes` entries (`*.png binary`, `dist/ linguist-generated`) to reduce diff noise, or disable `diff` and rely on CI environment variables (`GITHUB_SHA`, `CI_COMMIT_SHA`) for commit-level traceability instead.

---

### Pattern 301 — `page.requestGC()` — Triggering Garbage Collection for Memory Leak Detection (v1.48+) [official]

`page.requestGC()` asks the V8 JavaScript engine to perform a garbage collection cycle on the page's JS heap. This is not guaranteed to collect all unreachable objects — V8 may schedule collection asynchronously or skip it under memory pressure — but in practice it causes a major GC in Chromium, making `WeakRef` targets eligible for collection immediately. The canonical use case is asserting that application objects (components, event listeners, cached API responses) do not leak across navigation cycles by wrapping suspects in `WeakRef` and verifying they are collected after GC.

```typescript
test('navigating away releases the product detail component', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/123');

  // Plant a WeakRef to the suspect component instance exposed on window
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    // App exposes current route component for testing in non-production builds
    (globalThis as any).__ref = new WeakRef((globalThis as any).__currentComponent);
  });

  // Navigate away — component should be eligible for GC
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Request GC and verify the WeakRef target was collected
  await page.requestGC();

  const leaked = await page.evaluate(() => (globalThis as any).__ref.deref() !== undefined);
  expect(leaked).toBe(false);  // true means the component leaked
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.requestGC()` is only meaningful in Chromium; WebKit and Firefox do not expose a forced GC mechanism through the CDP interface Playwright uses, so the call is a no-op (or silently ignored) on those browsers. The lack of a GC guarantee means a passing assertion (`leaked === false`) is reliable, but a failing assertion should be retried — V8 may genuinely defer collection. Wrap the `requestGC` + `evaluate` check in `expect.poll()` with a short interval to tolerate deferred collection cycles.

---

### Pattern 302 — `page.screencast` + `screencast.onFrame` — Real-Time Frame Capture for Custom Video Processing (v1.59+) [official]

`page.screencast` exposes a first-class screencast API that provides real-time JPEG frame callbacks alongside optional video file output. `screencast.start({ path, onFrame, size, quality })` begins capture; the `onFrame` callback receives `{ data: Buffer, timestamp: number, width: number, height: number }` for every rendered frame. This enables custom screenshot diffing, streaming to external tools, or per-frame assertions without post-processing a video file. `screencast.stop()` finalizes any video file and stops the frame stream.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';

test('loading animation completes within 30 frames', async ({ page }) => {
  const frames: Buffer[] = [];

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Start screencast collecting raw JPEG frames
  await using capture = await page.screencast.start({
    size: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
    quality: 60,
    onFrame: ({ data }) => {
      frames.push(data);
    },
  });

  // Trigger the loading animation
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Load Report' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });

  // Capture is auto-stopped by `await using` block exit
  // Assert the animation resolved within 30 rendered frames
  expect(frames.length).toBeLessThan(30);
  // Optionally save last frame for visual debugging
  if (frames.length > 0) {
    fs.writeFileSync('test-results/last-frame.jpg', frames[frames.length - 1]);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `onFrame` callbacks are invoked synchronously in the CDP event loop — heavy computation (compression, network upload) inside the callback will block frame delivery and cause visible rendering delays in the browser. Offload non-trivial processing to a `Worker` thread or push frames to a queue for async processing. `screencast.start()` returns an async disposable — use `await using` (TypeScript 5.2+) to guarantee `stop()` is called even on test failure; manually call `await capture.stop()` in `afterEach` if targeting environments without `await using` support.

---

### Pattern 303 — `testConfig.webServer.wait` with Regex Named Capture Groups — Dynamic Port Discovery for Dev Servers (v1.57+) [official]

The `wait` field in `testConfig.webServer` accepts a regex applied to the server's stdout. When the regex matches, the server is considered ready. Named capture groups in the regex are automatically promoted to environment variables (upper-cased) — allowing tests to read dynamically assigned ports without a hardcoded `baseURL`. This replaces fragile polling of known ports or custom `waitForPort` scripts.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'node server.js',          // server logs "Listening on port 54321"
    wait: {
      stdout: /Listening on port (?<server_port>\d+)/,
      // Playwright sets process.env.SERVER_PORT = '54321' from the capture group
    },
    timeout: 30_000,
  },

  use: {
    // Read the captured port at config evaluation time
    baseURL: `http://localhost:${process.env.SERVER_PORT ?? 3000}`,
  },
});

// server.js — logs port to stdout for Playwright to capture:
// const port = 0;  // OS assigns a free port
// server.listen(port, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${server.address().port}`));
```

**Tradeoff.** The environment variable set by named capture groups is populated only *after* the webServer process emits the matching output — it is not available at the top-level module evaluation of `playwright.config.ts` but is available when `use.baseURL` is evaluated as a function. Use a factory function for `baseURL` rather than string interpolation at config load time to reliably access the captured value. Named groups must be valid JavaScript identifiers; hyphens or dots in group names cause silent capture failures. Group names are normalized to `UPPER_CASE` — a group named `server_port` sets `process.env.SERVER_PORT`, not `process.env.server_port`.

---

### Pattern 304 — `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` — Page-Level ARIA Snapshot Assertions with `boxes` Coordinates (v1.60+) [official]

`expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` extends the existing `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` assertion to the full page body, capturing the complete accessibility tree from the `<body>` element downward. The v1.60 `boxes: true` option on `page.ariaSnapshot()` appends bounding box data (`[box=x,y,width,height]` in CSS pixels) to each element's ARIA snapshot entry, enabling spatial assertions — for example, verifying that a call-to-action button appears below the fold boundary. The `{ name: 'snapshot.aria.yml' }` form stores the snapshot in a versioned file for change-detection across releases.

```typescript
test('homepage layout matches ARIA snapshot', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // Basic page-level aria snapshot — asserts full accessibility tree structure
  await expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Main menu"
    - main:
      - heading "Welcome to Acme" [level=1]
      - button "Get Started"
    - contentinfo "Footer"
  `);

  // With boxes: capture spatial data for layout regression detection
  const snapshot = await page.ariaSnapshot({ boxes: true, mode: 'default' });
  // snapshot entries contain [box=x,y,width,height] — parse for spatial assertions
  const ctaMatch = snapshot.match(/button "Get Started" \[box=(\d+),(\d+),(\d+),(\d+)\]/);
  if (ctaMatch) {
    const [, , y, , h] = ctaMatch.map(Number);
    expect(y + h).toBeGreaterThan(300);  // CTA is below the hero fold boundary
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` traverses the *entire* page accessibility tree, which can be hundreds of nodes for complex SPAs — the assertion is slower than `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` on a specific region. Use the `depth` option (`page.ariaSnapshot({ depth: 3 })`) to limit traversal when asserting structural layout rather than leaf content. The `boxes` bounding box values are viewport-relative CSS pixels and change when viewport size or zoom level changes — pin `use.viewport` in `playwright.config.ts` to ensure spatial assertions are deterministic across CI environments.

---

### Pattern 305 — `testConfig.updateSourceMethod: '3way'` — Merge-Conflict-Style Snapshot Updates for Team Review (v1.50+) [official]

`testConfig.updateSourceMethod: '3way'` changes how Playwright writes snapshot updates (`--update-snapshots`) into source files. Instead of overwriting the old value, it inserts standard Git merge conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`) around the old and new snapshot values. This enables the team to review snapshot changes using standard merge-conflict IDE tooling (VS Code "Accept Incoming", GitLens diff) before committing — preventing accidental acceptance of incorrect snapshot regressions. The `'patch'` mode (default) generates a `.patch` file for later `git apply`; `'overwrite'` directly replaces values; `'3way'` is the review-friendly middle ground.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — use 3-way for deliberate review of snapshot changes
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // During snapshot update runs, insert merge-conflict markers for human review
  updateSourceMethod: process.env.UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS ? '3way' : 'overwrite',
  updateSnapshots: process.env.UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS ? 'changed' : 'none',
});

// Usage workflow:
// 1. Run:  UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 npx playwright test --update-snapshots
// 2. Open updated .aria.yml / test files in VS Code — conflict markers show old vs new
// 3. Review each change: Accept (new snapshot correct) or Reject (regression found)
// 4. Stage resolved files and commit

// Example conflict marker in a snapshot file after step 1:
// <<<<<<< HEAD (old snapshot)
// - heading "Welcome" [level=1]
// =======
// - heading "Welcome to Acme" [level=1]
// >>>>>>> Updated snapshot
```

**Tradeoff.** `updateSourceMethod: '3way'` requires the test files to be writable and tracked by git — it uses `git merge-file` semantics internally. Untracked or `.gitignore`d snapshot files cause the conflict insertion to fall back to `'overwrite'` silently. The conflict markers make the test file temporarily unparseable by TypeScript, so `tsc --noEmit` will fail until conflicts are resolved — do not run `npm test` again without resolving markers first or CI will report false type errors unrelated to actual test failures.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 45

### Gotcha #100: `expect(locator).toContainClass()` with an array argument fails if the locator matches *more* elements than array entries — excess elements cause an assertion error even if all listed classes are correct [community]

When `toContainClass(['class-a', 'class-b'])` is called and the locator resolves to three elements, Playwright asserts that element[0] contains `'class-a'`, element[1] contains `'class-b'`, and then finds element[2] has no corresponding expected entry — the assertion fails with "expected 2 elements, but got 3". The error message focuses on the count mismatch rather than the class mismatch, which confuses developers who assume the array form is a "match any" check rather than a positional per-element assertion.

```typescript
// ❌ toContainClass array form is POSITIONAL — fails if list has 3 items but array has 2
const items = page.getByRole('listitem');
await expect(items).toContainClass(['active', 'active']);  // FAILS if 3 items exist

// ✅ Scope the locator to the exact count expected, or use individual assertions
const activeItems = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: /Active/ });
await expect(activeItems).toHaveCount(2);
await expect(activeItems).toContainClass(['active', 'active']);

// ✅ Or assert one element at a time for variable-length lists
for (const item of await page.getByRole('listitem').all()) {
  await expect(item).toContainClass('item');  // every item has base class
}
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's multi-element assertion model (`toHaveText`, `toHaveClass`, `toContainClass` with arrays) always performs a *positional* check — the array length must exactly match the locator's resolved element count. This design mirrors `toHaveText(['a', 'b', 'c'])` which checks element[0]='a', element[1]='b', element[2]='c'. The positional contract is intentional: it prevents false-green assertions where "at least two items are active" passes silently when five items become active. The engine resolves the locator count first and validates array length parity before comparing class lists. Use `locator.filter()` to constrain the set before applying the array form. [community]

---

### Gotcha #101: `page.requestGC()` is a no-op in WebKit and Firefox — memory leak tests written exclusively with `requestGC()` produce false-green results on non-Chromium browsers [community]

`page.requestGC()` sends a CDP `HeapProfiler.collectGarbage` command, which is a Chrome DevTools Protocol method. WebKit's WebDriver implementation does not expose an equivalent CDP surface, and Firefox's BiDi/CDP bridge does not implement `HeapProfiler`. Playwright silently ignores the call on non-Chromium browser types rather than throwing, so a test that asserts a `WeakRef` target was collected after `requestGC()` will consistently pass on WebKit because the `WeakRef.deref()` may also return `undefined` — not because GC ran, but because WebKit's own GC happened to run at an opportune moment.

```typescript
// ❌ Platform-agnostic GC test — silently vacuous on WebKit/Firefox
await page.requestGC();
const leaked = await page.evaluate(() => (globalThis as any).__ref.deref() !== undefined);
expect(leaked).toBe(false);  // passes vacuously on WebKit if object happened to be GC'd

// ✅ Gate requestGC memory leak tests to Chromium only
test('memory leak detection (Chromium only)', async ({ page, browserName }) => {
  test.skip(browserName !== 'chromium', 'requestGC() is only meaningful in Chromium');

  await page.goto('/heavy-component');
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    (globalThis as any).__ref = new WeakRef((globalThis as any).__currentComponent);
  });
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.requestGC();

  const leaked = await page.evaluate(() => (globalThis as any).__ref.deref() !== undefined);
  expect(leaked).toBe(false);
});
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's browser abstraction layer maps `page.requestGC()` to `HeapProfiler.collectGarbage` over CDP. CDP is natively supported in Chromium; Playwright emulates a CDP-compatible interface for WebKit and Firefox using their respective DevTools protocols, but `HeapProfiler.collectGarbage` has no equivalent in the WebKit Remote Debugging Protocol or the Firefox BiDi spec. When Playwright encounters an unsupported CDP command on non-Chromium browsers, it either silently no-ops or logs a warning at debug level — it does not throw, preserving cross-browser test compatibility. Memory leak assertions must therefore be explicitly scoped to `browserName === 'chromium'` to be meaningful. [community]

---

### Gotcha #102: `screencast.onFrame` callbacks block the CDP event loop when they perform synchronous I/O — writing frames to disk inside `onFrame` causes visible frame drops in the recorded output [community]

`screencast.onFrame` is called synchronously on every rendered frame within Playwright's CDP event dispatch thread. If the callback performs synchronous file I/O (e.g., `fs.writeFileSync(path, data)`), it blocks the thread for the duration of the write. During this blocking period, new frames queued by the browser's rendering engine cannot be dispatched from the CDP socket buffer. When the thread unblocks, the queued frames are delivered in rapid succession — the resulting video file has irregular timestamps, and frame-count-based assertions (e.g., "animation completed in under 30 frames") become unreliable.

```typescript
// ❌ Synchronous file write inside onFrame blocks CDP event loop — causes frame drops
await page.screencast.start({
  onFrame: ({ data, timestamp }) => {
    fs.writeFileSync(`frames/frame-${timestamp}.jpg`, data);  // BLOCKS CDP thread
  },
});

// ✅ Buffer frames in memory for async processing after screencast stops
const frameQueue: Array<{ data: Buffer; timestamp: number }> = [];
await using capture = await page.screencast.start({
  onFrame: ({ data, timestamp }) => {
    frameQueue.push({ data, timestamp });  // non-blocking in-memory push
  },
});

// ... run test steps ...
// capture auto-stopped by `await using`

// Process frames asynchronously after capture ends
await Promise.all(
  frameQueue.map(({ data, timestamp }) =>
    fs.promises.writeFile(`frames/frame-${timestamp}.jpg`, data)
  )
);
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's CDP client runs on a single Node.js async I/O thread with a synchronous event dispatch model for CDP events — the `onFrame` callback is invoked inline during `CDPSession.on('Page.screencastFrame', ...)` event handling. Node.js's `fs.writeFileSync` blocks the entire event loop, not just the current callback: while the write is in progress, no other I/O, timers, or CDP event callbacks can run. The browser's CDP socket backpressures during this period; frames are not lost but their delivery is delayed, creating timestamp clustering in the output. Async file I/O (`fs.promises.writeFile`) returns immediately to the event loop and performs the write on libuv's thread pool — the CDP event thread remains unblocked, preserving frame cadence. [community]

---

### Gotcha #103: `testConfig.webServer.wait` named capture groups use upper-cased environment variable names — a group named `server_port` sets `process.env.SERVER_PORT`, not `process.env.server_port` [community]

The `wait.stdout` regex named capture group names are transformed to `UPPER_CASE` before being set as environment variables. A group named `(?<my_app_port>\d+)` sets `process.env.MY_APP_PORT`, not `process.env.my_app_port`. This transformation follows the Unix convention for environment variable names but is not prominently documented, and developers who access the captured value via the lowercase name (as used in the regex) will always get `undefined` — causing `baseURL` to silently fall back to a hardcoded port or `undefined`.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — demonstrate the uppercase transformation
export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'node server.js',
    wait: {
      // Named group 'app_port' → process.env.APP_PORT  (UPPERCASE)
      stdout: /Server started on port (?<app_port>\d+)/,
    },
  },
  use: {
    // ❌ WRONG: process.env.app_port is always undefined
    // baseURL: `http://localhost:${process.env.app_port}`,

    // ✅ CORRECT: use UPPER_CASE version of the capture group name
    baseURL: `http://localhost:${process.env.APP_PORT ?? 3000}`,
  },
});
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's webServer implementation normalizes capture group names using `name.toUpperCase()` before calling `process.env[name] = value`. This mirrors POSIX convention where environment variable names are conventionally uppercase, and avoids conflicts with Node.js built-in lowercase env vars (like `path`, `home`). The regex itself uses the lowercase name (JavaScript's `RegExp` named groups are case-sensitive and match the authored case), but the resulting environment variable is always the uppercase equivalent. Developers debugging this issue with `console.log(process.env)` will see the uppercase key in the output — the fix is to always reference the captured value via its upper-cased name. [community]

---

### Gotcha #104: `locator.describe()` labels do not propagate to child locators derived from a described locator — `described.locator('.child')` has no description and appears as raw selectors in traces [community]

When you call `locator.describe('My Button')` and then derive a child locator (`locator.describe('My Button').locator('.icon')`), the child locator has no description. In the trace viewer and HTML report, the parent interaction shows "My Button" but any subsequent actions on the derived `.icon` locator appear as raw selectors (`locator('.icon')`), breaking the intent-driven naming established for the parent. This is particularly confusing in component-level fixture patterns where a described "Product Card" locator has many unnamed child locators for individual fields.

```typescript
// ❌ Description does NOT inherit to child locators
const card = page.getByTestId('product-card').first().describe('Product card');
const title = card.getByRole('heading');   // no description — appears raw in traces
const price = card.getByTestId('price');  // no description — appears raw in traces

await expect(title).toBeVisible();  // trace shows: locator.getByRole("heading")
await expect(price).toBeVisible();  // trace shows: locator.getByTestId("price")

// ✅ Explicitly describe each child locator used in assertions or interactions
const describedTitle = card.getByRole('heading').describe('Product card title');
const describedPrice = card.getByTestId('price').describe('Product card price');

await expect(describedTitle).toBeVisible();  // trace shows: "Product card title"
await expect(describedPrice).toBeVisible();  // trace shows: "Product card price"

// ✅ For component patterns, encapsulate descriptions in a factory function
function productCard(page: Page, index = 0) {
  const root = page.getByTestId('product-card').nth(index).describe(`Product card #${index}`);
  return {
    title: root.getByRole('heading').describe(`Product card #${index} title`),
    price: root.getByTestId('price').describe(`Product card #${index} price`),
    addToCart: root.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).describe(`Product card #${index} add-to-cart`),
  };
}
```

> **WHY:** `locator.describe()` stores the label as a metadata annotation on the specific `Locator` object instance — it is not part of the selector chain and is not serialized into child locator derivations. When `locator.locator('.child')` creates a new `Locator` instance, it copies the selector composition but not the metadata annotations. This is analogous to how CSS class names don't inherit to child elements — the label belongs to the locator object, not to the DOM subtree it resolves to. The `Locator` class is designed as an immutable value object with each derivation producing a fresh instance; inheriting parent descriptions into child locators would create ambiguity when a described locator is used as a base for many different children (which one "inherits" the label?). The solution is always to describe at the leaf level — the point of interaction or assertion. [community]

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 306 — `page.addLocatorHandler()` for overlay dismissal [official]

`page.addLocatorHandler()` registers a callback that Playwright fires automatically whenever a specified locator becomes visible during any subsequent action. This is the idiomatic solution for cookie banners, chat widgets, cookie consent overlays, and newsletter pop-ups that appear non-deterministically during a test run. The handler receives the locator as its first argument and should dismiss the overlay; Playwright re-checks actionability of the original target locator after the handler resolves. Since v1.44, the `{ noWaitAfter, times }` options control whether Playwright re-waits for the overlay to disappear and how many times the handler fires before auto-deregistering.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Register once per test — fires automatically on any blocking overlay
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie consent/i }),
    async (overlay) => {
      await overlay.getByRole('button', { name: /accept/i }).click();
    },
    { times: 3 }   // auto-deregister after 3 dismissals to prevent infinite loops
  );
});

test('checkout flow ignores cookie banner', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');
  // No manual cookie banner handling needed — handler fires if overlay appears
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Your cart' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The handler fires synchronously inside Playwright's actionability retry loop, so a handler that itself triggers another overlay can cause unbounded recursion. Always pass `times` to cap invocations, and avoid navigating inside the handler — navigation inside a handler aborts the outer action queue.

### Pattern 307 — `locator.ariaSnapshot()` for component-level ARIA tree assertions [official]

`locator.ariaSnapshot()` generates an ARIA-tree YAML string scoped to a specific locator rather than the full page. This is ideal for asserting the accessible structure of individual components — a navigation menu, data table, or modal dialog — without coupling the assertion to surrounding page structure. The snapshot is written to a `.aria.yaml` file when running with `--update-snapshots` and compared on subsequent runs using Playwright's structural diff. Pair with `{ ref: true }` to capture element refs for follow-up interactions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('data table ARIA structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports');

  const table = page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Sales report' });

  // Assert component-scoped ARIA tree — fails if headers or row count change
  await expect(table).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - table "Sales report":
      - rowgroup:
        - row:
          - columnheader "Region"
          - columnheader "Q1"
          - columnheader "Q2"
      - rowgroup:
        - row /Region: .+/:
          - cell /[A-Z][a-z]+/
          - cell /\\$[\\d,]+/
          - cell /\\$[\\d,]+/
  `);

  // With { ref: true } — snapshot includes aria-ref attributes for follow-up clicks
  const snapshot = await table.ariaSnapshot({ ref: true });
  expect(snapshot).toContain('aria-ref');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** ARIA snapshots are verbose for complex components — a 10-column table produces a 50+ line YAML file. Prefer scoped `locator.ariaSnapshot()` over `page.ariaSnapshot()` to keep snapshot files reviewable. Regex cell patterns (`/\\$[\\d,]+/`) prevent brittle data-coupling but require escaping backslashes in template literals.

---

### Pattern 308 — `route.fetch()` with `{ maxRedirects: 0 }` for redirect chain testing [official]

`route.fetch()` re-issues the intercepted request from Playwright's network layer, giving the test full control over request modification before forwarding. Setting `maxRedirects: 0` prevents Playwright from following redirects automatically, so the test can assert the intermediate redirect location header before allowing the chain to continue. This is essential for OAuth flows, URL shorteners, and multi-hop SSO redirects where the intermediate Location header carries state tokens that must be validated.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('OAuth redirect carries state parameter', async ({ page }) => {
  const redirectLocations: string[] = [];

  await page.route('**/oauth/authorize**', async (route) => {
    // Capture redirect without following it
    const response = await route.fetch({ maxRedirects: 0 });
    const location = response.headers()['location'] ?? '';
    redirectLocations.push(location);

    // Allow the browser to follow the redirect normally
    await route.fulfill({
      status: response.status(),
      headers: response.headers(),
      body: await response.body(),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login with SSO' }).click();

  expect(redirectLocations.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(redirectLocations[0]).toContain('state=');
  expect(redirectLocations[0]).toContain('code_challenge=');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `maxRedirects: 0` only stops Playwright's fetch layer from following redirects — the browser's network stack still follows the redirect for the original navigation. Use `page.route` (not `page.context().route`) to intercept the specific navigation request. For fully mocking OAuth without a real IdP, combine with `route.fulfill()` on subsequent legs.

---

### Pattern 309 — `expect.configure({ timeout, message })` for assertion-level timeout overrides [official]

`expect.configure()` creates a scoped `expect` instance with custom defaults, allowing specific assertions in a test to use longer (or shorter) timeouts than the global `expect.timeout` without changing the configuration for the rest of the suite. The `message` option prepends a custom failure prefix to every assertion made with the configured instance, replacing the generic "Received…/Expected…" output with a domain-meaningful label that shows up in CI logs and HTML reports.

```typescript
import { test, expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';

test('slow chart renders within SLA', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Chart renders via async data fetch — needs a longer timeout than default
  const slowExpect = baseExpect.configure({
    timeout: 15_000,
    message: 'Chart SLA: canvas element must render within 15 s of page load',
  });

  await slowExpect(
    page.getByRole('img', { name: 'Revenue chart' })
  ).toBeVisible();

  // Subsequent assertions still use default timeout
  await expect(page.getByText('Last updated')).toBeVisible();

  // Scoped expect for soft assertions with custom prefix
  const softExpect = baseExpect.configure({ soft: true, message: 'Dashboard widget' });
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('kpi-revenue')).toBeVisible();
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('kpi-conversions')).toBeVisible();
  baseExpect(page).not.toHaveURL(/error/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.configure()` creates a new object on every call — call it once at the top of the test (or in a fixture) rather than inline in a loop. The `message` string is prepended as-is; Playwright does not append the locator description, so include enough context in the message string to identify the failing assertion in large tests.

### Pattern 310 — `page.pickLocator()` for interactive locator authoring during debugging [official]

`page.pickLocator()` opens an interactive element picker in the browser — equivalent to clicking "Pick locator" in VS Code or the Playwright Inspector — but callable from test code or a REPL. When called in headed mode, it returns a `Promise<string>` that resolves with the auto-generated locator string when the user clicks an element. This bridges the gap between exploratory inspection and codegen, letting developers iteratively refine a test's locator strategy without leaving the test file.

```typescript
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Only run this "authoring" test locally in headed mode to pick locators
test.skip(!!process.env.CI, 'Locator authoring test — headed only');

test('pick locators for new checkout flow', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/step-2');

  // Opens browser picker — resolves when user clicks an element
  const locatorStr = await page.pickLocator();
  console.log('Picked locator:', locatorStr);
  // e.g. "getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Card number' })"

  // Copy the output into the real test — then delete this authoring test
  // Optionally validate the picked locator resolves correctly:
  const locator = page.locator(locatorStr);
  await expect(locator).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.pickLocator()` is exclusively a developer-ergonomics tool — it pauses test execution indefinitely waiting for user input, making it unsuitable for any CI environment. Always gate with `test.skip(!!process.env.CI, ...)` and delete the authoring test before committing. It does not offer a timeout option; the promise only rejects if the page closes.

---

### Pattern 311 — `browserContext.setHTTPCredentials()` for mid-test Basic Auth credential rotation [official]

`browserContext.setHTTPCredentials()` updates the Basic Auth credentials used for all subsequent requests in the context without creating a new context. This is needed for tests that verify credential-based access transitions — e.g., logging in as a read-only user, performing a scoped action, then rotating to an admin credential to verify the elevated operation. The credentials apply to all `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` challenges; digest auth requires a separate approach.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('read-only user cannot delete; admin can', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    httpCredentials: { username: 'readonly', password: 'pass1' },
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/admin/items');
  // Read-only user sees items but delete button is absent
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toHaveCount(0);

  // Rotate credentials to admin without re-creating context (preserves cookies/session)
  await context.setHTTPCredentials({ username: 'admin', password: 'adminpass' });
  await page.reload();

  // Admin sees delete buttons
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).not.toHaveCount(0);

  await context.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `setHTTPCredentials()` only affects Basic Auth challenges — it has no effect on Bearer token or session-cookie authentication flows. For apps that mix Basic Auth on the CDN/reverse-proxy layer with session cookies for the app layer, rotating HTTP credentials does not rotate the app session; you may also need to clear cookies or call a logout endpoint.

### Pattern 312 — `page.waitForResponse()` with a predicate function for semantic response matching [official]

`page.waitForResponse()` accepts either a URL glob/string or a predicate function `(response) => boolean`. The predicate form enables matching on status code, response body, or custom response headers — making it possible to wait for the specific successful response in a sequence of retried API calls (e.g., waiting for a 201 after a series of 409 conflict retries). Combining with `Promise.all` and the triggering click prevents a race where the response arrives before the listener is registered.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form submission returns 201 with resource URL', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/projects/new');

  // Register listener BEFORE the click to avoid race condition
  const [response] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForResponse(
      (res) =>
        res.url().includes('/api/projects') &&
        res.request().method() === 'POST' &&
        res.status() === 201,
      { timeout: 10_000 }
    ),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create project' }).click(),
  ]);

  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ id: expect.any(String), name: expect.any(String) });

  // Assert the UI reflects the new project
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: body.name })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** A predicate that is never satisfied causes the test to time out with a generic "Timeout waiting for response" error that does not indicate which requests were received. For easier debugging, log all matching-URL responses inside the predicate with `console.log(res.url(), res.status())` when investigating failures — remove before committing.

---

### Pattern 313 — `worker`-scoped fixtures for expensive shared setup (database seeding, auth tokens) [official]

Worker-scoped fixtures are created once per worker process and shared across all tests running in that worker. This is the right scope for expensive initialization that is safe to share — authentication token acquisition, database schema migration, or static test-data seeding. Worker fixtures receive a `workerInfo` argument (index, project) and must accept a `use` callback; they are torn down after the last test in the worker completes.

```typescript
// fixtures.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = {
  authToken: string;
  seededUserId: string;
};

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  authToken: [
    async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
      // Called once per worker — expensive token fetch amortized across all tests
      const res = await fetch('https://auth.example.com/token', {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ client_id: 'test', worker: workerInfo.workerIndex }),
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      });
      const { access_token } = await res.json();
      await use(access_token);
      // Teardown: revoke token after all tests in worker complete
      await fetch('https://auth.example.com/revoke', {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ token: access_token }),
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      });
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
  seededUserId: [
    async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
      const userId = `test-user-worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}`;
      // Seed DB record once; each test in this worker shares the same user
      await db.seed({ userId });
      await use(userId);
      await db.cleanup({ userId });
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker fixtures are shared — tests that mutate the shared state (e.g., changing the seeded user's email) corrupt state for subsequent tests in the same worker. Treat worker-fixture data as read-only within tests and isolate mutations by using the worker-scoped data as a template to clone into test-scoped records.

---

### Pattern 314 — `page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme, forcedColors, reducedMotion })` for accessibility and theme testing [official]

`page.emulateMedia()` sets CSS media features mid-test without re-creating the context, enabling a single test to verify multiple appearance modes sequentially. `colorScheme: 'dark'` or `'light'` sets the `prefers-color-scheme` media query; `forcedColors: 'active'` emulates Windows High Contrast mode triggering `forced-colors` CSS; `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` fires `prefers-reduced-motion`. All three can be combined and changed dynamically after navigation.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('header renders correctly in all color modes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Light mode (default)
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'light' });
  await expect(page.getByRole('banner')).toHaveScreenshot('header-light.png');

  // Dark mode
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' });
  await expect(page.getByRole('banner')).toHaveScreenshot('header-dark.png');

  // High Contrast (Windows accessibility mode)
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark', forcedColors: 'active' });
  await expect(page.getByRole('banner')).toHaveScreenshot('header-high-contrast.png');

  // Reduced motion — verify no CSS animation classes present
  await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce', colorScheme: 'light' });
  const spinner = page.getByTestId('loading-spinner');
  // App should replace animation with static indicator under prefers-reduced-motion
  await expect(spinner).not.toHaveClass(/animate-spin/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `emulateMedia()` only sets CSS media features — it does not change the OS-level color scheme in the browser process. JavaScript that reads `window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches` will correctly reflect the emulated value, but native browser UI (scrollbars, form controls) renders in the actual OS theme. For pixel-perfect screenshots, also set `colorScheme` at context creation to ensure consistent initial render.

---

### Pattern 315 — `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with `{ ignoreCase, timeout }` for case-insensitive URL assertions [official]

`expect(page).toHaveURL()` supports `ignoreCase: true` (since v1.44) for case-insensitive URL comparison, and accepts string, regex, or function predicates. The function form enables complex URL state assertions — checking that a query parameter exists regardless of ordering, or that a fragment identifier matches a pattern. Combining with `timeout` avoids the need for manual `page.waitForURL()` calls before the assertion.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search results URL reflects query params in any order', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');
  await page.getByRole('searchbox').fill('playwright testing');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  // Function predicate: assert both params exist, order-independent
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(
    (url) => url.searchParams.has('q') && url.searchParams.has('page'),
    { timeout: 8_000 }
  );

  // Case-insensitive match for slug-based routing
  await page.goto('/Products/FEATURED');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/products\/featured/i, { ignoreCase: true });

  // Assert fragment (hash) navigation after in-page link click
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'API Reference' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL((url) => url.hash === '#api-reference', { timeout: 3_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The function predicate form receives a `URL` object (not a string), so `url.href.includes('q=')` works but is less reliable than `url.searchParams.has('q')` due to encoding differences. When asserting on `searchParams`, use `.has()` / `.get()` rather than string-matching the full URL to avoid false failures caused by parameter encoding or ordering.

---

### Pattern 316 — `page.addInitScript()` for deterministic `Date`, `Math.random()`, and `crypto` overrides [official]

`page.addInitScript()` injects a script that runs in the page's JavaScript context before any page scripts execute, making it the correct place to freeze time, stub random values, or override `crypto.randomUUID()` for deterministic test data. The script runs for every new page load in the same context and receives no arguments; closures over external variables are not supported — serialize all needed values into the script string.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice date frozen to 2026-01-15', async ({ page }) => {
  const frozenDate = new Date('2026-01-15T10:00:00Z').getTime();

  await page.addInitScript((ts) => {
    // Override Date globally — runs before any page JS
    const OrigDate = Date;
    class FrozenDate extends OrigDate {
      constructor(...args: ConstructorParameters<typeof OrigDate>) {
        if (args.length === 0) super(ts);
        else super(...args);
      }
      static now() { return ts; }
    }
    // @ts-ignore — intentional global override in browser context
    window.Date = FrozenDate;

    // Deterministic UUID for snapshot stability
    let uuidCounter = 0;
    const origRandomUUID = crypto.randomUUID.bind(crypto);
    crypto.randomUUID = () =>
      `00000000-0000-4000-8000-${String(++uuidCounter).padStart(12, '0')}`;
  }, frozenDate);

  await page.goto('/invoices/new');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText('Jan 15, 2026');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-id')).toHaveText(/^INV-00000000/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `addInitScript()` runs in the browser's JavaScript VM — it cannot import Node.js modules or access the test's Node.js scope. Serialize all test-side data as JSON-safe primitives via the second argument to `addInitScript(script, arg)`. Overriding `Date` globally can break third-party scripts that depend on real timestamps (analytics, error reporters) — scope overrides to specific window properties when possible.

---

### Pattern 317 — `request` fixture and `APIRequestContext.storageState()` for API-first authentication [official]

The `request` fixture provides an `APIRequestContext` bound to the test's browser context, sharing cookies and storage state. Calling `request.storageState()` after a successful API login serializes the resulting auth cookies to a file; subsequent contexts load it via `storageState: 'auth.json'` to skip the UI login flow entirely. This is the canonical Playwright pattern for separating authentication from functional test logic.

```typescript
// auth.setup.ts — runs once before all tests via project dependencies
import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const AUTH_FILE = path.resolve('.playwright/auth/user.json');

setup('authenticate via API', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.post('https://api.example.com/auth/login', {
    data: { email: 'test@example.com', password: process.env.TEST_PASSWORD },
  });
  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  // Persist cookies + localStorage to disk
  await request.storageState({ path: AUTH_FILE });
});

// playwright.config.ts — project dependency wiring
// export default defineConfig({
//   projects: [
//     { name: 'setup', testMatch: '**/auth.setup.ts' },
//     { name: 'tests', dependencies: ['setup'],
//       use: { storageState: AUTH_FILE } },
//   ],
// });

// any.test.ts — no login steps needed
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
test('authenticated page loads', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `storageState` files contain sensitive cookies — add `.playwright/auth/` to `.gitignore` and never commit them. The file is shared across all tests using that project; if one test invalidates the session (logout, token revocation), all subsequent tests fail. Use per-worker storage state files (parameterized by `workerInfo.workerIndex`) when tests must mutate auth state.

---

### Pattern 318 — `page.coverage` (Istanbul) for collecting JavaScript code coverage from E2E tests [official]

`page.coverage.startJSCoverage()` instruments the page's JavaScript using V8's coverage API, collecting per-function and per-block hit counts. After navigation and test interactions, `page.coverage.stopJSCoverage()` returns an array of coverage entries that can be written to a format istanbul/nyc understands. This surfaces which application code paths are exercised by E2E tests — useful for identifying dead code or validating that critical paths are covered.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { writeFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'fs';
import v8toIstanbul from 'v8-to-istanbul';

test('collect JS coverage for checkout flow', async ({ page, browserName }) => {
  test.skip(browserName !== 'chromium', 'V8 coverage is Chromium-only');

  await page.coverage.startJSCoverage({ resetOnNavigation: false });

  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Card number' }).fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();

  const coverage = await page.coverage.stopJSCoverage();

  // Convert V8 format to Istanbul for nyc/c8 compatibility
  mkdirSync('.nyc_output', { recursive: true });
  for (const entry of coverage) {
    if (!entry.url.includes('localhost')) continue;
    const converter = v8toIstanbul(entry.url, 0, { source: entry.source ?? '' });
    await converter.load();
    converter.applyCoverage(entry.functions);
    const istanbul = converter.toIstanbul();
    writeFileSync(`.nyc_output/${Date.now()}.json`, JSON.stringify(istanbul));
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** V8 coverage is Chromium-only — `page.coverage` is `null` on Firefox and WebKit. `resetOnNavigation: false` is required for multi-page flows; with the default `true`, navigating to `/checkout` after `/cart` discards the `/cart` coverage. The `v8-to-istanbul` conversion is lossy for heavily minified bundles without source maps; always configure the dev server to emit source maps in test runs.

---

### Pattern 319 — `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` for opaque reusable action blocks [official]

`test.step()` groups a sequence of actions under a named step visible in the trace viewer and HTML report. Adding `{ box: true }` (since v1.46) makes the step "boxed" — the trace viewer collapses all internal actions into a single top-level step entry, hiding implementation details and showing only the step name and pass/fail status. This is the idiomatic way to write reusable page-object-style helpers without exposing every `fill` and `click` in the trace.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

async function fillShippingForm(page: Page, data: {
  name: string; address: string; city: string; zip: string;
}) {
  await test.step('Fill shipping form', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Full name' }).fill(data.name);
    await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Address' }).fill(data.address);
    await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'City' }).fill(data.city);
    await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'ZIP code' }).fill(data.zip);
  }, { box: true });  // All 4 fills collapsed to one "Fill shipping form" entry in trace
}

test('checkout with standard shipping', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  await fillShippingForm(page, {
    name: 'Jane Doe',
    address: '123 Main St',
    city: 'Springfield',
    zip: '12345',
  });

  await test.step('Submit order', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  }, { box: true });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Boxed steps hide all internal trace actions — when a boxed step fails, the trace viewer shows the step-level error but not which internal action caused it. During active debugging, remove `{ box: true }` temporarily to see the full action sequence. Boxed steps are best applied to stable, well-understood helpers rather than newly-authored code paths still being debugged.

---

### Pattern 320 — `expect(locator).toHaveValues()` for multi-select listbox assertion [official]

`expect(locator).toHaveValues()` asserts the selected option values of a `<select multiple>` element, accepting an array of strings or regular expressions. It retries until the selection matches, making it safe to call immediately after programmatic selection changes triggered by keyboard events or JavaScript. This is the only built-in Playwright assertion for multi-select state — `toHaveValue()` (singular) only works for single-select elements.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('multi-select filter controls', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports/filter');

  const regionSelect = page.getByRole('listbox', { name: 'Regions' });

  // Programmatic multi-select via selectOption
  await regionSelect.selectOption(['north', 'south', 'east']);
  await expect(regionSelect).toHaveValues(['north', 'south', 'east']);

  // Deselect one and verify the updated selection
  await regionSelect.selectOption(['north', 'east']);
  await expect(regionSelect).toHaveValues(['north', 'east']);

  // Regex matching for dynamic option values
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Select all EU regions' }).click();
  await expect(regionSelect).toHaveValues([/^eu-/, /^eu-/, /^eu-/]);

  // Assert empty selection after "Clear filters"
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Clear filters' }).click();
  await expect(regionSelect).toHaveValues([]);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toHaveValues()` compares the `value` attribute of `<option>` elements — not the visible text label. If the app uses display names as values (`value="North America"`) rather than slugs (`value="north-america"`), the assertion strings must match the raw `value` attribute. Use `page.evaluate(() => [...selectEl.options].filter(o => o.selected).map(o => o.value))` to inspect actual values when debugging unexpected assertion failures.
