### Gotcha #115: `locator.describe()` labels do not appear in `expect()` failure messages — only in trace/report action logs [community]

Developers who adopt `locator.describe()` expecting the label to surface in `TimeoutError` assertion messages are surprised to find that the failure output still shows the raw selector string (e.g., `locator('[data-id="42"]').first()`) rather than the human-readable description. The `describe()` label is injected into Playwright's action-recording infrastructure (Trace Viewer, HTML reporter), not into the assertion formatting path.

```typescript
// ❌ Expect: TimeoutError: "First line item in cart" not visible
// Actual:  TimeoutError: locator('[data-id="42"]').first() not visible
const firstItem = page.locator('[data-id="42"]').first().describe('First line item in cart');
await expect(firstItem).toBeVisible({ timeout: 1000 }); // raw selector in error message

// ✅ Use the expect() message option for assertion-level failure context
await expect(firstItem, 'Expected first line item to be visible in cart').toBeVisible({ timeout: 1000 });
// TimeoutError: Expected first line item to be visible in cart
//   Locator: locator('[data-id="42"]').first()
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's `Locator` object maintains its selector tree in a `_selector` field (a private `ParsedSelector` struct). `locator.describe()` stores the human-readable label in a separate `_description` field that was added alongside `_selector`. Assertion helpers like `toBeVisible()` construct their error messages by serializing `_selector` through `stringifySelector()`, which has no visibility into `_description`. The Trace Viewer and HTML reporter, in contrast, call `locator.toString()` after the `_description` annotation was applied to a forked code path in the action recorder — so descriptions appear there but not in error messages. Pair `describe()` with explicit `expect(locator, message)` calls for full coverage. [community]

---

### Gotcha #116: `route.continue()` can no longer override the `Cookie` header in v1.52+ — the real context cookies are sent silently instead [community]

Since Playwright v1.52, calling `route.continue({ headers: { Cookie: 'session=fake' } })` is a silent no-op for the `Cookie` header — the intercepted request is forwarded with the browser context's real cookies, ignoring the override. Prior to v1.52, teams relied on this technique to inject fake session cookies for specific intercepted requests. The change was made to close a CORS bypass vector, but it breaks any test that depended on per-route cookie spoofing.

```typescript
// ❌ Cookie override silently ignored since v1.52
await page.route('/api/me', async (route) => {
  await route.continue({
    headers: {
      ...route.request().headers(),
      Cookie: 'session=spoofed-value', // silently dropped in v1.52+
    },
  });
});

// ✅ Use browserContext.addCookies() before navigation instead
await page.context().addCookies([{
  name: 'session',
  value: 'spoofed-value',
  domain: 'app.example.com',
  path: '/',
}]);
await page.goto('/dashboard'); // all requests from this point carry the spoofed cookie
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's network interception stack routes through the browser's `Network.continueInterceptedRequest` CDP command (Chromium) and equivalent protocol commands in Firefox and WebKit. Starting with v1.52, Playwright's `route.continue()` implementation explicitly strips the `Cookie` key from the headers map before forwarding to the browser protocol, because allowing arbitrary `Cookie` overrides in conjunction with SameSite=None cookies and CORS pre-flight caching created a scenario where test-injected cookies could bypass the browser's CORS preflight cache, causing divergence between test-only behavior and real-browser behavior. The only supported way to control cookie values is through the browser context's cookie jar via `addCookies()`. [community]

---

### Gotcha #117: `apiRequest.newContext()` with `maxRedirects: 0` throws rather than returning the 3xx response — you cannot inspect the redirect location via the thrown error reliably [community]

Many developers expect `maxRedirects: 0` to behave like `fetch({ redirect: 'manual' })` in the browser — returning the 3xx response object so they can inspect `location` and `status`. Playwright's implementation throws a `playwright.errors.Error` (wrapping the Node.js `MaxRedirectsError`) instead of returning the response, making it impossible to read `response.status()` or `response.headers()['location']` without fragile error-message parsing.

```typescript
// ❌ Attempting to inspect the 3xx response via maxRedirects: 0
const api = await playwright.request.newContext({ maxRedirects: 0 });
try {
  const r = await api.get('/old-url');
  // Never reached — redirect throws before returning
} catch (e) {
  // e.message is implementation-dependent — NOT a reliable interface
  console.log(e.message); // "Request failed: exceeded maxRedirects" or similar
}

// ✅ Use page.goto() with waitUntil: 'commit' to inspect the initial 3xx response
const response = await page.goto('/old-url', { waitUntil: 'commit' });
// waitUntil: 'commit' resolves on the first response (the redirect itself, before following)
expect(response!.status()).toBe(301);
expect(response!.headers()['location']).toBe('/new-url');
```

> **WHY:** Playwright's `APIRequestContext` is built on Node.js's `http`/`https` modules, which follow redirects by making a new request internally. The `maxRedirects` option in Playwright maps to the Node.js `http` module's `maxRedirects` option, which throws a `MaxRedirectsError` rather than returning the redirect response to the caller — this is a Node.js design decision rooted in the `http.ClientRequest` API surfacing redirect-followed responses through event chains rather than the initial response object. There is no mechanism in Node.js's built-in HTTP stack to intercept and return a redirect response without following it; `waitUntil: 'commit'` in `page.goto()` uses the CDP protocol's `Page.frameNavigated` event which fires before redirect following completes in the browser. [community]

---

### Gotcha #118: ARIA snapshot `/children: true` strict matching fails on `aria-hidden`-less decorative SVG nodes injected by icon libraries [community]

When using `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` with `/children: true` on a button that contains an icon library component (e.g., Heroicons, FontAwesome `<i>` tags, or SVG sprites without `aria-hidden="true"`), the ARIA tree may include decorative `img ""` or `presentation` role nodes. The `/children: true` assertion fails because the live tree has more nodes than the snapshot specifies — but the failure message names ARIA node types that appear invisible in the rendered UI, making the mismatch confusing to diagnose.

```typescript
// ❌ Strict children matching fails if icon injects an 'img ""' ARIA node
await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
  - button "Delete":
    /children: true
    - text "Delete"
`);
// Fails: expected 1 child, found 2
// Extra node: - img ""  ← the SVG icon (aria-hidden not set by the icon library)

// ✅ Option A: Add aria-hidden to the icon SVG (fix the component)
// <svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">...</svg>

// ✅ Option B: Use default (non-strict) children matching for icon-bearing buttons
await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
  - button "Delete"
`);

// ✅ Option C: Include the icon node explicitly in the strict snapshot
await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
  - button "Delete":
    /children: true
    - img ""
    - text "Delete"
`);
```

> **WHY:** The Playwright ARIA snapshot serializer calls `AccessibilityTree.snapshot()` which uses the browser's accessibility API to enumerate all nodes including those with `role="img"` for SVGs that lack `aria-hidden="true"`. Icon library SVGs frequently omit `aria-hidden="true"` in older package versions, causing the accessibility tree to expose them as unnamed image nodes. The `/children: true` flag in the YAML snapshot compares the full ordered list of child nodes using strict array equality — a single extra `img ""` node at any position causes a mismatch. The browser's accessibility engine includes these nodes in the tree by default; only `aria-hidden="true"` (or `role="presentation"` with no focusable descendants) suppresses them from the serialized snapshot. [community]

---

### Gotcha #119: `testInfo.snapshotPath({ kind })` is silently ignored when `snapshotPathTemplate` is a plain string — both kinds resolve to the same template [community]

Teams that upgrade to Playwright v1.53 and call `testInfo.snapshotPath('name', { kind: 'aria' })` expecting a different path from `testInfo.snapshotPath('name', { kind: 'screenshot' })` are surprised when both return identical paths. The `kind` discriminator only works when `snapshotPathTemplate` is configured as a `Record<string, string>` object — if it is a plain string (the format from v1.52 and earlier), the `kind` option is silently ignored and all kinds resolve through the same template.

```typescript
// ❌ String template ignores kind — all calls return identical paths
// playwright.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',
});

// In test: both return the same path regardless of kind
// testInfo.snapshotPath('product', { kind: 'screenshot' })
// → tests/__snapshots__/product.e2e.ts/product.png
// testInfo.snapshotPath('product', { kind: 'aria' })
// → tests/__snapshots__/product.e2e.ts/product.png  ← SAME — kind ignored!

// ✅ Object template required for kind-based routing (v1.53+)
export default defineConfig({
  snapshotPathTemplate: {
    screenshot: '{testDir}/__screenshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',
    aria:       '{testDir}/__aria__/{testFilePath}/{arg}.yaml',
    default:    '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',
  },
});
// Now the two calls return distinct paths with distinct extensions
```

> **WHY:** `testInfo.snapshotPath()` is implemented in `TestInfoImpl._snapshotPath()`. In v1.53, the implementation checks whether `config.snapshotPathTemplate` is a `string` or a `Record<string, string>`. When it is a plain `string`, the method ignores the `kind` parameter entirely and applies the single template to all calls — the `kind` key is used only as a lookup key into the object form. This is an intentional backward-compatibility choice: projects using the string form from v1.52 continue to work without modification, but they silently do not benefit from the new kind-based routing. The only indication of this behavior is a single sentence in the v1.53 release notes describing the object form as required for kind routing. [community]

## Cycle 50 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern #351: `page.screencast` — Unified Video Recording with Action Annotations [official]

Playwright v1.59 introduced `page.screencast` as a first-class API for recording video with overlaid action markers and chapter cards. Unlike `recordVideo` in context options, `screencast` starts and stops on demand mid-test and exposes real-time JPEG frames via an `onFrame` callback — enabling AI vision pipelines or thumbnail previews without writing to disk.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('record purchase flow with chapter overlays', async ({ page }) => {
  // Start recording to disk; onFrame enables concurrent live streaming
  await page.screencast.start({ path: 'purchase-flow.webm' });

  await page.goto('/products/42');

  // Chapter card overlaid on the recording at this timestamp
  await page.screencast.showChapter('Product Page', {
    description: 'Verifying price and stock badge',
    duration: 2000,
  });

  const addToCart = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' });
  await addToCart.click();

  await page.screencast.showChapter('Cart', {
    description: 'Item added — proceeding to checkout',
    duration: 1500,
  });

  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order summary' })).toBeVisible();

  // showActions overlays click-highlight circles on playback
  const dismissActions = await page.screencast.showActions({ position: 'bottom-right' });
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  dismissActions[Symbol.dispose](); // remove overlay before stop

  await page.screencast.stop();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `screencast` produces a single `.webm` per `start()`/`stop()` call and cannot be paused/resumed mid-recording. Chapters and action overlays are baked into the video at playback time, not stored separately — you cannot strip them after the fact. For CI artifact size, prefer `trace: 'on-first-retry'` over always-on screencast; screencast is best for demo recordings or AI vision pipelines that consume `onFrame` callbacks in real time.

### Pattern #352: `browser.bind()` — Expose a Launched Browser for External Clients [official]

`browser.bind()` makes a running Playwright-controlled browser available for connection by external processes (CLI tools, MCP servers, other Node processes) over a WebSocket endpoint. This is the mechanism behind `npx playwright show` and LLM agent toolchains that need a persistent browsing session without re-launching.

```typescript
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';

async function startSharedBrowser() {
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();

  // Bind browser under a named session; returns the WebSocket endpoint
  const { endpoint } = await browser.bind('qa-session', {
    workspaceDir: process.cwd(),
  });

  console.log(`Browser available at: ${endpoint}`);
  // External tool connects via: npx playwright connect <endpoint>
  // or: chromium.connectOverCDP(endpoint)

  // Keep alive until signal
  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
    process.on('SIGINT', async () => {
      await browser.unbind('qa-session'); // reject new connections
      await browser.close();
      resolve();
    });
  });
}

startSharedBrowser();
```

> **Tradeoff:** `browser.bind()` enables multi-client access to a single browser instance, but all clients share the same process — a crash in one client's context can destabilize others. `browser.unbind()` stops accepting new connections but does not disconnect already-connected clients. This API is designed for developer tooling (CLI, MCP), not for parallelizing test suites; use `--shard` or worker-level contexts for test parallelism.

---

### Pattern #353: `browserContext.setStorageState()` — Hot-Swap Auth State Without Re-Creating a Context [official]

`context.setStorageState()` replaces all cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB for a context in-place, avoiding the overhead of closing and re-opening a context when testing multi-account flows or toggling between login states mid-test.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { adminStorageState, editorStorageState } from './fixtures/storage-states';

test('admin can publish; editor can only draft', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: adminStorageState });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Publish' })).toBeEnabled();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Publish' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Published');

  // Hot-swap to editor credentials — no new context required
  await context.setStorageState(editorStorageState);
  await page.reload(); // force re-auth check

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Publish' })).toBeDisabled();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save draft' })).toBeEnabled();

  await context.close();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `context.setStorageState()` is atomic in its clearing step — all existing cookies and storage are wiped before the new state is applied. Any in-flight requests that depend on the old session will fail after the call. For tests that assert seamless session handoff (e.g., "user remains logged in on refresh"), use a new context with `storageState` set at creation time instead, which never goes through a cleared state.

### Pattern #354: `locator.normalize()` — Convert Fragile Selectors to Best-Practice Locators [official]

`locator.normalize()` converts an existing locator that uses fragile strategies (CSS class chains, XPath, positional `nth()` alone) into the closest idiomatic equivalent preferring test IDs and ARIA roles. It is designed for codegen post-processing and automated locator healing workflows.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('normalize codegen-produced selectors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Codegen sometimes emits brittle CSS — normalize before committing
  const fragileLocator = page.locator('.checkout-form > div:nth-child(2) > input');
  const normalized = fragileLocator.normalize();

  // normalized will prefer: page.getByLabel('Email address')
  // or page.getByTestId('email-input') if data-testid is present
  console.log(normalized.toString()); // inspect the improved selector

  await normalized.fill('user@example.com');
  await expect(normalized).toHaveValue('user@example.com');

  // Use normalized form in assertions and interactions
  const submitBtn = page.locator('button[type="submit"].btn-primary').normalize();
  await submitBtn.click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `locator.normalize()` is a best-effort heuristic — it may not find a unique semantic alternative for every element and will fall back to the original selector if no better option exists. It is a one-shot transformation at call time; it does not continuously re-evaluate if the DOM changes between test runs. Do not rely on it as a substitute for writing semantic locators at authoring time — use it only for healing legacy or codegen-produced selectors.

---

### Pattern #355: `page.pickLocator()` — Interactive Element Selection in Running Tests [official]

`page.pickLocator()` pauses the test and enters an interactive "inspector" mode where hovering over an element highlights it and displays its best-practice Playwright locator. Clicking an element resolves the promise with the `Locator` object. Useful for diagnosing hard-to-select elements in headed mode without switching to the full codegen CLI.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.only('diagnose locator for date-picker input', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/booking');

  // In headed mode: hover elements to see locators, click to select
  // In CI (headless): skip the pick step, use the locator you collected locally
  let dateInput: import('@playwright/test').Locator;

  if (process.env.PICK_LOCATOR) {
    // Developer workflow: pick the element interactively
    dateInput = await page.pickLocator();
    console.log('Picked locator:', dateInput.toString());
    // Output example: page.getByLabel('Check-in date')
    await page.cancelPickLocator(); // clean up inspector state
  } else {
    // CI workflow: use the locator collected in a prior session
    dateInput = page.getByLabel('Check-in date');
  }

  await dateInput.fill('2026-06-15');
  await expect(dateInput).toHaveValue('2026-06-15');
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `page.pickLocator()` only works in headed mode — calling it in headless mode throws immediately. It is a developer ergonomics tool, not for CI or automated pipelines. Always gate it behind an environment variable or `test.only` and never commit a test that calls `page.pickLocator()` unconditionally, as it will hang CI indefinitely waiting for a click that never comes.

### Pattern #356: `page.clearConsoleMessages()` / `page.consoleMessages()` — Per-Action Console Assertion Windows [official]

Playwright v1.59 added `page.consoleMessages()` to retrieve buffered console output and `page.clearConsoleMessages()` to reset the buffer, enabling precise "only messages emitted during this action" assertion windows without a persistent `page.on('console')` listener.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('no console errors emitted during file upload', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/upload');

  // Clear any startup noise before the action under test
  await page.clearConsoleMessages();

  const [fileChooser] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('filechooser'),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Choose file' }).click(),
  ]);
  await fileChooser.setFiles('tests/fixtures/sample.pdf');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Upload' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Upload complete');

  // Assert no console errors were emitted during the upload flow
  const messages = await page.consoleMessages();
  const errors = messages.filter((m) => m.type() === 'error');
  expect(errors, `Unexpected console errors: ${errors.map((e) => e.text()).join(', ')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `page.consoleMessages()` returns a snapshot of the buffer at call time — it is not a live stream. Messages emitted after the call but before your assertion are not captured in that snapshot. For continuous monitoring across the full test lifetime, combine `clearConsoleMessages()` windows with a `page.on('console')` listener that pushes to an external array. The buffer has an internal size limit; very chatty applications may overflow it, losing early messages silently.

---

### Pattern #357: `consoleMessage.timestamp()` — Correlate Console Events with Network Timeline [official]

`consoleMessage.timestamp()` returns the Unix timestamp (milliseconds) when the browser emitted the console message. Combined with `response.timing()` or `page.requests()`, this enables correlating client-side log events with their triggering network responses — useful for diagnosing race conditions in async initialization code.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('console init log fires after config fetch completes', async ({ page }) => {
  const consoleEvents: Array<{ text: string; timestamp: number }> = [];
  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    consoleEvents.push({ text: msg.text(), timestamp: msg.timestamp() });
  });

  let configResponseEnd = 0;
  page.on('response', (response) => {
    if (response.url().includes('/api/config')) {
      configResponseEnd = response.timing().responseEnd;
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/app');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  const initLog = consoleEvents.find((e) => e.text.startsWith('[App] initialized'));
  expect(initLog).toBeDefined();

  // Init log should be emitted after the config response completes
  expect(initLog!.timestamp).toBeGreaterThan(configResponseEnd);
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `consoleMessage.timestamp()` reports the browser-side emission time using the browser's internal clock, which may differ from the Node.js process clock by a few milliseconds due to IPC latency. Do not use it to assert sub-millisecond ordering; use it for coarse-grained "A happened before B" reasoning. For precise ordering, use `page.clock` to freeze time and control the timeline.

---

### Pattern #358: `tracing.start({ live: true })` — Real-Time Trace Updates for Long-Running Tests [official]

Setting `live: true` in `tracing.start()` causes the trace file to be flushed incrementally as actions complete, rather than only at `tracing.stop()`. This allows external monitoring tools to read a partial trace from a running test — useful for test-in-production monitoring or AI agent pipelines that want to inspect intermediate state.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('long checkout flow with live trace', async ({ context, page }, testInfo) => {
  const tracePath = testInfo.outputPath('checkout-live.zip');

  await context.tracing.start({
    screenshots: true,
    snapshots: true,
    live: true,  // flush incrementally; external reader can open partial trace
  });

  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();

  // At this point, an external monitoring process can already read tracePath
  // even though the test is still running
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/29');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment successful' })).toBeVisible();

  await context.tracing.stop({ path: tracePath });
  testInfo.attachments.push({ name: 'trace', path: tracePath, contentType: 'application/zip' });
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `live: true` increases I/O overhead because each action triggers a partial flush to disk. On high-frequency action tests (>50 actions/second), this can slow down execution by 5–15%. Only enable `live` when you have an external consumer actively reading the trace file — otherwise use the default (flush at stop) to minimize overhead. Live traces are write-once-read-many; do not attempt to write to the file from the reader process.

### Pattern #359: `webSocketRoute.protocols()` — Negotiate WebSocket Subprotocols in Route Handlers [official]

`webSocketRoute.protocols()` returns the list of subprotocols the page requested during the WebSocket handshake (`Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header). Route handlers can use this to simulate a server that selects a specific protocol — enabling tests to verify how the client handles different protocol negotiation outcomes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('client falls back to json-v1 when json-v2 is unavailable', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://api.example.com/stream', async (ws) => {
    const requested = ws.protocols();
    // Client requests ['json-v2', 'json-v1'] in priority order
    expect(requested).toEqual(['json-v2', 'json-v1']);

    // Simulate server accepting only the fallback protocol
    const selectedProtocol = requested.includes('json-v1') ? 'json-v1' : requested[0];

    // Accept with the negotiated protocol and proxy messages
    const server = ws.connectToServer({ protocol: selectedProtocol });

    ws.onMessage((msg) => {
      // json-v1 wraps payload in { data: ... }
      const payload = selectedProtocol === 'json-v1' ? JSON.stringify({ data: msg }) : msg;
      server.send(payload);
    });
    server.onMessage((msg) => ws.send(msg));
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('connection-status')).toHaveText('Connected (json-v1)');
  await expect(page.getByRole('log')).toContainText('Fallback protocol active');
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `webSocketRoute.protocols()` is only available inside a `page.routeWebSocket()` handler — it cannot be called before the route is triggered. The returned array reflects what the browser sent; if the application code does not set `protocols` in the `WebSocket()` constructor, the array will be empty. Negotiated protocol selection on the mock server side requires manually calling `ws.connectToServer({ protocol })` with the chosen value; Playwright does not auto-negotiate.

---

### Pattern #360: `page.getByRole()` with `description` Option — Accessible Description Matching [official]

Playwright v1.60 added a `description` option to `getByRole()` that matches elements by their computed accessible description (`aria-describedby`, `aria-description`, or `title` attribute), not just their accessible name. This enables precise selection in UIs with multiple similarly-named controls differentiated only by their descriptions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('select delete button by accessible description to avoid ambiguity', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/file-manager');

  // Page has multiple "Delete" buttons, each described by the file name:
  // <button aria-label="Delete" aria-describedby="desc-report">
  // <span id="desc-report">Annual Report Q4.pdf</span>
  const deleteReport = page.getByRole('button', {
    name: 'Delete',
    description: 'Annual Report Q4.pdf',
  });
  const deleteInvoice = page.getByRole('button', {
    name: 'Delete',
    description: 'Invoice-2026-04.pdf',
  });

  await expect(deleteReport).toBeVisible();
  await expect(deleteInvoice).toBeVisible();

  // Click the correct delete without positional nth() fragility
  await deleteReport.click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm delete' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Annual Report Q4.pdf')).not.toBeVisible();
  // Invoice still present — correct file was deleted
  await expect(page.getByText('Invoice-2026-04.pdf')).toBeVisible();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** The `description` option matches the _computed_ accessible description, which Playwright evaluates via `AccessibilityNode.description` in the browser. If the description is provided via `aria-describedby` pointing to a hidden element (e.g., a tooltip not yet rendered), the description may be empty at match time. Always prefer `aria-description` (the string attribute, not `aria-describedby`) for stable descriptions that do not depend on DOM presence.

---

### Pattern #361: `expect(locator).toHaveCSS()` with `pseudo` Option — Assert Pseudo-Element Styles [official]

Playwright v1.60 added a `pseudo` option to `toHaveCSS()` for asserting computed styles on `::before` and `::after` pseudo-elements. This enables testing CSS-driven decorations (loading spinners, status indicators, icons injected via `content: ''`) that are not accessible via `locator.evaluate()` on the element itself.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('required field indicator renders as red asterisk via ::before', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/registration');

  const emailLabel = page.getByText('Email address');

  // Assert the ::before pseudo-element renders the required indicator
  await expect(emailLabel).toHaveCSS('content', '"*"', { pseudo: '::before' });
  await expect(emailLabel).toHaveCSS('color', 'rgb(220, 38, 38)', { pseudo: '::before' });

  // After marking optional, the pseudo-element should be suppressed
  await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Email is optional' }).check();
  await expect(emailLabel).toHaveCSS('content', 'none', { pseudo: '::before' });

  // Assert the actual label element color is unaffected (no pseudo — element itself)
  await expect(emailLabel).toHaveCSS('color', 'rgb(17, 24, 39)');
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `toHaveCSS({ pseudo })` reads the _computed_ style from the pseudo-element, which is the final browser-resolved value including inheritance. The `content` value for a string literal is returned with surrounding quotes (`'"*"'` not `'*'`) — always include the surrounding quotes in your assertion string. This option does not support `:hover`, `:focus`, or other state-based pseudo-classes; it only works with `::before` and `::after`.

---

### Pattern #362: `testInfoError.errorContext` — Surface Diagnostic Context at Failure Time [official]

Playwright v1.60 added `errorContext` to `testInfoError` objects surfaced in custom reporters. When a matcher fails, Playwright populates `errorContext` with diagnostic data (e.g., the current ARIA snapshot at the moment of failure), making it easier to write reporter plugins that include rich failure context without a full trace.

```typescript
import type {
  Reporter,
  TestCase,
  TestResult,
  TestError,
} from '@playwright/test/reporter';

class AriaContextReporter implements Reporter {
  onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult): void {
    if (result.status !== 'failed') return;

    for (const error of result.errors) {
      // errorContext is set by Playwright when an assertion includes diagnostic data
      if (error.errorContext) {
        console.log(`\n--- Diagnostic context for: ${test.title} ---`);
        console.log(error.errorContext);
        // e.g. prints the ARIA snapshot of the page at assertion failure time:
        // - heading "Login" [level=1]
        // - textbox "Email"
        // - textbox "Password"  ← field was missing from aria snapshot assertion
        console.log('--- End context ---\n');
      } else {
        console.log(`[${test.title}] Error: ${error.message}`);
      }
    }
  }
}

export default AriaContextReporter;
```

> **Tradeoff:** `errorContext` is only populated for failures in matchers that explicitly attach diagnostic data — primarily ARIA snapshot matchers and a subset of accessibility assertions. Generic assertion failures (`expect(x).toBe(y)`) do not populate `errorContext`. If `errorContext` is `undefined`, fall back to parsing `error.message` for the diff. Do not assume `errorContext` is always a string; its type is `string | undefined` and its format may change between versions.

---

### Pattern #363: `browser.on('context')` — Intercept All Newly Created Contexts [official]

The `browser.on('context')` event fires whenever a new `BrowserContext` is created on the browser instance — including contexts opened by the application under test (e.g., via `window.open()` or PWA service worker). This enables centralized setup (cookie injection, route handler registration) across dynamically created contexts without needing a reference to each context at creation time.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('inject auth headers into all contexts including popup windows', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();

  // Attach handler BEFORE pages navigate — fires for all future contexts on this browser
  browser.on('context', async (newContext) => {
    // Inject auth cookie into every dynamically spawned context
    await newContext.addCookies([
      { name: 'session', value: 'test-session-token', domain: 'example.com', path: '/' },
    ]);
    // Register route handler on all contexts
    await newContext.route('**/api/**', (route) => {
      route.continue({
        headers: { ...route.request().headers(), 'X-Test-Auth': 'true' },
      });
    });
  });

  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');
  // Click a link that opens window.open() — the new context is auto-configured
  const [popup] = await Promise.all([
    context.waitForEvent('page'),
    page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Open in new window' }).click(),
  ]);
  await expect(popup.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `browser.on('context')` fires for every context including those created by Playwright's own framework (e.g., service worker contexts). Filtering by context origin or type is not supported — your handler must defensively guard against unexpected context types. The event fires synchronously before the context is returned to the caller, so async operations in the handler (like `addCookies`) execute before the context's first page load only if you `await` them in the handler body.

---

### Pattern #364: `test.abort()` — Terminate a Test Programmatically from Fixtures or Hooks [official]

`test.abort()` terminates the currently running test immediately with an optional message. Unlike `test.skip()`, which marks the test as skipped before it starts, `test.abort()` can be called from within fixtures, `beforeEach` hooks, or route handlers to halt a test that has already begun executing — useful for invariant checks that must stop further actions.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Fixture that aborts if a required feature flag is disabled
const test = base.extend<{ featureGuard: void }>({
  featureGuard: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    const featureEnabled = await page.evaluate(() =>
      (window as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__?.newCheckout === true
    );
    if (!featureEnabled) {
      test.abort('newCheckout feature flag is disabled — skipping test suite for this build');
      // Execution stops here; no further fixture code or test body runs
    }
    await use();
  }, { auto: true }],
});

test('new checkout flow completes successfully', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'New checkout' })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `test.abort()` marks the test result as `'failed'` with status `'aborted'` — it does not appear as `'skipped'` in reports. If you want the test to appear as skipped rather than failed, use `test.skip()` in a `beforeEach` hook before the test body starts. `test.abort()` is the right choice when the abort condition is detected _after_ the test has already begun executing and you want to prevent further potentially destructive actions from running.

---

### Pattern #365: `browserType.connectOverCDP({ noDefaults: true })` — Connect to User Browsers Without Playwright Overrides [official]

`noDefaults: true` in `connectOverCDP()` prevents Playwright from applying its standard browser context overrides (viewport injection, user-agent spoofing, JavaScript dialog auto-dismissal, etc.) when connecting to an externally launched Chrome or Edge instance. This is essential for testing against a user's actual browser profile without contaminating its state.

```typescript
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';

async function auditExistingSession() {
  // Connect to a Chrome instance started externally with --remote-debugging-port=9222
  const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222', {
    noDefaults: true, // do not inject viewport, user-agent, or dialog handlers
  });

  // Use the first existing context rather than creating a new one
  const contexts = browser.contexts();
  if (contexts.length === 0) throw new Error('No open contexts in target browser');
  const context = contexts[0];

  const pages = context.pages();
  const page = pages.find((p) => p.url().includes('example.com')) ?? pages[0];

  // Assert the application state as the real user sees it
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'My Account' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();

  // Do NOT close the browser — we connected to an external instance
  await browser.disconnect();
}

auditExistingSession();
```

> **Tradeoff:** `noDefaults: true` means Playwright will not set a default viewport, meaning `page.setViewportSize()` calls may not work as expected and screenshots may capture at the OS window size. Dialog handlers are not auto-dismissed — an `alert()` call in the page will block execution indefinitely unless you add a `page.on('dialog')` listener. Only use `noDefaults: true` for read-only auditing or debugging against real browser sessions; never for automated test suites where predictable viewport and dialog behavior is required.

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

### Gotcha #120: `page.screencast.start()` returns immediately but the first frame is not available until the browser emits a paint event — checking `onFrame` synchronously after start yields zero frames [community]

Teams using `page.screencast.start({ onFrame })` to capture the initial page state are surprised when the first `onFrame` callback fires several hundred milliseconds after `start()` resolves — not immediately. Calling `start()` and then immediately trying to read the frame count from the `onFrame` accumulator yields zero because the browser has not yet emitted a paint event over the CDP screencast channel.

```typescript
// ❌ Frame accumulator is empty immediately after start() — first frame not yet emitted
const frames: Buffer[] = [];
await page.screencast.start({ onFrame: ({ data }) => frames.push(data) });
console.log(frames.length); // 0 — first CDP screencast frame not yet received

// ✅ Wait for at least one navigation and paint before expecting frames
await page.screencast.start({ onFrame: ({ data }) => frames.push(data) });
await page.goto('/app');
await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');
// First frame arrives after DOMContentLoaded paints; accumulator now has data
console.log(frames.length); // 1+
```

> **WHY:** `page.screencast.start()` sends a CDP `Page.startScreencast` command to the browser, which acknowledges the command immediately but only emits `Page.screencastFrame` events after the browser has painted a frame to the compositor. The compositor paint pipeline is asynchronous relative to the CDP command channel — there is no synchronous acknowledgment that a frame is ready. `start()` resolving means only that the CDP command was acknowledged, not that the first frame buffer has been populated. This is the same underlying behavior as `page.screenshot()` requiring an implicit paint before capturing — the `onFrame` path just makes the async nature explicit. [community]

---

### Gotcha #121: `context.setStorageState()` clears IndexedDB for ALL origins in the context, not just the origin of the provided state — third-party iframe databases are wiped [community]

Teams using `context.setStorageState()` to rotate auth credentials discover that IndexedDB databases belonging to third-party iframes (analytics, chat widgets, embedded maps) are also wiped, causing those iframes to re-initialize on the next navigation and emit unexpected console errors or network requests that can destabilize timing-sensitive tests.

```typescript
// ❌ setStorageState clears ALL origins' IndexedDB — third-party iframes lose their state
await context.setStorageState({ cookies: newAuth.cookies, origins: newAuth.origins });
// IndexedDB for embedded analytics iframe is now gone
// → iframe re-initializes and emits "IDBVersionError: database not found" on next page load

// ✅ Option A: Block third-party iframes that use IndexedDB during auth-rotation tests
await context.route('https://analytics.thirdparty.com/**', (route) => route.abort());
await context.setStorageState(newAuth);

// ✅ Option B: Re-create the context instead of hot-swapping (avoids clearing third-party state)
await context.close();
const freshContext = await browser.newContext({ storageState: newAuth });
```

> **WHY:** `context.setStorageState()` is implemented in `BrowserContext._setStorageState()` which calls `clearStorageForOrigin()` for all tracked origins before applying the new state. "All tracked origins" includes origins of all frames that have loaded in the context, not just the primary origin — any cross-origin iframe that called `indexedDB.open()` registers its origin in the context's storage tracker. The CDPSession `Storage.clearDataForOrigin` command is issued for each registered origin with the `indexedDB` data type included. There is no opt-out mechanism; if you need to preserve third-party storage, you must block those origins before calling `setStorageState()`. [community]

---

### Gotcha #122: `locator.normalize()` may silently return the original locator unchanged when no semantic alternative exists — callers have no way to detect whether normalization succeeded [community]

Teams using `locator.normalize()` in locator-healing scripts check the return value hoping to detect whether a better locator was found, but `normalize()` always returns a `Locator` object regardless of whether it found a semantic improvement. There is no `normalized: boolean` property or thrown error when normalization produces no change — the only way to detect identity is to compare `toString()` output.

```typescript
// ❌ Cannot tell from the return value alone whether normalization improved anything
const original = page.locator('div.card:nth-child(3) > span.price');
const normalized = original.normalize();
// If no semantic alternative found, normalized === original selector
// normalized is still a valid Locator — no error, no flag

// ✅ Compare toString() to detect whether normalization produced a change
const originalStr = original.toString();
const normalizedStr = normalized.toString();

if (normalizedStr === originalStr) {
  console.warn(`normalize() found no improvement for: ${originalStr}`);
  // Consider adding data-testid to the element, then re-running
} else {
  console.log(`Normalized: ${originalStr} → ${normalizedStr}`);
}
```

> **WHY:** `locator.normalize()` is implemented as a heuristic selector upgrade pass that queries the accessibility tree and `data-testid` / `data-test-id` attributes of the target element. When none of those attributes are present and the element has no unique ARIA role/name pair, the algorithm has no semantic information to produce a better locator and returns the input locator unmodified. The return type is `Locator` (not `Locator | null`) because Playwright's API design principle is that locators are always valid — a locator that couldn't be improved is still a usable locator. The API provides no success discriminant because it would require the caller to handle a nullable type in every normalization call, which the Playwright team considered worse ergonomics than the silent identity behavior. [community]

---

### Gotcha #123: `test.abort()` in a fixture teardown (after `await use()`) does NOT abort the test — it throws an unhandled rejection that marks the test as failed with a confusing error message [community]

Teams calling `test.abort()` in fixture teardown code (after the `await use()` call) to enforce cleanup invariants discover that `abort()` is silently ineffective after the test body has completed — the call throws a rejected promise that bubbles up as an unexpected fixture error rather than a clean abort status.

```typescript
// ❌ test.abort() after await use() throws, does NOT abort cleanly
const test = base.extend<{ envGuard: void }>({
  envGuard: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(); // test body runs here
    // ❌ Calling abort() after use() is after-the-fact — the test already completed
    const leaked = await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__LEAKED_MUTATION__);
    if (leaked) {
      test.abort('Mutation leaked into shared state'); // ← throws UnhandledRejection
    }
  },
});

// ✅ Check invariants BEFORE await use() — abort() works only pre-execution
const test = base.extend<{ envGuard: void }>({
  envGuard: async ({ page }, use) => {
    const ready = await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__ENV_READY__);
    if (!ready) {
      test.abort('Environment not ready — aborting before test body runs');
    }
    await use();
    // Post-use teardown: use expect() assertions, not test.abort()
    const leaked = await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__LEAKED_MUTATION__);
    expect(leaked, 'Mutation leaked into shared state').toBeFalsy();
  },
});
```

> **WHY:** `test.abort()` works by throwing a special `TestAbortError` that the Playwright test runner catches in its execution coordinator and translates to an `'aborted'` result. This interception only works during the test body execution phase, which runs inside the coordinator's try/catch boundary. Fixture teardown (code after `await use()`) runs in a separate cleanup phase that is outside the abort-interception boundary — the `TestAbortError` thrown by `test.abort()` is not caught by the coordinator in this phase and surfaces as an unhandled fixture error. The design is intentional: once the test body has finished, the result is considered final and cannot be retroactively changed to `'aborted'`. [community]

---

### Gotcha #124: `browserType.connectOverCDP({ noDefaults: true })` causes `page.waitForNavigation()` to never resolve on SPAs because Playwright's navigation hooks are part of the "defaults" that are disabled [community]

Teams using `connectOverCDP({ noDefaults: true })` to audit real browser sessions find that `page.waitForNavigation()` hangs indefinitely on SPA route changes (React Router, Vue Router, Next.js client-side navigation). This helper relies on Playwright's internal navigation tracking hooks which are injected as part of the "defaults" disabled by `noDefaults: true`.

```typescript
// ❌ waitForNavigation() hangs on SPA client-side route changes with noDefaults: true
const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222', { noDefaults: true });
const page = browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0];
await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' }).click();
await page.waitForNavigation(); // ← hangs; navigation hook not installed

// ✅ Use page.waitForURL() with a timeout — polls URL rather than relying on hooks
await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' }).click();
await page.waitForURL('**/settings', { timeout: 5000 });

// ✅ Alternatively: poll a visible element on the target page
await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Settings' })).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });
```

> **WHY:** `noDefaults: true` in `connectOverCDP()` disables `BrowserContext._setupDefaults()`, which injects several JavaScript bindings and CDP event listeners into every new page. Among these is the `__playwright_navigation__` binding that fires on `history.pushState()` and `history.replaceState()` — the mechanism Playwright uses to detect SPA client-side navigations and resolve `waitForNavigation()`. Without this binding, Playwright has no notification that a SPA route change occurred and `waitForNavigation()` waits for a full page reload event that never comes on a SPA. `waitForURL()` works as a fallback because it polls `page.url()` on a timer rather than relying on the navigation binding. [community]

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern #366: `locator.filter({ visible: true })` — Scope Assertions to Visible Elements Only

Added in v1.51, `locator.filter({ visible: true })` narrows a multi-match locator to only the elements currently visible in the DOM. This prevents false positives in accordion, tab, and carousel UIs where multiple semantically identical elements exist but only one is visible at a time. Combining it with `{ visible: false }` allows asserting the hidden state as well, giving tests full visibility control without brittle CSS hacks.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('only visible tab panel is asserted', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // All three tab panels exist in the DOM; only the active one is visible
  const panels = page.getByRole('tabpanel');

  // Scope the assertion to the visible panel
  const visiblePanel = panels.filter({ visible: true });
  await expect(visiblePanel).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(visiblePanel).toContainText('Overview');

  // After switching tabs, the previously visible panel is now hidden
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Details' }).click();
  const hiddenOverview = panels.filter({ visible: false }).filter({ hasText: 'Overview' });
  await expect(hiddenOverview).toHaveCount(1);

  const newVisiblePanel = panels.filter({ visible: true });
  await expect(newVisiblePanel).toContainText('Details');
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `filter({ visible: true })` checks CSS visibility and `display` but does NOT check whether the element is within the viewport. An element with `opacity: 0` or `visibility: hidden` is considered not visible, but an off-screen element with `display: block` is visible. Use `locator.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded()` before interaction if viewport membership matters. [official]

---

### Pattern #367: `expect(locator).toContainClass()` — Assert Individual CSS Classes Without Brittle `className` String Matching

Introduced in v1.52, `toContainClass()` asserts that an element's `classList` includes the specified class names in any order, ignoring other classes. This is more resilient than `toHaveClass()` (which matches the full class string) and avoids the fragile `{ toContainText: 'active' }` workaround on non-text elements. For arrays of locators, each element can be checked against a corresponding class in one assertion call.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('active tab has correct CSS state classes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings');

  const settingsTab = page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Settings' });
  await settingsTab.click();

  // Assert only the presence of specific classes; other classes are ignored
  await expect(settingsTab).toContainClass('active');
  await expect(settingsTab).toContainClass('tab--selected tab--visible');

  // Array form: assert each list item in parallel
  const navItems = page.locator('nav > li');
  await expect(navItems).toContainClass([
    'nav-item--active',   // first item
    'nav-item',           // second item (not active)
    'nav-item',           // third item
  ]);

  // Negative form using not
  const inactiveTab = page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Profile' });
  await expect(inactiveTab).not.toContainClass('active');
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `toContainClass()` retries until timeout like all web-first assertions, so it handles async class application (e.g., CSS transitions). However, it is case-sensitive — `'Active'` will not match `'active'`. For dynamically generated class names (CSS Modules, Tailwind JIT), fall back to an aria-snapshot or `toHaveAttribute('data-state', 'active')` if class names are unpredictable. [official]

---

### Pattern #368: `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` — Assert `aria-errormessage` for Form Validation UX

Added in v1.50, `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` asserts the text of the element referenced by the `aria-errormessage` attribute, providing a semantic test for form validation error states. This is more meaningful than asserting `aria-invalid: 'true'` alone because it verifies the content of the error that screen-reader users actually hear. Works with both static `aria-errormessage` IDs and dynamically rendered error spans.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('email field shows accessible error on invalid submit', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  const emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email address');
  const submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' });

  // Submit without filling email
  await submitButton.click();

  // Assert the aria-errormessage content — retries until the error appears
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Email address is required.');
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');

  // Fill an invalid email and re-assert
  await emailInput.fill('not-an-email');
  await submitButton.click();
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/must be a valid email/i);

  // Fix the email and assert error disappears
  await emailInput.fill('user@example.com');
  await submitButton.click();
  await expect(emailInput).not.toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage();
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` resolves the `aria-errormessage` ID reference at assertion time, not continuously — if the referenced element's text changes mid-animation, the assertion captures the final stable value. The referenced element must be in the DOM and visible; if the error is conditionally rendered via `v-if`/`ngIf`, the element must exist before the assertion is evaluated. [official]

---

### Pattern #369: `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` — Persist Firebase/IndexedDB Authentication Tokens Across Tests

Introduced in v1.51, the `indexedDB: true` option on `browserContext.storageState()` captures IndexedDB data alongside cookies and localStorage. This is essential for applications that store auth tokens in IndexedDB (Firebase Authentication, Supabase local storage, Dexie.js caches). Without it, `storageState()` snapshots miss the token store and tests appear unauthenticated even after login.

```typescript
// e2e/auth.setup.ts
import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const authFile = path.join(__dirname, '../.auth/firebase-user.json');

setup('authenticate with Firebase', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(process.env.TEST_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  // Wait for Firebase to complete token exchange and write to IndexedDB
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();

  // Capture auth state including IndexedDB (Firebase stores tokens here)
  await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile, indexedDB: true });
});

// playwright.config.ts — reference auth file in all authenticated projects
// projects: [{ name: 'authenticated', use: { storageState: authFile } }]
```

> **Tradeoff:** IndexedDB serialization can produce large state files (several MB) because Firebase stores multiple token entries per user. Add the `.auth/` directory to `.gitignore` and CI artifact exclusions. IndexedDB state is origin-bound — the saved state works only when tests navigate to the exact same origin as the login page. [official]

---

### Pattern #370: `test.step()` with `timeout` Option — Enforce Per-Step Time Budgets for Slow Operations

Since v1.50, `test.step()` accepts a `timeout` option that independently bounds a single step without affecting the global test timeout. This is valuable for steps that wrap slow third-party APIs, file uploads, or chart renders — a step timeout produces a clear `TimeoutError` naming the step, rather than a cryptic global timeout message pointing at an arbitrary line.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('file export completes within SLA', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports');

  await test.step('generate report', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Generate' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Report ready');
  }, { timeout: 15_000 }); // SLA: generation must complete in 15s

  await test.step('export to CSV', async () => {
    const [download] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForEvent('download'),
      page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export CSV' }).click(),
    ]);
    const fileName = download.suggestedFilename();
    expect(fileName).toMatch(/report-\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\.csv/);
    await download.saveAs(`/tmp/${fileName}`);
  }, { timeout: 10_000 }); // Export must complete in 10s
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** Step timeouts do not pause the global test timeout clock — a step that uses its full 15s budget still consumes 15s from the test's global timeout. If all steps hit their individual timeouts, the test will still exceed the global timeout and be killed. Use step timeouts for SLA enforcement (raise a named failure), not for slowing down fast-path tests. [official]

---

### Pattern #371: `test.step.skip()` — Conditionally Disable Steps Without Commenting Out Code

`test.step.skip()` (available since v1.50) marks a step as skipped so it appears in the trace viewer and reporter as `skipped` rather than simply not running. Unlike commenting out a step body, `skip()` preserves the step label in reports, making it visible to reviewers that a step was intentionally bypassed. This is the right tool for platform-conditional steps (e.g., skip a mobile-only step on desktop) or in-progress features.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow with optional gift wrapping', async ({ page, isMobile }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  await test.step('add item to cart', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Item added');
  });

  // Gift wrapping UI is not yet implemented on mobile
  await test.step.skip('apply gift wrapping', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Add gift wrapping' }).check();
    await page.getByLabel('Gift message').fill('Happy Birthday!');
  });

  await test.step('proceed to checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout/);
  });

  await test.step('complete payment', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** Skipped steps still consume a small overhead in test execution (metadata tracking) but do not run their body. `test.step.skip()` is unconditional — the entire step body is bypassed. For conditional logic, use a regular `if` inside the step body; `skip()` is for permanently or deliberately disabled steps that you want tracked in CI artifacts. [official]

---

### Pattern #372: External ARIA Snapshot YAML Files — Version-Controlled Accessibility Baselines

Since v1.50, `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot({ name: 'component.aria.yml' })` stores the accessibility tree snapshot in a separate `.aria.yml` file rather than inline in the test file. External YAML baselines are easier to diff in PRs, can be reviewed by accessibility specialists, and allow snapshot updates without touching test code. The `--update-snapshots` CLI flag updates only the YAML files while leaving test assertions intact.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('navigation menu has correct ARIA structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Snapshot stored in e2e/snapshots/nav-menu.aria.yml
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main menu' }))
    .toMatchAriaSnapshot({ name: 'nav-menu.aria.yml' });
});

test('search results list is accessible', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search?q=playwright');
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Search results' }))
    .toMatchAriaSnapshot({ name: 'search-results.aria.yml' });
});

// e2e/snapshots/nav-menu.aria.yml (generated, then committed)
// - navigation "Main menu":
//   - link "Home"
//   - link "Docs"
//   - link "Blog"
//   - link "Community"
```

> **Tradeoff:** External ARIA YAML files add file-system surface to the test suite. Keep them in an `e2e/snapshots/` directory and commit them alongside tests — treat them like golden screenshots. Use `updateSnapshots: 'changed'` in config to avoid inadvertently resetting snapshots that did not change between runs. [official]

---

### Pattern #373: `updateSnapshots: 'changed'` — Surgical Snapshot Updates Without Wholesale Reset

The `updateSnapshots: 'changed'` option (v1.50+) in `playwright.config.ts` or via `--update-snapshots=changed` CLI flag updates only snapshots whose comparison failed, leaving passing snapshots untouched. The default `'all'` mode resets every snapshot on every update run, which masks regressions introduced between update runs. Using `'changed'` is the safer production workflow: it acts as a scalpel, not a sledgehammer.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/snapshots/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',

  // Only update snapshots that actually diffed — don't reset passing ones
  updateSnapshots: 'changed',

  // 3-way merge for inline snapshot updates (produces cleaner git diffs)
  updateSourceMethod: '3way',

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
});

// CLI usage:
// npx playwright test --update-snapshots=changed
// npx playwright test --update-snapshots=all      ← nuclear option, use with care
// npx playwright test --update-snapshots=none     ← default; fail on any diff
```

> **Tradeoff:** `updateSnapshots: 'changed'` only updates snapshots for test files that were actually run. If you run a filtered subset (e.g., `--grep @smoke`), snapshots for skipped tests are not updated even if their UI changed. Always run the full suite before committing snapshot updates to avoid stale baselines for untested paths. [official]

---

### Pattern #374: `testProject.workers` — Per-Project Worker Budgets for Mixed-Speed Suites

Since v1.52, `testProject.workers` overrides the global `workers` count for an individual project. This is essential in monorepo configs where a fast unit-like API project and a slow E2E project run in the same `playwright.config.ts` — the API project can use 8 workers while the E2E project uses 2 to avoid browser resource contention. The value accepts both absolute counts and percentage strings (`'50%'`).

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : 2, // global default

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'api-tests',
      testDir: './e2e/api',
      workers: 8, // API tests are stateless — max parallelism
      use: { baseURL: process.env.API_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3001' },
    },
    {
      name: 'chromium-e2e',
      testDir: './e2e/browser',
      workers: 2, // Browser tests are resource-heavy — limit concurrency
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'mobile-e2e',
      testDir: './e2e/browser',
      workers: 1, // Mobile emulation conflicts at high concurrency
      use: { ...devices['iPhone 14'] },
    },
  ],
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `testProject.workers` overrides the global value but the OS-level browser process pool is still shared. Setting one project to 8 workers while another runs simultaneously may still contend on CPU. Use `fullyParallel: false` on the global config and rely on project-level workers only when projects run sequentially (e.g., with `dependencies`). [official]

---

### Pattern #375: `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` — Fail CI When Retries Reveal Flakiness

`testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` (v1.52+) exits with a non-zero status code when any test passes on retry after an initial failure — i.e., a test that is flaky. By default Playwright treats a pass-on-retry as a success; enabling this option treats it as a signal to investigate rather than silently paper over. This is the correct posture for mature CI pipelines where flakiness budget is tracked explicitly.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // CI: fail the pipeline if any test needed a retry to pass
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
    ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results/results.json' }],
  ],

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
});

// In the reporter output, flaky tests appear with status "flaky"
// Combined with the HTML reporter's filter, teams can track flake rate over time
```

> **Tradeoff:** Enabling `failOnFlakyTests` in a newly-migrated or actively-developed suite will likely break CI immediately because some flakiness is expected during feature development. Roll this out gradually: enable it per-project starting with the most stable project, or add a `FAIL_ON_FLAKY=true` environment variable guard so it can be toggled per-branch without a config change. [official]

---

### Pattern #376: `webServer.wait.stdout` with Named Capture Groups — Dynamic Port Injection

Since v1.57, the `webServer.wait.stdout` regex supports named capture groups whose values are automatically injected as environment variables for use in `baseURL` and test fixtures. This eliminates the need for hardcoded ports in configs — the test runner listens for the server's own port announcement and wires it through automatically, solving port-conflict issues in parallel CI shards.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    // Named capture group 'PORT' → process.env.PORT in tests
    wait: {
      stdout: /Local:\s+http:\/\/localhost:(?<PORT>\d+)/,
    },
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    timeout: 30_000,
  },

  use: {
    // Reads the captured PORT env var — resolves after server announces it
    baseURL: `http://localhost:${process.env.PORT ?? '5173'}`,
  },

  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { channel: 'chrome' } },
  ],
});

// Vite's output: "Local: http://localhost:5173/" → PORT=5173
// Next.js output: "Ready - started server on 0.0.0.0:3000" → requires matching regex
```

> **Tradeoff:** Named capture groups require `wait.stdout` (not `wait.url`), so the server must print the port to stdout. Servers that print to stderr only (some Express apps) require a wrapper script that merges streams. The env var is set after the regex matches, meaning it's unavailable in the `webServer` object itself — use the fallback value in `baseURL` for local dev without the server running. [official]

---

### Pattern #377: Playwright Test Agents (Planner/Generator/Healer) — LLM-Driven Test Authoring Workflow

Introduced in v1.56, the `npx playwright init-agents` command initializes three agent definitions (Planner, Generator, Healer) for use with Claude Code, VS Code Copilot, and OpenCode. The workflow is: (1) Planner explores the app and writes Markdown specs; (2) Generator reads specs and emits `.spec.ts` files with live selector verification; (3) Healer reruns failing tests, inspects UI state, and patches locators. Teams use a `seed.spec.ts` to inject custom fixtures into agent-generated tests.

```typescript
// e2e/seed.spec.ts — bootstraps agent context with app-specific fixtures
import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('seed', async ({ page, apiClient }) => {
  // Verify the app is reachable and fixtures are wired correctly
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toBeVisible();

  // Agent-generated tests will import from './fixtures' and inherit apiClient
});

// e2e/specs/checkout.md (Planner output — committed, human-reviewable)
// # Checkout Flow
// ## Scenario: Guest checkout with credit card
// 1. Add item to cart from product page
// 2. Proceed to checkout without creating account
// 3. Fill shipping address form
// 4. Enter valid credit card details
// 5. Assert order confirmation page with order number

// Run agents via VS Code or CLI:
// npx playwright test --agent=planner --spec="checkout flow"
// npx playwright test --agent=generator --plan=e2e/specs/checkout.md
// npx playwright test --agent=healer --test=e2e/tests/checkout.spec.ts
```

> **Tradeoff:** Agent-generated tests require a running application and headed browser; they cannot generate tests for apps behind authentication barriers without a configured `seed.spec.ts` that handles login. Generated tests inherit the locator strategy of the Generator agent (prefers `getByRole`/`getByLabel`) but may require manual review for complex data-driven scenarios. [official]

---

### Pattern #378: `await using` Disposable Pattern — Automatic Resource Cleanup for Playwright APIs

Many Playwright APIs (v1.59+) return `AsyncDisposable` objects compatible with the TC39 `using`/`await using` proposal (Stage 4, supported in TypeScript 5.2+ with `--target ES2017` and `--lib ES2022`). `await using` ensures `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` is called at scope exit, eliminating try/finally boilerplate for tracing, screencast recording, and route handlers. This is the idiomatic cleanup pattern for Playwright's newer APIs.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('trace is always stopped even on failure', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // await using automatically calls tracing.stop() at scope exit
  await using _tracing = await context.tracing.start({
    screenshots: true,
    snapshots: true,
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();

  // Even if this assertion throws, _tracing.stop() runs via asyncDispose
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('1 item in cart');

  // Explicit save before scope exit — dispose just stops, not saves
  await context.tracing.stop({ path: 'trace.zip' });
});

// Route cleanup example
test('mock API call with auto-cleanup', async ({ page }) => {
  await using _route = await page.routeFromHAR('./fixtures/api.har', {
    url: '**/api/**',
    update: false,
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toContainText('Welcome');
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `await using` requires TypeScript 5.2+ and `"lib": ["ES2022"]` or later in `tsconfig.json`. The `[Symbol.asyncDispose]` method is not available on all Playwright APIs — check the return type in the API docs. In older TypeScript targets, fall back to explicit `try/finally` cleanup. Do not mix `await using` with manual `stop()`/`dispose()` calls on the same resource — calling both leads to double-dispose errors. [community]

---

### Pattern #379: `locator.filter({ hasNot })` — Exclude Sub-Element Matches in Complex List Assertions

`locator.filter({ hasNot })` (v1.33+) narrows a multi-element locator by excluding elements that contain a specified nested locator. This solves the common pattern of "find all cards that have NOT been dismissed" or "find the form row that does NOT have an error state" without resorting to complex CSS `:not()` combinators or `evaluate()` calls. Combining `hasNot` with `has` produces highly precise scoped selections.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('incomplete tasks are shown, completed tasks are hidden', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/todo');

  const allTasks = page.getByRole('listitem');

  // Find tasks that do NOT have a checkmark icon (not yet completed)
  const incompleteTasks = allTasks.filter({
    hasNot: page.getByRole('img', { name: 'Completed' }),
  });

  // Find tasks that DO have error state AND are NOT dismissed
  const activeErrors = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({
    has: page.getByRole('alert'),
    hasNot: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Dismiss' }).filter({ visible: false }),
  });

  await expect(incompleteTasks).toHaveCount(3);
  await expect(activeErrors).toHaveCount(1);

  // Complete the first task
  await incompleteTasks.first().getByRole('checkbox').check();
  await expect(incompleteTasks).toHaveCount(2);
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** `hasNot` evaluates the nested locator in the context of each parent element's subtree at assertion time. If the nested element is outside the parent's subtree (e.g., a sibling), `hasNot` does not exclude correctly. Both outer and inner locators must belong to the same frame — `FrameLocator` inside `hasNot` throws at evaluation. [official]

---

### Pattern #380: Multi-Server `webServer` Array — Frontend + Backend with Named Server Labels

Since v1.27 and enhanced in v1.57, `webServer` accepts an array of server configs, each with a `name` label that appears in the test reporter and log output. The reporter-visible names make it immediately clear which server failed to start on CI. Each entry has an independent `timeout`, `reuseExistingServer`, and readiness `url`, enabling polyglot stacks (Vite + Express, Next.js + FastAPI) to boot cleanly before any test runs.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: [
    {
      name: 'Frontend (Vite)',
      command: 'npm run dev --workspace=frontend',
      url: 'http://localhost:5173',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      timeout: 30_000,
    },
    {
      name: 'API (Express)',
      command: 'npm run start --workspace=api',
      url: 'http://localhost:3001/health',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      timeout: 20_000,
      env: {
        NODE_ENV: 'test',
        DATABASE_URL: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL ?? 'sqlite::memory:',
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'Mock SMTP',
      command: 'npx maildev --port 1080 --smtp 1025',
      url: 'http://localhost:1080',
      reuseExistingServer: true, // always reuse; maildev is lightweight
      timeout: 5_000,
    },
  ],

  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:5173',
  },
});
```

> **Tradeoff:** All `webServer` entries start in parallel but Playwright waits for all of them to become ready before running any test. If one server takes 90s and the others take 5s, the slowest determines startup time. Use `reuseExistingServer: true` for services that are already running in your dev environment to avoid startup overhead locally. [official]
