**Pattern 480** — `page.addLocatorHandler()` with `noWaitAfter` for Async Overlay Chains
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('complete onboarding wizard with multi-step overlay chain', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/app/onboarding');

  // Register handler for each overlay in the chain — they appear in sequence
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Welcome' }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Get Started' }).click();
      // Do NOT wait for the dialog to disappear — next dialog appears immediately
    },
    { noWaitAfter: true, times: 1 },
  );

  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Choose Your Plan' }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('radio', { name: 'Free' }).click();
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
    },
    { noWaitAfter: true, times: 1 },
  );

  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Enable Notifications' }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Skip' }).click();
    },
    { times: 1 },  // last in chain — wait for it to close before proceeding
  );

  // Main test action — handlers fire automatically as overlays appear
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Start Setup' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `noWaitAfter: true` in `addLocatorHandler()` tells Playwright not to wait for the overlay to detach before resuming the action that triggered the handler. This is necessary when one overlay triggers another immediately on close (chained dialogs, wizard steps, notification prompts in sequence). Without `noWaitAfter`, Playwright times out waiting for the first dialog to disappear while the second dialog has already appeared and is blocking the same area. The tradeoff is that you lose the safety net of confirming the overlay closed — if the "Get Started" click fails silently, the handler returns and Playwright may re-invoke it. Use `times: N` to limit re-invocation and add an assertion inside the handler (e.g., `await expect(dialog).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 2000 })`) when `noWaitAfter` is not required.

**Pattern 481** — `test.fixme()` with Condition for Environment-Aware Skipping
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Payment processing', () => {
  test('Stripe checkout completes in staging', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
    // Skip in local dev — Stripe test keys not configured outside CI/staging
    test.fixme(
      !process.env.STRIPE_TEST_KEY,
      'Skipped: STRIPE_TEST_KEY not set. Run in CI or staging.',
    );

    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();

    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /payment successful/i })).toBeVisible({
      timeout: 30_000,
    });
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/[0-9]+\/confirmation/);
  });

  test('invalid card shows inline error', async ({ page }) => {
    // This test has no external dependency — always runs
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4000 0000 0000 0002');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/card was declined/i);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.fixme(condition, message)` marks a test as expected-to-fail (or should-be-skipped) when a runtime condition is true, without removing the test from the suite. Unlike `test.skip()`, `fixme` signals "this test is known to be broken or unavailable in this environment" — it appears in the HTML report with a distinctive status, reminding engineers that the test exists and should eventually pass. The tradeoff vs. `test.skip()` is semantic: use `fixme` for tests that are temporarily broken or require a missing dependency, and `skip` for tests that are intentionally excluded for a permanent reason (e.g., a feature not yet implemented on a specific platform). Both accept a condition as the first argument for environment-aware branching.

**Pattern 482** — `locator.selectOption()` with Label for Accessible Dropdown Testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shipping rate updates when country is changed', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/shipping');

  // Select by visible label text — most resilient to value/index changes
  await page.getByLabel('Country').selectOption({ label: 'Germany' });

  // Confirm the shipping rate region updated
  const shippingRate = page.getByRole('region', { name: 'Shipping Rate' });
  await expect(shippingRate).toContainText('€');

  // Assert specific rate for Germany (mocked in test environment)
  await expect(shippingRate.getByRole('term')).toHaveText('Standard Shipping');
  await expect(shippingRate.getByRole('definition')).toHaveText('€4.99');

  // Test multi-select when the select element has multiple attribute
  const multiSelect = page.getByLabel('Notify me about');
  await multiSelect.selectOption([
    { label: 'Order Updates' },
    { label: 'Promotions' },
  ]);
  await expect(multiSelect).toHaveValues(['order-updates', 'promotions']);
});
```
Tradeoff: `selectOption({ label: '...' })` selects a `<select>` option by its visible text, which is more resilient than selecting by `value` (which may be a database ID or internal code that changes without UI impact) or by `index` (which breaks if options are reordered). For multi-select elements, passing an array of label objects selects multiple options atomically. The limitation is that `selectOption()` only works with native `<select>` elements — custom dropdown components built with `<div>` and ARIA `role="listbox"` require `getByRole('option')` + `.click()` or a custom fixture. Always verify the accessible name of the `<select>` via `getByLabel()` rather than `locator('select')` to ensure the label association is correct.

---

**Pattern 483** — `page.dragAndDrop()` with Precise Coordinates for Kanban Board Testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dragging a card between Kanban columns updates its status', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/board');

  const todoColumn = page.getByRole('region', { name: 'To Do' });
  const inProgressColumn = page.getByRole('region', { name: 'In Progress' });

  // Locate the card to drag by its title
  const card = todoColumn.getByRole('article', { name: 'Write unit tests' });
  await expect(card).toBeVisible();

  // Use dragAndDrop for HTML5 drag — target the column's drop zone
  await page.dragAndDrop(
    '[data-testid="card-write-unit-tests"]',
    '[data-testid="column-in-progress"]',
  );

  // Assert the card moved to the In Progress column
  await expect(inProgressColumn.getByRole('article', { name: 'Write unit tests' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(todoColumn.getByRole('article', { name: 'Write unit tests' })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Assert the status label within the card updated
  await expect(
    inProgressColumn.getByRole('article', { name: 'Write unit tests' })
      .getByRole('status'),
  ).toHaveText('In Progress');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.dragAndDrop(source, target)` is the highest-level drag API — it dispatches `pointerdown`, `dragstart`, `dragenter`, `dragover`, `drop`, and `dragend` events in the correct sequence and handles element coordinates automatically. It works reliably for HTML5 native drag-and-drop (elements with `draggable="true"` and `ondrop` handlers). The limitation is that many modern Kanban libraries (react-beautiful-dnd, dnd-kit) use pointer events rather than the HTML5 drag API — for these, use `locator.dragTo()` with `{ force: true }` or manually simulate the pointer event sequence with `page.mouse.move()`, `page.mouse.down()`, a series of `page.mouse.move()` calls, and `page.mouse.up()`. Always verify which event model the component uses by checking source code or DevTools event listeners before choosing the drag API.

---

**Pattern 484** — `APIRequestContext.dispose()` for Manual Request Context Lifecycle
```typescript
import { test, expect, request } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Admin API with dedicated auth context', () => {
  let adminRequest: import('@playwright/test').APIRequestContext;

  test.beforeAll(async () => {
    // Create a standalone request context with admin credentials
    // separate from the test's built-in `request` fixture
    adminRequest = await request.newContext({
      baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3001',
      extraHTTPHeaders: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.ADMIN_TOKEN}`,
        'X-Admin-Secret': process.env.ADMIN_SECRET ?? '',
      },
    });
  });

  test.afterAll(async () => {
    // Dispose explicitly to flush cookies/credentials from memory
    await adminRequest.dispose();
  });

  test('admin can list all users', async ({ page }) => {
    const res = await adminRequest.get('/admin/users');
    expect(res.status()).toBe(200);
    const { users } = await res.json();
    expect(users.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

  test('admin can deactivate a user account', async ({ page }) => {
    const createRes = await adminRequest.post('/admin/users', {
      data: { email: `test-${Date.now()}@example.com`, role: 'viewer' },
    });
    const { id } = await createRes.json();

    const deactivateRes = await adminRequest.patch(`/admin/users/${id}`, {
      data: { active: false },
    });
    expect(deactivateRes.status()).toBe(200);
    await adminRequest.delete(`/admin/users/${id}`);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `request.newContext()` creates a request context with custom credentials that is completely independent of the test's built-in `request` fixture and any browser page contexts — changes to its cookie jar do not bleed into browser tests running in the same worker. This is the correct pattern when you need two concurrent credential levels in one test (e.g., admin API calls alongside a regular-user browser session). The mandatory `dispose()` in `afterAll` flushes all credential state from memory; omitting it is a security risk in CI environments where worker processes may be reused across test runs. The tradeoff vs. using the built-in `request` fixture is that `newContext()` requires explicit lifecycle management — if `beforeAll` throws, `afterAll` still runs but `adminRequest` may be undefined, so guard with `if (adminRequest) await adminRequest.dispose()`.

---

**Pattern 485** — `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleDescription()` for Tooltip and Help-Text Validation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form fields have correct accessible descriptions and error associations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile/edit');

  // Verify help text is associated via aria-describedby
  const passwordField = page.getByLabel('New Password');
  await expect(passwordField).toHaveAccessibleDescription(
    /at least 8 characters.*one uppercase.*one number/i,
  );

  // Submit with invalid data to trigger inline errors
  await passwordField.fill('weak');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Changes' }).click();

  // After validation, the error message should become the accessible description
  await expect(passwordField).toHaveAccessibleDescription(/password must be at least 8/i);

  // Assert the error element itself is visible and correctly associated
  const errorMsg = page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: /password must be at least 8/i });
  await expect(errorMsg).toBeVisible();

  // Verify a tooltip-described button has the right description
  const helpButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'What is this?' });
  await helpButton.hover();
  await expect(helpButton).toHaveAccessibleDescription(/your unique username shown in your profile URL/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: `toHaveAccessibleDescription()` asserts the value of `aria-describedby` or `title` as resolved by the accessibility tree — it validates that help text and error messages are correctly wired to their form controls, not just visually co-located. This catches the common bug where an error `<span>` is rendered next to a field but not referenced by `aria-describedby`, making the error invisible to screen readers. The assertion retries until the description matches, so it naturally waits for error messages that appear after async validation. The limitation is that `toHaveAccessibleDescription()` reads the computed accessible description — if the associated element is `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, the description may be empty even though the element is in the DOM; always pair with a `toBeVisible()` check on the describing element.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G160** — `page.route()` glob patterns with a single `*` do not match across path separators, silently falling through to the real network
Why this matters: Playwright's URL glob matching follows the rule that `*` matches any string except `/`, while `**` matches across path separators. A route registered as `page.route('*/api/users', ...)` does NOT match `https://app.example.com/api/users` because the single `*` cannot cross the `://` and `/` characters in the origin. The route silently falls through, the real network request completes, and the test appears to pass — until the CI environment has no backend and the request 404s. This is one of the hardest-to-diagnose route failures because there is no warning when a `route()` handler is never invoked.
Fix: Always use `**/` at the start of route globs that should match any origin: `page.route('**/api/users', ...)`. To assert that your route was actually invoked, add a counter: `let intercepted = 0; await page.route('**/api/users', (r) => { intercepted++; r.fulfill(...); }); /* ... action ... */ expect(intercepted).toBe(1);`. Alternatively, use a URL predicate function `page.route((url) => url.pathname === '/api/users', ...)` for exact path matching without glob ambiguity.

---

**Gotcha G161** — `locator.fill()` on a `contenteditable` element sets the value but does not trigger framework input events
Why this matters: `locator.fill()` uses the `input` event to set a value in form fields. For standard `<input>` and `<textarea>` elements, this works correctly and triggers React/Vue/Angular's synthetic event system. However, rich text editors built on `contenteditable` divs (Tiptap, Quill, Draft.js, Lexical) listen to `beforeinput`, `keydown`, and mutation observer events — not the `input` event. Calling `fill()` on a `contenteditable` element sets the text content visually but does not fire the events the editor framework expects, leaving the editor's internal state desynchronized. The text appears in the DOM but the editor's `onChange` is never called, so form submission sends an empty or stale value.
Fix: For `contenteditable` editors, use `locator.click()` to focus, then `page.keyboard.type('your text')` to simulate real keystrokes. This fires the full `keydown`→`beforeinput`→`input`→`keyup` sequence that rich text editors require. For editors with a ProseMirror-based architecture, check if the library exposes a `.commands.setContent()` API accessible via `page.evaluate()` — programmatic content injection is more reliable than keystroke simulation for long text. Never mix `fill()` and `keyboard.type()` on the same `contenteditable` in one test — `fill()` clears selection state that `keyboard.type()` expects.

---

**Gotcha G162** — `context.storageState()` does not capture `IndexedDB` data by default, silently omitting auth tokens stored by Firebase or Supabase
Why this matters: `context.storageState()` serializes `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and cookies to a JSON file. It does NOT serialize `IndexedDB`, which is where Firebase Auth SDK, Supabase Auth, and several other auth libraries persist session tokens. When `storageState` is used for auth persistence in `globalSetup` and restored in each test, the browser context loads with empty `IndexedDB` — the Firebase SDK finds no token, silently re-initializes in an unauthenticated state, and the test redirects to the login page. Because `localStorage` and cookies are restored correctly, no error is thrown — the test just sees the login page and times out on dashboard assertions.
Fix: Use `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` (introduced in Playwright 1.45) when saving state from a Firebase/Supabase authenticated session: `await context.storageState({ path: '.auth/user.json', indexedDB: true })`. Restore it the same way in `playwright.config.ts` under `use.storageState`. To verify the fix, add a sanity-check test that asserts `await page.evaluate(() => indexedDB.databases())` returns entries with names matching the Firebase app name before running the full suite.

---

**Gotcha G163** — `test.setTimeout()` called inside `test.beforeAll()` only affects the `beforeAll` hook timeout, not the individual tests in the suite
Why this matters: `test.setTimeout(ms)` sets the timeout for the currently running test or hook. When called inside `test.beforeAll()`, it extends the timeout of the `beforeAll` hook itself — which is often the intention for slow global setup. However, developers frequently place `test.setTimeout(60_000)` inside `beforeAll` expecting it to apply to all subsequent tests in the `describe` block, especially when doing slow database seeding. The individual tests still run with the default timeout (30 seconds by default), causing them to time out during long operations while the `beforeAll` hook completes fine.
Fix: To set a timeout for all tests in a `describe` block, use `test.describe.configure({ timeout: 60_000 })` at the top of the block — this sets the timeout for all tests and hooks within that describe scope. To override the timeout for a single test, call `test.setTimeout(ms)` at the top of that test's callback. To set a global default, use `timeout` in `playwright.config.ts` under `use`. Never rely on `test.setTimeout()` inside `beforeAll` to affect sibling tests — the call is scoped to the currently executing hook.

---

**Gotcha G164** — `page.screenshot()` with `fullPage: true` captures the scroll overflow but misses fixed-position elements at their scrolled positions
Why this matters: `page.screenshot({ fullPage: true })` stitches together a full-page screenshot by virtually scrolling the viewport and combining screenshots. Fixed-position elements (sticky headers, floating action buttons, cookie banners, chat widgets) that are `position: fixed` or `position: sticky` in CSS appear at their original viewport position in every stitched segment — so in a `fullPage` screenshot, a fixed header appears repeated every viewport-height in the final image. This causes visual regression tests to fail after any content change that alters page height (adding a paragraph, expanding an accordion), because the stitch point changes and the repeated header shifts by a few pixels.
Fix: For pages with fixed headers or sticky elements, avoid `fullPage: true` and instead test specific regions: use `locator.screenshot()` to capture individual components, or use `page.screenshot({ clip: { x, y, width, height } })` to snapshot a specific viewport region. For full-page visual regression without repeated-header artifacts, inject CSS before the screenshot: `await page.addStyleTag({ content: 'header, [data-testid="sticky-nav"] { position: static !important; }' })` to unfix the element, take the screenshot, then remove the style tag. Document this workaround with a comment so future maintainers understand why the injection exists.

**Pattern 486** — Worker-Scoped Database Fixture for Expensive Seed Operations
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = {
  dbConnection: { baseUrl: string; seedId: string };
};

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  dbConnection: [
    async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
      // Worker-scoped: runs once per worker process, shared across all tests in the worker
      const seedId = `seed-${workerInfo.workerIndex}-${Date.now()}`;
      const baseUrl = process.env.API_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000';

      // Expensive one-time seed using a dedicated API context
      const apiContext = await browser.newContext();
      const apiPage = await apiContext.newPage();
      const seedRes = await apiPage.request.post(`${baseUrl}/api/test/seed`, {
        data: { id: seedId, products: 50, users: 10 },
      });
      expect(seedRes.ok()).toBeTruthy();
      await apiContext.close();

      await use({ baseUrl, seedId });

      // Teardown: clean up the seeded data once all tests in this worker complete
      const cleanupContext = await browser.newContext();
      const cleanupPage = await cleanupContext.newPage();
      await cleanupPage.request.delete(`${baseUrl}/api/test/seed/${seedId}`);
      await cleanupContext.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('product listing shows seeded items', async ({ page, dbConnection }) => {
  await page.goto(`${dbConnection.baseUrl}/products?seed=${dbConnection.seedId}`);
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Products' }).getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(50);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toContainText('Products');
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures amortize expensive database seeding across all tests in a worker — a 50-product seed runs once per worker instead of once per test, reducing suite time proportionally to the test count. The risk is shared state between tests in the same worker: if one test mutates the seeded data (deletes a product, changes a price), subsequent tests in the same worker see the modified state, causing order-dependent failures. Mitigate by having tests only read from the shared seed and create their own ephemeral mutations in test-scoped fixtures that clean up after themselves. Never share a mutable `page` instance in a worker-scoped fixture — only share stable data like IDs and URLs.

**Pattern 487** — `page.exposeFunction()` for Injecting Node.js Crypto into the Browser
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createHmac } from 'crypto';

test('signed API request from page-level JavaScript is accepted by server', async ({ page }) => {
  // Expose a Node.js crypto function so page-level JS can call it synchronously
  await page.exposeFunction(
    'signPayload',
    (payload: string, secret: string): string => {
      return createHmac('sha256', secret).update(payload).digest('hex');
    }
  );

  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Fill cart and trigger client-side signature generation
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();

  // Assert that the page JS called signPayload and the signed request was accepted
  const signatureVisible = page.getByTestId('request-signature');
  await expect(signatureVisible).toBeVisible();
  await expect(signatureVisible).toHaveText(/^[a-f0-9]{64}$/);

  // Verify the checkout form submits successfully with the signed payload
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.exposeFunction()` bridges the browser sandbox and Node.js — it allows page-level JavaScript to call Node APIs (crypto, file system, database) that are unavailable in the browser. The function survives navigations, making it safe to expose once per test and use across page transitions. The limitation is that the exposed function is asynchronous from the browser's perspective even if your Node implementation is synchronous; page JS must `await window.signPayload(...)`. Additionally, all arguments and return values must be JSON-serializable — passing class instances, Buffers, or circular references throws a serialization error. For testing signed-request flows, this pattern avoids the fragile alternative of hard-coding HMAC signatures as test constants.

**Pattern 488** — `page.emulateMedia()` for Dark Mode and Print Stylesheet Testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('theming and print layout', () => {
  test('dark mode applies correct color tokens to navigation', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' });
    await page.goto('/');

    const nav = page.getByRole('navigation');
    await expect(nav).toBeVisible();
    // Assert CSS custom property resolves to the dark token value
    await expect(nav).toHaveCSS('background-color', 'rgb(18, 18, 18)');
    await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Home' })).toHaveCSS('color', 'rgb(230, 230, 230)');
  });

  test('print stylesheet hides navigation and shows print-only summary', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.emulateMedia({ media: 'print' });
    await page.goto('/invoice/123');

    // Navigation hidden in print layout
    await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeHidden();

    // Print-only footer visible
    const printFooter = page.getByTestId('print-summary');
    await expect(printFooter).toBeVisible();
    await expect(printFooter).toContainText('Invoice #123');
  });

  test('reduced motion disables animated transitions', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' });
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open Menu' }).click();
    // Assert animation-duration is 0ms under reduced-motion
    const sidebar = page.getByRole('complementary', { name: 'Sidebar' });
    await expect(sidebar).toHaveCSS('animation-duration', '0s');
    await expect(sidebar).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.emulateMedia()` sets the CSS media features at the browser level, so `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and `@media print` rules activate exactly as they do for real users — no JavaScript theme injection needed. The call can be made after `page.goto()` to test dynamic theme switching mid-session, or before to test initial render. The limitation is that `toHaveCSS()` reads computed style values including browser defaults and CSS variable resolution — if your design system uses CSS custom properties, assert the final computed RGB value, not the variable name, since `toHaveCSS('color', 'var(--fg-default)')` always fails. For print, `page.emulateMedia({ media: 'print' })` does not trigger the browser's print dialog — it only applies print CSS; use `page.pdf()` if you need to test actual PDF output.

**Pattern 489** — `locator.filter()` Chaining for Complex Table Row Assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('order table shows correct status badge for each order state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/admin/orders');

  const rows = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasNot: page.getByRole('columnheader') });

  // Pending rows have a yellow badge and no action buttons
  const pendingRows = rows.filter({
    has: page.getByRole('status').filter({ hasText: 'Pending' }),
  });
  await expect(pendingRows.getByRole('status')).toHaveText(['Pending', 'Pending']);
  await expect(pendingRows.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' })).toHaveCount(2);

  // Shipped rows have a green badge and a tracking link
  const shippedRow = rows.filter({
    has: page.getByRole('status').filter({ hasText: 'Shipped' }),
  });
  await expect(shippedRow).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(shippedRow.getByRole('link', { name: /track/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(shippedRow.getByRole('status')).toHaveCSS('color', 'rgb(22, 163, 74)');

  // Cancelled rows are visually de-emphasised and have no action buttons
  const cancelledRows = rows.filter({
    has: page.getByRole('status').filter({ hasText: 'Cancelled' }),
  });
  await expect(cancelledRows.getByRole('button')).toHaveCount(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.filter()` with `has` and `hasNot` enables scoped assertions within a matching set without resorting to nth-child indices or CSS attribute selectors — it stays in Playwright's retry-safe locator graph, so each assertion automatically retries until the condition is met. Chaining multiple `.filter()` calls is additive (AND semantics), and each filter locator must be relative to the outer locator, not rooted at the document. The limitation is that `hasNot` is only available from Playwright 1.33 onward — older projects need `locator.filter({ hasNotText: ... })` as a workaround for simple text exclusions. Avoid using `.filter()` on very large tables (500+ rows) in the DOM — each filter evaluates all candidate elements synchronously in the browser, which can cause perceptible slowdowns compared to backend-filtered queries.

**Pattern 490** — `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` for Reusable Reporting Helpers
```typescript
import { test, expect, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

// Reusable step function — boxed so errors surface at the call site, not inside the helper
async function completeCheckout(page: Page, card: string): Promise<string> {
  return test.step('Complete checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Payment' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill(card);
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/26');
    await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();
    const confirmationHeading = page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order #\d+/i });
    await expect(confirmationHeading).toBeVisible();
    const text = await confirmationHeading.textContent() ?? '';
    return text.match(/order #(\d+)/i)?.[1] ?? '';
  }, { box: true });
}

async function verifyEmailConfirmation(page: Page, orderId: string): Promise<void> {
  return test.step(`Verify email confirmation for order ${orderId}`, async () => {
    await page.goto(`/admin/emails?orderId=${orderId}`);
    await expect(page.getByRole('cell', { name: `Order #${orderId} Confirmed` })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('cell', { name: 'Sent' })).toBeVisible();
  }, { box: true });
}

test('end-to-end checkout sends confirmation email', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await test.step('Add product to cart', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status', { name: 'Cart' })).toContainText('1 item');
  });
  const orderId = await completeCheckout(page, '4242424242424242');
  expect(orderId).toMatch(/^\d+$/);
  await verifyEmailConfirmation(page, orderId);
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` collapses the call stack inside helper functions so that when an assertion fails, the error message points to the `completeCheckout(page, card)` call in the test body, not to the specific `expect` line inside the helper — this dramatically improves readability in Trace Viewer and CI log output when helpers are called from many tests. The step name also appears in structured test reports, enabling fine-grained timing analysis per step. The limitation is that `box: true` makes it harder to debug the helper itself — temporarily remove the option to get the exact failing line during active development, then re-add before committing. Nested steps are supported and appear hierarchically in Trace Viewer, but avoid nesting more than two levels deep as report readability degrades.

**Pattern 491** — `page.waitForEvent()` for Dialog and Popup Synchronization
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('export CSV triggers download dialog and file is valid', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports/sales');

  // Set up listeners before the action that triggers them
  const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download');
  const dialogPromise = page.waitForEvent('dialog');

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export CSV' }).click();

  // Handle the native confirm dialog that appears before the download
  const dialog = await dialogPromise;
  expect(dialog.message()).toContain('Export 1,234 rows?');
  await dialog.accept();

  // Now await the download that follows dialog acceptance
  const download = await downloadPromise;
  expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toMatch(/sales-report-\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\.csv/);

  // Save and verify content
  const downloadPath = await download.path();
  expect(downloadPath).not.toBeNull();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status', { name: 'Export status' })).toContainText('Export complete');
});

test('new-tab link opens product detail in separate page', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // waitForEvent('page') on the context catches any new tab opened during the action
  const newPagePromise = context.waitForEvent('page');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View Details', exact: false }).first().click();
  const newPage = await newPagePromise;

  await newPage.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');
  await expect(newPage.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(newPage).toHaveURL(/\/products\/\d+/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForEvent()` returns a Promise that resolves to the event payload — it must be created before the action that triggers the event, not after, otherwise the event fires before the listener is registered and the Promise never resolves. Registering both `downloadPromise` and `dialogPromise` before clicking is the idiomatic pattern. For dialogs, `page.on('dialog', handler)` auto-dismisses with the default accept/dismiss behavior if no `waitForEvent` is registered — always use `waitForEvent` when you need to assert the dialog message. For popup windows, `context.waitForEvent('page')` is preferred over `page.waitForEvent('popup')` when the exact triggering element is ambiguous, because `context` catches all new pages regardless of opener.

**Pattern 492** — `frameLocator()` for Embedded Payment iframes
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Stripe payment iframe accepts card details and submits order', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment Details' })).toBeVisible();

  // Enter the outer-frame context first, then the inner card-number frame
  const stripeFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[name="stripe-frame"]');
  const cardNumberFrame = stripeFrame.frameLocator('iframe[title="Secure card number input frame"]');

  await cardNumberFrame.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Card number' }).fill('4242424242424242');

  const expiryFrame = stripeFrame.frameLocator('iframe[title="Secure expiration date input frame"]');
  await expiryFrame.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Expiration date' }).fill('12 / 26');

  const cvcFrame = stripeFrame.frameLocator('iframe[title="Secure CVC input frame"]');
  await cvcFrame.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'CVC' }).fill('123');

  // Back to main page to submit
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay $99.00' }).click();

  // Assert confirmation on main page
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment Successful' })).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });
  await expect(page.getByRole('paragraph').filter({ hasText: /order #\d+/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `frameLocator()` creates a scoped locator that automatically enters the iframe before resolving child elements — no manual `page.frames()` iteration or frame handle juggling is required. It supports chaining for nested iframes (wrapper frame to leaf input frame), which is exactly Stripe's structure. All locators inside a `frameLocator` inherit the same retry and auto-waiting behavior as top-level locators. The limitation is that `frameLocator()` cannot cross into iframes from a different origin in headless browsers without `--disable-web-security` (which changes test behavior); for cross-origin iframes like Stripe in test mode, use Stripe's test environment domain that serves the iframe from the same scheme/host as your app, or use `page.route('**/stripe.com/**', ...)` to substitute a local mock. Closed-mode shadow roots and `sandbox="allow-same-origin"` missing from the iframe tag also block `frameLocator` access.

**Pattern 493** — `locator.all()` with `test.step()` for Parameterized Row Validation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('all product cards display required fields and valid prices', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  const cards = page.getByRole('article').filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading') });
  const allCards = await cards.all();

  expect(allCards.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);

  for (const [index, card] of allCards.entries()) {
    await test.step(`Validate product card ${index + 1}`, async () => {
      // Each heading must be non-empty
      const heading = card.getByRole('heading');
      await expect(heading).not.toBeEmpty();

      // Price must match currency pattern
      const price = card.getByTestId('price');
      await expect(price).toHaveText(/^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/);

      // Add-to-cart button must be enabled
      const addBtn = card.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i });
      await expect(addBtn).toBeEnabled();

      // Image must have non-empty alt text for accessibility
      const img = card.getByRole('img');
      await expect(img).not.toHaveAttribute('alt', '');
    });
  }

  // Assert aggregate count matches pagination header
  const countLabel = page.getByRole('status', { name: 'Product count' });
  await expect(countLabel).toContainText(`${allCards.length} products`);
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.all()` resolves the locator to a JavaScript array of `Locator` instances at a single point in time — it does not auto-retry the collection itself. If the page adds or removes cards asynchronously after `all()` is called, the loop iterates over a stale snapshot. Always call `all()` after the page has reached a stable state (after a `waitForLoadState` or after asserting the expected count with `toHaveCount`). The advantage over `locator.nth(i)` inside a loop is that `all()` makes the total count explicit and avoids off-by-one errors. Wrapping each card validation in `test.step()` creates per-card step entries in Trace Viewer, making it easy to identify which card failed without re-running with `--debug`.

**Pattern 494** — `page.addInitScript()` with Arguments for Deterministic Random Values
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('referral code generator produces stable output for snapshot testing', async ({ page }) => {
  // Inject deterministic Math.random before ANY page script runs
  await page.addInitScript(
    ({ seed }: { seed: number }) => {
      let state = seed;
      // Simple seeded LCG replacing Math.random
      window.Math.random = () => {
        state = (state * 1664525 + 1013904223) & 0xffffffff;
        return (state >>> 0) / 4294967296;
      };
    },
    { seed: 42 }
  );

  await page.goto('/dashboard/referrals');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Generate Referral Code' }).click();

  const code = page.getByTestId('referral-code');
  await expect(code).toBeVisible();

  // With seed=42, the generated code is deterministic — safe to snapshot
  const codeText = await code.textContent();
  expect(codeText).toBe('REF-7B4A9D'); // stable across runs with this seed

  // Generate a second code and assert it is different (randomness is consumed)
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Generate Referral Code' }).click();
  await expect(code).not.toHaveText(codeText ?? '');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.addInitScript()` executes the provided function before the page's own scripts run on every navigation, making it ideal for seeding non-deterministic globals like `Math.random`, `Date.now`, or `crypto.getRandomValues`. The function argument (second parameter) must be JSON-serializable — passing functions, class instances, or Symbols throws. The init script runs in the page context, not in Node, so it has no access to the test's Node.js scope. The injection applies to all child frames attached after the call, but not to iframes that were already attached before `addInitScript()` was called. For `Date` determinism, prefer `page.clock.setFixedTime()` (introduced in Playwright 1.45) over init script date patching — the clock API handles `setTimeout` and `setInterval` as well, which an init script Date stub does not.

---

**Pattern 495** — `page.waitForFunction()` for Custom Browser-Side Readiness Conditions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('infinite scroll loads additional items when user scrolls to bottom', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/feed');

  // Wait until the virtual scroll container reports at least 20 items rendered
  await page.waitForFunction(
    (selector: string) => {
      const container = document.querySelector(selector);
      return container ? container.querySelectorAll('[data-item]').length >= 20 : false;
    },
    '[data-testid="feed-container"]',
    { timeout: 10_000 }
  );

  const initialCount = await page.locator('[data-item]').count();
  expect(initialCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(20);

  // Scroll to bottom of the container to trigger next page load
  await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight));

  // Wait for the item count to grow beyond the initial count
  await page.waitForFunction(
    (threshold: number) => document.querySelectorAll('[data-item]').length > threshold,
    initialCount,
    { timeout: 15_000 }
  );

  const newCount = await page.locator('[data-item]').count();
  expect(newCount).toBeGreaterThan(initialCount);
  await expect(page.getByRole('status', { name: 'Feed' })).toContainText(`${newCount} posts`);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForFunction()` polls a browser-side predicate until it returns truthy — it is the escape hatch for readiness conditions that cannot be expressed with locator assertions. Unlike `locator.waitFor()` which requires an element to exist, `waitForFunction` can check arbitrary DOM state, window properties, or JS framework internals. The function argument is serialized and executed in the page context; it must be a pure function with no closure over test-scope variables — pass all required values via the second parameter. The limitation is that `waitForFunction` polling is not as efficient as Playwright's built-in mutation observers used by locator assertions; default polling interval is 100ms. For simple element-count thresholds, prefer `expect(locator).toHaveCount(n)` which uses mutation observers; use `waitForFunction` only for compound or non-element conditions like checking a property on `window.__APP_STATE__`.

---

**Pattern 496** — `locator.and()` for Multi-Attribute State Assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('submit button is enabled only when all required fields are valid', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  const submitBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create Account' });

  // Initially disabled — and() narrows to button with both role AND disabled state
  await expect(submitBtn.and(page.locator('[disabled]'))).toBeVisible();

  // Fill email only
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('user@example.com');
  await expect(submitBtn).toBeDisabled();

  // Fill password but too short — button still disabled
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('abc');
  await expect(submitBtn).toBeDisabled();

  // Fill valid password — button becomes enabled
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('SecurePass123!');
  await expect(submitBtn).toBeEnabled();
  // Confirm the submit button now lacks the disabled attribute
  await expect(submitBtn.and(page.locator(':not([disabled])'))).toBeVisible();

  // Fill mismatched confirm password — button disabled again
  await page.getByLabel('Confirm Password').fill('WrongPass');
  await expect(submitBtn).toBeDisabled();

  await page.getByLabel('Confirm Password').fill('SecurePass123!');
  await expect(submitBtn).toBeEnabled();

  await submitBtn.click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Check your email' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.and(otherLocator)` combines two locator queries with AND semantics — it matches elements that satisfy both the original locator and the additional locator simultaneously. This is useful for asserting that the same element has multiple independent attributes or roles at once, without resorting to CSS attribute selectors that bypass the accessibility tree. The limitation is that both locators must resolve to the same element set — if the original locator matches element A and the `and()` locator matches element B, the combined locator matches nothing and the assertion fails with a misleading "element not found" error rather than a set mismatch error. For state assertions on a single element (enabled/disabled, checked), prefer `toBeEnabled()` / `toBeDisabled()` / `toBeChecked()` — they are semantically clearer than `and(page.locator('[disabled]'))` and produce better error messages.

**Pattern 497** — `page.pdf()` for Invoice and Report Print Fidelity Testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { join } from 'path';

test('invoice PDF contains all required fields and correct total', async ({ page }) => {
  // PDF generation requires headless Chromium — skip if running in headed mode
  test.skip(!!process.env.CI_HEADED, 'PDF test requires headless Chromium');

  await page.goto('/invoices/INV-2024-001');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Invoice #INV-2024-001' })).toBeVisible();

  const pdfPath = join(test.info().outputDir, 'invoice-INV-2024-001.pdf');
  await page.pdf({
    path: pdfPath,
    format: 'A4',
    margin: { top: '20mm', bottom: '20mm', left: '15mm', right: '15mm' },
    printBackground: true,
    tagged: true,    // embed accessibility tags in PDF
    outline: true,   // include heading outline for PDF navigation
  });

  // Verify the file was created and is a valid PDF (starts with %PDF header)
  const pdfBytes = readFileSync(pdfPath);
  expect(pdfBytes.slice(0, 4).toString('ascii')).toBe('%PDF');
  expect(pdfBytes.length).toBeGreaterThan(5_000); // non-trivial content

  // Attach the PDF to the test report for manual review
  await test.info().attach('Invoice PDF', {
    path: pdfPath,
    contentType: 'application/pdf',
  });

  // Assert the invoice page itself has the expected total before PDF comparison
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-total')).toContainText('$1,234.50');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.pdf()` generates a PDF from the current page using Chromium's print engine and is only supported in headless Chromium (not Firefox or WebKit). It applies `@media print` CSS rules, so you get the same output as a user clicking Print then Save as PDF — layout, page breaks, and print-only elements all behave as in the browser. The `tagged: true` option embeds PDF/UA accessibility tags, enabling screen-reader testing of generated PDFs. The limitation is that automated visual comparison of PDF content requires a PDF parsing library (e.g., `pdf-parse`) — Playwright has no built-in `toMatchPDF()` assertion. For CI, the recommended pattern is to attach the PDF to the test report via `test.info().attach()` and use snapshot testing on specific page text content rather than pixel-comparing the PDF binary.

**Pattern 498** — Worker-Scoped Authentication State with `browser` Fixture
```typescript
import { test as base, expect, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerAuth = {
  authenticatedContext: BrowserContext;
};

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerAuth>({
  authenticatedContext: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      // Log in once per worker and reuse the context across all tests in this worker
      const context = await browser.newContext();
      const loginPage = await context.newPage();

      await loginPage.goto('/login');
      await loginPage.getByLabel('Email').fill('admin@example.com');
      await loginPage.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_ADMIN_PASSWORD ?? '');
      await loginPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
      await expect(loginPage.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();

      // Persist auth state to a temp file for this worker
      const authFile = `playwright/.auth/worker-${process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX ?? '0'}.json`;
      await context.storageState({ path: authFile });
      await loginPage.close();

      await use(context);

      // Cleanup: invalidate the session after all worker tests complete
      const logoutPage = await context.newPage();
      await logoutPage.goto('/api/auth/signout');
      await context.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// Tests use a fresh page within the shared authenticated context
test('admin can view all user accounts', async ({ authenticatedContext }) => {
  const page = await authenticatedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'User Management' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasNot: page.getByRole('columnheader') })).toHaveCount(10);
  await page.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using a worker-scoped `BrowserContext` for auth means the login flow runs once per worker process and all tests in that worker share the authenticated session — dramatically reducing auth overhead in large suites. The risk is cookie/session cross-contamination between tests: if test A modifies session data (changes user preferences, triggers a force-logout), test B in the same worker inherits that state. Mitigate by having each test open its own `newPage()` from the shared context rather than sharing a page instance, and avoid tests that intentionally expire or invalidate the session. For tests that need a clean unauthenticated state, override the fixture with a test-scoped unauthenticated context. Do not pass the `BrowserContext` itself between tests via shared module state — always go through the fixture.

**Pattern 499** — `page.requestGC()` for Detecting Memory Leaks via WeakRef
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('route handler is garbage collected after page navigation away', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Inject a WeakRef tracker into the page before component mounts
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const registry = new FinalizationRegistry((label: string) => {
      (window as any).__gcLog = (window as any).__gcLog ?? [];
      (window as any).__gcLog.push(`${label} collected`);
    });

    // Track the chart component element that should be freed on navigation
    const chartEl = document.querySelector('[data-testid="sales-chart"]');
    if (chartEl) {
      registry.register(chartEl, 'sales-chart');
      (window as any).__chartRef = new WeakRef(chartEl);
    }
  });

  // Assert the chart is visible before navigation
  await expect(page.getByTestId('sales-chart')).toBeVisible();

  // Navigate away to trigger component unmount and release DOM references
  await page.goto('/settings');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Settings' })).toBeVisible();

  // Trigger GC explicitly — best-effort hint to V8
  await page.requestGC();

  // Check if the FinalizationRegistry fired for the chart element
  const gcLog = await page.evaluate(() => (window as any).__gcLog ?? []);
  expect(gcLog).toContain('sales-chart collected');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.requestGC()` triggers a browser garbage collection cycle, making it possible to test that components and event listeners are properly freed after unmount or navigation. Without it, the GC timing is non-deterministic and a `FinalizationRegistry` callback might not fire within the test's lifetime even if the object is collectible. This pattern is particularly valuable for SPAs where unmounted components can silently retain DOM references through closure captures in event handlers, preventing GC. The limitation is that `requestGC()` is a best-effort hint — the V8 GC may still defer collection of objects with ambiguous reference graphs. If the `gcLog` array is empty after `requestGC()`, retry with a second call or add a short `page.waitForTimeout(200)` before the assertion. This pattern should live in a dedicated memory-leak test suite, not in functional tests, as it increases test time and depends on GC internals.

---

**Pattern 500** — `page.emulateMedia({ forcedColors: 'active' })` for Windows High-Contrast Mode Testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('application is usable under Windows forced-colors (high contrast) mode', async ({ page }) => {
  // Simulate Windows High Contrast / Edge forced-colors media feature
  await page.emulateMedia({ forcedColors: 'active', colorScheme: 'dark' });
  await page.goto('/');

  // Navigation links must be distinguishable — forced-colors strips background colors
  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation');
  await expect(nav).toBeVisible();
  const links = nav.getByRole('link');
  await expect(links).toHaveCount(5);

  // Interactive elements must rely on outline/border, not background-color only
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Get Started' }).focus();
  const focusedBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Get Started' });
  // Under forced-colors, outline must not be 'none' — CSS should use forced-color-adjust
  await expect(focusedBtn).not.toHaveCSS('outline-style', 'none');

  // Form fields must be visible — borders are recolored to ButtonText by the UA
  const emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email address');
  await expect(emailInput).toBeVisible();
  await emailInput.fill('test@example.com');
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveValue('test@example.com');

  // Assert error message text is not conveyed by color alone
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Subscribe' }).click();
  const error = page.getByRole('alert');
  await expect(error).toBeVisible();
  await expect(error).not.toBeEmpty();
  // Error should have an icon or text prefix, not just red color
  await expect(error).toContainText(/error|invalid|required/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.emulateMedia({ forcedColors: 'active' })` activates the CSS `@media (forced-colors: active)` feature, which simulates Windows High Contrast Mode — a critical accessibility requirement for enterprise and government applications. Under forced-colors, the browser overrides all author-specified colors with system colors (ButtonText, Highlight, ButtonFace), effectively testing whether your UI communicates state through shape, border, and text rather than color alone. This catches the common pattern of using only `background-color` changes to indicate focus or error states, which become invisible in forced-colors mode. The limitation is that Playwright's forced-colors emulation applies the CSS media query but does not fully replicate the Windows system color palette substitution that a real Windows High Contrast Mode would apply — visual regression screenshots taken under emulation may differ from actual Windows HCM screenshots. Use `toHaveCSS('outline-style', ...)` assertions rather than color assertions for forced-colors tests.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G165** — `locator.all()` snapshot is taken at call time and does not re-evaluate if the DOM changes during iteration
Why this matters: `locator.all()` resolves the locator immediately and returns a static JavaScript array of `Locator` instances. If the page adds, removes, or re-orders elements between the `all()` call and the loop body executing on a given element (e.g., a lazy-loaded list that appends items during scroll, or a live filter that removes items as the user types), the array reflects the DOM state at snapshot time. Assertions on a stale locator from the array still succeed if the element remains in the DOM — but `locator.nth(i)` would re-evaluate and pick up the new element at that position. The silent failure mode is an array that contains fewer elements than are actually present, causing the test to miss validating the newly appended items entirely.
Fix: Always stabilize the page before calling `all()`: wait for an expected count with `await expect(locator).toHaveCount(expectedN)` first, then call `all()`. For lists that grow during interaction, capture the count before and after the interaction separately rather than iterating over a single snapshot. If the list is fully server-rendered and static after `networkidle`, `all()` is safe without additional guards.

---

**Gotcha G166** — `page.exposeFunction()` callback executes in the Node.js event loop, not in the browser microtask queue, causing unexpected ordering when awaited from page JS
Why this matters: When page JavaScript calls `await window.myNodeFn()`, the await suspends the browser microtask queue and sends a message to the Playwright server, which invokes the Node.js callback, waits for its Promise to resolve, and sends the result back. This round-trip crosses the CDP boundary and takes on the order of milliseconds, even for trivial callbacks. If page code calls `exposeFunction` inside a `requestAnimationFrame` or a `MutationObserver` callback and awaits the result, the awaited suspension may cause the next animation frame to be missed or the mutation batch to be processed before the callback returns — leading to visible rendering glitches in tests that do not exist in production (where the function would be synchronous). The effect is that tests using `exposeFunction` for stubbing can exhibit timing issues that make them pass locally but fail under CPU throttling.
Fix: Design `exposeFunction` callbacks to be non-blocking from the browser's perspective by having the page call the function in a fire-and-forget pattern (`window.logEvent(data)` without `await`) when ordering guarantees are not needed. When a synchronous result is required from page JS, use `page.evaluate()` from the test side to push data into the page rather than pulling it through `exposeFunction`. For crypto operations, consider `page.addInitScript()` to inject a synchronous stub at page load time instead of an exposed async function.

---

**Gotcha G167** — `frameLocator()` silently matches the first frame if the selector matches multiple iframes, causing flaky cross-iframe assertion failures
Why this matters: `page.frameLocator('iframe')` without a disambiguating selector matches all iframes on the page and uses strict mode — it throws a "strict mode violation" error if more than one iframe matches. However, `page.frameLocator('iframe[name]')` with a name attribute that appears on multiple frames (e.g., multiple `<iframe name="stripe-frame">` for different card fields, as in Stripe's multi-frame layout) matches only the first element in DOM order. Playwright does not throw a strict mode error for `frameLocator` the way it does for `locator` — it silently uses the first match. If the page re-renders and the DOM order of iframes changes (lazy load, conditional rendering), the "first stripe-frame" may now be the CVC frame instead of the card-number frame, filling the wrong field and causing a silent wrong-value failure.
Fix: Use the most specific selector available for `frameLocator`: prefer `iframe[title="Secure card number input frame"]` (the `title` attribute is set by Stripe for accessibility) over `iframe[name]`. If the application renders iframes without stable disambiguating attributes, add `data-testid` to each iframe wrapper in the application code. Verify the frame count with `await expect(page.locator('iframe[name="stripe-frame"]')).toHaveCount(1)` before calling `frameLocator`, so unexpected duplicate frames fail loudly rather than silently misfilling a field.

---

**Gotcha G168** — `test.slow()` triples the timeout relative to the current effective timeout, not the global config default, causing unexpected timeout values when called after `test.setTimeout()`
Why this matters: `test.slow()` multiplies the test's current timeout by 3. If `test.setTimeout(20_000)` is called earlier in the test body (or in `beforeEach`) to extend the timeout to 20 seconds, and then `test.slow()` is called, the final timeout becomes 60 seconds — not 3x the playwright.config `timeout` default. Developers who use both `test.setTimeout()` and `test.slow()` in the same test end up with non-obvious timeout values that vary based on call order, making timeout management hard to reason about across a large test suite. The silent failure mode is a test that is implicitly much longer or shorter than intended, either masking slow operations or timing out legitimate slow paths.
Fix: Choose one timeout mechanism per test: use `test.slow()` for semantically slow tests where 3x the project default is the right timeout, or use `test.setTimeout(ms)` for an explicit millisecond value. Never combine both in the same test body. For suite-wide timeout overrides, use `test.describe.configure({ timeout: ms })` at the describe block level, which sets a fixed value that `test.slow()` then triples for individual tests within the block. Document the intent with a comment: `test.slow(); // this test hits a real payment processor — allow 3x default` so reviewers understand why the slowness annotation is present.

---

**Gotcha G169** — `page.pdf()` silently produces a blank page when called before fonts loaded via CSS `@font-face` with `font-display: optional` have resolved
Why this matters: `page.pdf()` triggers Chromium's print engine synchronously after the call — it does not wait for pending network requests or font loads to complete. When a page uses `font-display: optional`, the browser omits fallback font rendering if the web font has not loaded within a ~100ms budget. In `networkidle`-based tests where the font CDN request completes just after the `networkidle` threshold, the PDF is generated before font bytes arrive and all text renders in the system fallback font — or, in worst cases, renders as blank boxes if the fallback font is not available in the headless environment. This produces a PDF that appears visually correct in the browser screenshot but has garbled or missing text in the PDF artifact.
Fix: Before calling `page.pdf()`, explicitly wait for fonts to load via `page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready)`, which returns a Promise that resolves only when all `@font-face` fonts referenced by the current document have either loaded or been deemed unavailable. Chain this after page navigation: `await page.goto(url); await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready); const pdf = await page.pdf(...)`. For CI environments without internet access to font CDNs, add a `page.route('**/fonts.googleapis.com/**', route => route.abort())` before navigation to force immediate font fallback rather than waiting for a CDN timeout.

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 501** — `page.clock.install()` with `fastForward` for deterministic timer-driven UI testing
```typescript
test('session-timeout banner appears after 15 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install clock BEFORE navigation so all timers created during page load are fake
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Confirm no banner yet
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeHidden();

  // Advance fake time by 14 minutes 59 seconds — banner should still be hidden
  await page.clock.fastForward('14:59');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeHidden();

  // Cross the 15-minute threshold
  await page.clock.fastForward('00:02');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/your session will expire/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` must be called before any navigation that initialises the timers under test — if called after `page.goto()`, timers already scheduled with the real `setTimeout` are not intercepted and will fire at real-clock times, causing the test to hang waiting for a banner that never appears under the fake clock. `fastForward` skips intermediate time without firing every accumulated callback, making it appropriate for long timeout periods; use `runFor` instead when you need every `setInterval` tick to fire (e.g., a progress bar that updates every second), because `fastForward` may skip those intermediate callbacks if the engine coalesces jumps.

---

**Pattern 502** — `page.clock.setFixedTime()` for stable `Date.now()` without intercepting timers
```typescript
test('invoice date stamp reflects current date at submission', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze only Date — do NOT call install() so real timers continue to fire
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-03-31T00:00:00Z'));
  await page.goto('/invoices/new');
  await page.getByLabel('Description').fill('Consulting services');
  await page.getByLabel('Amount').fill('5000');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit Invoice' }).click();

  // The invoice should show today's frozen date
  const invoiceRow = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Consulting services' });
  await expect(invoiceRow).toContainText('2026-03-31');

  // Real timers still run — polling and animations are unaffected
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/saved/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: `setFixedTime` affects only `Date.now()` and `new Date()` — it does not intercept `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, or `requestAnimationFrame`. This makes it the safest choice when the UI relies on real timers for polling, animations, or debouncing and you only need to stabilise a displayed date-stamp. The trade-off is that you cannot advance time with `fastForward` after calling only `setFixedTime`; to advance time you must first call `install()`, which does intercept timers. Using `setFixedTime` after `install()` is valid and resets the fake clock to the given moment without changing the interception mode.

---

**Pattern 503** — `page.routeFromHAR()` for deterministic API playback in integration tests
```typescript
// First run: record with update:true to populate the HAR
// Subsequent runs: replay from stored HAR — no network needed
test('product listing renders from recorded API responses', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeFromHAR('./fixtures/product-api.har', {
    url: '**/api/v1/**',
    update: false,            // replay mode — fail if request has no HAR match
    updateContent: 'embed',   // response bodies embedded in HAR (not separate files)
    notFound: 'abort',        // abort unmatched requests rather than passing through
  });

  await page.goto('/products');

  // All /api/v1/* requests are now served from the HAR — network is not used
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Products' })).toBeVisible();
  const items = page.getByRole('listitem');
  await expect(items).toHaveCount(12);
  await expect(items.first()).toContainText('Widget Pro');
});
```
Tradeoff: HAR replay matches URL and HTTP method strictly — for POST requests it also matches the POST body strictly, so even a single differing query-parameter or body field causes the request to be treated as unmatched and aborted when `notFound: 'abort'` is set. The `update: true` mode re-records the HAR from live network traffic, which is useful for refreshing stale data; set it back to `false` before committing to ensure tests are hermetic. HAR files stored as `.zip` archives bundle response bodies as separate entries and are preferred for binary payloads (images, PDFs) because embedding large base64 bodies inside the JSON HAR file inflates file size significantly.

---

**Pattern 504** — `context.routeFromHAR()` for full-context API isolation including cross-origin requests
```typescript
test('checkout flow with payment iframe uses HAR for cross-origin calls', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();

  // Route at context level — captures cross-origin requests from iframes too
  await context.routeFromHAR('./fixtures/checkout.har', {
    url: /stripe\.com\/v1\//,
    update: process.env.UPDATE_HAR === '1',
    notFound: 'fallback',     // pass unmatched requests through to real network
  });

  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  const cardFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[title="Secure card number input frame"]');
  await cardFrame.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.frameLocator('iframe[title="Secure expiration date input frame"]')
    .getByLabel('Expiration').fill('12/30');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /payment successful/i })).toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.routeFromHAR()` intercepts all requests in the entire browser context — including those from nested iframes and service workers — whereas `page.routeFromHAR()` only intercepts requests originating from the top-level page. Using `notFound: 'fallback'` passes unmatched requests to the real network, which is useful when only a subset of endpoints (e.g., third-party payment APIs) needs to be mocked while the application's own API is exercised live; however it means the test is not fully hermetic and can still fail due to external network issues.

---

**Pattern 505** — `page.coverage.startJSCoverage()` / `stopJSCoverage()` for dead-code detection
```typescript
test('critical user path exercises all auth module code paths', async ({ page }) => {
  // Must start before navigation to capture module-load-time execution
  await page.coverage.startJSCoverage({ resetOnNavigation: false });

  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('user@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');

  const jsCoverage = await page.coverage.stopJSCoverage();

  // Find the auth bundle and calculate coverage percentage
  const authEntry = jsCoverage.find(e => e.url.includes('auth.bundle'));
  expect(authEntry).toBeDefined();

  const totalBytes = authEntry!.source!.length;
  const coveredBytes = authEntry!.ranges.reduce((sum, r) => sum + (r.end - r.start), 0);
  const coveragePct = (coveredBytes / totalBytes) * 100;

  // Fail if less than 80% of the auth bundle was executed
  expect(coveragePct).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(80);
  console.log(`Auth bundle coverage: ${coveragePct.toFixed(1)}%`);
});
```
Tradeoff: The coverage API is Chromium-only — tests using it cannot run against Firefox or WebKit, so they should be isolated in a dedicated Chromium-only project in `playwright.config.ts` using `projects: [{ name: 'coverage', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } }]`. Anonymous scripts generated via `eval()` or `new Function()` are not included by default; enable `reportAnonymousScripts: true` in `startJSCoverage()` options to capture them. `resetOnNavigation: false` is required when the user journey spans multiple page loads, otherwise coverage data is discarded on each navigation and only the final page's execution is captured.

---

**Pattern 506** — `page.coverage.startCSSCoverage()` for identifying unused stylesheet rules
```typescript
test('landing page does not load excessive unused CSS', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.coverage.startCSSCoverage({ resetOnNavigation: false });
  await page.goto('/');

  // Interact to trigger hover states, modals, and active pseudo-classes
  await page.getByRole('navigation').getByRole('link', { name: 'Features' }).hover();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Learn more' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');

  const cssCoverage = await page.coverage.stopCSSCoverage();

  for (const entry of cssCoverage) {
    if (!entry.url.includes('main.css')) continue;
    const totalChars = entry.text!.length;
    const usedChars = entry.ranges.reduce((sum, r) => sum + (r.end - r.start), 0);
    const unusedPct = ((totalChars - usedChars) / totalChars) * 100;

    // Warn (not fail) if more than 60% of CSS is unused on the landing page
    if (unusedPct > 60) {
      console.warn(`main.css has ${unusedPct.toFixed(1)}% unused rules — consider code splitting`);
    }
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: CSS coverage ranges report character offsets into the stylesheet text, not rule counts — a single long rule with many selectors counts as many characters even if few selectors are active, and a tiny `display:none` override that is critical may appear as negligible coverage. Dynamically injected `<style>` tags without a `sourceURL` comment are excluded from coverage results. Coverage measures execution during the test run, not all possible states — rules for hover, focus, and error states will appear uncovered unless the test explicitly triggers those states, making raw coverage percentages misleading without comprehensive interaction coverage.
