**Pattern 507** — `page.addLocatorHandler()` for auto-dismissing overlays that block actionability checks
```typescript
test('checkout flow completes despite GDPR consent banner', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register handler BEFORE the overlay can appear
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie consent/i }),
    async (dialog) => {
      // Accept all cookies to make dialog disappear
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all/i }).click();
    },
    {
      times: 1,          // dismiss at most once (prevent infinite loop if dismiss fails)
      noWaitAfter: false // default: wait for the overlay to disappear after handler runs
    }
  );

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('buyer@example.com');
  // If the cookie banner appears during any of these actions, the handler fires automatically
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `addLocatorHandler` fires during actionability checks — specifically when Playwright is about to perform a click, fill, or assertion and the registered locator is visible. It does not fire proactively in the background; if the overlay appears between actionability checks (e.g., during a `page.waitForTimeout` or a long network request), the handler is not triggered until the next Playwright action. Handlers alter page state: the mouse moves and focus shifts during handler execution, which can break subsequent actions that depend on hover state or keyboard focus; use `locator.click({ position: ... })` inside handlers rather than relying on the previous focus state.

---

**Pattern 508** — `mergeTests()` for composing fixtures from multiple utility modules
```typescript
// fixtures/db.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export const test = base.extend<{ db: DbClient }>({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const client = await DbClient.connect(process.env.TEST_DB_URL!);
    await use(client);
    await client.disconnect();
  },
});

// fixtures/auth.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export const test = base.extend<{ authToken: string }>({
  authToken: async ({ request }, use) => {
    const resp = await request.post('/api/auth/token', { data: { user: 'testuser' } });
    const { token } = await resp.json();
    await use(token);
  },
});

// fixtures/index.ts — compose both fixture sets into one test object
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as dbTest } from './db';
import { test as authTest } from './auth';
export const test = mergeTests(dbTest, authTest);
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// my.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures';
test('user data is returned for authenticated request', async ({ page, db, authToken }) => {
  const user = await db.findUser('testuser');
  await page.goto(`/profile?token=${authToken}`);
  await expect(page.getByText(user.email)).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` requires that fixture names across all merged modules are unique — if two modules define a fixture with the same name (e.g., both define `page`), the merge will throw a runtime error. The built-in `page`, `context`, `browser`, and `request` fixtures from `@playwright/test` can be overridden individually in each module before merging, but the overrides must not conflict. When merging more than two modules, chain the merges: `mergeTests(mergeTests(a, b), c)` is equivalent to `mergeTests(a, b, c)` (the function accepts variadic arguments since Playwright v1.39).

---

**Pattern 509** — Option fixtures with `{ option: true }` for project-level test configuration
```typescript
// fixtures/theme.ts — declare a typed option fixture
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type ThemeOptions = { colorScheme: 'light' | 'dark'; locale: string };

export const test = base.extend<ThemeOptions>({
  // Tuple syntax: [defaultValue, { option: true }]
  colorScheme: ['light', { option: true }],
  locale:      ['en-US', { option: true }],
});

// playwright.config.ts — set values per project
export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    { name: 'light-en', use: { colorScheme: 'light', locale: 'en-US' } },
    { name: 'dark-de',  use: { colorScheme: 'dark',  locale: 'de-DE' } },
  ],
});

// my.spec.ts — consume option fixtures just like any other fixture
import { test } from '../fixtures/theme';
test('header adapts to color scheme and locale', async ({ page, colorScheme, locale }) => {
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme });
  await page.goto(`/?locale=${locale}`);
  const heading = page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 });
  await expect(heading).toBeVisible();
  if (colorScheme === 'dark') {
    await expect(heading).toHaveCSS('color', 'rgb(255, 255, 255)');
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Option fixtures use tuple syntax for declaration — `[defaultValue, { option: true }]` — and the default value must be a scalar or a JSON-serialisable value. Array defaults require double-wrapping: `[['a', 'b'], { option: true }]` (the outer array is the tuple; the inner is the default). Omitting the outer tuple and writing `colorScheme: 'light'` instead of `colorScheme: ['light', { option: true }]` creates a normal test-scoped fixture, not an option — the `use:` property in `playwright.config.ts` then silently has no effect, and the fixture always returns its hardcoded default regardless of project configuration.

---

**Pattern 510** — `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` for structural accessibility regression testing
```typescript
test('navigation menu has correct ARIA structure after authenticated login', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main navigation' });
  await expect(nav).toBeVisible();

  // Snapshot assertion: YAML format captures role, name, and attributes
  await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Main navigation":
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Dashboard" [current=page]
        - listitem:
          - link "Projects"
        - listitem:
          - link "Settings"
        - listitem:
          - link /Notifications \\d+/
  `);
  // Regex pattern /Notifications \d+/ matches dynamic badge counts
});
```
Tradeoff: `toMatchAriaSnapshot` matching is order-sensitive — list items must appear in the same order in the snapshot template as they do in the DOM. The snapshot captures the full accessibility tree under the locator including off-viewport content that is attached to the DOM but not visible; elements hidden with `display:none` or `visibility:hidden` are excluded, but elements scrolled off-screen are included, which can cause snapshot mismatches after pagination or infinite-scroll renders new items into the DOM above the fold. Use `locator.ariaSnapshot()` during test development to generate the initial YAML template and then paste it into the assertion; do not hand-author the YAML format from scratch as role names must exactly match the ARIA role spec.

---

**Pattern 511** — `page.ariaSnapshot()` with regex patterns for asserting dynamic accessibility tree content
```typescript
test('search results list announces result count to screen readers', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');
  await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search' }).fill('playwright');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL(/\/search\?q=playwright/);

  // Capture raw ARIA snapshot for inspection during development
  const rawSnapshot = await page.ariaSnapshot();
  console.log('Full ARIA tree:', rawSnapshot);

  // Assert that the results region announces the count dynamically
  const resultsRegion = page.getByRole('region', { name: /search results/i });
  await expect(resultsRegion).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - region /search results/i:
      - status:
        - text /\\d+ results? for "playwright"/
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - heading /Playwright/
          - link /playwright\\.dev/
  `);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.ariaSnapshot()` without a locator captures the full-page accessibility tree, which can be hundreds of lines for complex SPAs — always prefer `locator.ariaSnapshot()` scoped to the component under test to keep snapshots maintainable. Regex patterns in the ARIA snapshot YAML use the `/pattern/flags` literal syntax inside the template string; backslashes inside template literals require double-escaping (`\\d+` in the template string becomes `\d+` in the regex). The snapshot waits up to the expect timeout for the tree to stabilise — if the test times out during snapshot generation, increase the timeout via `await expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot(template, { timeout: 10_000 })`.

**Pattern 512** — `page.consoleMessages()` for asserting no errors or warnings after user interactions
```typescript
test('form submission does not produce console errors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');
  await page.getByLabel('Name').fill('Alice');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Message').fill('Hello world');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/message sent/i);

  // page.consoleMessages() returns up to the last 200 messages
  const messages = await page.consoleMessages({ filter: 'since-navigation' });
  const errors = messages.filter(m => m.type() === 'error');
  const warnings = messages.filter(m =>
    m.type() === 'warning' &&
    !m.text().includes('favicon') // ignore known benign warning
  );

  expect(errors).toHaveLength(0);
  expect(warnings).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.consoleMessages()` returns a static snapshot of up to 200 messages buffered since the last navigation (or since page creation if `filter: 'since-navigation'` is omitted). If the test triggers more than 200 console events (e.g., a verbose debug build), older messages are silently dropped from the buffer — use a `page.on('console', ...)` event listener registered before navigation to capture all messages into an unbounded array for high-volume scenarios. The `filter: 'since-navigation'` option restricts results to messages emitted after the most recent navigation, which avoids false positives from errors that occurred during page load before the test interaction began.

---

**Pattern 513** — `page.pageErrors()` for detecting uncaught JavaScript exceptions in the page
```typescript
test('lazy-loaded widget does not throw uncaught exceptions', async ({ page }) => {
  // Collect errors via event listener for complete capture (no 200-message limit)
  const uncaughtErrors: Error[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', err => uncaughtErrors.push(err));

  await page.goto('/widgets');
  // Scroll to trigger lazy loading of widgets below the fold
  await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight));
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // page.pageErrors() provides a point-in-time snapshot (added v1.56)
  const snapshotErrors = await page.pageErrors();
  expect(snapshotErrors).toHaveLength(0);

  // The event-listener array catches anything not yet in the snapshot buffer
  expect(uncaughtErrors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.pageErrors()` (added in Playwright v1.56) returns up to 200 uncaught page exceptions buffered since the last navigation. Like `consoleMessages()`, it is a snapshot — errors that occurred before `page.pageErrors()` is called are included, but errors that occur after are not. When the test needs to assert no errors occur during an animation loop or a polling interval that runs for the duration of a long test, the `page.on('pageerror', ...)` event listener is more reliable because it captures exceptions in real time as they are thrown, without a buffer size limit. Both approaches report the same `Error` objects including `message` and `stack` properties.

---

**Pattern 514** — Auto-use fixture with `{ auto: true }` for zero-config per-test console error assertion
```typescript
// fixtures/no-console-errors.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  // Auto-use fixture — runs for every test without needing to declare it as a parameter
  assertNoConsoleErrors: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    const errors: string[] = [];
    page.on('console', msg => {
      if (msg.type() === 'error') errors.push(msg.text());
    });

    await use(undefined); // test body runs here

    // Teardown: assert after every test automatically
    if (errors.length > 0) {
      throw new Error(
        `Test produced ${errors.length} console error(s):\n${errors.join('\n')}`
      );
    }
  }, { auto: true }], // runs automatically for every test that imports this test object
});

// my.spec.ts — no explicit parameter needed; errors are asserted automatically
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/no-console-errors';
test('login page renders without errors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Sign in' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Auto-use fixtures with `{ auto: true }` run for every test in the suite that imports the extended `test` object — they cannot be selectively disabled per individual test without restructuring the fixture. If a test legitimately triggers a console error (e.g., testing error boundary rendering), maintain a known-errors allowlist inside the fixture using a regex pattern check rather than a hard `.toHaveLength(0)` assertion. Auto fixtures do not appear as named steps in test reports by default; add `test.step('assert no console errors', ...)` inside the fixture teardown to make the assertion visible in traces and HTML reports.

---

**Pattern 515** — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` for ordered stateful test flows
```typescript
// Use serial mode only for flows where test N depends on state created by test N-1
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

let orderId: string;

test.describe('order lifecycle', () => {
  test('create order', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/orders/new');
    await page.getByLabel('Product').selectOption('Widget Pro');
    await page.getByLabel('Quantity').fill('3');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText(/order created/i);

    // Capture ID for subsequent tests in this serial block
    orderId = await page.getByTestId('order-id').textContent() ?? '';
    expect(orderId).toBeTruthy();
  });

  test('ship order', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`/orders/${orderId}`);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Mark as shipped' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-status')).toHaveText('Shipped');
  });

  test('close order', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`/orders/${orderId}`);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Close order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-status')).toHaveText('Closed');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mode: 'serial'` makes tests in the describe block run in file order within a single worker, and if one test fails, all subsequent tests in the block are automatically skipped — this cascading skip can mask independent failures and produce misleading test reports that show many skipped tests with no actionable information. Serial mode also prevents the tests from benefiting from Playwright's parallel sharding, so a large serial suite significantly increases CI wall-clock time. Use serial mode only for workflows that are inherently stateful and impossible to isolate (e.g., external system state that cannot be reset between tests); for most flows, prefer independent tests with `beforeEach` setup that creates fresh state.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G170** — `page.clock.install()` called after `page.goto()` does not intercept timers set during page load, causing fake-clock tests to hang
Why this matters: `page.clock.install()` replaces the browser's `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and related globals with fake implementations. However, any timer that was already scheduled by JavaScript executing during `page.goto()` — before `install()` was called — used the real `setTimeout` and is already queued in the browser's native timer heap with a real-clock expiry. Those timers will still fire at their real scheduled times regardless of the fake clock state. A common manifestation is a session-timeout test: the page schedules a 15-minute `setTimeout` during load, `install()` is called after navigation, and then `fastForward('15:00')` has no effect on the already-scheduled real timer — the test waits 15 real minutes and then times out. The issue is silent: no error is thrown at `install()` time to warn that timers already exist.
Fix: Always call `page.clock.install({ time: startTime })` before `page.goto()`. Per the documentation: "If you call `install` at any point in your test, the call MUST occur before any other clock related calls." The `time` option sets the initial fake date so that `new Date()` in page-load code also sees the frozen time. If pre-navigation clock installation is not possible (e.g., the page is shared across tests via a worker-scoped fixture), recreate the page in a test-scoped fixture that installs the clock before navigation.

---

**Gotcha G171** — `page.routeFromHAR()` with `notFound: 'fallback'` silently passes requests to real network, making tests non-hermetic and environment-dependent
Why this matters: `routeFromHAR()` has two `notFound` modes: `'abort'` (return a network error for unmatched requests) and `'fallback'` (pass unmatched requests to the real network). Teams that choose `'fallback'` to avoid breaking tests when the HAR is incomplete unknowingly create tests that succeed in development (where the real network is reachable) and fail in CI (where egress is blocked) — or vice versa when the external service has an outage. The failure manifests as a timeout waiting for a response that never arrives, with no indication in the test output that the request fell through HAR playback to a blocked network. Because `'fallback'` is the more permissive option, many teams discover the problem only when CI starts flaking after a network policy change.
Fix: Use `notFound: 'abort'` in all committed tests — this makes HAR coverage gaps fail loudly with a `net::ERR_FAILED` error that points directly to the unmatched URL, making it easy to identify which requests need to be added to the HAR. Keep a separate re-recording workflow guarded by `update: process.env.UPDATE_HAR === '1'` for refreshing the HAR against live network. Treat HAR files as committed fixtures that must be updated when API contracts change, and run the re-recording step as part of your dependency-update workflow.

---

**Gotcha G172** — `mergeTests()` fixture name collision produces a runtime error that does not identify which fixture is conflicting or in which module
Why this matters: `mergeTests(a, b)` throws a runtime error — not a TypeScript compile-time error — if both modules define a fixture with the same name. The error message is generic and does not indicate which fixture name is duplicated or in which files it was defined, making diagnosis time-consuming in codebases with many fixture modules. Because the collision is discovered only when a test that imports the merged object is first executed (not at import time), CI can pass in branches that do not exercise the conflicting test file, only to fail when the merged fixture is first used. The built-in fixtures (`page`, `context`, `browser`, `request`) are the most common collision source when two modules both try to override the same built-in.
Fix: Establish a naming convention for custom fixtures that includes the module name as a prefix (e.g., `db_client` instead of `client`, `auth_token` instead of `token`) to prevent accidental collisions. TypeScript can surface conflicts at compile time: define a merged type alias `type MergedFixtures = DbFixtures & AuthFixtures` — TypeScript will report an error on duplicate keys because an intersection type with conflicting property types produces `never`, making the conflict visible before any test runs.

---

**Gotcha G173** — `page.coverage.stopJSCoverage()` returns `null` for `source` when bundles are minified without source maps, producing meaningless coverage ranges
Why this matters: `stopJSCoverage()` returns an array of coverage entries, each with a `ranges` array of `{ start, end }` character offsets into the `source` property. When a bundler (Webpack, Rollup, esbuild) tree-shakes and minifies the output without generating source maps, the `source` property on each entry is `null` or contains only the minified single-line bundle. Coverage ranges against a minified bundle are meaningless — the offset numbers have no correspondence to the original source files. Teams that implement coverage assertions without checking for source availability silently get measurements against minified bytes, producing false high-coverage results: a 30-character minified expression that replaced 500 lines of source code counts as covered even though the untaken branches were eliminated at build time.
Fix: Configure the test build to emit source maps alongside bundles (Webpack: `devtool: 'source-map'`; Vite: `build.sourcemap: true`). Check that `entry.source !== null` before computing coverage percentages and skip entries without source. For production builds that intentionally omit source maps, restrict coverage tests to development builds by setting `process.env.NODE_ENV=development` in the Playwright test worker or using a dedicated `coverage` project in `playwright.config.ts` that points to a dev server rather than the production bundle.

---

**Gotcha G174** — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` combined with project-level `retries` causes the entire serial group to restart from the first test on each retry, not just the failing test
Why this matters: In serial mode, when a test within a `describe` block fails and retries are configured at the project or file level, Playwright re-runs the entire serial group from the first test — not from the failing test. This is by design: serial tests may share state (e.g., a captured `orderId` variable set in the first test), so retrying only the failing test would skip the setup that created that shared state. However, teams that add `retries: 2` to a serial test file expecting individual test retries discover that a single flaky test in the middle of a 10-test serial group triggers 2 full re-runs of all 10 tests, tripling CI time. The Playwright HTML report shows the first tests as "passed on retry" even though they did not fail, obscuring which test was actually flaky.
Fix: Do not combine `mode: 'serial'` with file-level or project-level retries unless the entire group is expected to be retried as a unit. Set `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial', retries: 0 })` to explicitly disable retries within the serial group, and rely on deterministic setup and increased action timeouts (e.g., `await expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 })`) to handle timing variability rather than retries. If retries are genuinely needed for a serial group, ensure the shared state variables are reset in a `beforeAll` hook so that a full-group re-run does not carry over stale values from the previous (failed) attempt.

## Cycle 62 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern #516** — `page.addInitScript()` with serialized argument to inject typed mock data before any page script runs

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface FeatureFlags { enableBeta: boolean; maxItems: number; }

test('feature-flag-gated UI renders correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  const flags: FeatureFlags = { enableBeta: true, maxItems: 5 };

  // Injects BEFORE the page's own JS executes — including module loaders
  await page.addInitScript((flags: FeatureFlags) => {
    (window as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__ = flags;
  }, flags);

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // The app reads window.__FEATURE_FLAGS__ at module init time
  await expect(page.getByTestId('beta-banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(5);
});
```
Tradeoff: `addInitScript` runs in every frame and is re-injected on every navigation within the same page object, making it reliable for SPAs that rehydrate on route changes — but because the script runs before any network request completes, values must be synchronously available; you cannot `await` an API call inside the init script, so all injected data must be determined at test time and passed as serializable arguments.

**Pattern #517** — `page.exposeFunction()` to bridge Node.js crypto/file-system capabilities into browser evaluation context

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import crypto from 'node:crypto';

test('HMAC signature field is computed correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  // Expose a Node.js function — callable as window.hmacSign() in page JS
  await page.exposeFunction('hmacSign', (payload: string) =>
    crypto
      .createHmac('sha256', process.env.SIGNING_SECRET!)
      .update(payload)
      .digest('hex')
  );

  await page.goto('/checkout/review');
  const payload = await page.getByTestId('order-payload').textContent();
  const expectedSig = await crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', process.env.SIGNING_SECRET!)
    .update(payload!)
    .digest('hex');

  const displayedSig = await page
    .getByTestId('order-signature')
    .textContent();

  expect(displayedSig?.trim()).toBe(expectedSig);
});
```
Tradeoff: `exposeFunction` registers the binding on the `Page` object and survives navigations, meaning every subsequent page load in that test has access to the function — which is useful for multi-step flows that re-navigate — but means the exposed function is available in `page.evaluate()` calls too, so avoid exposing sensitive secrets (like raw private keys) through this channel if the page can be tricked into calling the function with attacker-controlled arguments.

**Pattern #518** — `page.exposeBinding()` with `{ handle: true }` to receive a live `JSHandle` instead of a serialized value, enabling large-object inspection without serialization overhead

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('virtual-list renders only visible rows', async ({ page }) => {
  let capturedHandle: any;

  await page.exposeBinding(
    'captureRowData',
    async ({ page: _p }, handle) => {
      // handle is a JSHandle — no serialization round-trip
      capturedHandle = handle;
    },
    { handle: true }
  );

  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // App calls this when virtual list mounts
    (window as any).captureRowData(window.__VIRTUAL_LIST_STATE__);
  });

  await page.goto('/data-grid');
  await page.waitForFunction(() => (window as any).__VIRTUAL_LIST_STATE__);

  const renderedCount: number = await capturedHandle.evaluate(
    (state: { renderedRows: unknown[] }) => state.renderedRows.length
  );

  expect(renderedCount).toBeLessThan(20); // only ~15 rows in viewport
});
```
Tradeoff: The `{ handle: true }` variant avoids the cost of JSON-serializing potentially megabyte-scale objects (e.g., entire store snapshots) but requires you to keep the `JSHandle` in scope and call `.evaluate()` or `.jsonValue()` before the page navigates away — after navigation the handle is invalid and any subsequent `.evaluate()` call throws `Target page, context or browser has been closed`.

**Pattern #519** — `page.route()` with a handler that reads the real response before deciding whether to modify it, using `route.fetch()` for pass-through with selective mutation

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('price override banner appears when API returns discounted price', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/v2/products/*', async route => {
    // Fetch the real response first
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const body = await response.json();

    // Mutate only the field under test
    body.pricing.discountedPrice = 0.01;
    body.pricing.isDiscounted = true;

    await route.fulfill({
      response,               // inherit status, headers
      json: body,             // override body only
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('discount-banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-display')).toHaveText('$0.01');
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `route.fetch()` inside a route handler makes the test partially network-dependent — the real endpoint must be reachable for the route to resolve; in CI environments with egress restrictions, this pattern silently hangs. Prefer fully-stubbed `route.fulfill({ json: completeFixture })` for hermetic tests and reserve `route.fetch()` mutations for exploratory local runs or staging environments where the real API is always accessible.

**Pattern #520** — `page.routeWebSocket()` to intercept and inject WebSocket messages, enabling real-time feature testing without a live WS server

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('live-price ticker updates DOM on WebSocket push', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://prices.example.com/stream', ws => {
    // Relay messages from server -> client (pass-through)
    ws.onmessage = msg => ws.send(msg);

    // After 100 ms, inject a synthetic price update
    setTimeout(() => {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ symbol: 'ACME', price: 42.99, change: +1.5 }));
    }, 100);
  });

  await page.goto('/market/ACME');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('live-price')).toHaveText('42.99', {
    timeout: 3_000,
  });
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-change')).toHaveText('+1.50');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.routeWebSocket()` intercepts only WebSocket connections opened after the route is registered; any connection initiated during `page.goto()` (before the handler fires) is not intercepted — so register the route before navigation. The synthetic `ws.send()` from the handler side simulates server-push; to simulate client-to-server messages for echo-back testing, use the returned mock object's `.close()` and relay methods rather than attempting to call the real server.

**Pattern #521** — `page.waitForRequest()` / `page.waitForResponse()` with a predicate to assert both request payload and response code in a single awaitable

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form submission sends correct payload and receives 201', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');
  await page.getByLabel('Name').fill('Alice');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Message').fill('Hello!');

  // Set up the wait BEFORE triggering the action
  const [response] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForResponse(
      res =>
        res.url().includes('/api/contact') &&
        res.request().method() === 'POST' &&
        res.status() === 201
    ),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click(),
  ]);

  const requestBody = JSON.parse(
    (await response.request().postData()) ?? '{}'
  );
  expect(requestBody.email).toBe('alice@example.com');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
});
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping `waitForResponse` and the triggering action in `Promise.all` is essential — setting up the wait after `.click()` introduces a race condition where the response may arrive before the listener is registered and the test hangs indefinitely. This pattern couples the test to the network layer and will fail if the endpoint is unavailable; for offline test environments, prefer `page.route()` stubs and assert the stub's recorded call arguments instead.

**Pattern #522** — Custom worker-scoped fixture that creates a shared authenticated `APIRequestContext` used by all tests in a worker without re-authenticating

```typescript
import { test as base, APIRequestContext, request } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { apiContext: APIRequestContext };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  apiContext: [
    async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
      // One login per worker process — not per test
      const ctx = await request.newContext({
        baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL,
        extraHTTPHeaders: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_TOKEN}`,
        },
      });

      await use(ctx);
      // Teardown: dispose context (releases connection pool)
      await ctx.dispose();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// Usage in a test file:
test('GET /users returns 200', async ({ apiContext }) => {
  const response = await apiContext.get('/users');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures share state across all tests running in the same worker process, which reduces authentication overhead from O(n tests) to O(n workers) — a significant speedup for large suites. The risk is that state mutations on the shared context (e.g., cookies set by one test) leak into subsequent tests in the same worker; mitigate by creating test-scoped child contexts when mutation isolation is required, or by using stateless `Authorization` header auth rather than cookie-based sessions that accumulate across requests.

**Pattern #523** — Box fixture (`{ box: true }`) to hide multi-step helper setup from the HTML report while keeping it visible in code

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type Fixtures = { loginAs: (role: 'admin' | 'viewer') => Promise<void> };

export const test = base.extend<Fixtures>({
  loginAs: [
    async ({ page }, use) => {
      await use(async (role) => {
        await page.goto('/login');
        await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(
          role === 'admin' ? 'admin@co.com' : 'view@co.com'
        );
        await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('s3cr3t');
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
        await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
      });
    },
    { box: true }, // Steps collapsed in HTML report under fixture name
  ],
});

test('admin can delete a record', async ({ page, loginAs }) => {
  await loginAs('admin');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete record #1' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('toast')).toHaveText('Record deleted');
});
```
Tradeoff: The `{ box: true }` option collapses all steps inside the fixture into a single fixture entry in the Playwright HTML report, reducing report noise for multi-step helpers like login flows — but this also means errors thrown inside a boxed fixture are attributed to the fixture entry rather than the specific failing line, which can make debugging harder. Use box fixtures for well-understood, stable helpers; keep non-boxed fixtures for anything under active development where line-level attribution is valuable.

**Pattern #524** — `page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` combined with `toHaveScreenshot()` to run dual-theme visual regression in a single test

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard renders correctly in both light and dark themes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Light theme baseline
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'light' });
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('dashboard-light.png', {
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
  });

  // Switch to dark — no reload required
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' });
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('dashboard-dark.png', {
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
  });

  // Verify CSS custom properties respond correctly
  const bgColor = await page
    .locator('body')
    .evaluate(el => getComputedStyle(el).backgroundColor);
  expect(bgColor).not.toBe('rgb(255, 255, 255)'); // not white in dark mode
});
```
Tradeoff: `emulateMedia` changes the media query at the OS emulation layer, so `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` CSS rules and `window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')` JS listeners both respond correctly — but the emulation only applies to CSS media queries; JavaScript code that reads `localStorage.theme` or a React context for theme state will not automatically switch and must be updated via `page.evaluate()` or fixture before the screenshot assertion.

**Pattern #525** — `page.pdf()` with `printBackground: true` and custom header/footer templates for testing generated-PDF content programmatically

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import * as path from 'node:path';

test('invoice PDF contains correct content structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/invoices/INV-2024-001');
  await page.emulateMedia({ media: 'print' });

  const pdfBuffer = await page.pdf({
    printBackground: true,
    format: 'A4',
    displayHeaderFooter: true,
    headerTemplate: '<span class="title"></span>',
    footerTemplate:
      '<span style="font-size:9px">Page <span class="pageNumber"></span></span>',
  });

  // Persist for artifact upload in CI
  const outputPath = path.join(test.info().outputDir, 'invoice.pdf');
  await fs.writeFile(outputPath, pdfBuffer);
  test.info().attach('invoice-pdf', { path: outputPath, contentType: 'application/pdf' });

  // Assert buffer is a valid PDF by magic bytes
  expect(pdfBuffer.subarray(0, 5).toString('ascii')).toBe('%PDF-');
  // Assert non-trivial content size (not an empty page)
  expect(pdfBuffer.byteLength).toBeGreaterThan(10_000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.pdf()` is Chromium-only and requires a headless context (the method throws if called in headed mode); in CI you must ensure `chromium` is installed rather than relying on the `--browser=firefox` flag. PDF content cannot be inspected as DOM, so testing specific text requires a secondary PDF-parsing library (e.g., `pdf-parse`) — the pattern above only validates format validity and size as a smoke test; for text-content assertions, install `pdf-parse` and assert on extracted text strings.

**Pattern #526** — `expect.soft()` accumulating multiple independent assertions before a hard stop, used for multi-field form-validation testing

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('registration form shows all validation errors simultaneously', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/register');
  // Submit with intentionally invalid data
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();

  // Soft assertions — all run even if earlier ones fail
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('email-error')).toHaveText('Email is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('password-error')).toHaveText(
    'Password must be at least 8 characters'
  );
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('username-error')).toHaveText('Username is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('terms-error')).toHaveText(
    'You must accept the terms'
  );

  // Hard assertion — fails fast if the form itself disappeared
  await expect(page.getByRole('form', { name: 'Registration' })).toBeVisible();

  // Verify all soft assertions passed
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft()` defers failure accumulation until the test ends (or until a hard `expect()` fails), making it ideal for multi-field validation where you want a complete picture of all broken assertions in one run — but the test continues executing after a soft assertion failure, which can cause misleading subsequent steps if the UI is in an unexpected state after the first failure. Avoid using `expect.soft()` for assertions whose truth is a precondition for later steps (e.g., asserting a redirect happened before clicking a link on the new page).

**Pattern #527** — `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` to create named, collapsible checkpoints in the HTML report for long multi-action tests

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('end-to-end order placement flow', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('Navigate and add item to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/shop');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart: Widget Pro' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  await test.step('Proceed to checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View cart' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('/checkout');
  });

  await test.step('Fill shipping details', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Alice Smith');
    await page.getByLabel('Address').fill('1 Infinite Loop');
    await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Cupertino');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('Confirm order', { box: true }, async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('confirmation-number')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step()` groups related actions into named checkpoints in the HTML trace and report, improving readability of long tests — but steps do not create isolation boundaries: a failure in one step does not prevent subsequent steps from running unless you re-throw or use `test.fail()`. The `{ box: true }` variant available from Playwright 1.39 further collapses sub-steps for steps you treat as black-box helpers; without `{ box: true }`, each inner action appears expanded in the report, which is useful for debugging but noisy for stable flows.

**Pattern #528** — `page.locator().filter({ has, hasNot, hasText, hasNotText })` chaining to target a list item by multiple simultaneous conditions

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('in-stock items with discount badge can be added to cart', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Chain two filter conditions: has discount AND is in-stock (no "Out of stock" text)
  const discountedInStock = page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByTestId('discount-badge') })
    .filter({ hasNotText: 'Out of stock' });

  const count = await discountedInStock.count();
  expect(count).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Act on the first qualifying item
  await discountedInStock
    .first()
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
    .click();

  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).not.toHaveText('0');
});
```
Tradeoff: Chained `.filter()` calls compose as a logical AND — each filter further narrows the matching set — and all filtering is evaluated lazily at action time, meaning the locator re-evaluates on each interaction to pick up DOM changes. The downside is that deeply-chained filters can be slow on large lists (hundreds of items) because Playwright evaluates each filter condition against every matching element; for lists exceeding ~200 items, prefer a CSS `:has()` selector or a direct `page.locator()` with a compound CSS expression for better performance.

**Pattern #529** — `page.getByRole()` with `name` regex to match ARIA labels that include dynamic suffixes (counts, statuses)

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('notification bell with dynamic unread count is accessible', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/inbox');

  // ARIA label is "Notifications (3 unread)" — dynamic count embedded in label
  const bell = page.getByRole('button', { name: /notifications/i });
  await expect(bell).toBeVisible();
  await expect(bell).toHaveAttribute('aria-label', /\d+ unread/i);

  await bell.click();
  // Panel opens
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('region', { name: /notification/i })
  ).toBeVisible();

  // Mark all read — label should update
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /mark all as read/i }).click();
  await expect(bell).toHaveAttribute('aria-label', /0 unread/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: Using a `RegExp` for the `name` option in `getByRole()` makes the locator resilient to label changes that embed dynamic values — but overly broad patterns like `/button/i` can match multiple elements accidentally. Always use the most specific regex that uniquely identifies the target (e.g., anchor to the static prefix `notifications` rather than a generic noun) and confirm uniqueness with `await expect(locator).toHaveCount(1)` in a sanity-check test to catch regressions if the page adds a similarly-named control.

**Pattern #530** — `page.dragAndDrop()` with explicit `sourcePosition` and `targetPosition` offsets for drag-and-drop reordering in sortable lists

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('kanban card can be moved from To Do to In Progress', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/kanban');

  const sourceCard = page
    .getByTestId('column-todo')
    .getByRole('article', { name: 'Fix login bug' });

  const targetColumn = page.getByTestId('column-in-progress');

  // Drag from the card's grab handle area to the target column's drop zone
  await page.dragAndDrop(
    '[data-testid="column-todo"] [aria-label="Fix login bug"]',
    '[data-testid="column-in-progress"]',
    {
      sourcePosition: { x: 10, y: 10 },   // grab handle offset
      targetPosition: { x: 50, y: 100 },  // mid-column drop zone
    }
  );

  // Verify card moved
  await expect(sourceCard).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(
    targetColumn.getByRole('article', { name: 'Fix login bug' })
  ).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.dragAndDrop()` dispatches `dragstart`, `drag`, `dragover`, `dragenter`, `dragleave`, `drop`, and `dragend` events in sequence with Playwright's synthetic mouse movements — but some drag-and-drop libraries (React DnD, `@dnd-kit`) rely on pointer events (`pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`) rather than HTML5 drag events, and `page.dragAndDrop()` does not emit pointer events. For pointer-event-based DnD, use `page.mouse.move()` + `page.mouse.down()` + a series of `page.mouse.move()` calls + `page.mouse.up()` to simulate the full pointer gesture.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G175** — `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` causes flaky hangs on pages with polling or long-polling endpoints that never go truly idle
Why this matters: `networkidle` resolves only when there are no more than 0 in-flight network requests for at least 500 ms. Pages that implement periodic polling (e.g., a dashboard refreshing every 10 seconds) or long-poll connections (e.g., SSE, WebSocket keepalives, background fetch) never satisfy this condition — Playwright waits the full navigation timeout (default 30 s) and then throws `TimeoutError`. The failure is misleading because the page is visually complete and fully interactive; the "pending" request is a background polling request that has nothing to do with the UI the test wants to interact with. Teams that copy `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` from tutorials into every navigation silently degrade their suite's speed even when pages don't hang, because `networkidle` adds at least 500 ms of artificial delay after the last request on every navigation.
Fix: Replace `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` with a specific element-based wait: `await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible()` or `await page.waitForSelector('[data-ready="true"]')`. For navigation assertions, `waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded')` is sufficient for most SPAs. Reserve `networkidle` only for pages with no background network activity (e.g., static documents) and document why it is used to prevent future developers from copying the pattern blindly.

---

**Gotcha G176** — Locator actions on `locator.nth(0)` after a list re-render silently act on a stale element reference, producing a mismatch between the clicked item and the expected item
Why this matters: `page.locator('css >> nth=0')` is evaluated lazily — it re-queries the DOM at the moment of each action. If a list dynamically reorders between the locator construction and the `.click()` call (e.g., an async sort triggered by a prior interaction), the element at index 0 may be a different item than the one the test intended to target. The test passes (the click succeeds on whatever is now first), but the subsequent assertion fails with a confusing message about wrong text. Developers seeing the failure often blame async timing or animation and add `waitForTimeout()` calls rather than diagnosing the root cause: the locator is correct but the list reordered.
Fix: Use semantic locators that identify by stable attributes rather than position: `page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Widget Pro' })` instead of `page.getByRole('listitem').nth(0)`. If position is genuinely meaningful (e.g., testing that sort order is correct), capture the text of the expected first item before triggering the sort and assert via `page.getByRole('listitem').first().toHaveText(expectedFirstItem)` after the sort completes. Never use position-based locators for items that may move.

---

**Gotcha G177** — `page.fill()` on a `contenteditable` div does not clear existing text in some browser/framework combinations, causing appended rather than replaced content
Why this matters: `page.fill()` is specified for `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and `contenteditable` elements. For `<input>` and `<textarea>`, it reliably selects all and replaces. For `contenteditable` divs — used by rich-text editors like ProseMirror, Tiptap, and Quill — `fill()` behavior is inconsistent across browser engines: on Chromium it typically clears first, but on Firefox and WebKit the existing content may not be fully selected before the fill, resulting in appended text. A test that sets an editor field to `'New title'` when it already contains `'Old title'` can produce `'Old titleNew title'`, causing the subsequent `toHaveText` assertion to fail with a value that looks like a concatenation bug in the application rather than a test authoring issue.
Fix: Before calling `fill()` on a `contenteditable` element, explicitly triple-click to select all content: `await page.locator('[contenteditable]').click({ clickCount: 3 })` then `await page.keyboard.press('Control+a')` (or `Meta+a` on macOS), then `await page.keyboard.type('New title')`. Alternatively, use `page.locator('[contenteditable]').evaluate(el => { el.textContent = ''; })` to clear via JS before `fill()`. For rich-text editors with their own APIs (e.g., `.commands.setContent()` in Tiptap), call the editor API via `page.evaluate()` rather than simulating keyboard input.

---

**Gotcha G178** — `page.screenshot({ clip })` with coordinates from `locator.boundingBox()` returns an empty or misaligned image when the element is inside a CSS `transform: scale()` container
Why this matters: `locator.boundingBox()` returns coordinates in the CSS layout space — the box before transforms are applied. When a parent element has `transform: scale(0.5)` or `transform: translate(100px, 0)`, the bounding box returned is the pre-transform logical box, but `page.screenshot({ clip })` clips against the visual viewport in device pixels after transforms are applied. The result is a screenshot that captures a different region than the element's visual location, producing misaligned snapshots that either include surrounding elements or miss the target element entirely. This is a known discrepancy between CSS layout coordinates and visual rendering coordinates that is not documented in the `boundingBox()` API.
Fix: Use `locator.screenshot()` instead of `page.screenshot({ clip })` — it resolves the element's visual bounding box correctly even inside transformed containers and handles scroll offsets. If you must use `page.screenshot({ clip })`, compute the clip rect by evaluating `el.getBoundingClientRect()` via `locator.evaluate()` which returns viewport-relative visual coordinates: `const rect = await locator.evaluate(el => el.getBoundingClientRect())` then clip to `{ x: rect.x, y: rect.y, width: rect.width, height: rect.height }`.

---

**Gotcha G179** — Auto-use fixtures with teardown side effects run after the test timeout expires, causing teardown code to execute against a context that has already been torn down by Playwright's own cleanup
Why this matters: When a test times out, Playwright immediately begins its own cleanup: it closes the page, context, and browser objects. Auto-use fixtures with teardown code (code after `await use()`) are then called as part of fixture teardown — but by the time the teardown runs, the `page` and `context` objects are already closed or in a closing state. Any teardown action that calls `page.evaluate()`, `context.storageState()`, or similar methods throws `Target page, context or browser has been closed`, masking the original `TimeoutError` with a secondary fixture teardown error in the HTML report. Teams investigating the failure see the fixture teardown error and focus on the wrong cause.
Fix: Wrap auto-use fixture teardown in a try/catch that ignores `Target closed` errors and re-surfaces any other unexpected errors: `try { await page.evaluate(() => cleanup()); } catch (e) { if (!String(e).includes('Target closed')) throw e; }`. For teardown actions that are critical (e.g., database cleanup that must run even after test failure), move them to a `test.afterAll()` hook in a `workerFixture` teardown where the context lifecycle is separate from the test's page, ensuring cleanup runs against a fresh context rather than the closed test page.

### Patterns

**Pattern 531** — Worker-scoped browser context with saved storage state for authenticated test suites
```typescript
import { test as base, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { authedContext: BrowserContext };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  authedContext: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      // Perform login once per worker, save to storage state
      const setupPage = await browser.newPage();
      await setupPage.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
      await setupPage.getByLabel('Email').fill('qa@example.com');
      await setupPage.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.QA_PASSWORD!);
      await setupPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
      await setupPage.waitForURL('**/dashboard');
      const storageState = await setupPage.context().storageState();
      await setupPage.close();

      // All tests in this worker share this authenticated context
      const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState });
      await use(context);
      await context.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('dashboard loads user profile', async ({ authedContext }) => {
  const page = await authedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/profile');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /qa@example\.com/ })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped contexts eliminate per-test login round-trips (often 500–2000 ms each), but all tests sharing the worker context mutate the same cookie jar and localStorage — a test that logs out, changes user roles, or clears session storage will corrupt the shared state for subsequent tests in the same worker, causing misleading auth failures that disappear on isolated re-runs.

**Pattern 532** — `locator.and()` to intersect two independent locator conditions without CSS combinators
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('active admin row is highlighted', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/users');

  // Locate rows that are both in the "admin" role AND currently active
  const adminRole = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Admin' });
  const activeRow = page.getByRole('row').filter({ has: page.locator('[data-status="active"]') });

  // .and() narrows to elements that satisfy BOTH locators simultaneously
  const activeAdminRow = adminRole.and(activeRow);

  // Should be exactly one match; strictness check enforces it
  await expect(activeAdminRow).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(activeAdminRow).toHaveCSS('background-color', 'rgb(220, 252, 231)');

  // Interact with the narrowed result
  await activeAdminRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Edit User' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.and()` performs a lazy DOM intersection — it does not create a CSS selector combining both constraints but re-evaluates both locators independently at action time and takes the intersection. This means it cannot be used when you need a single CSS query for performance on large tables (thousands of rows), because two full DOM queries are issued; prefer a single `locator('[data-role="admin"][data-status="active"]')` CSS attribute selector when both conditions map to attributes on the same element.

**Pattern 533** — `locator.or()` to handle alternative UI states within a single assertion path
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment confirmation shows success or pending state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();

  // Payment processor may respond instantly (success) or queue (pending)
  const successBanner = page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: 'Payment successful' });
  const pendingBanner = page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: 'Payment processing' });

  // .or() matches whichever appears first — resolves as soon as either is visible
  const confirmation = successBanner.or(pendingBanner);
  await expect(confirmation).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });

  // Narrow back to the matched variant for further assertions
  const isSuccess = await successBanner.isVisible();
  if (isSuccess) {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-number')).toBeVisible();
  } else {
    await expect(page.getByText('You will receive an email')).toBeVisible();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.or()` resolves as soon as the first matching locator becomes visible, which is ideal for handling legitimate UI state variations, but it can mask regressions where the application should always show the success state but starts intermittently showing pending — the test passes in both cases and hides the behavioral change. Use `locator.or()` only for genuinely equivalent outcomes and add a separate test that mocks the payment gateway to assert each branch deterministically.

---

**Pattern 534** — `browserContext.route()` with `**` glob to intercept all API calls for offline/error scenario testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard shows error state when API is unavailable', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // Intercept all requests to the API origin and return 503
  await context.route('**/api/**', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 503,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Service temporarily unavailable' }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Verify each widget gracefully degrades
  await expect(page.getByTestId('metrics-widget')).toContainText('Unable to load metrics');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('activity-feed')).toContainText('Feed unavailable');

  // Confirm the retry button appears
  const retryButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Retry' });
  await expect(retryButton).toBeVisible();

  // Remove the route intercept and verify recovery
  await context.unroute('**/api/**');
  await retryButton.click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('metrics-widget')).not.toContainText('Unable to load');
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.route()` intercepts apply to all pages opened in the context from registration forward — including any background tabs or service worker fetches — so a route that fulfills `**/api/**` with 503 will also block requests made by pages the test opens for navigation assertions; call `context.unroute()` or use `page.route()` with per-page scope when only one page should see the error condition.

**Pattern 535** — `page.route()` with `route.continue({ headers })` for injecting feature flags via request headers
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('beta feature is visible when feature-flag header is set', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept requests to the app and inject a feature-flag header
  await page.route('https://app.example.com/**', async (route) => {
    const request = route.request();
    await route.continue({
      headers: {
        ...request.headers(),
        'X-Feature-Flag': 'new-dashboard:enabled,dark-mode:enabled',
      },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Beta features should now be visible
  await expect(page.getByTestId('new-dashboard-banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('switch', { name: 'Dark Mode' })).toBeVisible();

  // Confirm non-flagged elements are still present
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `route.continue({ headers })` to inject feature flags is a clean way to test flag-gated paths without modifying application code or seeding a flag service, but it only applies to browser-initiated requests — server-side rendering (SSR) that reads the flag from the initial HTTP request will not see the injected header because the navigation request itself must be intercepted before the browser receives the SSR HTML; combine with `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` for SSR scenarios where the header must be present on the initial document request.

**Pattern 536** — `page.waitForRequest()` combined with `Promise.all` to prevent request/action race conditions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form submission triggers correct API request with expected payload', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/create-project');

  await page.getByLabel('Project Name').fill('Alpha Launch');
  await page.getByLabel('Description').fill('Q3 release project');
  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Team' }).selectOption('engineering');

  // Start waiting for the request BEFORE triggering the action that causes it
  const [request] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForRequest((req) =>
      req.url().includes('/api/projects') && req.method() === 'POST'
    ),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create Project' }).click(),
  ]);

  // Assert the payload matches what the form submitted
  const body = JSON.parse(request.postData() ?? '{}');
  expect(body.name).toBe('Alpha Launch');
  expect(body.description).toBe('Q3 release project');
  expect(body.teamId).toBe('engineering');

  // Also assert the UI response
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Alpha Launch' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForRequest()` must be registered before the action that triggers the network call — the `Promise.all` pattern enforces this ordering. However, `waitForRequest()` resolves as soon as the request is sent (before the response arrives), so it cannot assert response status or response body; use `page.waitForResponse()` in the same `Promise.all` pattern when you need to assert on the API response rather than the outgoing request payload.

**Pattern 537** — Custom `test.extend()` fixture with `{ option: true }` for environment-parameterized test configurations
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type EnvOptions = {
  apiVersion: 'v1' | 'v2' | 'v3';
  featureSet: 'core' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';
};

export const test = base.extend<EnvOptions>({
  apiVersion: [
    'v2',
    { option: true },  // becomes a configurable option in playwright.config.ts
  ],
  featureSet: [
    'core',
    { option: true },
  ],
});

// In playwright.config.ts, projects can override:
// projects: [
//   { name: 'enterprise-v3', use: { apiVersion: 'v3', featureSet: 'enterprise' } },
//   { name: 'core-v1', use: { apiVersion: 'v1', featureSet: 'core' } },
// ]

test('API response shape matches version contract', async ({ page, apiVersion, featureSet }) => {
  await page.goto(`https://app.example.com/api-explorer?version=${apiVersion}`);

  const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(`**/api/${apiVersion}/schema`);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Load Schema' }).click();
  const response = await responsePromise;

  const schema = await response.json();
  expect(schema.version).toBe(apiVersion);

  if (featureSet === 'enterprise') {
    expect(schema.features).toContain('audit-logs');
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Fixture options declared with `{ option: true }` make the test matrix explicit in `playwright.config.ts` and avoid runtime `process.env` checks scattered across test files — but every unique combination of options spawns a separate project entry in the config, and with many options the config grows combinatorially; use options for high-value axis variations (API version, feature tier) and keep them to 2–3 per suite to avoid an unmanageable project matrix.

**Pattern 538** — `context.storageState()` snapshot between test phases for stateful multi-step flow isolation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

test.describe('multi-step onboarding flow', () => {
  const stateDir = path.join(__dirname, '.test-states');

  test('step 1: account creation saves storage state for step 2', async ({ page, context }) => {
    fs.mkdirSync(stateDir, { recursive: true });
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/onboarding/step-1');

    await page.getByLabel('Full Name').fill('Jane Tester');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('jane@test.example.com');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('**/onboarding/step-2');

    // Snapshot context state after step 1 completes
    await context.storageState({ path: path.join(stateDir, 'after-step1.json') });
    await expect(page.getByText('Tell us about yourself')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('step 2: profile setup (resumes from step 1 state)', async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      storageState: path.join(stateDir, 'after-step1.json'),
    });
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/onboarding/step-2');

    await page.getByLabel('Job Title').fill('QA Engineer');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Complete Setup' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');

    await expect(page.getByText('Welcome, Jane Tester')).toBeVisible();
    await context.close();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Snapshotting `storageState` between test phases enables precise resumption of multi-step flows without re-running all prior steps, but the saved state files are written to disk and persist between CI runs — if the application changes session token formats or adds new required cookies between runs, a stale snapshot causes cryptic authentication failures that are difficult to trace; add the state directory to `.gitignore` and include a cleanup step in CI to purge state files before each pipeline run.

**Pattern 539** — `page.on('dialog')` handler with conditional accept/dismiss for alert and confirm dialogs
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('delete confirmation dialog requires explicit user approval', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/files');

  // Register dialog handler BEFORE triggering the action that opens it
  let dialogMessage = '';
  page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => {
    dialogMessage = dialog.message();
    if (dialog.type() === 'confirm' && dialog.message().includes('permanently delete')) {
      await dialog.accept();
    } else {
      // Dismiss unexpected dialogs to prevent test hang
      await dialog.dismiss();
    }
  });

  // Trigger the delete action
  await page.getByRole('row', { name: 'quarterly-report.pdf' })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })
    .click();

  // Verify the dialog message was correct
  expect(dialogMessage).toContain('permanently delete');
  expect(dialogMessage).toContain('quarterly-report.pdf');

  // Verify the file was removed after confirmation
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('row', { name: 'quarterly-report.pdf' })
  ).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Registering a `page.on('dialog')` listener before the triggering action is mandatory — an unhandled dialog freezes the test until timeout because Playwright will not auto-dismiss dialogs. However, a single static handler cannot selectively respond to sequences of dialogs (e.g., confirm then alert), so for multi-step dialog flows register the listener inside the test body using `page.once('dialog')` per expected dialog to handle each occurrence independently with distinct logic.

---

**Pattern 540** — `context.grantPermissions()` with geolocation emulation for location-aware feature testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('store locator shows nearest branch for emulated coordinates', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Create a context with a specific geolocation and permission pre-granted
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    geolocation: { latitude: 37.7749, longitude: -122.4194 },  // San Francisco
    permissions: ['geolocation'],
    locale: 'en-US',
    timezoneId: 'America/Los_Angeles',
  });

  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/store-locator');

  // Click "Use my location" — browser permission is already granted
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Use my location' }).click();

  // Nearest branch to SF coordinates should appear first
  const firstResult = page.getByRole('listitem').first();
  await expect(firstResult).toContainText('San Francisco');

  // Override geolocation mid-test to simulate user moving
  await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 40.7128, longitude: -74.0060 });  // New York
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh location' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toContainText('New York');

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Passing `geolocation` and `permissions` at context creation time ensures the permission dialog never appears and the coordinates are available from the first frame, but `context.setGeolocation()` only changes the coordinates Playwright returns for `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition()` — it does not re-trigger Geolocation API callbacks that the application may have registered via `watchPosition()`, so applications using `watchPosition()` for live tracking will not react to `setGeolocation()` changes unless the test also calls the application's refresh mechanism or re-navigates.

**Pattern 541** — HAR file recording with `context.routeFromHAR()` for deterministic replay of complex API sequences
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const harPath = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', 'dashboard-api.har');

// RECORD mode: run once to capture real API traffic
// await context.recordHar({ path: harPath, url: '**/api/**' });

test('dashboard renders correctly from HAR-replayed API responses', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();

  // Replay all matching requests from the HAR file
  await context.routeFromHAR(harPath, {
    url: '**/api/**',
    update: false,  // set to true to re-record on mismatch
    notFound: 'abort',  // abort any API request not in the HAR
  });

  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Assertions against HAR-replayed data are fully deterministic
  await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-total')).toHaveText('$142,530');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('active-users')).toHaveText('1,284');
  await expect(page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Recent Orders' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('row')).toHaveCount(11);  // header + 10 data rows

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: HAR replay makes tests fast and fully deterministic — no network dependency, consistent data — but HAR files must be manually re-recorded when the API contract changes (new fields, endpoint renames, auth token formats), and stale HAR files silently test against outdated response shapes; include HAR re-recording as a scheduled CI job (weekly or on API schema change PRs) and commit the updated HAR file alongside the schema change to keep the two in sync.

---

**Pattern 542** — `expect(locator).toHaveAttribute()` with regex for partial dynamic attribute value assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

test('upload progress indicator reflects dynamic percentage', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/upload');

  // Intercept upload to control progress timing
  await page.route('**/api/upload', async (route) => {
    // Simulate a slow upload by delaying the response
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
    await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ fileId: 'abc123' }) });
  });

  const fileInput = page.locator('input[type="file"]');
  await fileInput.setInputFiles(path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', 'sample.pdf'));

  // aria-valuenow is dynamic — assert it's a valid percentage string
  const progressBar = page.getByRole('progressbar');
  await expect(progressBar).toHaveAttribute('aria-valuenow', /^\d{1,3}$/);
  await expect(progressBar).toHaveAttribute('aria-valuemax', '100');

  // Wait for completion — aria-valuenow becomes '100'
  await expect(progressBar).toHaveAttribute('aria-valuenow', '100', { timeout: 10_000 });

  // Confirm success state
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Upload complete');
  await expect(page.getByText('abc123')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `toHaveAttribute()` with a regex pattern retries the assertion until the attribute value matches — making it resilient to intermediate animation frames — but the regex is evaluated as a JavaScript `RegExp` against the attribute string value, not as a CSS selector or XPath expression; for attributes that contain JSON-encoded values (e.g., `data-config='{"theme":"dark"}'`), regex matching becomes fragile due to key ordering and whitespace variations; use `locator.evaluate()` to parse the attribute as JSON and assert individual properties instead.

---

**Pattern 543** — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` with isolated fixtures for intra-file parallelism
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Run all tests in this describe block in parallel within a single worker
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' });

test.describe('settings page — independent panel tests', () => {
  // Each test gets its own page (default fixture) — no shared state
  test('profile panel updates display name', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/settings/profile');
    await page.getByLabel('Display Name').fill('Updated Name');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Profile saved');
  });

  test('notifications panel saves email preferences', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/settings/notifications');
    await page.getByLabel('Weekly digest').check();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save preferences' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Preferences saved');
  });

  test('security panel shows active sessions', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://app.example.com/settings/security');
    await expect(page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Active sessions' })).toBeVisible();
    const rowCount = await page.getByRole('row').count();
    expect(rowCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` runs the describe block's tests in parallel using separate worker slots, which can cut block execution time proportionally to the number of workers — but it only parallelizes within the describe block using the number of workers available; if `workers` in `playwright.config.ts` is set to `1` (common in CI with resource constraints), this has no effect. Additionally, parallel tests in the same describe block can compete for the same user account's server-side state (e.g., two tests simultaneously modifying the same user's settings), so parallel execution requires either test-account isolation or backend idempotency for the mutations being tested.
