**Pattern 544** — `locator.tap()` with `hasTouch: true` context for mobile gesture testing
```typescript
import { test, expect, devices } from '@playwright/test';

// Configure context to emulate a touch-capable mobile device
const iPhone14 = devices['iPhone 14'];

test('mobile notification tap expands detail view', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    ...iPhone14,
    hasTouch: true,
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/notifications');

  const notification = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'New message from Alice' });
  await expect(notification).toBeVisible();

  // Use touch tap to expand the notification
  await notification.tap();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toContainText('Alice');

  // Dismiss with touch gesture on close button
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Dismiss' }).tap();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Verify notification marked as read
  await expect(notification.getByTestId('unread-dot')).not.toBeVisible();

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.tap()` dispatches `touchstart`, `touchend`, and `click` events, which correctly triggers touch-specific event handlers that `locator.click()` does not emit — however, swipe gestures (e.g., swipe-to-dismiss) require `page.touchscreen.tap()` with coordinates or a sequence of `touchstart` → `touchmove` → `touchend` dispatches via `locator.dispatchEvent()`, because there is no built-in `locator.swipe()` API; for gesture-heavy mobile UIs, implement a `swipeLeft(locator, distance)` helper that calls `page.touchscreen` APIs to simulate the full touch sequence.

---

**Pattern 545** — `page.evaluate()` with a typed `PageFunction` returning structured data for batched DOM state assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface TableSummary {
  rowCount: number;
  columnHeaders: string[];
  firstRowData: Record<string, string>;
  hasScrollbar: boolean;
}

test('data table renders complete schema after async load', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/reports/sales');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Load Full Report' }).click();

  // Wait for the skeleton loader to disappear
  await expect(page.getByTestId('skeleton-loader')).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });

  // Extract structured state in a single evaluate call to minimize CDP round-trips
  const summary = await page.evaluate((): TableSummary => {
    const table = document.querySelector('[data-testid="sales-table"]')!;
    const headers = Array.from(table.querySelectorAll('thead th')).map(
      (th) => th.textContent?.trim() ?? ''
    );
    const rows = Array.from(table.querySelectorAll('tbody tr'));
    const firstCells = Array.from(rows[0]?.querySelectorAll('td') ?? []);
    const firstRowData: Record<string, string> = {};
    headers.forEach((h, i) => {
      firstRowData[h] = firstCells[i]?.textContent?.trim() ?? '';
    });
    const wrapper = table.closest('[data-testid="table-wrapper"]') as HTMLElement | null;
    return {
      rowCount: rows.length,
      columnHeaders: headers,
      firstRowData,
      hasScrollbar: wrapper ? wrapper.scrollWidth > wrapper.clientWidth : false,
    };
  });

  expect(summary.rowCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(50);
  expect(summary.columnHeaders).toEqual(['Date', 'Region', 'Product', 'Units', 'Revenue']);
  expect(summary.firstRowData['Region']).toBeTruthy();
  expect(summary.hasScrollbar).toBe(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: Batching multiple DOM reads into a single `page.evaluate()` call eliminates the network round-trip overhead of multiple separate Playwright API calls (each `locator.textContent()` or `locator.count()` is a CDP message), which is especially valuable when asserting table schemas with many columns — but the `PageFunction` runs in the browser context and has no access to Node.js modules or Playwright fixtures; complex assertions that need Playwright's retry semantics (e.g., waiting for a count to stabilize) must use `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` rather than `page.evaluate()`, because `page.evaluate()` does not retry.

### Community Gotchas

**G180** — `page.getByLabel()` fails to find an input when the `<label>` element uses `aria-labelledby` instead of a `for`/`id` pairing
Why this matters: `page.getByLabel('Email')` resolves by finding a `<label>` whose text content matches and then locating the associated form control via the `for`/`id` attribute pairing or by containment (label wrapping the input). When developers use `aria-labelledby` on the input element pointing to a `<span>` or `<div>` as the label — a common pattern in design-system components where the label is not a `<label>` element — `getByLabel()` cannot find the association and throws a strict-mode violation or returns zero matches. The failure message says "no elements" and developers waste time checking whether the selector text matches, not realizing the association mechanism is the issue.
Fix: For `aria-labelledby` associations, use `page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Email' })` — it resolves the accessible name using the full ARIA computation including `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, and label containment. Alternatively, add a `for`/`id` pairing to the label markup alongside `aria-labelledby` so both `getByLabel()` and assistive technology work correctly. If the component cannot be modified, use `page.locator('[aria-labelledby="email-label"]')` as a targeted fallback.

---

**G181** — `page.route()` registered inside `test.beforeEach()` accumulates duplicate handlers when the test body also registers the same route pattern
Why this matters: `page.route(pattern, handler)` adds a new handler to the front of an internal handler stack — it does not replace an existing handler for the same pattern. When `test.beforeEach()` registers `page.route('**/api/user', handler)` and a test also calls `page.route('**/api/user', overrideHandler)` locally, both handlers are active. Playwright executes the most-recently-registered handler first; if that handler calls `route.continue()`, the earlier `beforeEach` handler runs next and may call `route.fulfill()` on the already-continued request, throwing "Request already handled" and failing the test with an error that appears to be a framework bug rather than a double-registration issue.
Fix: Call `page.unroute('**/api/user')` at the start of any test that needs to override a `beforeEach`-registered route before registering the new handler. Alternatively, structure `beforeEach` routes to accept an override by checking a test-level variable inside a single shared handler: define `let mockResponse = realData` and have the handler call `route.fulfill({ body: JSON.stringify(mockResponse) })`, letting each test reassign `mockResponse` to customize the response without re-registering the route.

---

**G182** — `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` passes for elements with `opacity: 0` because Playwright's visibility definition excludes CSS opacity from its hidden check
Why this matters: Playwright considers an element "visible" if it has a non-zero bounding box and none of its ancestors (or itself) have `display: none` or `visibility: hidden` applied — but `opacity: 0` does not make an element invisible by Playwright's definition because the element still occupies space in the layout and can be interacted with programmatically. An element fading out via a CSS `opacity` transition is considered visible by Playwright until it is explicitly hidden with `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`. A test asserting that a tooltip "disappears" after mouse-out via `toBeHidden()` will fail while the tooltip is mid-fade at `opacity: 0.1`, but will also pass when the tooltip is fully faded to `opacity: 0` because the element remains in the DOM and is not hidden by Playwright's definition.
Fix: For elements that use `opacity` transitions to show/hide, assert with `toHaveCSS('opacity', '0')` or `toHaveCSS('opacity', '1')` rather than `toBeVisible()`/`toBeHidden()`. If the element is removed from the DOM at animation end, `toBeHidden()` will correctly pass after removal; if it remains in DOM at `opacity: 0`, use `toHaveCSS('opacity', '0')` to assert the hidden state. For maximum reliability, add a `data-visible` attribute that the application sets synchronously when the animation completes and assert `toHaveAttribute('data-visible', 'false')`.

---

**G183** — `locator.selectOption()` throws on custom `role="listbox"` select replacements because it only works with native `<select>` elements
Why this matters: `page.locator('select').selectOption('value')` works reliably for native `<select>` elements, dispatching the native `change` event that framework bindings (React's `onChange`, Vue's `v-model`) listen to. Many UI libraries (Material UI, Ant Design, Headless UI) replace native `<select>` with a custom ARIA listbox pattern: a trigger button opens a `role="listbox"` popup, and items are `role="option"` elements. Calling `selectOption()` on the visual trigger button throws "Element is not a `<select>` element". Teams often attempt `.evaluate()` workarounds that set `.value` directly on the hidden native select without dispatching events, causing the framework to not detect the change and leaving form state stale with no visible error.
Fix: Interact with custom select dropdowns exactly as a user would: `await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Country' }).click()` to open the dropdown, then `await page.getByRole('option', { name: 'Germany' }).click()` to select the option. This dispatches the click events that the library's own event handlers listen to, properly updating framework state. If the custom select wraps a hidden native `<select>`, triggering the ARIA interaction will keep the hidden element in sync automatically via the library's internal logic.

---

**G184** — `test.setTimeout()` inside `test.beforeAll()` sets the timeout for the hook only, not for tests within the describe block
Why this matters: `test.setTimeout(60_000)` inside `test.beforeAll()` extends the timeout for the `beforeAll` hook's own execution, which is useful when the hook performs a slow setup (e.g., seeding a database). Developers expect it to also extend the default timeout for all tests in the block — a natural inference from its placement inside the describe scope — but it does not. Tests within the block still run with the global default timeout (30 seconds). When those tests perform slow operations that succeed during local development but fail under the 30-second test timeout in CI, the error message `Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded` appears inside test bodies rather than in the hook, misleading developers into thinking the tests themselves are slow rather than that the timeout configuration is misapplied.
Fix: To set a custom timeout for all tests within a describe block, call `test.describe.configure({ timeout: 60_000 })` at the top of the `describe` block — this sets the per-test timeout for every test inside that block. To extend only the `beforeAll` hook's timeout, use `test.setTimeout()` inside the hook. To extend both, call `test.describe.configure({ timeout: 60_000 })` for tests and `test.setTimeout()` inside `beforeAll()` for the hook. Document both explicitly to prevent future maintainers from removing one thinking it is redundant.

## Cycle 64 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 546** — Custom test fixture with automatic teardown for authenticated browser context
```typescript
import { test as base, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type AuthFixtures = { authenticatedContext: BrowserContext };

export const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  authenticatedContext: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
    });
    // Yield the context to the test body
    await use(context);
    // Automatic teardown — always runs even if the test throws
    await context.close();
  },
});

test('dashboard shows user name', async ({ authenticatedContext }) => {
  const page = await authenticatedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Welcome/ })).toBeVisible();
  await page.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping `browser.newContext()` in a fixture guarantees teardown via the `use()` boundary even when tests throw mid-execution, but every test using this fixture pays the cost of creating a new context (including loading cookies from disk) rather than sharing a single worker-scoped authenticated context — for suites with hundreds of tests, prefer a `scope: 'worker'` fixture with a single `storageState` load to avoid per-test context creation overhead.

---

**Pattern 547** — Worker-scoped fixture for one-time global setup (database seeding)
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { seededDb: void };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  seededDb: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Runs once per worker process — not once per test
      await seedTestDatabase({ schemaVersion: 'v3' });
      await use();
      // Teardown runs once when the worker shuts down
      await cleanTestDatabase();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test.describe('product catalog', () => {
  test('shows 50 products', async ({ page, seededDb }) => {
    await page.goto('/products');
    await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(50);
  });

  test('product detail loads', async ({ page, seededDb }) => {
    await page.goto('/products/1');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `scope: 'worker'` reduces database seed/teardown calls from N (one per test) to one per Playwright worker process, dramatically lowering total setup cost for large suites — but any test in a worker that mutates seeded data (e.g., deletes a product) contaminates all subsequent tests in that same worker; either enforce read-only access in seeded data tests or reset to a clean snapshot between tests using `beforeEach`.

---

**Pattern 548** — `locator.filter({ has })` to target a row in a dynamic data table
```typescript
test('edit action targets the correct table row', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/admin/users');

  // Wait for the table to be populated
  await page.waitForSelector('table tbody tr');

  // Locate the specific row by its content, then click its action button
  const targetRow = page
    .getByRole('row')
    .filter({ has: page.getByText('alice@example.com') });

  await expect(targetRow).toHaveCount(1);
  await targetRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' }).click();

  // Confirm the edit modal opened for the right user
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('dialog').getByLabel('Email')
  ).toHaveValue('alice@example.com');
});
```
Tradeoff: `filter({ has })` resolves to only rows that contain the specified sub-locator, making the row selection robust against row ordering changes and new rows being inserted — but performing nested locator evaluation on every matched row adds a DOM query per row, so filtering a table with thousands of rows is slower than a targeted CSS attribute selector like `[data-email="alice@example.com"]`; reserve `filter({ has })` for tables without reliable data attributes.

---

**Pattern 549** — `locator.filter({ hasNotText })` to assert a list no longer contains a deleted item
```typescript
test('deleted item disappears from list', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/tasks');

  const taskList = page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Task list' });
  const taskToDelete = taskList
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasText: 'Buy groceries' });

  await expect(taskToDelete).toHaveCount(1);

  // Click the delete button inside that specific item
  await taskToDelete.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).click();

  // After deletion, no listitem with that text should remain
  await expect(
    taskList.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Buy groceries' })
  ).toHaveCount(0);

  // Sibling items are unaffected — list is not empty
  await expect(taskList.getByRole('listitem')).not.toHaveCount(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `filter({ hasText })` then asserting `toHaveCount(0)` tests deletion without relying on index positions or brittle CSS selectors, making the assertion survive list reordering — but `toHaveCount(0)` on a filtered locator retries until timeout before passing, so if the deleted item re-appears due to an optimistic-update rollback, the test will hang for the full timeout rather than failing fast; set a shorter timeout on the assertion when covering rollback scenarios.

---

**Pattern 550** — `route.fulfill()` with a dynamically constructed JSON response body
```typescript
test('dashboard displays fallback when API returns empty data', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/dashboard/metrics', async (route) => {
    // Inspect the real request before deciding what to return
    const request = route.request();
    const headers = request.headers();
    const isAuthenticated = !!headers['authorization'];

    await route.fulfill({
      status: isAuthenticated ? 200 : 401,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify(
        isAuthenticated
          ? { metrics: [], message: 'No data available yet' }
          : { error: 'Unauthorized' }
      ),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Revenue card should show a placeholder, not throw a JS error
  await expect(page.getByText('No data available yet')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('table')).not.toBeAttached();
});
```
Tradeoff: Inspecting the intercepted request's headers inside `route.fulfill()` allows a single route handler to branch on auth state, locale, or feature-flag headers without registering multiple overlapping route patterns — but constructing the response body dynamically in the handler couples test logic to API contract details (field names, status codes), so if the real API changes its response schema the mock silently diverges; validate mock shapes against a shared TypeScript response type or OpenAPI schema to catch drift early.

---

**Pattern 551** — `route.continue()` to inject a custom request header for server-side feature flag activation
```typescript
test('experimental checkout flow is shown when feature flag header is set', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.route('**/*', async (route) => {
    const headers = {
      ...route.request().headers(),
      'x-feature-flag': 'new-checkout=true',
    };
    await route.continue({ headers });
  });

  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();

  // New checkout flow renders a multi-step stepper, old flow does not
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Checkout steps' })
  ).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('step-indicator')).toHaveText('Step 1 of 3');
});
```
Tradeoff: Injecting feature-flag headers via `route.continue({ headers })` on a `**/*` glob pattern is the only reliable way to set custom request headers for all navigation requests (including the initial page load), since `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` sets headers on subsequent requests only after the page object is created — but intercepting every request with a `**/*` handler measurably increases test execution time due to handler invocation overhead on every asset request; narrow the pattern to `**/api/**` or the specific pages that read the flag header to limit overhead.

---

**Pattern 552** — `page.waitForResponse()` with a predicate to assert API payload after form submission
```typescript
test('submitting the contact form sends the correct payload', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');

  await page.getByLabel('Name').fill('Jane Doe');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('jane@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Message').fill('Hello, I need help.');

  // Race the click against the network response before the navigation
  const [response] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForResponse(
      (res) =>
        res.url().includes('/api/contact') && res.request().method() === 'POST'
    ),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click(),
  ]);

  expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ name: 'Jane Doe', email: 'jane@example.com' });
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForResponse()` with a predicate resolves as soon as the response headers arrive, allowing payload inspection before the page navigates away — but `await response.json()` reads the body stream after `waitForResponse()` resolves, and if the server sends a large streaming response the body may not be fully buffered yet, causing a race; use `await response.body()` followed by `JSON.parse()` on the buffer for responses with a `Content-Length` header to ensure the full body is read.

**Pattern 553** — `browserContext.addInitScript()` to inject test helpers into every page before any script runs
```typescript
test('date-dependent logic uses a fixed clock', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // Inject a fake Date constructor into every page opened in this context
  await context.addInitScript(() => {
    const FIXED_DATE = new Date('2024-01-15T12:00:00Z');
    const OriginalDate = Date;
    // Replace global Date for test isolation
    (globalThis as any).Date = class extends OriginalDate {
      constructor(...args: any[]) {
        if (args.length === 0) {
          super(FIXED_DATE.getTime());
        } else {
          super(...(args as []));
        }
      }
      static now() {
        return FIXED_DATE.getTime();
      }
    };
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // Application renders "Last updated: Jan 15, 2024" using new Date()
  await expect(page.getByText('Last updated: Jan 15, 2024')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.addInitScript()` runs before any page script (including framework bootstrap), making it the only reliable way to override browser globals like `Date`, `Math.random`, or `window.fetch` before the application code reads them — but the injected script runs in the browser context and cannot access Node.js variables or Playwright fixtures; any dynamic values (like the desired fixed date) must be hardcoded or serialized into the script string at test definition time using template literals.

---

**Pattern 554** — `expect.soft()` to collect multiple assertion failures without stopping the test
```typescript
test('product detail page shows all required fields', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/42');

  // Collect all assertion failures rather than stopping at the first
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-price')).toContainText('$');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-sku')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('img', { name: /product/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
  ).toBeEnabled();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('stock-status')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-description')).not.toBeEmpty();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('breadcrumb')).toBeVisible();

  // Test fails here listing all collected soft-assertion errors at once
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft()` continues test execution after a failing assertion and reports all failures at the end, which is ideal for content-completeness checks (e.g., verifying all fields on a product page) because a single run reveals all missing elements rather than requiring repeated reruns — but soft assertions do not halt subsequent steps that depend on previous ones; if the heading is missing, the test continues to click "Add to cart" which may throw an unrelated error that obscures the real failure, so use `expect.soft()` only for independent assertions with no execution dependencies.

---

**Pattern 555** — `locator.first()` and `locator.last()` for dynamic feed position assertions
```typescript
test('latest activity entry appears at the top of the feed', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/activity');

  const initialCount = await page.getByRole('listitem').count();

  // Trigger a new activity event
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Post update' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Update text').fill('Shipped v2.0!');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();

  // Wait for list to grow by exactly one item
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(initialCount + 1);

  // Newest entry is inserted at the top (index 0)
  const newestEntry = page.getByRole('listitem').first();
  await expect(newestEntry).toContainText('Shipped v2.0!');

  // Oldest entry moved to last position — verify it is not the new item
  const oldestEntry = page.getByRole('listitem').last();
  await expect(oldestEntry).not.toContainText('Shipped v2.0!');
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.first()` and `locator.last()` are robust to list size changes because they always reference the boundary elements rather than a fixed index — but if the feed uses virtual scrolling and only renders visible items, `locator.first()` targets the first rendered item (which may not be the absolute top when scrolled down); call `page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, 0))` before asserting position to ensure the full list top is rendered.

**Pattern 556** — `page.on('requestfailed')` to surface silent network errors in test output
```typescript
test('no network requests fail silently during checkout flow', async ({ page }) => {
  const failedRequests: string[] = [];

  page.on('requestfailed', (request) => {
    // Ignore browser-initiated prefetch failures for third-party analytics
    if (!request.url().includes('analytics.example.com')) {
      failedRequests.push(
        `${request.method()} ${request.url()} — ${request.failure()?.errorText}`
      );
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Payment confirmed')).toBeVisible();
  expect(failedRequests).toEqual([]);
});
```
Tradeoff: Attaching a `requestfailed` listener captures network errors (DNS failures, TCP resets, aborted requests) that do not cause visible UI changes and would otherwise be invisible to the test — but the listener fires for all resource types including fonts, images, and prefetch hints that are non-critical; maintaining an allowlist of acceptable failure URLs requires ongoing maintenance as the application loads new third-party scripts, so run this pattern in a dedicated "network health" suite rather than in every functional test.

---

**Pattern 557** — `route.fetch()` to proxy and surgically modify a real API response
```typescript
test('dashboard degrades gracefully when metrics API omits the revenue field', async ({
  context,
  page,
}) => {
  await context.route('**/api/metrics', async (route) => {
    // Fetch the real response from the origin server
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const json = await response.json();

    // Surgically remove one field to simulate a partial API response
    const { revenue: _removed, ...rest } = json;

    await route.fulfill({
      response,           // Inherit status and headers from the real response
      body: JSON.stringify(rest),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Revenue card should show a placeholder, not throw a JS error
  await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-card')).toContainText('—');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeAttached();
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.fetch()` proxies the real request to the origin and returns the live response, allowing tests to modify only the fields under test while leaving all other fields realistic — but this makes the test network-dependent; if the backend is unavailable (CI offline mode, preview environments without a running API), `route.fetch()` throws and the test fails for infrastructure reasons rather than code quality; gate these tests with a `test.skip` condition that checks for API reachability, or use fully static `route.fulfill()` mocks in CI.

**Pattern 558** — `page.getByRole('combobox')` with keyboard navigation for accessible dropdown interaction
```typescript
test('country dropdown accepts keyboard selection', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  const countryDropdown = page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Country' });
  await countryDropdown.click();

  // Type to filter options
  await countryDropdown.fill('Ger');

  // Wait for the filtered listbox to appear
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('listbox').getByRole('option', { name: 'Germany' })
  ).toBeVisible();

  // Select with keyboard to validate keyboard accessibility compliance
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');

  await expect(countryDropdown).toHaveValue('Germany');

  // Submit and verify the form payload contains the correct value
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('selected-country')).toHaveText('Germany');
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `getByRole('combobox')` combined with keyboard events (`ArrowDown`, `Enter`) tests both the visual interaction and keyboard accessibility compliance as required by WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.1 — but ARIA combobox keyboard behavior differs between pattern implementations (some require `ArrowDown` to open the popup before it is populated, others open on focus); inspect the actual ARIA pattern your design system implements and adjust the key sequence accordingly, otherwise `ArrowDown` may select the first option of an empty list before filtering completes.

**Pattern 559** — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` for stateful multi-step flows that share a page object
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Declare serial mode — tests in this block run sequentially and share a context
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

let page: import('@playwright/test').Page;

test.describe('onboarding wizard', () => {
  test.beforeAll(async ({ browser }) => {
    page = await browser.newPage();
  });

  test.afterAll(async () => {
    await page.close();
  });

  test('step 1: profile information', async () => {
    await page.goto('/onboarding');
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Alex Kim');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Step 2 of 4')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('step 2: company details', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Company').fill('Acme Corp');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Step 3 of 4')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('step 3: preferences', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Email notifications' }).check();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Step 4 of 4')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('step 4: confirmation', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Finish setup' }).click();
    await expect(
      page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Welcome, Alex Kim!' })
    ).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mode: 'serial'` with a shared `page` object across steps allows each test to continue from where the previous left off, making multi-step wizard flows testable without re-navigating from scratch in every test — but if step 1 fails, Playwright skips all remaining tests in the block (they show as "skipped" not "failed"), which hides the real failure count in CI dashboards; always check the first failed test name rather than the skipped count to diagnose wizard failures.

**Pattern 560** — `page.addLocatorHandler()` to dismiss transient overlays that block element interaction
```typescript
test('user can complete purchase despite cookie consent overlay', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register a handler that automatically dismisses the cookie banner
  // whenever it appears and blocks a locator from being interacted with
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Cookie consent' }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Accept all' }).click();
      await expect(dialog).not.toBeAttached();
    }
  );

  await page.goto('/store/product/123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();

  // The handler fires automatically if the dialog reappears during navigation
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Shipping address' })
  ).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.addLocatorHandler()` detects when a registered overlay locator becomes visible and blocks an actionability check, then runs the handler automatically to dismiss it before retrying the blocked action — this is strictly more reliable than injecting `display: none` CSS to hide cookie banners because it exercises the real dismissal code path and verifies the banner is actually removed — but the handler adds latency to every actionability check while the overlay is present; if the overlay is shown on every page navigation in a long test, the cumulative delay may push the test past its timeout.

### Community Gotchas

**G185** — `test.extend()` fixture teardown is skipped when `use()` is never called inside the fixture body
Why this matters: In a Playwright fixture defined with `test.extend()`, the teardown code after `await use(value)` only runs if `use()` is reached during setup. If the fixture throws an error before reaching `use()` — for example, when a database connection fails — the teardown block is skipped entirely and resources allocated before the throw (open file handles, partially created test users) are never cleaned up. Developers often discover this as flaky test infrastructure failures that accumulate across CI runs: leaked database rows, unclosed connections hitting pool limits, or temporary directories that fill disk.
Fix: Wrap all setup code that allocates resources in a `try/finally` block inside the fixture, calling cleanup in the `finally` clause so it runs regardless of whether `use()` was reached: `try { const conn = await openDb(); await use(conn); } finally { await conn?.close(); }`. Alternatively, restructure the fixture so `use()` is always called (even with a null/error value) and handle the invalid state inside the test body.

---

**G186** — `page.getByRole('button', { name })` matches hidden buttons when `exact: false` is the default
Why this matters: `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` with `exact: false` (the default) matches any button whose accessible name contains the substring "Submit", including visually hidden "Submit form" buttons rendered for screen readers that are positioned off-screen with `position: absolute; left: -9999px`. When a visible "Submit" button and a hidden "Submit form" button both exist in the DOM, the locator matches two elements and Playwright throws a strict-mode violation — "strict mode violation: getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }) resolved to 2 elements". The error message lists both matches, but the second element's coordinates show `(−9999, 0)`, which is easy to overlook.
Fix: Use `{ exact: true }` when the button name is a complete string — `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit', exact: true })` — to prevent substring matching against hidden assistive-technology buttons. If both visible and hidden buttons share the same exact accessible name, add `.filter({ visible: true })` to restrict to rendered elements: `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).filter({ visible: true })`.

---

**G187** — `context.addInitScript()` does not run on pages opened via `window.open()` when a new context is created
Why this matters: `context.addInitScript(script)` injects the script into every new `Page` created within that `BrowserContext`. However, when application code calls `window.open('https://external-app.example.com', '_blank')` or sets `target="_blank"` on an anchor, the opened page may be captured by Playwright as a `Page` event on the existing context — and `addInitScript` will run there — but if the navigation crosses an origin boundary to a page that opens its own popup via `window.open()` in a new context (e.g., OAuth flows), the injected script is not present. Developers are surprised when their `Date` mock or `window.fetch` stub disappears mid-OAuth and the test fails with "Cannot read properties of undefined" on mocked globals.
Fix: For popup windows that Playwright captures as new pages within the same context, `addInitScript` will run automatically. For cross-origin popups that create new browser contexts, attach an event listener on `context` to capture new pages: `context.on('page', async (newPage) => { await newPage.addInitScript(script); })`. If the OAuth flow can be avoided by seeding auth tokens directly into `storageState`, do that instead to eliminate the popup entirely.

---

**G188** — `expect(locator).toHaveText()` fails on trimmed whitespace when the element contains non-breaking spaces
Why this matters: `expect(locator).toHaveText('Total: $42.00')` extracts the element's `textContent`, which concatenates all descendant text nodes. When the element is `<div>Total: <span class="price">$42.00</span></div>` and the `<span>` has `padding-left: 4px` (CSS space), `textContent` returns `"Total: $42.00"` with no extra whitespace and the assertion passes. But when the spacing is implemented as a Unicode non-breaking space (`&nbsp;`) inside the HTML — `Total:&nbsp;<span>$42.00</span>` — `textContent` returns `"Total: $42.00"`, which does not match the regular space in `'Total: $42.00'`. The assertion fails with a confusing diff that looks identical in most terminal fonts because ` ` renders like a space.
Fix: Use a regex with `\s+` to match flexible whitespace: `expect(locator).toHaveText(/Total:\s+\$42\.00/)`. Alternatively, normalize the text content using `page.evaluate()` with `.innerText.replace(/ /g, ' ').trim()` for assertions that must match exact strings. If you control the HTML, replace `&nbsp;` entities with CSS `gap`, `margin`, or `padding` so spacing is purely presentational and not embedded in `textContent`.

---

**G189** — Registering `page.on('dialog')` after `page.goto()` misses `beforeunload` dialogs triggered by navigation
Why this matters: When a page has a `beforeunload` event listener that triggers a browser confirmation dialog (the "Are you sure you want to leave?" prompt), Playwright must have the `dialog` event handler registered on the page object before the navigation that triggers the dialog. If a test calls `page.goto('/form')`, fills a form, then registers `page.on('dialog', handler)`, and then calls `page.goto('/other')` to trigger the `beforeunload`, the dialog fires during the second navigation before the handler is active and Playwright auto-dismisses it — or the dialog blocks the navigation indefinitely in headed mode — causing the test to hang or produce unexpected navigation behavior with no clear error message.
Fix: Register all `page.on('dialog', handler)` listeners before any navigation that could trigger the dialog: call `page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => await dialog.accept())` immediately after creating the page object, before the first `goto()`. For `beforeunload` dialogs specifically, use `page.once('dialog', handler)` registered just before the navigation that triggers the unload, combined with `page.evaluate(() => window.dispatchEvent(new Event('beforeunload')))` to test the behavior in isolation without a full navigation.

## Cycle 67 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 576** — `page.clock.install()` + `page.clock.runFor()` for deterministic time-dependent UI
```typescript
test('session expiry banner appears after 30-minute inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install fake clock before navigation so all Date/setTimeout calls use it
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Advance clock by 29 minutes — banner should NOT be visible yet
  await page.clock.runFor(29 * 60 * 1000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance one more minute — banner should now appear
  await page.clock.runFor(60 * 1000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Verify the countdown in the banner reflects the correct remaining seconds
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-countdown')).toHaveText('60 seconds');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` replaces the browser's `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `requestAnimationFrame` with a synthetic clock that advances only when `runFor()` or `tick()` is called — this eliminates all timing flakiness for inactivity timers and countdown components — but the synthetic clock breaks real-time `fetch` retry logic that uses `setTimeout` internally; if the component under test fires a background refresh via `setTimeout(() => fetch('/api/heartbeat'), 60000)`, the clock's jump will immediately trigger that fetch and may interfere with route handlers, so pair `page.clock.install()` with `route.abort()` on heartbeat endpoints or call `page.clock.pauseAt()` to freeze time after each advance.

---

**Pattern 577** — `test.step()` with screenshot capture for structured sub-step reporting
```typescript
test('multi-step checkout produces order confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to product and add to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/store/widget-pro');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-badge')).toHaveText('1');
    await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshots/step1-cart.png' });
  });

  await test.step('proceed through checkout address form', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View Cart' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Street address').fill('123 Main St');
    await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Springfield');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to Payment' }).click();
    await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshots/step2-address.png' });
  });

  await test.step('submit payment and verify confirmation', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
    await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshots/step3-confirmation.png' });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step()` groups assertions and actions into named sub-steps that appear as collapsible sections in Playwright HTML reporter and VS Code extension, making failure diagnosis dramatically faster in long checkout or wizard flows — but each `test.step()` creates a nested scope that captures its own start/end timestamps and status; if a step throws, subsequent steps are skipped and their screenshots are never taken, so a failure in step 2 loses the step-3 screenshot evidence; work around this by using `test.step('...', { box: true })` (boxed steps, Playwright 1.39+) which surfaces inner errors at the step boundary without propagating early exit to siblings.

**Pattern 578** — `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with regex for dynamic segment assertions
```typescript
test('saving a draft redirects to the draft-specific edit URL', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/articles/new');

  await page.getByLabel('Title').fill('My Draft Article');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save Draft' }).click();

  // The URL will be /articles/<uuid>/edit — assert the shape, not the exact UUID
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/articles\/[0-9a-f-]{36}\/edit$/);

  // Extract the generated ID for subsequent assertions
  const url = page.url();
  const articleId = url.match(/\/articles\/([0-9a-f-]{36})\/edit$/)?.[1];
  expect(articleId).toBeTruthy();

  // Reload to confirm the draft persists under the same ID
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(new RegExp(`/articles/${articleId}/edit$`));
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Title')).toHaveValue('My Draft Article');
});
```
Tradeoff: Using a regex with `toHaveURL()` asserts the URL shape (path structure and segment count) without coupling the test to a specific server-generated ID, which makes the test stable across test runs — but loose regexes like `/edit/` match any URL containing the substring "edit", including `/users/edit` if a redirect goes wrong; always anchor the regex to the full path structure (`/\/articles\/[0-9a-f-]{36}\/edit$/`) so an incorrect redirect to a similar-looking path still fails the assertion.

**Pattern 579** — `locator.dragTo()` for drag-and-drop reordering with position verification
```typescript
test('kanban card drag-and-drop moves item between columns', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/board');

  const todoColumn = page.getByTestId('column-todo');
  const inProgressColumn = page.getByTestId('column-in-progress');

  // Confirm initial state
  await expect(todoColumn.getByTestId('card-fix-login-bug')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(inProgressColumn.getByTestId('card-fix-login-bug')).not.toBeAttached();

  // Drag the card to the In Progress column
  await page.getByTestId('card-fix-login-bug').dragTo(inProgressColumn, {
    targetPosition: { x: 50, y: 80 }, // Drop in the upper portion of the column
  });

  // Verify the card moved to the new column
  await expect(inProgressColumn.getByTestId('card-fix-login-bug')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(todoColumn.getByTestId('card-fix-login-bug')).not.toBeAttached();

  // Verify column counts updated
  await expect(todoColumn.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(2);
  await expect(inProgressColumn.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(3);
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.dragTo()` performs a full pointer-events sequence (mousedown → mousemove → mouseup) that exercises the real drag-and-drop logic including event handlers and drop-zone detection — but HTML5 `drag`/`drop` events and pointer-events-based drag libraries (react-beautiful-dnd, dnd-kit) fire different event sequences; `dragTo()` uses pointer events and works with pointer-events libraries but may not fire `dragstart`/`dragover`/`drop` HTML5 events that older libraries rely on — verify with `page.evaluate(() => window.__lastDragEvent)` tracing if drops are silently ignored.

---

**Pattern 580** — `page.accessibility.snapshot()` for asserting ARIA tree structure
```typescript
test('modal dialog has correct accessible name and focus management', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings');

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete Account' }).click();

  // Wait for the modal to be fully rendered
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();

  const snapshot = await page.accessibility.snapshot({ root: page.getByRole('dialog') });

  // Assert the dialog role and accessible name
  expect(snapshot?.role).toBe('dialog');
  expect(snapshot?.name).toMatch(/delete account/i);

  // Focus should be inside the dialog — first interactive element should be focused
  const focusedNode = snapshot?.children?.find((n) => n.focused);
  expect(focusedNode).toBeTruthy();
  expect(focusedNode?.role).toBe('button');

  // Confirm the cancel button is present and reachable in the tree
  const cancelButton = snapshot?.children?.find(
    (n) => n.role === 'button' && /cancel/i.test(n.name ?? '')
  );
  expect(cancelButton).toBeTruthy();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.accessibility.snapshot()` returns the browser's computed accessibility tree as a JSON object, enabling assertions about ARIA roles, names, states, and focus order that are invisible to DOM locators — but the snapshot reflects the accessibility tree after browser-side ARIA computation, not the raw HTML attributes; elements with `role="none"` are flattened out of the tree, and browser vendors compute accessible names slightly differently (especially for SVG and custom elements), so a snapshot assertion that passes in Chromium may differ in Firefox or WebKit; scope snapshot assertions to the specific subtree under test and avoid asserting exact child counts across browsers.

---

**Pattern 581** — `test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` scoped to a describe block for dark-mode visual regression
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('dashboard — dark mode', () => {
  test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' });

  test('revenue chart renders legibly in dark mode', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');

    // Wait for chart to finish rendering (canvas-based or SVG)
    await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-chart')).toBeVisible();
    await page.waitForFunction(
      () => document.querySelector('[data-testid="revenue-chart"]')?.getAttribute('data-loaded') === 'true'
    );

    // Visual snapshot scoped to the chart component only
    await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-chart')).toHaveScreenshot('revenue-chart-dark.png', {
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.02,
    });
  });

  test('sidebar text contrast meets WCAG AA in dark mode', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('sidebar')).toHaveScreenshot('sidebar-dark.png', {
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
    });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` inside a `test.describe` block scopes the dark-mode setting only to tests in that block without affecting the default light-mode tests in the same file — but `colorScheme` only sets the `prefers-color-scheme` media query; if the application's dark mode is controlled by a CSS class on `<html>` (e.g., `class="dark"`) or a localStorage flag rather than the media query, `test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` has no effect, and you must instead inject the class or flag via `page.addInitScript()` before navigation.

---

**Pattern 582** — `context.grantPermissions(['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write'])` for clipboard integration tests
```typescript
test('copy-to-clipboard button copies the API key to the clipboard', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Create context with clipboard permissions pre-granted
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    permissions: ['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write'],
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/settings/api-keys');

  const apiKeyDisplay = page.getByTestId('api-key-value');
  const expectedKey = await apiKeyDisplay.textContent();
  expect(expectedKey).toMatch(/^sk-[a-z0-9]{32}$/);

  // Click the copy button
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Copy API Key' }).click();

  // Confirm the success indicator appears
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Copied!');

  // Read the clipboard to verify the exact value was written
  const clipboardText = await page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.readText());
  expect(clipboardText).toBe(expectedKey?.trim());

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Granting `clipboard-read` and `clipboard-write` at context creation via `browser.newContext({ permissions: [...] })` is the only reliable cross-browser way to test `navigator.clipboard` API calls without triggering the native permission prompt — but clipboard permissions are only supported in Chromium-based browsers in Playwright; Firefox and WebKit do not support `clipboard-read` in `context.grantPermissions()` and will throw a `permissions not supported` error, so wrap clipboard tests with `test.skip(browserName !== 'chromium', 'Clipboard API only testable in Chromium')` to prevent false failures in cross-browser matrix runs.

---

**Pattern 583** — `page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` to stabilize animation-sensitive assertions
```typescript
test('file upload progress bar completes and shows success state', async ({ page }) => {
  // Disable CSS animations and transitions to prevent race conditions
  // between animation frames and assertion timing
  await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' });

  await page.goto('/upload');

  // Intercept the upload endpoint and simulate a slow response
  await page.route('**/api/upload', async (route) => {
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ fileId: 'f-abc123', url: '/files/f-abc123' }),
    });
  });

  const fileChooserPromise = page.waitForEvent('filechooser');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Choose File' }).click();
  const fileChooser = await fileChooserPromise;
  await fileChooser.setFiles({ name: 'report.pdf', mimeType: 'application/pdf', buffer: Buffer.from('PDF content') });

  // With reducedMotion: 'reduce', the success state transition is instant — no animation wait needed
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Upload complete');
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'report.pdf' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` sets `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` in the browser, which causes well-implemented CSS transitions and animations to complete instantly or be skipped — this eliminates a whole class of timing-sensitive failures where an assertion fires while an animation is mid-frame — but this only works if the application actually respects `prefers-reduced-motion` in its CSS (i.e., uses `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rules); if animations are driven by JavaScript timers or a third-party library that ignores the media query, `emulateMedia` has no effect and you must fall back to `page.clock.install()` to control the animation timer directly.

---

**Pattern 584** — `locator.selectOption()` with `{ value }` vs `{ label }` for robust `<select>` interactions
```typescript
test('billing cycle select updates price summary correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/pricing/configure');

  const billingSelect = page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Billing cycle' });

  // Use { value } (the HTML option value attribute) when backend receives the value field
  await billingSelect.selectOption({ value: 'annual' });
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-per-seat')).toHaveText('$8/month');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('billing-note')).toContainText('billed annually');

  // Switch to monthly using { label } (the visible text) to test the label path
  await billingSelect.selectOption({ label: 'Monthly' });
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-per-seat')).toHaveText('$12/month');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('billing-note')).toContainText('billed monthly');

  // Verify the select itself shows the correct displayed label
  await expect(billingSelect).toHaveValue('monthly');

  // Test the summary card recalculates for 5 seats
  await page.getByLabel('Number of seats').fill('5');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('total-price')).toHaveText('$60/month');
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.selectOption({ value: 'annual' })` targets the `<option value="annual">` attribute and is immune to display-text changes — if marketing renames "Annual" to "Yearly", the value-based selector still works — but using `{ label }` verifies that the text the user actually reads matches expectations, which value-based selection misses; use `{ value }` when asserting backend-correct data submission, and `{ label }` when asserting UI copy correctness, rather than picking one approach for all select interactions.

---

**Pattern 585** — `route.abort()` for simulating hard network failures and verifying error UI
```typescript
test('dashboard shows error state when analytics API is unreachable', async ({ page }) => {
  // Abort all requests to the analytics endpoint to simulate a network failure
  await page.route('**/api/analytics/**', (route) => route.abort('failed'));

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // The main content should still load (analytics is non-critical)
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();

  // Analytics widgets should show error states, not empty/loading states
  await expect(page.getByTestId('analytics-widget')).toHaveCount(3);
  for (const widget of await page.getByTestId('analytics-widget').all()) {
    await expect(widget.getByRole('alert')).toBeVisible();
    await expect(widget.getByText('Unable to load data')).toBeVisible();
  }

  // Retry button should be present and functional
  const retryButton = page.getByTestId('analytics-widget').first().getByRole('button', { name: 'Retry' });
  await expect(retryButton).toBeVisible();

  // Remove the abort handler to allow the retry to succeed
  await page.unroute('**/api/analytics/**');
  await retryButton.click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('analytics-widget').first().getByRole('alert')).not.toBeAttached();
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.abort('failed')` simulates a TCP connection failure (not an HTTP error response) and triggers `fetch` to reject with a `TypeError: Failed to fetch`, which tests the application's handling of true network unreachability rather than a 500 response — but `abort('failed')` is indistinguishable from `abort('connectionrefused')` or `abort('timedout')` at the JavaScript `fetch` catch-handler level; if the UI needs to show different messages for timeout vs connection-refused, use a `route.fulfill({ status: 504 })` stub for the timeout case instead, since `abort()` cannot simulate the timeout error type specifically.

---

**Pattern 586** — `page.screenshot({ mask })` for masking dynamic content in visual regression tests
```typescript
test('invoice page visual appearance is stable across runs', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/invoices/inv-2026-001');

  // Wait for the invoice to fully render
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-container')).toBeVisible();

  // Take a screenshot masking all dynamic fields so the snapshot is stable
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('invoice-page.png', {
    mask: [
      page.getByTestId('invoice-date'),        // Changes based on current date
      page.getByTestId('invoice-number'),      // Incrementing number
      page.getByTestId('generated-timestamp'), // Server render time
      page.getByTestId('due-date'),            // Relative to invoice date
    ],
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
    fullPage: true,
  });

  // Separately assert the dynamic fields have correct format (without visual snapshot)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-number')).toHaveText(/^INV-\d{4}-\d{3}$/);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText(/^\d{2}\/\d{2}\/\d{4}$/);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `mask` array in `toHaveScreenshot()` replaces the bounding boxes of specified locators with a solid magenta rectangle before pixel comparison, making the snapshot stable across runs without hard-coding dates or IDs into fixtures — but the masking approach hides layout shifts inside the masked region; if a dynamic element's content grows (e.g., the invoice number becomes wider and pushes adjacent text), the surrounding layout change will not be caught because only the locator's original bounding box is masked; complement masked snapshots with separate text-format assertions (`toHaveText(/regex/)`) so format regressions are still caught.

---

**Pattern 587** — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` with per-test isolated fixtures to maximise throughput
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Create a per-test user fixture so parallel tests never share credentials
const test = base.extend<{
  uniqueUser: { email: string; password: string; authToken: string };
}>({
  uniqueUser: async ({ request }, use) => {
    // Create a test user via API — unique per test worker
    const id = `${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}`;
    const email = `testuser-${id}@qa.example.com`;
    const password = 'Test1234!';

    const createRes = await request.post('/api/test/users', {
      data: { email, password },
    });
    expect(createRes.ok()).toBeTruthy();
    const { authToken } = await createRes.json();

    await use({ email, password, authToken });

    // Teardown: delete the user after the test completes
    await request.delete('/api/test/users', { data: { email } });
  },
});

// Parallel mode: each test in this block runs in its own worker simultaneously
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' });

test.describe('user profile settings', () => {
  test('user can update display name', async ({ page, uniqueUser }) => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(uniqueUser.email);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(uniqueUser.password);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Profile' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('QA Tester');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Profile updated');
  });

  test('user can change notification preferences', async ({ page, uniqueUser }) => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(uniqueUser.email);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(uniqueUser.password);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Notifications' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Email notifications').uncheck();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save preferences' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Preferences saved');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` combined with a `uniqueUser` fixture that provisions and tears down isolated test data per-test allows all tests in the block to run simultaneously without shared-state conflicts — but each test now pays the full cost of an API round-trip to create and delete a user; at scale (50+ parallel tests), this can spike the test-user-creation endpoint and hit rate limits or database connection pool exhaustion; implement a user pool (pre-provision N users before the suite, lease/return them via a worker-scoped fixture) when the provisioning overhead becomes a bottleneck.

---

**Pattern 588** — `locator.evaluate()` for asserting computed CSS properties invisible to DOM locators
```typescript
test('disabled submit button has correct cursor and opacity styling', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/payment');

  // Leave required fields empty — button should be disabled
  const submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' });
  await expect(submitButton).toBeDisabled();

  // Assert computed styles that are not testable via Playwright locator API
  const styles = await submitButton.evaluate((el) => {
    const computed = window.getComputedStyle(el);
    return {
      cursor: computed.cursor,
      opacity: computed.opacity,
      pointerEvents: computed.pointerEvents,
      backgroundColor: computed.backgroundColor,
    };
  });

  expect(styles.cursor).toBe('not-allowed');
  expect(parseFloat(styles.opacity)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(0.5);
  expect(styles.pointerEvents).toBe('none');

  // Fill required fields and verify styles update
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');

  const enabledStyles = await submitButton.evaluate((el) => {
    const computed = window.getComputedStyle(el);
    return { cursor: computed.cursor, opacity: computed.opacity };
  });

  expect(enabledStyles.cursor).toBe('pointer');
  expect(parseFloat(enabledStyles.opacity)).toBe(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.evaluate((el) => window.getComputedStyle(el).someProperty)` reads the browser-computed CSS value after cascade resolution and pseudo-class application, which is the only way to assert visual states like `cursor: not-allowed` or `opacity: 0.5` that have no Playwright assertion counterpart — but computed CSS values are returned as serialized strings in the browser's canonical format (e.g., `rgb(255, 0, 0)` not `red`, `0.5` not `50%`), so assertions must account for format normalization; use `parseFloat()` for numeric values and compare color strings as `rgb()` format, or write a helper that converts values to a common format before asserting.

---

**Pattern 589** — `page.unrouteAll()` to reset route handlers between phases of a single test
```typescript
test('payment form shows loading state then success, then handles retry on failure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');

  // Phase 1: Simulate slow payment processing to verify loading state
  await page.route('**/api/payment/charge', async (route) => {
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 500));
    await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: 'ord-001' }) });
  });

  const submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' });
  await submitButton.click();
  await expect(submitButton).toBeDisabled();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Processing payment…');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Phase 2: Reset ALL route handlers before testing the failure path
  await page.unrouteAll({ behavior: 'ignoreErrors' });

  await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4000000000000002'); // Declined card

  // Register failure handler for the second phase
  await page.route('**/api/payment/charge', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 402, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Card declined' }) })
  );

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toHaveText('Card declined. Please use a different card.');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.unrouteAll({ behavior: 'ignoreErrors' })` removes all registered route handlers atomically in a single call, which is safer than calling `page.unroute()` for each pattern individually when a test has registered multiple overlapping routes — but `unrouteAll` also removes any persistent handlers set up in `beforeEach` fixtures or by helper utilities called before the test body; if a shared fixture registers a route (e.g., an auth token refresh interceptor), calling `unrouteAll` mid-test will remove that fixture's handler and break subsequent requests that depend on it; prefer `page.unroute(specificPattern)` when only certain handlers need to be cleared.

---

**Pattern 590** — `page.waitForLoadState()` — choosing the correct state for different navigation types
```typescript
test('search results appear without waiting for unrelated third-party scripts', async ({ page }) => {
  // Block third-party analytics that would delay 'networkidle' for 30+ seconds
  await page.route('**googletagmanager.com/**', (route) => route.abort());
  await page.route('**hotjar.com/**', (route) => route.abort());

  await page.goto('/search', { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });

  // At 'domcontentloaded' the DOM is ready but resources may still be loading
  await page.getByLabel('Search').fill('playwright testing');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  // Wait for the API-driven results to populate rather than a load state
  await page.waitForResponse('**/api/search?q=playwright+testing');

  // Results should be in the DOM — no need for 'networkidle'
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Search results' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(10);

  // For a full page with fonts/images, 'load' is the right state
  await page.goto('/search/results/detail/1', { waitUntil: 'load' });
  await expect(page.getByTestId('result-thumbnail')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `waitUntil: 'networkidle'` waits until there are no more than 0 network requests for 500 ms, which is semantically correct for pages that signal readiness through inactivity — but modern SPAs with analytics, chat widgets, and background polling never reach `networkidle` and cause 30-second timeouts in CI; prefer `waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded'` combined with explicit `page.waitForResponse()` or locator visibility assertions that directly target the content you need, reserving `networkidle` only for server-rendered pages with no persistent background connections.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G195** — `locator.fill()` dispatches an `input` event but not `change`; React controlled inputs using `onChange` wired to `change` events miss the update
Why this matters: React's synthetic event system typically listens to the browser's `input` event for controlled `<input>` components, and Playwright's `locator.fill()` dispatches `input` — so most React forms work correctly. However, some third-party form libraries (older versions of Formik, React Final Form with custom adapters, or native `<select>` wrappers) register their change handler on the DOM `change` event rather than `input`. When `locator.fill()` writes to these inputs, the React state is never updated because the `change` event is never fired, and the field's value appears correct in the DOM (`locator.inputValue()` returns the typed text) but the component's state remains at the previous value. The symptom is a form that passes `toHaveValue()` assertions but submits the old pre-fill value to the server.
Fix: Use `locator.fill()` first, then programmatically dispatch the `change` event: `await locator.fill('new value'); await locator.dispatchEvent('change');`. For `<select>` elements specifically, use `locator.selectOption()` instead of `fill()` — `selectOption()` fires both `input` and `change` events in the correct order. For inputs controlled by libraries that rely on `change`, consider using `locator.type()` (which fires keydown/keypress/keyup/input per character) as an alternative that better mimics real user typing.

---

**G196** — `page.waitForSelector()` resolves to a detached element handle when the component remounts between the wait and the action
Why this matters: `page.waitForSelector('.submit-btn')` returns an `ElementHandle` pointing to the DOM node that existed when the selector first matched. In React and Vue apps that re-render in response to state changes (form validation, data loading), the component containing `.submit-btn` may unmount and remount between the moment `waitForSelector` resolves and the moment the returned handle is used for a click or assertion. The `ElementHandle` still points to the original (now-detached) DOM node, and Playwright throws "Element is not attached to the DOM". This happens most often in tests with a `waitForSelector` followed by `await handle.click()` separated by even a few milliseconds of async work (logging, fixture setup).
Fix: Replace `page.waitForSelector()` + `handle` usage with Playwright `Locator` API: `const btn = page.locator('.submit-btn')` creates a lazy locator that re-queries the DOM on every action, so if the component remounts, the locator finds the fresh element automatically. `page.waitForSelector()` returns a static `ElementHandle` — a snapshot of a DOM node — and should be avoided in favor of `await page.locator(selector).waitFor({ state: 'visible' })` which keeps the locator dynamic.

---

**G197** — `test.beforeEach` hooks in nested `describe` blocks run outer-to-inner but their fixtures are torn down inner-to-outer, causing fixture state to outlive the assertion scope
Why this matters: In a Playwright test file with nested `test.describe` blocks, each with their own `test.beforeEach`, the execution order is: outer `beforeEach` → inner `beforeEach` → test body → inner fixture teardown → outer fixture teardown. This is correct LIFO teardown order. However, developers are surprised when an outer `beforeEach` establishes state (e.g., logs in a user, seeds database rows) and an inner `beforeEach` modifies that state (e.g., deletes the user's profile), and then the outer fixture's teardown tries to clean up a resource that the inner hook already removed — throwing an error in teardown that marks the test as failed even though all assertions passed. This causes false-negative test results that are hard to diagnose because the teardown error message references a resource deletion that already happened.
Fix: Design `beforeEach` hooks to be idempotent in their teardown: use `DELETE ... WHERE EXISTS` SQL patterns, `request.delete()` calls with non-2xx response tolerance (`expect(res.status()).not.toBe(500)` rather than `expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy()`), or check-before-delete patterns. Alternatively, restructure nested fixtures so each level only owns the resources it creates and never depends on another level's resource being present at teardown time.

---

**G198** — `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` passes for elements with `opacity: 0` or `color: transparent` that are in the DOM and have non-zero layout dimensions
Why this matters: Playwright's `toBeVisible()` assertion checks that the element is attached to the DOM, is not hidden via `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, and has a non-zero bounding box. It does not check `opacity` or color values. An element rendered with `opacity: 0` (common for fade-in animations before they begin) passes `toBeVisible()` even though the user cannot see it. This creates false positives in tests that assert a "success toast is visible" or "error banner is visible" on components that fade in over 300 ms — the `opacity: 0` initial state passes the assertion, the test completes, and the toast fades in (or never does) after the test has already passed.
Fix: For components that may have opacity animations, wait for the animation to complete by asserting a CSS class change or using `page.waitForFunction()` to poll `getComputedStyle(el).opacity === '1'` before asserting visibility. Alternatively, assert the text content rather than just visibility: `expect(locator).toHaveText('Success!')` only passes when the element is both visible (non-zero box) and contains the expected text — a zero-opacity element still has text content, so also verify `await locator.evaluate(el => getComputedStyle(el).opacity)` equals `'1'` when opacity-based animations are involved.

---

**G199** — `page.reload()` inside a test does not re-run `context.addInitScript()` scripts when the page is controlled by a service worker that intercepts navigation
Why this matters: `context.addInitScript(script)` injects a script that runs before every page's JavaScript on navigation. For a standard navigation, this injection is reliable. However, when the application has a registered service worker that handles navigation requests (common in PWAs and offline-capable apps), `page.reload()` may cause the browser to serve the page from the service worker's cache rather than performing a real network navigation. In this case, Playwright's injection mechanism, which hooks into the browser's `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` CDP command, may not fire for service-worker-served navigations in some Playwright/Chromium version combinations, leaving globals mocked by `addInitScript` (Date overrides, feature flags, mock APIs) absent on the reloaded page.
Fix: For applications with service workers, prefer navigating with `page.goto(page.url(), { waitUntil: 'networkidle' })` instead of `page.reload()` — `goto()` always triggers Playwright's full navigation interception pipeline. Alternatively, unregister the service worker before reload: `await page.evaluate(() => navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistrations().then(regs => Promise.all(regs.map(r => r.unregister()))))` before `page.reload()`. In `playwright.config.ts`, set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the project config to prevent service worker registration entirely during tests, which is the safest option when PWA offline functionality is not itself under test.

### Patterns

**Pattern 561** — Worker-scoped fixture for shared database seed with per-test rollback
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface DbFixtures {
  db: { query: (sql: string) => Promise<unknown[]>; cleanup: () => Promise<void> };
}

export const test = base.extend<Record<string, never>, DbFixtures>({
  db: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const conn = await openDbConnection(process.env.TEST_DB_URL!);
      await conn.query('BEGIN');
      await seedTestData(conn);
      await use({ query: (sql) => conn.query(sql), cleanup: () => conn.query('ROLLBACK') });
      await conn.query('ROLLBACK');
      await conn.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('product search returns seeded items', async ({ page, db }) => {
  const rows = await db.query("SELECT id FROM products WHERE name = 'Test Widget'");
  await page.goto(`/products/${rows[0].id}`);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Test Widget' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures run once per worker and persist across multiple tests in that worker, which eliminates the per-test cost of opening a new database connection and seeding data — but when a test mutates the seeded rows without calling `db.cleanup()`, the mutation leaks into subsequent tests in the same worker, causing spurious failures that only appear when tests run in a specific order; pair worker-scoped fixtures with explicit rollback discipline or use savepoints per-test.

**Pattern 562** — `test.extend()` with automatic fixture for per-test trace annotation
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ annotateTrace: void }>({
  annotateTrace: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
      await page.evaluate((title) => {
        (window as Record<string, unknown>).__playwrightTestTitle = title;
      }, testInfo.title);
      await use();
      if (testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus) {
        await testInfo.attach('page-url-on-failure', {
          body: page.url(),
          contentType: 'text/plain',
        });
        const screenshot = await page.screenshot({ fullPage: true });
        await testInfo.attach('failure-screenshot', {
          body: screenshot,
          contentType: 'image/png',
        });
      }
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],
});

test('checkout flow completes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `{ auto: true }` fixtures inject into every test in the project without any per-test opt-in, which guarantees uniform failure evidence capture — but automatically running `page.screenshot({ fullPage: true })` on every failing test adds 200–800 ms of teardown time per failure and may surface sensitive user data in attachments; scope the screenshot to `testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus` and configure attachment retention policies in CI to avoid accumulating large artifacts.
