**Pattern 563** — `mergeTests()` to compose fixture sets from separate modules
```typescript
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as authTest } from './fixtures/auth';
import { test as apiTest } from './fixtures/api-client';
import { test as storageTest } from './fixtures/storage-state';

// Merge all three fixture namespaces into one test function
export const test = mergeTests(authTest, apiTest, storageTest);

// Now every test can destructure from all three fixture sets simultaneously
test('authenticated user can upload file via API and see it in UI', async ({
  page,          // from authTest (pre-authenticated page)
  apiClient,     // from apiTest (typed REST client)
  storageState,  // from storageTest (pre-seeded localStorage)
}) => {
  const { id } = await apiClient.post('/files', { name: 'report.pdf', size: 1024 });
  await page.goto('/files');
  await expect(page.getByText('report.pdf')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId(`file-${id}`)).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` composes multiple independent fixture namespaces into a single `test` function without requiring a deep inheritance chain, which keeps each fixture module independently testable and avoids the brittle re-export pyramid that accumulates when teams chain `base.extend()` calls — but fixture name collisions between merged modules silently favor the last-merged module's definition; always run `tsc --noEmit` on merged types because TypeScript will surface collisions as union-type errors before they cause runtime surprises.

**Pattern 564** — `locator.and()` to assert an element satisfies two independent constraints simultaneously
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('selected tab is both active and aria-selected', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Overview' }).click();

  // Build two independent locators and combine with .and()
  const activeTab = page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Overview' });
  const ariaSelectedTab = page.locator('[aria-selected="true"]');

  // .and() narrows to elements matching BOTH locators simultaneously
  const selectedActiveTab = activeTab.and(ariaSelectedTab);

  await expect(selectedActiveTab).toBeVisible();
  await expect(selectedActiveTab).toHaveClass(/tab--active/);

  // Verify exactly one tab satisfies both constraints
  await expect(selectedActiveTab).toHaveCount(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.and()` performs a simultaneous DOM intersection — it matches elements that satisfy both locator queries at the same point in time, which is strictly more reliable than chaining `.filter()` calls that evaluate in sequence and may observe intermediate DOM states during animations — but `and()` generates a compound selector that Playwright must re-evaluate on every auto-wait retry tick, doubling the number of DOM queries per retry cycle; for high-frequency animations, this doubles CPU overhead compared to a single precise CSS selector.

**Pattern 565** — `locator.or()` to handle two legitimate UI states in a single assertion
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment result shows either success or pending state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/payment/result');

  const successBanner = page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: 'Payment successful' });
  const pendingBanner = page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: 'Payment pending' });

  // .or() waits until at least one locator matches — handles race between
  // synchronous confirmation and async webhook-driven status update
  const resultBanner = successBanner.or(pendingBanner);
  await expect(resultBanner).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });

  // Narrow further to assert the correct messaging per state
  const bannerText = await resultBanner.innerText();
  if (bannerText.includes('pending')) {
    await expect(page.getByText('Check your email for confirmation')).toBeVisible();
  } else {
    await expect(page.getByText('Receipt sent to')).toBeVisible();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.or()` waits for the first matching locator to appear and resolves the auto-wait, which correctly handles legitimate UI states where timing determines which message renders — but `or()` disguises a flaky test as a stable one when only one state should ever be reachable; if the payment service always resolves synchronously in CI, a bug that surfaces the pending state will be masked because the assertion passes on whichever banner appears first.

**Pattern 566** — `context.storageState()` snapshot and restore for multi-step auth session reuse
```typescript
import { test, expect, Browser } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const AUTH_STATE_PATH = path.join(__dirname, '.auth/user.json');

// Global setup: authenticate once and persist storage state
async function globalSetup(browser: Browser) {
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('test@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
  await context.storageState({ path: AUTH_STATE_PATH });
  await context.close();
}

// Each test file reuses the stored state — no login overhead per test
test.use({ storageState: AUTH_STATE_PATH });

test('authenticated dashboard loads user data', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Welcome/ })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-email')).toHaveText('test@example.com');
});
```
Tradeoff: Persisting `storageState` to disk in global setup reduces per-test login time from ~2 s to ~0 ms for every test that declares `test.use({ storageState })`, enabling hundreds of tests to skip the login flow entirely — but the persisted state file captures cookies and localStorage tokens that expire on a wall-clock schedule; if a CI run starts just before token expiration, some tests will fail mid-suite with 401 responses while earlier tests passed, producing a confusing split-failure pattern that is difficult to reproduce locally.

**Pattern 567** — `context.grantPermissions()` for geolocation and notification testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('store locator shows nearest branch using geolocation', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Grant permissions and inject fake coordinates before creating the page
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    permissions: ['geolocation'],
    geolocation: { latitude: 51.5074, longitude: -0.1278 }, // London
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/store-locator');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Find stores near me' }).click();

  // Page reads navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition() — gets injected coords
  await expect(page.getByTestId('nearest-store')).toContainText('London Bridge');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('distance')).toHaveText(/0\.\d+ miles/);

  // Override mid-test to simulate user travelling
  await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 53.4808, longitude: -2.2426 }); // Manchester
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('nearest-store')).toContainText('Piccadilly');

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.grantPermissions(['geolocation'])` combined with `context.setGeolocation()` allows mid-test coordinate updates without page reload, which is the only reliable way to test location-aware features without hitting the browser's native permission dialog — but geolocation injection bypasses the browser's real permission flow entirely; features that rely on `PermissionState` changing from `prompt` to `granted` asynchronously may not behave correctly in tests because the permission is pre-granted before any page code runs.

**Pattern 568** — `page.route()` with `route.abort()` to test offline/network-failure error states
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard shows retry banner when analytics endpoint fails', async ({ page }) => {
  let analyticsCallCount = 0;

  // Abort the analytics call but let all other requests through
  await page.route('**/api/analytics/**', async (route) => {
    analyticsCallCount++;
    await route.abort('failed'); // simulate connection reset
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // App should show degraded-mode banner, not a blank screen
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /analytics unavailable/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('main-content')).toBeVisible();
  expect(analyticsCallCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);

  // Verify retry logic: remove the abort handler and trigger retry
  await page.unrouteAll({ behavior: 'ignoreErrors' });
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Retry' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /analytics unavailable/i })).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.abort('failed')` simulates a connection-level failure — the browser receives a network error rather than an HTTP error response — which correctly exercises `fetch()` `.catch()` branches and `onerror` handlers that HTTP 500 responses do not trigger; but `abort('failed')` does not preserve the request in the browser's DevTools network panel because it is intercepted before any bytes are sent, making it harder to inspect the aborted request URL during debugging compared to `route.fulfill({ status: 503 })`.

**Pattern 569** — `page.waitForRequest()` to assert outbound payload structure before response arrives
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout form sends correct line items in POST body', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add Widget' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add Gadget' }).click();

  // Register the expectation BEFORE the action that triggers the request
  const checkoutRequestPromise = page.waitForRequest((req) =>
    req.url().includes('/api/orders') && req.method() === 'POST'
  );

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();

  const checkoutRequest = await checkoutRequestPromise;
  const body = JSON.parse(checkoutRequest.postData() ?? '{}') as {
    items: Array<{ sku: string; qty: number }>;
  };

  expect(body.items).toHaveLength(2);
  expect(body.items).toContainEqual({ sku: 'WIDGET-001', qty: 1 });
  expect(body.items).toContainEqual({ sku: 'GADGET-007', qty: 1 });
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForRequest()` resolves as soon as the browser dispatches the request, before any response is received, allowing assertions on the outbound payload without coupling to server-side processing time — but the predicate receives every request fired during the wait period and can match an earlier unrelated POST to the same path if the page makes background calls; scope the predicate with both URL and method checks, and register the promise before the triggering action to avoid a race where the request fires between the action and the `waitForRequest()` call.

**Pattern 570** — `browserContext.route()` for context-wide API mocking shared across all pages
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('multi-tab workflow sees consistent mocked user profile', async ({ context }) => {
  // Single route registered on the context applies to all pages opened within it
  await context.route('**/api/v1/me', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ id: 'u-42', name: 'Ada Lovelace', plan: 'enterprise' }),
    });
  });

  const page1 = await context.newPage();
  const page2 = await context.newPage();

  await page1.goto('/profile');
  await page2.goto('/settings');

  // Both pages see the same mocked profile without per-page route setup
  await expect(page1.getByTestId('username')).toHaveText('Ada Lovelace');
  await expect(page2.getByTestId('plan-badge')).toHaveText('enterprise');

  // Verify pages are truly isolated — local storage doesn't bleed between them
  await page1.evaluate(() => localStorage.setItem('tab', 'profile'));
  const page2Storage = await page2.evaluate(() => localStorage.getItem('tab'));
  expect(page2Storage).toBeNull();
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.route()` registers the handler once and intercepts the matching URL on every `Page` created within that context, eliminating the boilerplate of calling `page.route()` for each tab in a multi-page test — but context-level routes persist for the lifetime of the context and cannot be temporarily suspended per page; if one tab in the test needs the real API response while other tabs need the mock, you must unregister the context route with `context.unroute()` and register a narrower per-page route on the specific page that needs the real response.

**Pattern 571** — `page.frameLocator()` to interact with embedded third-party iframe content
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('embedded payment iframe accepts card details and confirms charge', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/payment');

  // Target the iframe by its `name` or `src` attribute — frameLocator pierces the boundary
  const paymentFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[name="payment-frame"]');

  // All locator methods work inside the frameLocator as if it were the main frame
  await paymentFrame.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await paymentFrame.getByLabel('Expiry date').fill('12/29');
  await paymentFrame.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await paymentFrame.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  // Assert back in the main frame — the parent page updates after iframe postMessage
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment confirmed' })).toBeVisible({
    timeout: 10_000,
  });
  await expect(page.getByTestId('transaction-id')).toHaveText(/^txn_/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.frameLocator()` returns a locator scoped to the iframe's document and supports the full auto-waiting locator API, which is far more reliable than obtaining a raw `Frame` reference via `page.frame()` and losing auto-wait semantics — but `frameLocator()` requires the iframe to be same-origin or the test context to be configured without strict cross-origin policies; third-party payment iframes that enforce `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` will refuse to load in the test browser unless the test runs against a local mock of the payment provider.

**Pattern 572** — `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with regex for async router transition assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout wizard progresses through steps with valid URL slugs', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Step 1 — cart review
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/cart/);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to shipping' }).click();

  // Step 2 — shipping
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/shipping/);
  await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Test User');
  await page.getByLabel('Address').fill('123 Main St');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }).click();

  // Step 3 — payment
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/payment/);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();

  // Step 4 — confirmation with dynamic order ID
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/confirmation\/ord_[a-z0-9]+/);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-id')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect(page).toHaveURL(/regex/)` auto-retries until the URL matches, which correctly handles client-side router transitions that update the URL asynchronously after a React `setState` or Vue `router.push()` resolves — but regex URL assertions do not verify the page has fully rendered after the navigation; a fast router may update the URL before the new page's components mount, causing subsequent `getByRole()` locator calls to fail with "element not found" even though the URL assertion passed.

**Pattern 573** — `test.fixme()` with a condition for tracked known-broken tests
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const isCI = !!process.env.CI;
const FLAKY_TICKET = 'https://jira.example.com/browse/WEB-4421';

test.describe('file upload feature', () => {
  // Mark as fixme only in CI where the upload endpoint mock is unavailable
  test.fixme(isCI, `Upload mock unavailable in CI — tracked in ${FLAKY_TICKET}`);

  test('drag-and-drop upload shows progress bar and completion state', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/upload');

    const dropzone = page.getByTestId('upload-dropzone');
    await dropzone.dispatchEvent('dragenter');
    await dropzone.dispatchEvent('drop', {
      dataTransfer: await page.evaluateHandle(() => {
        const dt = new DataTransfer();
        dt.items.add(new File(['content'], 'test.pdf', { type: 'application/pdf' }));
        return dt;
      }),
    });

    await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByText('Upload complete')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.fixme(condition, message)` marks a test as expected-to-fail only when the condition is truthy — enabling the test to run and pass locally while being skipped in CI where the dependency is missing — but `fixme` causes the test runner to report the test as "skipped" rather than "failed", which means CI pipelines that gate merges on test passage will not catch regressions in the fixme condition itself; use `test.skip()` when the test must never run in a given environment, and reserve `test.fixme()` exclusively for tests expected to fail when infrastructure is present.

**Pattern 574** — `locator.filter({ hasNot })` to exclude loading skeleton rows from list assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product list renders real data cards after skeletons resolve', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Immediately after navigation, skeleton loaders are visible
  const allCards = page.getByTestId('product-card');
  const skeletonCards = allCards.filter({ has: page.locator('[data-skeleton="true"]') });
  const realCards = allCards.filter({ hasNot: page.locator('[data-skeleton="true"]') });

  // Wait for skeletons to disappear — real cards have no skeleton descendant
  await expect(skeletonCards).toHaveCount(0);

  // Now assert on real data cards only
  await expect(realCards).toHaveCount(12);
  await expect(realCards.first()).toContainText('$');
  await expect(realCards.first().getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })).toBeEnabled();

  // Ensure no card still shows placeholder text
  for (const card of await realCards.all()) {
    await expect(card.getByTestId('product-name')).not.toHaveText('Loading...');
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `filter({ hasNot: locator })` excludes DOM elements containing the specified descendant, which correctly separates skeleton placeholder cards from hydrated data cards without requiring a `page.waitForSelector()` timeout guess — but iterating `realCards.all()` inside a `for...of` loop snapshots the NodeList at call time and does not re-query on each iteration; if the component renders additional cards asynchronously after `all()` resolves (e.g., via infinite scroll), the loop will miss them and the 12-card count assertion may pass prematurely.

**Pattern 575** — `page.on('console')` listener for capturing and asserting JavaScript console errors
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('page navigation does not emit React hydration errors or unhandled rejections', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  const consoleErrors: string[] = [];
  const consoleWarnings: string[] = [];

  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') consoleErrors.push(msg.text());
    if (msg.type() === 'warning') consoleWarnings.push(msg.text());
  });

  page.on('pageerror', (err) => {
    consoleErrors.push(`[pageerror] ${err.message}`);
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await page.getByRole('navigation').getByRole('link', { name: 'About' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/about');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Contact' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/contact');

  // Filter known-acceptable warnings before asserting
  const unexpectedErrors = consoleErrors.filter(
    (e) => !e.includes('favicon.ico') && !e.includes('[HMR]')
  );
  expect(unexpectedErrors, `Unexpected console errors: ${unexpectedErrors.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: Attaching `page.on('console')` and `page.on('pageerror')` listeners before navigation captures all console output emitted during page load and user interactions, surfacing React hydration mismatches, unhandled promise rejections, and third-party script errors that are invisible to Playwright's assertion APIs — but the `console` event fires for every `console.log()` call in the application including verbose debug output, so the error array accumulates noise; always filter the array against a known-acceptable list before asserting, and store the full array in `testInfo.attach()` for post-mortem debugging when the filtered assertion fails.

### Community Gotchas

**G190** — `locator.all()` returns a static snapshot that does not re-query when the DOM mutates
Why this matters: `const rows = await locator.all()` captures a fixed JavaScript array of `Locator` objects representing elements that exist in the DOM at the moment `all()` is called. If the application removes, reorders, or appends rows after `all()` resolves — for example, because a sort operation completes asynchronously — iterating `rows` with `for (const row of rows)` operates on stale element handles. Calls on stale handles either resolve to wrong elements or throw "Element is not attached to the DOM" errors. Developers are caught off-guard because other Playwright locator methods re-query on every call, creating an inconsistency between `locator.all()` and methods like `locator.nth()`.
Fix: Use `locator.nth(i)` inside a loop driven by `await locator.count()` instead of `locator.all()` when the list may mutate: `for (let i = 0; i < await locator.count(); i++) { await locator.nth(i).click(); }`. Each call to `locator.nth(i)` re-queries the DOM, so it always resolves against the current DOM state. Reserve `locator.all()` for snapshot assertions on stable, fully-loaded lists where no mutations are expected.

---

**G191** — `page.waitForSelector()` accepts hidden elements and resolves before they are visible
Why this matters: `page.waitForSelector('.modal')` resolves as soon as a `.modal` element appears in the DOM, even if the element has `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, or `opacity: 0` — because the default state is `'attached'`, not `'visible'`. Tests that call `await page.waitForSelector('.modal')` then immediately try to click a button inside the modal fail with "element is not visible" because the CSS animation has not yet transitioned the modal to its visible state. This is a frequent source of flaky tests in applications that use CSS transitions to fade modals in.
Fix: Pass `{ state: 'visible' }` to ensure the selector resolves only once the element is both in the DOM and has non-zero dimensions with no `visibility: hidden` or `display: none` styles: `await page.waitForSelector('.modal', { state: 'visible' })`. Better yet, replace `waitForSelector` with a locator assertion — `await expect(page.locator('.modal')).toBeVisible()` — which uses auto-wait with visibility semantics by default and produces clearer timeout error messages.

---

**G192** — `browserContext.addCookies()` requires the `url` or both `domain` and `path` fields — omitting them silently drops the cookie
Why this matters: Calling `context.addCookies([{ name: 'session', value: 'abc123' }])` without specifying either a `url` or both `domain` and `path` does not throw an error — it silently accepts the call but the cookie is never associated with any origin and is therefore never sent with requests. Tests that set up session cookies this way and then navigate to the application find themselves on the login page with no indication that cookie injection failed. The bug is particularly deceptive because `context.cookies()` returns the malformed cookie entry in the list, making it appear as though the cookie was set correctly.
Fix: Always include either `url: 'https://app.example.com'` (which Playwright uses to derive domain and path) or explicit `domain: 'app.example.com'` and `path: '/'` fields in every cookie object: `context.addCookies([{ name: 'session', value: 'abc123', url: 'https://app.example.com' }])`. After calling `addCookies`, verify the cookie is present and correctly scoped with `const cookies = await context.cookies('https://app.example.com'); expect(cookies.find(c => c.name === 'session')).toBeDefined()`.

---

**G193** — `expect(locator).toBeEnabled()` passes on `<div>` elements that have no concept of disabled state
Why this matters: `expect(locator).toBeEnabled()` checks whether the element is not disabled — but for non-form elements like `<div>`, `<span>`, or `<a>`, there is no HTML `disabled` attribute or ARIA `aria-disabled` property set by default, so `toBeEnabled()` always returns true regardless of whether the element is visually or functionally disabled. Applications that implement custom disabled states by adding a CSS class like `.disabled` or by setting `pointer-events: none` via JavaScript will pass `toBeEnabled()` even when the element is non-interactive. Developers writing `await expect(page.getByTestId('submit-btn')).toBeEnabled()` against a custom `<div role="button">` component get false confidence.
Fix: For custom interactive elements that use ARIA roles, assert on `aria-disabled` explicitly: `expect(locator).not.toHaveAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true')`. For elements that signal disabled state via CSS class, use `expect(locator).not.toHaveClass(/disabled/)`. Reserve `toBeEnabled()` exclusively for native form elements (`<button>`, `<input>`, `<select>`, `<textarea>`) where the `disabled` property is a first-class DOM concept with defined semantics.

---

**G194** — `page.route()` handlers registered with string patterns are case-sensitive and will not match URL variants with different casing
Why this matters: `page.route('**/api/Users/**', handler)` matches requests to `/api/Users/profile` but silently misses requests to `/api/users/profile` — the glob pattern comparison is case-sensitive on all platforms because Playwright matches the literal URL string. Developers running tests on macOS, where the filesystem and many development servers are case-insensitive, may write route patterns that work locally but fail in Linux-based CI where the application server or reverse proxy normalizes URL casing differently. The route handler is simply never invoked, so the real network request goes through without mocking and the test fails with an unexpected API response or CORS error.
Fix: Always write route glob patterns in the exact casing that the application's HTTP client will use in the request URL — inspect the actual request URL in DevTools or via a `page.on('request', r => console.log(r.url()))` listener before writing the pattern. For APIs where casing varies across environments, use a regex pattern instead of a glob string: `page.route(/\/api\/users\//i, handler)` — regex patterns support the `i` flag for case-insensitive matching and will correctly intercept the request regardless of how the server normalizes the path.

## Cycle 69 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 591** — Page Object Model with typed locator properties and constructor-injected `Page`
```typescript
// pages/checkout-page.ts
import { type Page, type Locator, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export class CheckoutPage {
  readonly page: Page;
  readonly emailInput: Locator;
  readonly submitButton: Locator;
  readonly orderConfirmationHeading: Locator;
  readonly errorBanner: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email address');
    this.submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' });
    this.orderConfirmationHeading = page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' });
    this.errorBanner = page.getByRole('alert');
  }

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('/checkout');
    await expect(this.submitButton).toBeVisible();
  }

  async placeOrder(email: string) {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
    await this.submitButton.click();
    await expect(this.orderConfirmationHeading).toBeVisible();
  }
}

// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { CheckoutPage } from '../pages/checkout-page';

test('places an order with a valid email', async ({ page }) => {
  const checkout = new CheckoutPage(page);
  await checkout.goto();
  await checkout.placeOrder('buyer@example.com');
});
```
Tradeoff: Defining locators as `readonly` class properties in the constructor means all locators are created eagerly at instantiation time even if a test only exercises one method, which adds negligible overhead per-test but means any locator API typos (e.g., wrong role name) are not caught until the test runs that particular assertion — lazy locator evaluation via getter methods would surface errors earlier but adds boilerplate; the constructor pattern is preferred for readability and consistent IDE autocomplete.

**Pattern 592** — `test.step()` for hierarchical test structure with named sub-operations in the HTML report
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user completes profile setup', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('Navigate to profile setup wizard', async () => {
    await page.goto('/profile/setup');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Step 1 of 3' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('Fill in personal information', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Jane Doe');
    await page.getByLabel('Timezone').selectOption('America/New_York');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Step 2 of 3' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('Upload avatar and save', async () => {
    const fileChooserPromise = page.waitForEvent('filechooser');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Upload photo' }).click();
    const fileChooser = await fileChooserPromise;
    await fileChooser.setFiles('./fixtures/avatar.png');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Finish setup' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Profile saved');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step()` wraps async operations and names them in the HTML report trace timeline, making step-level failure attribution instant in CI — but each `test.step()` boundary introduces an additional async call frame, and nesting steps more than two levels deep produces report trees that are harder to scan than flat steps; reserve nesting for genuinely hierarchical operations (e.g., "Fill form" → "Enter billing details") and keep top-level steps to six or fewer per test.

**Pattern 593** — `expect.soft()` to collect multiple assertion failures before reporting
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product detail page displays all required metadata', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');

  // All soft assertions run even when earlier ones fail
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toContainText('Widget Pro');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-price')).toContainText('$49.99');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-sku')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('img', { name: 'Widget Pro product photo' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByLabel('Quantity')).toHaveValue('1');
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })).toBeEnabled();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('stock-status')).toContainText('In stock');

  // Hard assertion at the end — if any soft assertion failed, test fails here
  // with all accumulated soft failure messages listed together
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft()` continues test execution after failures and reports all violations together, which dramatically reduces the number of test re-runs needed to find all broken metadata fields after a content migration — but code that executes *after* a soft assertion failure may throw hard errors (e.g., clicking a button that doesn't exist because the earlier soft assertion caught its absence), which surface as a second unrelated failure in the report and obscure the root cause; structure tests so that soft assertions are grouped together at a stable page state rather than interspersed with interactions.

**Pattern 594** — CSV-driven parameterized tests loaded from external data file
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

// fixtures/search-queries.csv format: query,expectedResultCount
const csvPath = path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/search-queries.csv');
const rows = fs
  .readFileSync(csvPath, 'utf-8')
  .trim()
  .split('\n')
  .slice(1) // skip header
  .map((line) => {
    const [query, expectedCount] = line.split(',');
    return { query: query.trim(), expectedCount: parseInt(expectedCount.trim(), 10) };
  });

for (const { query, expectedCount } of rows) {
  test(`search for "${query}" returns ${expectedCount} results`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/search');
    await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search' }).fill(query);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('result-count')).toContainText(`${expectedCount} results`);
    const results = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: page.getByTestId('search-result') });
    await expect(results).toHaveCount(expectedCount);
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Parsing an external CSV at module evaluation time generates one `test()` entry per row so Playwright's test runner sees each row as a distinct test with its own retry budget, trace, and HTML report entry — but the CSV is read synchronously at load time before the test runner initialises its worker pool, which means `fs.readFileSync` failures (missing file, wrong path in CI) cause the entire spec file to be skipped with a cryptic "no tests found" error rather than a named test failure; always validate the CSV path exists at module load time and throw a descriptive error.

**Pattern 595** — `AxeBuilder` accessibility scan with snapshot fingerprinting to track known violations
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

type ViolationFingerprint = { rule: string; targets: string[] };

function fingerprint(violations: { id: string; nodes: { target: string[] }[] }[]): ViolationFingerprint[] {
  return violations.flatMap((v) =>
    v.nodes.map((n) => ({ rule: v.id, targets: n.target }))
  );
}

test('homepage has no new WCAG 2.1 AA violations beyond known baseline', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
    .exclude('#legacy-widget') // third-party widget with unfixable violation
    .analyze();

  // Attach full results for post-mortem debugging
  await testInfo.attach('axe-results', {
    body: JSON.stringify(results.violations, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  const prints = fingerprint(results.violations);

  // Snapshot fingerprints — update with `--update-snapshots` only after deliberate sign-off
  expect(prints).toMatchSnapshot('known-a11y-violations.json');
});
```
Tradeoff: Fingerprinting violation rule IDs and CSS target selectors into a snapshot file tracks whether the set of known violations has grown, shrunk, or shifted without blocking CI on pre-existing technical debt — but the snapshot must be committed and updated intentionally (`--update-snapshots`) whenever legitimate UI changes alter the selectors, and forgetting to update the snapshot after a benign DOM restructure causes false CI failures that erode team trust in the accessibility gate; establish a documented workflow for who approves snapshot updates and add a PR comment explaining the change.

**Pattern 596** — Custom `Reporter` that posts test results to an external webhook on suite completion
```typescript
// reporters/webhook-reporter.ts
import type { Reporter, TestCase, TestResult, FullResult } from '@playwright/test/reporter';

class WebhookReporter implements Reporter {
  private results: { title: string; status: string; duration: number }[] = [];
  private webhookUrl: string;

  constructor(options: { webhookUrl: string }) {
    this.webhookUrl = options.webhookUrl;
  }

  onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult) {
    this.results.push({
      title: test.titlePath().join(' > '),
      status: result.status,
      duration: result.duration,
    });
  }

  async onEnd(result: FullResult) {
    const payload = {
      outcome: result.status,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      tests: this.results,
      passed: this.results.filter((r) => r.status === 'passed').length,
      failed: this.results.filter((r) => r.status === 'failed').length,
    };
    await fetch(this.webhookUrl, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });
  }
}

export default WebhookReporter;

// playwright.config.ts excerpt
// reporter: [['list'], ['./reporters/webhook-reporter.ts', { webhookUrl: process.env.RESULTS_WEBHOOK_URL }]]
```
Tradeoff: Implementing `onEnd` as an `async` method and using `fetch` to post results gives the reporter access to the full suite outcome including final retry status and duration totals — but Playwright's reporter contract does not guarantee that `onEnd` awaits asynchronous operations in all runner configurations; if the Node.js process exits before the `fetch` promise resolves (possible when running with `--workers=1` on fast suites), the webhook call is silently dropped; use a fire-and-forget pattern with a `process.exitCode` guard or migrate to a plugin that explicitly awaits reporter teardown.

**Pattern 597** — API-driven test data setup and teardown via `request` fixture for true test isolation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('admin can deactivate a user account', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // SETUP: create a user via API so the test owns its own data
  const createResp = await request.post('/api/admin/users', {
    data: { email: 'temp-user@example.com', role: 'viewer', active: true },
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.ADMIN_API_TOKEN}` },
  });
  expect(createResp.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  const { id: userId } = await createResp.json();

  try {
    // ACT: exercise the UI to deactivate the user
    await page.goto(`/admin/users/${userId}`);
    await expect(page.getByTestId('user-status')).toContainText('Active');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Deactivate account' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('dialog').getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).click();

    // ASSERT: UI reflects new status
    await expect(page.getByTestId('user-status')).toContainText('Deactivated');
  } finally {
    // TEARDOWN: always delete the user regardless of test outcome
    await request.delete(`/api/admin/users/${userId}`, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.ADMIN_API_TOKEN}` },
    });
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `try/finally` to guarantee teardown via API calls means test data is cleaned up even on assertion failure or timeout, preventing stale fixture accumulation that causes future test runs to fail on uniqueness constraints — but the `request` fixture within `test()` body shares the browser context's cookie jar, so if the admin token is cookie-based rather than header-based the teardown request may inadvertently use the browser session's auth state; use `request.newContext()` with explicit auth headers for teardown calls that must be independent of the browser session.

**Pattern 598** — Component test with `mount()` and `update()` to verify prop-driven re-render behaviour
```typescript
// tests/badge.spec.tsx  (Playwright component test, React)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import { Badge } from '../src/components/Badge';

test('Badge updates label and variant when props change', async ({ mount }) => {
  // Initial render
  const component = await mount(
    <Badge label="Draft" variant="neutral" data-testid="badge" />
  );
  await expect(component).toContainText('Draft');
  await expect(component).toHaveAttribute('data-variant', 'neutral');

  // Re-render with updated props — simulates parent state change
  await component.update(
    <Badge label="Published" variant="success" data-testid="badge" />
  );
  await expect(component).toContainText('Published');
  await expect(component).toHaveAttribute('data-variant', 'success');

  // Verify no residual class from previous render (common with CSS Modules)
  await expect(component).not.toHaveClass(/neutral/);
  await expect(component).toHaveClass(/success/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `component.update()` triggers a real React re-render with new props inside the Playwright browser context, validating that the component correctly responds to prop changes without requiring a full parent/context setup — but component tests run in a stripped-down `playwright/index.html` harness that does not include the application's router, global CSS imports, or context providers by default; components that depend on a `ThemeProvider` or `RouterContext` at any level will throw "cannot read properties of undefined" errors unless those providers are wrapped in `beforeMount` hooks in `playwright/index.ts`.

**Pattern 599** — `toHaveScreenshot()` with `stylePath` to mask animated elements for stable visual baselines
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot: {
      maxDiffPixels: 50,
      stylePath: './tests/visual/mask-animations.css',
    },
  },
});

// tests/visual/mask-animations.css
/* Freeze all CSS animations and transitions for visual snapshot stability */
*, *::before, *::after {
  animation-duration: 0s !important;
  animation-delay: 0s !important;
  transition-duration: 0s !important;
  transition-delay: 0s !important;
}
/* Hide volatile third-party widgets */
[data-testid="chat-widget"],
iframe[src*="analytics"] {
  visibility: hidden !important;
}

// tests/visual/homepage.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('homepage hero section matches visual baseline', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('hero-section')).toHaveScreenshot('hero-section.png');
});
```
Tradeoff: Injecting a `stylePath` CSS file globally freezes all animations and hides volatile widgets before every screenshot comparison, eliminating the most common source of flaky visual tests (animated elements captured mid-transition) without modifying application source code — but the injected CSS runs in the actual browser context, meaning any `animation-duration: 0s` rule that a component reads via `window.getComputedStyle` to branch rendering logic will produce a different component state than production, causing the visual snapshot to reflect a non-production rendering path; audit components for CSS-query-driven logic before relying on the global animation-freeze approach.

**Pattern 600** — `test.use({ colorScheme })` in a describe block for dark-mode visual regression per project
```typescript
// tests/visual/dark-mode.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Dark mode visual regression', () => {
  test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' });

  test('settings page renders correctly in dark mode', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/settings');
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('settings-dark.png');
  });

  test('dashboard charts are legible in dark mode', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-chart')).toHaveScreenshot('revenue-chart-dark.png');
  });
});

// playwright.config.ts — separate projects for light and dark baselines
// projects: [
//   { name: 'chromium-light', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], colorScheme: 'light' } },
//   { name: 'chromium-dark',  use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], colorScheme: 'dark'  } },
// ]
```
Tradeoff: Scoping `test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` to a `test.describe()` block overrides the project-level setting for only those tests, allowing a single spec file to house both light and dark assertions without duplicating files — but snapshot baselines include the project name in their filename (e.g., `settings-dark-chromium-light.png` vs `settings-dark-chromium-dark.png`), so running dark-mode tests inside the `chromium-light` project generates a baseline with a misleading filename suffix that causes confusion when updating snapshots; use dedicated `chromium-dark` projects in the config rather than in-file `test.use()` overrides so snapshot filenames reflect the actual rendering context.

**Pattern 601** — `test.extend()` custom option for per-project feature-flag parameterization
```typescript
// fixtures/feature-flags.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type FeatureFlags = {
  newCheckoutEnabled: boolean;
  betaDashboardEnabled: boolean;
};

export const test = base.extend<FeatureFlags>({
  newCheckoutEnabled: [false, { option: true }],
  betaDashboardEnabled: [false, { option: true }],
});

// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test } from '../fixtures/feature-flags';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow uses new or legacy UI based on feature flag', async ({
  page,
  newCheckoutEnabled,
}) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  if (newCheckoutEnabled) {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('new-checkout-form')).toBeVisible();
  } else {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('legacy-checkout-form')).toBeVisible();
  }
});

// playwright.config.ts excerpt
// projects: [
//   { name: 'legacy-checkout', use: { newCheckoutEnabled: false } },
//   { name: 'new-checkout',    use: { newCheckoutEnabled: true  } },
// ]
```
Tradeoff: Declaring feature flags as typed `option: true` fixtures lets each Playwright project supply different flag values through `use:` config rather than through environment variables or test-file conditionals, enabling the same spec to cover both the old and new code paths in a single CI run — but adding a new flag to the `FeatureFlags` type requires updating the `test.extend()` call and every `playwright.config.ts` project entry that should set the flag, creating a maintenance surface that grows with the number of flags; consider a single `featureFlags: Record<string, boolean>` option fixture rather than one property per flag to avoid config sprawl.

---

**Pattern 602** — `route.fulfill()` with inline JSON for clean REST endpoint stubbing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user list page renders stubbed users from API', async ({ page }) => {
  const stubbedUsers = [
    { id: 1, name: 'Alice Nguyen', role: 'admin', active: true },
    { id: 2, name: 'Bob Chen',    role: 'viewer', active: false },
  ];

  // Intercept the API call before navigation so the stub is in place when the page loads
  await page.route('**/api/users', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ users: stubbedUsers, total: stubbedUsers.length }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  await expect(page.getByRole('row', { name: /Alice Nguyen/ })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('row', { name: /Bob Chen/ })).toBeVisible();
  // Verify inactive styling applied based on data field
  await expect(page.getByRole('row', { name: /Bob Chen/ })).toHaveClass(/inactive/);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-count')).toContainText('2 users');
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `route.fulfill()` with an inline `body` string gives complete control over response shape and avoids network dependencies, making the test deterministic regardless of API server state — but the stubbed JSON must exactly match the shape the frontend component expects, including field names, nesting, and pagination envelope (`{ users: [], total: N }`); when the API contract changes, stubs silently diverge from reality and the test continues to pass while production is broken; pair stub-based UI tests with a contract test or schema validation step that asserts the real API still returns the expected shape.

---

**Pattern 603** — `locator.filter({ hasText })` chained with `getByRole()` for precise table row assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice table shows correct status and amount per invoice', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/invoices');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  const invoiceTable = page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Invoices' });

  // Locate row by invoice number text, then assert cells within that row
  const targetRow = invoiceTable
    .getByRole('row')
    .filter({ hasText: 'INV-2024-0042' });

  await expect(targetRow).toBeVisible();
  await expect(targetRow.getByRole('cell', { name: /\$1,250\.00/ })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(targetRow.getByRole('cell', { name: 'Paid' })).toBeVisible();

  // Verify the paid row has the correct ARIA attribute for screen reader context
  await expect(targetRow).toHaveAttribute('data-status', 'paid');

  // Count unpaid rows without relying on row index
  const unpaidRows = invoiceTable.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Unpaid' });
  await expect(unpaidRows).toHaveCount(3);
});
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'INV-2024-0042' })` scopes all subsequent assertions inside the matched row and re-queries on every call so it tolerates row reordering from sort operations — but `filter({ hasText })` performs a substring match on the entire row's concatenated text content, meaning a row with text "INV-2024-0042 (amended)" also matches the filter for "INV-2024-0042"; use a more specific locator like `filter({ has: page.getByTestId('invoice-number').and(page.getByText('INV-2024-0042', { exact: true })) })` when invoice number strings can appear as substrings of other cell values.

**Pattern 604** — `request` fixture with `response.ok()` and `toContainEqual()` for API contract validation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('GET /api/products returns valid product list contract', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('/api/products', {
    params: { category: 'electronics', limit: '5' },
  });

  // Assert HTTP status is 2xx
  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(response.headers()['content-type']).toContain('application/json');

  const body = await response.json();

  // Assert envelope shape
  expect(body).toHaveProperty('products');
  expect(body).toHaveProperty('total');
  expect(Array.isArray(body.products)).toBe(true);
  expect(body.products.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(5);

  // Assert each product has required contract fields
  for (const product of body.products) {
    expect(product).toMatchObject({
      id: expect.any(Number),
      name: expect.any(String),
      price: expect.any(Number),
      category: 'electronics',
    });
  }

  // Assert at least one known product is present
  expect(body.products).toContainEqual(
    expect.objectContaining({ name: 'Wireless Headphones' })
  );
});
```
Tradeoff: Using the `request` fixture for pure API contract tests runs orders of magnitude faster than spinning up a browser page and navigating to a UI that calls the same endpoint — but `response.ok()` is a plain boolean accessor rather than a Playwright web-first assertion, so it does not retry on temporary 503 responses; wrap the request in a retry loop or use `page.waitForResponse()` if the endpoint has eventual-consistency behaviour during test setup.

---

**Pattern 605** — `page.waitForResponse()` with URL predicate to gate UI assertions on a specific API response
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search results update after debounce period', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  // Register the wait BEFORE triggering the action that causes the request
  const searchResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    (response) =>
      response.url().includes('/api/search') &&
      response.request().method() === 'GET' &&
      response.status() === 200,
    { timeout: 5000 }
  );

  // Type into the search box — debounce fires after 300ms
  await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search' }).fill('playwright');

  // Wait for the debounced API call to complete before asserting results
  const searchResponse = await searchResponsePromise;
  const { results } = await searchResponse.json();

  // Assert both the API payload and the rendered DOM are consistent
  expect(results.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('result-count')).toContainText(`${results.length} results`);
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toContainText(results[0].title);
});
```
Tradeoff: Storing the `waitForResponse()` promise *before* the triggering action and awaiting it *after* guarantees the listener is registered before the response arrives, eliminating the race condition where a fast server responds before the `waitForResponse` call executes — but the predicate receives every HTTP response in sequence and is called synchronously on each, so a predicate that calls async functions (e.g., `await response.json()`) will throw because `waitForResponse` predicates must be synchronous; filter on URL, method, and status code in the predicate and defer response body parsing to after the promise resolves.

### Community Gotchas

**G200** — `toHaveScreenshot()` baselines silently differ across operating systems due to font rendering
Why this matters: A screenshot baseline generated on macOS with Retina display sub-pixel font rendering will not match the same screenshot taken on Linux in CI because operating systems apply different font hinting algorithms, producing pixel-level differences in text edges. Playwright embeds the OS and browser name in the snapshot filename (e.g., `hero-chromium-darwin.png` vs `hero-chromium-linux.png`), so tests run locally on macOS silently generate separate baseline files that are never compared against the Linux CI baseline. Developers approve a macOS baseline in their PR but CI is comparing against a stale Linux baseline, causing permanent "screenshot mismatch" failures in CI that pass locally indefinitely.
Fix: Always generate and commit visual baselines from the same OS/browser combination used in CI — run `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` inside the same Docker image or GitHub Actions runner that CI uses, then commit the generated `*-linux.png` snapshot files. Use `--project=chromium` to limit baseline generation to one browser at a time. Add a CI step that asserts no un-committed snapshot files exist after the update run to catch stale baselines.

---

**G201** — `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` at file scope causes shared fixture mutation across parallel workers
Why this matters: Adding `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` at the top of a spec file causes all tests in that file to run in separate worker processes simultaneously rather than sequentially. If those tests share a worker-scoped fixture (e.g., a seeded database connection or a shared `storageState` file written by one test and read by another), parallel execution creates race conditions: one worker may truncate the database while another worker is mid-query, or the `storageState` file may be partially written when the second worker reads it. The failure manifests as intermittent "permission denied" or "unexpected end of JSON" errors in CI that never reproduce sequentially locally.
Fix: Audit every fixture transitively used by the tests before enabling parallel mode — ensure worker-scoped fixtures are truly stateless and read-only, or convert shared mutable state to test-scoped fixtures that each worker receives independently. For database-backed tests, use per-test schema namespaces or transaction-wrapped rollbacks rather than a shared seeded dataset. If tests must share state, keep `mode: 'serial'` within that describe block and parallelize at the file level using sharding instead.

---

**G202** — The `request` fixture does not share cookies with the `page` browser context by default
Why this matters: When a test uses both `page` (browser context) and `request` (API request context) fixtures, developers assume that logging in through the UI via `page` automatically propagates the session cookie to `request`, allowing API teardown calls to use the same authenticated session. This assumption is wrong: the `request` fixture creates an entirely independent `APIRequestContext` with its own cookie jar, isolated from `page`'s `BrowserContext`. API calls made via `request` after `page` has logged in return 401 Unauthorized, causing silent teardown failures that leave test data in the database and corrupt subsequent test runs.
Fix: To share auth state between `page` and `request`, use `page.context().request` instead of the standalone `request` fixture — `page.context().request` is the API request context bound to the same `BrowserContext` as `page` and shares its cookies: `const resp = await page.context().request.delete('/api/resource/123')`. Alternatively, extract the session token from `page.context().cookies()` and pass it as a header to the standalone `request` fixture for teardown calls that must be independent of the browser session.

---

**G203** — `mount()` in component tests silently drops non-serializable props (functions with closures over Node.js objects)
Why this matters: Playwright component tests run the test code in Node.js and the component in a real browser process — props passed to `mount()` are serialized over a postMessage-style bridge between the two environments. Functions are serialized as their source text using `Function.prototype.toString()` and re-evaluated in the browser context. Any function that closes over a Node.js-only object (e.g., a `Buffer`, a `stream`, or a module imported with `require('fs')`) loses that closed-over reference when re-evaluated in the browser, causing the component to receive a function that throws `ReferenceError: require is not defined` when invoked. The error is thrown inside the component, not at the `mount()` call, making it difficult to trace back to prop serialization.
Fix: Pass only plain JavaScript objects, strings, numbers, arrays, and pure functions (functions with no closed-over Node.js bindings) as component props in `mount()`. For complex behaviours that require Node.js resources, replace them with stub implementations that return hardcoded values or use Playwright's `page.exposeFunction()` to bridge Node.js logic into the browser context explicitly. Document prop serialization constraints in a JSDoc comment on the component's props interface so future test authors know which prop types are safe.

---

**G204** — `expect.soft()` failures do not halt execution — subsequent code after a soft failure can throw hard errors that obscure the real issue
Why this matters: `expect.soft()` is designed to continue test execution after an assertion fails, accumulating all failures for a combined report. However, if the *next line of code* after a failing soft assertion attempts to interact with a DOM element that the soft assertion just confirmed is absent (e.g., soft-asserting a button exists, then immediately clicking it), the click throws a hard `TimeoutError` rather than a named assertion failure. The HTML report shows the hard timeout error prominently and buries the soft assertion failure, misleading engineers into debugging the click timeout rather than the missing button. This is especially deceptive in loops that soft-assert properties of each item in a list.
Fix: Group soft assertions together at a stable, non-interactive page state — assert all properties of a page's current DOM state without performing any further navigation or interaction until the soft assertion block is complete. If you need to interact with an element that a soft assertion has just checked, add a guard: `if (await button.isVisible()) { await button.click(); }` to prevent the hard error. Alternatively, use `test.step()` to segment the test into discrete phases, with soft assertions confined to the "verify state" step and interactions in a separate "act" step so failures are clearly attributed.

## Cycle 66 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 606** — Page Object Model with Fluent Builder for Conditional Interactions
```typescript
// models/RegistrationPage.ts
import { type Page, type Locator, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export class RegistrationPage {
  readonly page: Page;
  readonly emailInput: Locator;
  readonly passwordInput: Locator;
  readonly confirmPasswordInput: Locator;
  readonly termsCheckbox: Locator;
  readonly submitButton: Locator;
  readonly successHeading: Locator;
  readonly errorSummary: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email address');
    this.passwordInput = page.getByLabel('Password', { exact: true });
    this.confirmPasswordInput = page.getByLabel('Confirm password');
    this.termsCheckbox = page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /terms and conditions/i });
    this.submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account', exact: true });
    this.successHeading = page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Account created' });
    this.errorSummary = page.getByRole('alert');
  }

  async goto(): Promise<this> {
    await this.page.goto('/register');
    return this;
  }

  async fillEmail(email: string): Promise<this> {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
    return this;
  }

  async fillPassword(password: string): Promise<this> {
    await this.passwordInput.fill(password);
    await this.confirmPasswordInput.fill(password);
    return this;
  }

  async acceptTerms(): Promise<this> {
    await this.termsCheckbox.check();
    return this;
  }

  async submit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.submitButton.click();
  }
}

// tests/registration.spec.ts
import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import { RegistrationPage } from '../models/RegistrationPage';

test('new user can register with valid data', async ({ page }) => {
  const reg = new RegistrationPage(page);
  await (await (await (await reg.goto()).fillEmail('user@example.com')).fillPassword('Secure123!')).acceptTerms();
  await reg.submit();
  await page.waitForURL(/\/dashboard/);
});
```
Tradeoff: Fluent builder methods (each returning `this`) allow chaining POM calls and keep the test body concise — but deeply chained `await` expressions like `(await (await reg.goto()).fill())` are syntactically awkward in TypeScript; consider collecting all setup steps into a single `register({ email, password })` method that calls the individual steps internally, reserving fluent chaining for POM interactions where partial-setup tests are required (e.g., testing validation with only email filled).

---

**Pattern 607** — `page.routeFromHAR()` with `updateMode: 'minimal'` for Incremental HAR Updates
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

// A single HAR file captures all API calls for the checkout flow
const checkoutHar = path.join(__dirname, '../fixtures/checkout.har');

test.describe('checkout flow — HAR replay', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await page.routeFromHAR(checkoutHar, {
      url: '*/**/api/**',
      // update: true refreshes the HAR; false replays existing entries
      update: process.env.REFRESH_HAR === '1',
    });
  });

  test('cart page loads products from HAR snapshot', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Cart items' })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(2);
  });

  test('shipping step pre-fills previously used address', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout/shipping');
    const addressField = page.getByLabel('Street address');
    await expect(addressField).not.toBeEmpty();
  });

  test('payment page shows correct order total', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-total')).toHaveText(/\$\d+\.\d{2}/);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: A single HAR file covering all steps in a multi-page checkout flow keeps related fixtures co-located and avoids per-test fixture management overhead — but when only one API endpoint changes (e.g., the cart API adds a `discount` field), the entire HAR must be regenerated with `REFRESH_HAR=1`; split large HAR files by domain or flow phase so that a change to the shipping API only requires refreshing `checkout-shipping.har` rather than the entire checkout HAR.

**Pattern 608** — `page.clock.setFixedTime()` for Stable Relative Date Labels in UI
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('activity feed shows "just now" label for events in the last minute', async ({ page }) => {
  // Pin time to a known moment before navigation
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-06-01T14:00:00.000Z'));
  await page.goto('/activity');

  // Events with timestamps < 60s ago should show "just now"
  const latestEntry = page.getByRole('listitem').first();
  await expect(latestEntry.getByTestId('timestamp-label')).toHaveText('just now');
});

test('dashboard shows "yesterday" for items from the previous calendar day', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-06-02T09:00:00.000Z'));
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Events from June 1st should appear as "yesterday" when viewed on June 2nd
  await expect(
    page.getByTestId('recent-activity').getByText('yesterday')
  ).toBeVisible();
});

test('invoice due date shows "overdue" badge when past due date', async ({ page }) => {
  // Set time to after the invoice due date
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-07-16T00:00:00.000Z'));
  await page.goto('/invoices/INV-2026-042');

  // Invoice due on July 15 2026 — should show overdue badge today (July 16)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('due-badge')).toHaveText('Overdue');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('due-badge')).toHaveAttribute('data-status', 'overdue');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.setFixedTime()` freezes `Date.now()` and `new Date()` without stopping setTimeout/setInterval, which is the correct tool for testing date-dependent display logic (labels like "just now", "yesterday", "overdue") that depends only on `Date.now()` comparisons — but when the component also uses `setTimeout` to auto-refresh the label (e.g., switching from "just now" to "1 min ago" after 60 seconds), the interval still fires on the real clock while the date stays frozen, causing the label update to use the frozen date value and producing an incorrect label; use `page.clock.install()` instead when both the date value and timer callbacks must be controlled together.

---

**Pattern 609** — `AxeBuilder.include()` Scoped Scan with Violation-Count Baseline Assertion
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

// Baseline violation counts accepted at current sprint — reduce each sprint
const BASELINE = {
  'color-contrast': 4, // 4 known contrast failures in legacy footer
  'label': 1,          // 1 unlabeled legacy input in address form
};

test.describe('dashboard page — accessibility gate', () => {
  test('violation count does not increase from baseline', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();

    const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .include('main')
      .withTags(['wcag2aa'])
      .analyze();

    const violationMap = Object.fromEntries(
      results.violations.map(v => [v.id, v.nodes.length])
    );

    for (const [ruleId, baselineCount] of Object.entries(BASELINE)) {
      const actual = violationMap[ruleId] ?? 0;
      expect(
        actual,
        `Rule '${ruleId}' has ${actual} violations but baseline allows ${baselineCount}. ` +
        `${actual > baselineCount ? 'Regression detected!' : 'Baseline can be reduced.'}`
      ).toBeLessThanOrEqual(baselineCount);
    }

    // Catch any violations not in the baseline at all
    const untracked = results.violations.filter(v => !(v.id in BASELINE));
    expect(untracked, `Untracked violations: ${untracked.map(v => v.id).join(', ')}`).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using per-rule node-count baselines allows gradual reduction — lowering `color-contrast` from 4 to 3 as each violation is fixed — and fails immediately when a code change adds new violations to a tracked rule; but the `BASELINE` object is a module-level constant shared across all tests in the file, so different pages tested in the same file share the same baseline even when they have different violation profiles; keep one baseline per page and one `test.describe` per page, or move baselines into a shared JSON config keyed by page path.

---

**Pattern 610** — `context.tracing` Auto-Fixture with Selective Retention Based on Test Duration
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

// Capture traces for slow tests (> 10s) even if they pass
const SLOW_THRESHOLD_MS = 10_000;

export const test = base.extend<{ smartTrace: void }>({
  smartTrace: [
    async ({ context }, use, testInfo) => {
      const startTime = Date.now();
      await context.tracing.start({
        screenshots: true,
        snapshots: true,
        sources: false, // omit sources to keep trace files small
      });

      await use();

      const duration = Date.now() - startTime;
      const isFailed = testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus;
      const isSlow = duration > SLOW_THRESHOLD_MS;

      if (isFailed || isSlow) {
        const tracePath = testInfo.outputPath('trace.zip');
        await context.tracing.stop({ path: tracePath });
        await testInfo.attach('trace', { path: tracePath, contentType: 'application/zip' });
        if (isSlow && !isFailed) {
          testInfo.annotations.push({
            type: 'warning',
            description: `Slow test (${duration}ms) — trace attached for performance investigation`,
          });
        }
      } else {
        await context.tracing.stop(); // discard trace — no path written
      }
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: Retaining traces for slow-but-passing tests surfaces performance regressions that conventional test reports miss — a test that starts taking 15 seconds instead of 3 seconds indicates an underlying performance issue — but `{ auto: true }` means tracing overhead applies to every test, including fast unit-style Playwright tests where the per-test overhead (snapshot capture, screenshot recording) can dominate the actual test time; benchmark the tracing overhead on your fastest tests before enabling `{ auto: true }` globally and consider scoping to integration test suites only.

---

**Pattern 611** — `page.frameLocator()` for Third-Party OAuth Popup Handling
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can log in via Google OAuth popup', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');

  // Listen for the popup window before triggering the click
  const popupPromise = context.waitForEvent('page');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue with Google' }).click();
  const popup = await popupPromise;

  // Wait for the Google sign-in page to load in the popup
  await popup.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');
  await expect(popup).toHaveURL(/accounts\.google\.com/);

  // In test environments, a fake OAuth server serves a simplified login form
  await popup.getByLabel('Email or phone').fill('test@example.com');
  await popup.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
  await popup.getByLabel('Enter your password').fill('test-password');
  await popup.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();

  // Wait for popup to close after OAuth completes
  await popup.waitForEvent('close', { timeout: 10_000 });

  // Main page should now show the authenticated state
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `context.waitForEvent('page')` before clicking the OAuth button ensures Playwright captures the popup even if it opens and closes very quickly — registering the listener before the click is critical because the popup may fire before the `await click()` promise resolves — but real-world OAuth flows (Google, GitHub, Microsoft) use multiple redirect hops and CORS checks that Playwright cannot fully automate against production OAuth servers; always use a fake OAuth server (e.g., `node-oidc-provider`) in test environments and restrict real-OAuth tests to a dedicated manual verification suite.

**Pattern 612** — `route.fulfill()` with `json` Shorthand and Per-Test Variant via Fixture Override
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface ProductFixtures {
  mockProducts: Array<{ id: number; name: string; inStock: boolean; price: number }>;
}

const test = base.extend<ProductFixtures>({
  mockProducts: async ({ page }, use) => {
    const defaultProducts = [
      { id: 1, name: 'Widget Pro', inStock: true, price: 49.99 },
      { id: 2, name: 'Gadget Lite', inStock: false, price: 19.99 },
    ];

    await page.route('*/**/api/products', route =>
      route.fulfill({ json: defaultProducts })
    );

    await use(defaultProducts);
  },
});

test('product list renders in-stock badge for available items', async ({ page, mockProducts }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  const inStockCount = mockProducts.filter(p => p.inStock).length;
  await expect(page.getByTestId('in-stock-badge')).toHaveCount(inStockCount);
});

test('all-out-of-stock state shows restock banner', async ({ page }) => {
  // Override route BEFORE the fixture-registered route for this one test
  await page.route('*/**/api/products', route =>
    route.fulfill({ json: [{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', inStock: false, price: 49 }] })
  );
  await page.goto('/products');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /out of stock/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Defining default mock data in a fixture and allowing per-test overrides via additional `page.route()` registrations works because Playwright processes route handlers in reverse-registration order (last registered wins) — so a test-body `page.route()` call overrides the fixture-registered handler — but this registration-order dependency is implicit and fragile; if the fixture is refactored to register the route after `use()` (for teardown purposes), the order inverts and per-test overrides no longer take precedence; document the ordering contract explicitly in the fixture's JSDoc.

**Pattern 613** — `test.extend()` Worker Fixture with `workerIndex` for Parallel Database User Isolation
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { createTestUser, cleanupTestUser } from '../helpers/test-db';

interface IsolatedUser {
  email: string;
  password: string;
  userId: string;
}

export const test = base.extend<{}, { isolatedUser: IsolatedUser }>({
  isolatedUser: [
    async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
      // Each worker gets its own user — no shared state between parallel workers
      const email = `e2e-worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}@test.example.com`;
      const password = `TestPass-${workerInfo.workerIndex}!`;

      const { userId } = await createTestUser({ email, password, role: 'member' });
      await use({ email, password, userId });
      await cleanupTestUser(userId);
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// tests/profile.spec.ts
import { test } from '../fixtures/isolated-user';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('worker-isolated user can update profile bio', async ({ page, isolatedUser }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(isolatedUser.email);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(isolatedUser.password);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Profile' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Bio').fill('Automated QA engineer');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save profile' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText(/profile updated/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped user fixtures amortize database user creation across all tests in a worker rather than creating a new user per test — reducing per-test setup cost from ~200ms to ~5ms — but because the user row persists across tests in the same worker, a test that modifies the user's role or email permanently alters the state for subsequent tests in that worker; restrict worker-scoped users to read-only assertion tests and use per-test fixtures (`scope: 'test'`) for flows that mutate user data.

**Pattern 614** — `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with `timeout` for Slow-Loading SPA Routes
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('deep link to settings tab resolves despite lazy-loaded module', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings/integrations/github');

  // The integrations module is lazy-loaded; route may take 3–5s to fully resolve
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/settings/integrations/github', { timeout: 8_000 });
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'GitHub Integration' })).toBeVisible();
});

test('browser back button restores previous route', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Reports' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/reports$/);

  await page.goBack();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard$/, { timeout: 5_000 });
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
});

test('invalid route redirects to 404 page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/this-route-does-not-exist');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/404|\/not-found/, { timeout: 5_000 });
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /page not found/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Go home' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Passing an explicit `timeout` to `expect(page).toHaveURL()` overrides the global `expect` timeout for this specific assertion — which is correct when a known-slow lazy-loaded module makes 5s the expected resolution time — but raising the timeout for individual assertions in test files is a maintenance hazard: if the assertion starts passing in under 1s (e.g., after code splitting is optimized), the 8s timeout is never revisited and silently masks future regressions where the route takes 6s; periodically audit custom timeouts and lower them to be 2x the current observed p99 resolution time.
